Something is expendable if it is considered not important enough to be worth keeping, protecting, or saving — especially when getting rid of it, using it up, or sacrificing it helps achieve a bigger goal.
Expenditure means the spending of money, or the total amount of money that is spent. Think of it as a formal, precise way of saying "spending."
An expense is money that you have to pay out — money that leaves your pocket or account in order to pay for something. It is the cost of having, doing, or obtaining something.
"Experience" is about contact with life — either a specific event you go through, or the wisdom you build up from going through many events over time.
Experimental describes anything that is based on trying something out — whether to test if it works, to discover something new, or to push beyond what is already known and accepted.
An expert is a person who knows a subject or can do something at a level that is significantly above what most other people can do.
Expertise means a deep, high-level mastery of a specific subject, skill, or field — the kind that goes far beyond ordinary knowledge or ability.
To expiate something means to actively do something to make up for a wrong you have committed — in a way that is meant to cancel out, or settle the debt of, the guilt or harm caused by that wrong.
Expiation is the act of wiping out guilt or the moral weight of a wrongdoing through a deliberate act of suffering, sacrifice, or reparation.
Done to make up for a wrongdoing or sin, as in "an expiatory sacrifice."
Expiration means the reaching of an end. It describes the moment or the process by which something comes to its final point — after which it is no longer valid, no longer active, or no longer alive.
Something is explanatory if its purpose is to explain — to take something that is unclear, complex, or confusing and make it easier to understand.
A swear word or offensive exclamation. In grammar, an expletive is a word like "it" or "there" that fills a gap in a sentence without adding meaning.
Explicable means capable of being explained.
To explicate something means to carefully unfold and explain it in full detail, making every part of it clear and understandable.
An explication is a careful, thorough, and detailed explanation of something — especially something that is complex, layered, or difficult to understand at first glance.

Something is explicit when it is clearly and fully stated or shown, leaving absolutely nothing to guesswork, assumption, or imagination. If something is explicit, it does the work for you — everything is right there, laid out in the open. Nothing is hidden.
When you do or say something explicitly, you do it in a way that is completely clear, direct, and fully stated — leaving absolutely nothing to be guessed, assumed, or figured out by the other person.
Explode captures one fundamental image: something that has been under pressure suddenly bursts outward with great force.

An exploit is a remarkable, daring, or impressive act that someone has done — something bold enough to be worth telling others about. Think of it as a deed that makes people say, "Wow, they actually did that?"
"Exploit" means to use something or someone in order to gain an advantage or benefit from it. That's the seed of the word. Everything else grows from there.
Exploitation means the act of using something or someone — primarily for your own gain.
Something is exploitative when it unfairly takes advantage of a person, group, or situation — usually to benefit one side while harming or shortchanging the other.

When someone or something is described as exploited, it means they have been used in an unfair, selfish, or harmful way — typically by someone with more power — where the person doing the using takes the benefits while the person being used suffers or gets very little in return.

When something is exploratory, it means it is done for the purpose of finding out, discovering, or investigating — especially when you don't yet know what you'll find, and the point is simply to look and learn.
"Explore every avenue" means to try every possible way or method to achieve something or solve a problem — leaving no option untested and no possibility ignored.
An exponent is a person who actively supports, promotes, and demonstrates a particular idea, belief, skill, style, or cause at a high level.

When something grows (or shrinks) exponentially, it does not grow by adding the same fixed amount each time. Instead, it grows by multiplying by the same number each time. That multiplication is the entire soul of the word.

When something grows exponentially, it doesn't just keep adding the same amount over and over. Instead, it keeps multiplying by the same amount over and over. That multiplication causes the growth to accelerate — the bigger it gets, the faster it grows.

To reveal something that was hidden, especially a wrongdoing, as in "the journalist exposed the scandal." It can also mean to uncover something, or to leave someone unprotected from something harmful.
Exposed describes something — or someone — that has lost its covering, protection, or concealment.
A detailed explanation of a theory or idea. In a story, exposition is the background information given at the start. It is also a large public exhibition.

Expository describes something — most often writing, speech, or text — whose primary purpose is to explain, inform, or clarify. If a piece of writing is expository, its job is to take a subject and make it understandable to the reader or listener.

To expostulate means to express strong disagreement, disapproval, or protest to someone — especially by reasoning with them earnestly and seriously, trying to make them see that what they are doing (or are about to do) is wrong, unwise, or unfair.

An expostulation is a serious, earnest protest or objection that someone makes — usually directed at another person — to express that they strongly disagree with what that person is doing, has done, or is about to do, and to try to reason them out of it.
Exposure means the condition or act of being open to something — with no shield, barrier, or protection in between.
To expound means to explain something in a thorough, detailed, and careful way — usually an idea, theory, belief, or philosophy — so that the listener or reader truly understands it at a deep level.
"Express" means to take something that exists inside you — a feeling, a thought, an idea — and bring it out into a form that others can perceive.

Expression is about making something internal — a thought, feeling, idea, or hidden quality — visible or perceptible to the outside world. Think of it as a bridge: it carries something from the inside to the outside.
"Expressly" always means something is direct, deliberate, and specific — never vague, accidental, or implied.

To expropriate something means to take someone's property away from them by authority — usually a government or state power — often without the owner's agreement, and sometimes without paying them fairly for it.
Expropriation is the act of an authority — almost always a government — taking away privately owned property from its owner. The key word here is authority. This is not theft by a random person.

Expulsion means the act of officially and forcibly pushing someone or something out — out of a place, a group, an organization, or even a body. Think of it as a forced exit that is decided by someone in authority.
To expunge something means to remove it completely and permanently — wiping it out so thoroughly that it is as if it never existed in the first place.

To expurgate something means to deliberately remove parts of a written work — a book, a script, a song, a speech, a letter, or any similar material — because those parts are considered offensive, indecent, immoral, politically dangerous, or otherwise unfit for a particular audience.

Expurgation is the act of deliberately removing parts of a written work, speech, film, or any other piece of content that someone considers offensive, immoral, inappropriate, or unsuitable — before that content is published or made available to an audience.

Exquisite means something that is so beautifully made, so perfectly crafted, or so intensely felt that it rises far above the ordinary — reaching a level of refinement and near-perfection that feels almost rare and untouchable.
To exsanguinate means to drain blood from a living body — either so severely that it causes death or near-death, or deliberately as a controlled medical procedure.
To exscind something means to cut it out or cut it off — completely and deliberately removing it from something larger.
Extant means still existing right now — something that has survived to the present day and has not been lost, destroyed, or wiped out.
"Extemporaneous" describes something — most often speech or performance — that is done on the spot, without a script, without formal preparation, and without rehearsal.
When you do something extempore, you do it without any preparation beforehand — right there on the spot, with no notes, no script, and no rehearsal.

To extemporize means to do something — most often speak, perform, or create — without any preparation, making it up as you go, using only the knowledge, skill, or creativity you already have inside you.
Extend means to make something reach further than it currently does — or, when nothing is being acted upon, to already reach across a distance or span.
Extension means the act of stretching or pushing something further beyond where it currently is — or the result of that stretching (the extra part itself).
Extensive describes something that is large in scope, range, or coverage — something that spreads widely, covers a lot of ground, or includes a great many things.

"Extent" is a measuring word. It tells you how far something reaches, how large something is, or how much something applies — whether you're talking about a physical space or an abstract idea like damage, trust, knowledge, or influence.

To extenuate means to make a wrongdoing, fault, or offense seem less serious or less blameworthy — not by denying it happened, not by saying it was the right thing to do, but by pointing to circumstances that reduce how harshly it should be judged.

"Extenuating" is an adjective that describes something that partially excuses a mistake, wrongdoing, or failure — not by denying that it happened, but by providing a special reason that makes it more understandable and less blameworthy.
Special conditions that make a wrongdoing or failure more understandable and deserving of a more lenient response.

Extenuation is the act of making a fault, a wrongdoing, or a crime appear less serious or less blameworthy than it might first seem — not by denying it, but by presenting circumstances that help explain or soften it.
To exterminate means to completely destroy every single member of a group of living things — so that not one survives.

When we say something is extinct, we mean it no longer exists anywhere in the world. Every single member, example, or instance of it has disappeared — permanently. Nothing is left. It is gone completely, and it cannot return on its own.

Extinction is the process by which something is completely and permanently wiped out — ended so thoroughly that nothing of it remains. The word always carries a strong sense of total, final disappearance.

To extinguish something means to completely put an end to it — to make it stop existing entirely. The word is almost always used for things that were once active, alive, glowing, or burning. Think of it as the act of bringing something to a total, final stop.
To extirpate something means to destroy it so completely that absolutely nothing of it remains. Not reduce it. Not weaken it. Not push it to the edges. Gone. Entirely. Without a trace.

Extirpation means the complete and total wiping out of something — so thoroughly that nothing of it remains. It's not just removal. It's not just reduction. It is absolute, utter, 100% elimination. Whatever was there before is now completely gone.
To extol someone or something means to praise it very enthusiastically and in a big way — to speak or write about it with great admiration, making it sound wonderful, impressive, or excellent.
When someone extols the virtues of something or someone, they are enthusiastically praising its good qualities — often going on and on about how wonderful, beneficial, or admirable it is.

To extort someone means to force them into giving you something — usually money, but sometimes a service, a favor, or some action — by threatening them with harm. The person being extorted doesn't give willingly.
Extortion is the act of obtaining something valuable — usually money — from a person by threatening to cause them harm if they refuse to comply.
Extortionate means grossly and unfairly excessive, especially in price, charge, or demand — to a degree that feels like exploitation or near-robbery.

To extract something means to take it out from inside something else — usually through a deliberate, careful, or effortful process. The thing you're extracting is buried, hidden, trapped, or mixed within something, and you're pulling it free.
"Extraction" means the act, process, or result of taking something out from a place where it is held, embedded, mixed in, or trapped — and doing so with deliberate effort or method.
"Extracurricular" means outside of that curriculum — any activity that is connected to the school but does not happen inside a regular class and is not part of the official coursework.
To extradite someone means for a government to officially hand over a person to another government so that person can face justice there.
The formal process of one country handing over a person accused or convicted of a crime to another country where they will face trial or punishment.
Done outside the authority of the law or the courts, as in "extrajudicial killings."
Extramarital describes anything that happens outside the boundaries of a marriage — most commonly, a romantic or sexual relationship that a married person has with someone who is not their spouse.
Outside the walls or normal programme of an institution, especially a university course for people who are not full-time students.
Extraneous means not belonging to, or not relevant to, the thing being discussed, examined, or focused on.

Extraordinaire means exceptionally outstanding — someone who is so remarkably skilled, talented, or impressive in what they do that they stand far above everyone else in that role. It's a word of high, emphatic praise.
Extraordinary means far beyond what is normal, usual, or expected. Think of it this way: "ordinary" describes what you'd normally expect — nothing special, nothing surprising, just the usual.

To extrapolate is to take information you already know — facts, data, patterns, or trends — and use them to make a reasoned prediction or conclusion about something that lies beyond what you currently know.
Extrapolation is the process of taking known information, data, or a pattern, and extending it beyond what you have directly observed, in order to estimate or predict something unknown.
Beyond the normal five senses, as in "extrasensory perception" — the supposed ability to sense things through the mind alone.

The adjective extraterrestrial describes anything that exists, originates, or occurs outside of planet Earth — including its atmosphere. If something is not from Earth, not on Earth, and not happening on or within Earth, it can be called extraterrestrial.
Existing or operating outside a country's territory, as when a country applies its laws to its citizens abroad.

Extravagance means going far beyond what is necessary, sensible, or affordable — most often with money, but sometimes with behavior, language, or emotion too. It is not simply "spending money" or "doing a lot."

When something is extravagant, it goes far past the normal limit — in spending, in behaviour, in style, or in claims. It always signals excess. Think of it as crossing a line that sensible, moderate people would not cross.
An extravaganza is a large, spectacular, and wildly elaborate event, show, or production that is designed specifically to dazzle, impress, and overwhelm people with its sheer scale and grandeur.

Extremism is the holding of beliefs or the taking of actions that are far outside what most people in a society consider normal, reasonable, or acceptable — especially in the areas of politics, religion, or ideology.

An extremist is a person who holds beliefs or views that are far outside what most people consider normal, reasonable, or balanced — and who is typically willing to take severe, aggressive, or even violent actions to push those beliefs onto the world.
An extremity is the outermost point of something — the place where it ends, beyond which nothing more exists.
To extricate means to free someone or something from a difficult, tangled, or complicated situation — usually through effort and skill.

Extrication is the act or process of freeing someone or something from a situation, place, or condition that is difficult, dangerous, complicated, or tangled — and where getting free requires real effort.
Extrinsic means coming from outside something — not part of its own inner nature, but something that exists or acts on it from the external world.

Extroversion is a personality trait — a natural, consistent tendency in a person to direct their energy outward, toward other people, social activity, and the external world. A person who has this trait is called an extrovert.
An extrovert is a person who feels energized and recharged by being around other people and engaging with the outside world.
When we say someone is extroverted, we mean they are a person who gains energy from being around other people and feels most alive, comfortable, and happy in social situations.
To extrude means to push or force a material through a shaped opening so that it comes out the other side in a specific shape.

Extrusion means one of two closely related things: 1. The act or process of pushing or squeezing a material through a shaped opening to produce a continuous object with a specific form. 2. The object itself that is produced by that process.

Exuberance is the quality of being so full of energy, enthusiasm, and joy that it seems to overflow and spill outward — almost as if the feeling is too big to be contained inside a person. It is not just happiness or excitement in a quiet, private sense.

Exuberant means overflowing with joy, energy, and enthusiasm in a way that is impossible to miss or contain. Think of a shaken bottle of soda — the fizz doesn't just sit quietly inside; it bursts outward. An exuberant person is exactly like that.
The slow oozing of a liquid through pores or small openings, as sap does from a tree. It can also mean the liquid itself that oozes out.
To exude something means to slowly and naturally give it off, release it, or radiate it — as if it is flowing outward from the inside, almost effortlessly.
To exult means to feel or show an intense, overflowing joy — especially because of a personal success, victory, or achievement. It's not quiet, private happiness.

Exultant means feeling or showing an intense, triumphant joy — the kind that bursts out of you because you have won something, achieved something difficult, or overcome a challenge. It is not just ordinary happiness.

Exultation is a feeling of very great joy — but not just any joy. It is specifically the kind of intense, triumphant happiness that bursts out of you when you have achieved something, won something, or overcome something difficult.

An exurb is a community that sits beyond a city's suburbs — farther out, quieter, more spread out — but whose residents still depend on that city for their jobs, shopping, culture, and overall way of life. It is the outermost ring of a city's reach.
Eye candy refers to something or someone that is very pleasing to look at but usually lacks depth, substance, or real value beyond its visual appeal.
"An eye for an eye" means that a person who harms someone else deserves to receive the exact same harm in return. Simply put: if you hurt me, I get to hurt you back in the same way.
When people say someone or something is "in the eye of the storm," they mean that person or thing is right at the center of a big conflict, controversy, or crisis.

Something is eye-catching when it grabs your attention the moment you see it — without you even trying. It "catches your eye" the way a sudden movement catches your gaze. You don't go looking for it; it pulls you in on its own, automatically.
When something surprises you so much that it completely changes the way you see or understand a thing, we say it opened your eyes.

To eyeball something or someone means to look at it very carefully and directly, using your eyes alone — with full attention and focus. The word captures a very deliberate, intentional kind of looking. It is not a casual glance. Your eyes are doing real work.
An eyelet is a small, round hole made in a piece of material — such as cloth, leather, canvas, or paper — that has been reinforced around its edges so it doesn't tear or fray.

An eyesore is something that is very ugly or unpleasant to look at — so ugly that it bothers or offends you just by being visible. It is something that stands out in a bad way and disturbs your sense of what looks good or acceptable.

In its most straightforward sense, eyewash is a mild, gentle liquid solution used to rinse, clean, or soothe the eyes. Think of it as a special water for your eyes — it removes dust, dirt, chemical splashes, or other irritants from the eye safely.
An eyewitness is a person who personally sees an event happen — with their own eyes, at the moment it occurs, while being physically present at that place.
An eyrie is the nest of an eagle or another large bird of prey — such as a hawk, falcon, or osprey. But it is not an ordinary nest.
A fable is a short, made-up story whose entire purpose is to teach a lesson about life, wisdom, or human behavior. That lesson is called the moral, and it is the whole reason the story exists.
Fabric is a material made by interweaving, knitting, or otherwise interlocking threads or fibers together into a flat, flexible sheet. In simpler words: it is cloth.

To fabricate means to make, construct, or build something — especially by putting together materials or parts to create a finished product. This meaning is most common in industrial, technical, or engineering contexts.
When something is fabricated, it means it was deliberately made up or invented — it has no basis in reality. It did not actually happen, it does not actually exist, or it is not actually true.
A fabrication is something that someone has made up entirely — a false story, a false statement, a false excuse, or a false account of events — and presented as if it were true.
A fabulist is either a skilled storyteller of invented tales, or — more commonly in everyday use — someone who fabricates elaborate lies and presents them as truth.

When someone calls something fabulous, they mean it is so impressive, so pleasing, or so wonderful that it almost feels hard to believe. It is a strong, enthusiastic word — much more powerful than simply saying "good" or "nice."
In its physical, architectural sense, a facade is the front-facing exterior wall of a building — the side it "shows" to the world, typically the side facing a street or public space.
"Face the music" means to accept the unpleasant consequences of something you have done.
"Face up to" means to honestly accept that something difficult or unpleasant is true, and then deal with it bravely — instead of running away from it, ignoring it, or pretending it doesn't exist.

Face-saving describes something — an action, statement, deal, gesture, or arrangement — that helps a person protect their dignity, reputation, or honor, especially in a situation where they are in danger of looking foolish, weak, defeated, or wrong in front of others.
A facet is one distinct side or aspect of something that has many sides or aspects.
When something is described as faceted, it means it has facets — it is made up of, or defined by, multiple distinct flat surfaces or aspects, each presenting a different angle or view of the whole.

Facetious describes someone who makes jokes or playful, silly comments in a situation that calls for seriousness. The key is the mismatch — the humor shows up where it doesn't belong, or at a moment when people expect a straight, genuine answer.
When someone says or does something facetiously, they are being playfully jokey about something that is serious, or in a situation where a serious response would normally be expected.

A facial cue is any movement, expression, or physical signal produced by the face that communicates information — about how a person is feeling, what they are thinking, whether they are telling the truth, how they are reacting to something, or what they are about to do next.

"Facile" means too easy in a way that is shallow or superficial. It describes something that appears simple or effortless, but only because it has ignored the real difficulty, nuance, or complexity of the situation.
To facilitate something means to make it easier for something to happen, or to help a process move forward smoothly — without necessarily doing that thing yourself.
A facilitator is a person whose job is to make something easier for others — not by doing the thing for them, but by creating the right conditions so that others can do it well themselves.

A building or place provided for a particular purpose, as in "sports facilities." It can also mean a natural ability to do something easily, as in "a facility for languages," or a feature of a machine or service.

A facsimile is an exact copy of something — usually a document, a piece of writing, a drawing, a painting, or any original work — that is reproduced to look identical to the original in every visible detail.

A faction is a group of people inside a larger group who share their own distinct beliefs, goals, or agenda — and who act together as a united bloc, often clashing with other groups within that same larger body.

Factionalism is the condition, pattern, or culture in which a group is heavily divided into competing factions that rival, undermine, or work against each other — often at the expense of the group's overall unity and shared goals.

Factious describes a person, group, or atmosphere that causes or promotes internal division and conflict within a larger group — usually by pushing a narrow self-serving agenda over the common good, and by forming or encouraging competing factions that fight against each other from the inside.
Factitious means artificially created, deliberately manufactured, or contrived — rather than arising naturally, spontaneously, or genuinely.
A piece of unreliable or false information that is repeated so often that people accept it as fact. In modern use, it often simply means a brief, interesting fact.
A factor is anything that plays a part in producing a result or making something happen the way it does.
To factor in something means to include it as one of the important things you think about when making a decision, plan, or calculation.
A factotum is a person who does all sorts of different tasks for someone else — a general all-purpose helper who handles whatever needs to be done, rather than having one specific job.

The word faculty means a power, ability, or capacity — or a group of people with a shared role or subject area. These two broad directions (ability vs. group) cover almost every use of this word you will ever encounter.
Briefly fashionable but unlikely to last, like a fad, as in "faddish diets."

"Fain" means willing — but it's a specific, layered kind of willingness. It sits somewhere between eager and content to accept. There are two closely related shades of meaning, and understanding both is the key to truly knowing this word.
"Fain" means "willingly" or "gladly." When someone says they would fain do something, they mean they would do it with willingness or pleasure.
Barely noticeable, as in "a faint sound" or "a faint smell." It can also mean slight, as in "a faint chance," or feeling weak and dizzy, as if about to lose consciousness.

When something or someone is described as "fair game," it means they are a legitimate and acceptable target — for criticism, jokes, investigation, pursuit, or any kind of action. There is nothing wrong, unfair, or against the rules about going after them.

A fair-weather friend is someone who is friendly, supportive, and pleasant to be around only when things are going well for you — but who disappears, pulls away, or even turns against you the moment you face trouble, hardship, or difficulty.

A fairway is a clear, open, designated path or channel — the safe, ideal route through a space that has less-ideal or more dangerous alternatives on either side. This idea plays out in two main areas where the word is used.

A fait accompli is something that has already been done — completely finished — before the people affected by it even had a chance to weigh in, object, or influence it. By the time they find out, it's too late.
Faith means a strong, confident belief or trust in someone or something — held even when you cannot fully prove it or verify it with your own eyes. It is not just a weak guess or a vague hope.

Faithless describes someone — or something — that has broken faith. "Breaking faith" means violating the trust, loyalty, or commitment that was expected of them. The word points directly at a betrayal of something that was owed.

A fake is something — or someone — that appears to be real, genuine, or authentic, but is not. The essential quality of a fake is this gap between appearance and reality. It looks like the real thing. It may even claim to be the real thing. But it isn't.
To "fake a facade" means to deliberately and consciously put on a false front — to project an image of yourself to the outside world that does not match your inner reality.
Falafel is a popular Middle Eastern food. It refers to small, round or slightly flattened balls (or sometimes patties) that are deep-fried until crispy on the outside.
A falcon is a bird of prey — meaning a bird that hunts and kills other animals for food.
To break into pieces. Figuratively, when a person falls apart, they lose emotional control; when a plan or relationship falls apart, it fails completely.
To fall back on something means to use it as a backup or a last resort when your main option has failed, run out, or isn't available. You rely on it because you have no better choice at that moment.
To "fall between two stools" means to fail because you tried to be two things at once, or aim for two goals at once, and ended up achieving neither.
When something or someone falls by the wayside, it means they fail to continue, get abandoned, or don't survive long enough to reach the finish line.
"Fall foul of" means to get into trouble with someone or something — especially by breaking a rule, violating a law, or doing something that causes conflict with a person or an authority.

To "fall from grace" means to lose the respect, favour, power, or good reputation that you once had — especially after doing something wrong, making a serious mistake, or behaving in a way that disappoints others.
A fall guy is a person who ends up taking the blame or suffering the consequences for something — often for something that was not entirely (or not at all) their fault.
When something "falls on deaf ears," it means that a request, warning, advice, or plea was completely ignored — as if the listener simply did not hear it at all.
To accept the blame or punishment for something, for example by resigning, usually to protect others or because it is the honourable thing to do.
"Fall out with" is a phrasal verb. It means to have a disagreement or quarrel with someone that damages or strains your relationship with them.
"Fall short of" means to fail to reach a goal, standard, amount, or expectation — to come close, but not close enough.
When a plan, deal, or arrangement falls through, it fails to happen or be completed.
Something is fallacious when it is wrong in a way that can fool you into thinking it is right.
A fallacy is a false or mistaken belief, OR a flawed piece of reasoning that looks convincing but is actually broken or wrong underneath.
Fallible means capable of making mistakes or being wrong.
The word fallout describes the bad things that happen as a result of something. Think of it as the negative aftermath — the mess, damage, or trouble that a situation leaves behind.
Of farmland, ploughed but deliberately left unplanted for a season so that the soil can recover. Figuratively, describing a period of inactivity, as in "a fallow period in her career."

When you say something is "a false dawn," you mean it is a situation that looks like something good, hopeful, or successful is beginning — but it is actually a misleading sign. The good thing never truly arrives, or it disappears very quickly.
A falsehood is simply something that is not true. It is a false statement — something said, written, or presented as a fact, when in reality it is not a fact at all.

When you use falsetto as an adjective, you are describing a voice, a sound, or a singing style that is unnaturally high-pitched — produced by a special technique where the singer pushes their voice far above their normal, comfortable speaking or singing range.
A way of singing or speaking, used especially by men, in which the voice is much higher and lighter than normal.

Falsification means the act of making something false — deliberately changing, distorting, or misrepresenting something so that it no longer reflects the truth. Think of it as intentional corruption of what is real or accurate.
To falsify something means to make it false — to deliberately alter, change, or misrepresent it so that it no longer reflects the truth. Think of it as "corrupting the truth on purpose."
Falsity is a noun that means the quality, condition, or state of being false — the property that something has when it is not true, not real, or not in agreement with the facts.
To falter means to become unsteady, weak, or hesitant — especially after a period of moving forward with strength or confidence. Think of it as a wobble or a stumble in the middle of something.
When something is described as faltering, it means it is losing its usual strength, steadiness, or confidence — not all at once, but gradually and visibly. It is still going, but barely.
Familial means "of, relating to, or characteristic of a family."
"Familiar" describes a kind of knowing that comes from experience — the feeling that you have encountered something before. It is the opposite of strange, new, or unknown.
Familiarity is the state of knowing something — or someone — well, not just intellectually, but through real, repeated, lived experience. It is deep, comfortable, first-hand knowledge.
The more you know someone or something very well, the more likely you are to lose your respect, admiration, or appreciation for them — and sometimes even start to dislike them.

To familiarize means to make yourself — or someone else — well enough acquainted with something new that it no longer feels strange or difficult. You move from a state of "I don't know this" to a state of "I know this well enough to feel comfortable with it."
The patterns of behaviour, communication, roles, and relationships that shape how a family works and how its members interact.

A famine is a severe, widespread shortage of food that affects a large number of people in a region, country, or area — lasting long enough that people begin to starve, fall seriously ill from lack of nutrition, and die in large numbers.
Famished means extremely hungry — not just a little hungry, but so hungry that it feels urgent and overwhelming. When someone is famished, their body is crying out for food.

When you describe something as fanatic (or its more common adjective form, fanatical — both mean the same thing), you mean that it involves a level of belief, devotion, or enthusiasm that has gone so far beyond normal that it has become unreasonable, extreme, and often dangerous.

Fanatical describes a level of belief, devotion, or enthusiasm toward something that is so extreme, so intense, and so beyond reason that it overrides a person's ability to think calmly, listen to others, or act with balance.

Fanaticism is an extreme, intense, and unquestioning devotion to a belief, cause, idea, or group — taken so far that the person loses the ability or the willingness to think about it reasonably, consider other perspectives, or recognize any limits to their commitment.
When something is described as "fancied," it means it exists only in someone's mind or imagination — it is believed or felt to be real, but it may not actually be real.

A fancier is a person who has a deep, serious, and knowledgeable passion for a specific type of animal or plant — and who is actively involved with it, usually by breeding, raising, collecting, or showing it.

Fanciful describes something that comes from imagination or fantasy rather than from reality, logic, or fact. Think of "fancy" as a playful, free-flying imagination — and fanciful is the adjective form of that.

A fanciful moment is a brief, self-aware spell of time in which a person allows their mind to drift freely into something imaginative, playful, whimsical, or unrealistic — not as a serious plan, not as a delusion, but as a light and entirely human indulgence in imagination.
"Fancy" describes something that is more elaborate, decorative, or impressive than what is ordinary or standard.

A fandom is a community of people who share a deep, passionate enthusiasm for the same thing — whether that's a musician, a movie series, a sports team, a TV show, a book, a video game, or even a fictional character.
A short, loud piece of music played on trumpets or horns to announce someone important. Figuratively, a great show of excitement or publicity, as in "launched with much fanfare."

A fanlight is a window built directly above a door (or sometimes above another window). Its job is simple: to let natural light flow into the space just inside the doorway — typically a hallway or entrance — that would otherwise be dark and gloomy.

To fantasize means to spend time in your mind imagining something pleasurable, exciting, or deeply desired — something that either doesn't exist in your life right now, hasn't happened yet, or may never happen at all.

"Fantastic" always signals that something is far beyond the ordinary — it stands out so sharply that it fills you with wonder, admiration, or disbelief. That sense of "far beyond the ordinary" shows up in three distinct ways depending on context.

A fantod (almost always used in its plural form, "the fantods") refers to a state of intense nervousness, anxiety, fidgety restlessness, or creeping unease — that deeply uncomfortable, jittery, on-edge feeling that grips you when something disturbs or unsettles you.
When someone says "far be it from me to [do something]," they are saying: "It is not my place to do this. I would not presume to do this. This is not something I would normally do."
Something is far-fetched when it is so unlikely, strange, or difficult to believe that it feels disconnected from reality.
Very far away, or spread out over a very wide area, as in "far-flung corners of the world."

When something is far-reaching, it means its effects, influence, or consequences spread widely — touching many people, many areas, or many aspects of life, often far beyond what is immediately and directly obvious.

"Faraway" describes something — or someone's mind — that is at a great distance. That distance can be physical (a place that is far from you) or mental (a mind that has drifted far from the present moment).
A farce is something so absurd, so chaotic, or so badly done that it becomes laughable — even when it was supposed to be serious.
Farcical means something is so absurdly ridiculous, chaotic, or badly handled that it stops being serious and becomes almost like a joke — even if nobody intended it to be one.
A fare is the amount of money you pay to ride a form of public or hired transportation — a bus, train, subway, ferry, taxi, or airplane.
Farina is a fine, flour-like powder made by grinding up starchy foods — most commonly cereal grains like wheat. Think of it as a step beyond grain and a step before fully cooked food.
Farming means the practice of working the land or raising animals — or both — to produce food, raw materials, or other useful things. It is the organized, ongoing activity of a farm.
Farouche describes a person who is deeply unsociable, sullen, and withdrawn — but in a way that carries a fierce, wild, even savage edge to it. It is not the same as being simply shy.
A farrago is a confused, chaotic jumble of things — especially ideas, claims, or arguments — thrown together with no logic, order, or coherence.
A farrier is a skilled tradesperson whose job is to care for horses' hooves — specifically by trimming them and fitting metal horseshoes onto them.
When used to describe eyesight, "farsighted" means that a person can see distant objects clearly, but struggles to see things up close.
"Fascia" refers to a flat, thin layer or band — something that wraps around, covers, or forms the outer surface of something else.

To fascinate someone means to attract and hold their attention so powerfully that they find it almost impossible to look away, stop thinking about it, or lose interest. It's not just mild curiosity — it's a strong, almost magnetic pull toward something.

When you are fascinated by something, you find it so interesting and captivating that you can barely look away or stop thinking about it. Your attention is pulled toward it completely, almost as if you have no choice in the matter.

Something fascinating has the power to capture your attention so completely that you feel pulled toward it — your mind wants to keep exploring, thinking, and learning more about it. It's not just that you find it nice or pleasant.
Fascination is a strong, deep feeling of being completely drawn to something or someone — so pulled in that it's hard to look away, walk away, or stop thinking about it. It's not casual interest.

Fascism is a political ideology and a form of government built on one central idea: the nation (or the state) is the highest thing that exists, and everything — every person, every institution, every right — must serve it.

When you call something fascist, you are saying it resembles, belongs to, or is characteristic of fascism — a specific, extreme political ideology that prizes absolute authority, aggressive nationalism, and the total crushing of any opposition.
Fashion means the style or way of doing things that is widely popular and accepted at a particular time.

At first glance, "fast" seems to mean only one thing — quick. But it actually carries two completely separate core ideas, and knowing both will help you understand the word in every situation you'll ever encounter.
To fasten something means to fix it firmly in place, close it securely, or join it to something else so that it stays put and doesn't move, come apart, or open on its own.

Fastidious means having very high, demanding standards — and being extremely careful to make sure those standards are always met, right down to the smallest detail. A fastidious person is never satisfied with "good enough."

Fastidiousness is the quality of having very high, precise standards — and being genuinely bothered when those standards aren't met. A person with fastidiousness is extremely particular, selective, and hard to satisfy.
A secure, well-protected place that is hard to reach or attack, such as a mountain stronghold. It can also mean the quality of being firmly fixed, as in "colour fastness."
Fatalism is the belief that everything that happens in life — every event, every outcome, every moment — has already been fixed in advance, and that nothing you do can change it.

A fatalist is a person who believes that everything that happens in life — every event, every outcome, every turn of fortune — was already decided in advance, and that no human effort, choice, or action can truly change it.

When someone is fatalistic, they believe that whatever is going to happen will happen — and that there is nothing they can do to change it. They see life's outcomes as already decided, fixed, and beyond their control.

A fatality is a death that results directly from a specific event, accident, or dangerous condition. Think of a car crash, a natural disaster, a war, or a disease outbreak — the deaths that happen because of those events are called fatalities.
Fate refers to a power or force that is believed to decide what happens to a person or thing — beyond anyone's control, as if it were already written before it even happens.
Having important, often disastrous, consequences that decide what happens in the future, as in "that fateful day."
Fatherless means without a father. When you describe someone as fatherless, you are saying that they do not have a father in their life — or never had one.
A fathom is a unit of measurement. Its one specific job is to measure depth — particularly the depth of water.
To fathom something means to fully and deeply understand it — especially something that feels mysterious, confusing, or almost impossible to wrap your head around.
Fathomless means so deep, vast, or complex that it cannot be fully measured, reached, or understood.

Fatigue means a state of deep, heavy exhaustion — the kind that is much more serious than just feeling a little tired. It is the feeling that your body, your mind, or both have been used up and have little energy or strength left to keep going.
Fatuity is a very particular kind of foolishness — one that is smug, self-satisfied, and completely unaware of itself. It isn't simply about being unintelligent or making an honest mistake.
Fatuous means foolish and pointless in a vacant, self-satisfied way, where the person showing this foolishness is completely unaware of how silly they look or sound.
A mistake, defect, or responsibility for something going wrong, as in "it was my fault." As a verb, to fault someone means to criticize them for a flaw or mistake.

Faultless means having absolutely no faults, errors, flaws, or imperfections — not even a single one. When something is described as faultless, it means it is completely and perfectly correct, clean, or right in every way that matters.

Fauna means all the animals living in a particular place or time period. When scientists, nature writers, or researchers use this word, they are talking about the entire animal life of a specific region, habitat, or era — taken as a whole group.
Faux means not real, but made or performed to look, feel, or seem like the real thing. It describes something that is a substitute or imitation of something genuine.
A faux pas is a social blunder — a mistake you make in a social situation that breaks an unwritten rule of behavior, causing embarrassment or awkwardness.

"To favor" doesn't have just one meaning — it has several, and they're all connected by a single thread: the idea of leaning toward something, or giving something an edge over others. Here is every important meaning explained clearly.
Liked more than all others of the same kind, as in "my favorite book."

Favourable means working in someone's benefit, showing approval, or helping something succeed. The easiest way to lock this in is through the phrase "in your favour" — when something is favourable, it is on your side.

Favouritism is the act or practice of giving special, unearned advantages or preferential treatment to a particular person or group, not because they have earned it or deserve it, but simply because of a personal connection, personal liking, or bias toward them.
A fawn is a baby deer, specifically one that is less than one year old. Once it turns a year old, it is no longer called a fawn — it becomes a "yearling." So "fawn" is a very age-specific word.

To fawn means to try to win someone's approval or favor by showering them with excessive praise, acting extremely submissive, and being overly eager to please — in a way that feels exaggerated, undignified, and driven by self-interest rather than genuine feeling.
When someone is fawning, they are showing excessive, over-the-top admiration or flattery toward someone — usually to impress them, please them, or gain something from them.
To faze someone means to disturb, unsettle, or bother them emotionally or mentally — to make them feel rattled, thrown off, or no longer calm and composed.

Fealty means a deep, solemn, and binding loyalty that a person pledges to someone or something that holds authority over them. It is not casual loyalty — it is the kind that comes with a sense of duty and obligation.

Something fearsome is so powerful, dangerous, or overwhelming that it makes you feel afraid — or at least deeply intimidated. When you call something fearsome, you are saying it has a quality that strikes fear into people. It isn't just a little scary.
Feasibility is a noun that refers to how possible, practical, and achievable something is — given the real-world conditions, resources, and constraints that actually exist.
Feasible means able to be done successfully in the real world, given the actual conditions.
To "feast one's eyes on" something means to look at something with great pleasure, joy, and admiration.
A feat is an act or achievement that is impressive because it required great skill, strength, courage, cleverness, or effort to pull off.
"A feather in one's cap" means an achievement, success, or honor that someone can be proud of — something that increases their reputation or standing in the eyes of others.

When someone "feathers their nest," it means they are secretly or dishonestly using their position, job, or power to enrich themselves or make their personal life more comfortable — usually at someone else's expense.
A feature is a notable, distinguishing part or quality of something — something that stands out, helps define it, or is worth pointing out.
Febrile means relating to fever or resembling a fever. That's its heart.

Feckless describes a person who is both irresponsible and ineffective — someone who fails to take charge of their own life, duties, or actions, and who lacks the drive, willpower, or sense of purpose to get anything meaningful done.
Feculence means filth, foulness, or impurity — specifically the kind that comes from waste, sediment, or excrement.

Feculent describes something that is foul, filthy, and disgusting — specifically because it is full of, covered in, or heavily contaminated with feces, excrement, sewage, or similarly repulsive waste matter.
Fecund means richly and abundantly productive. It describes something — or someone — that produces a great deal, whether that's offspring, ideas, creative works, or results.

Fecundity means the ability to produce a large amount of something — most often offspring, but also ideas, creative works, or anything that "gives birth" to more of itself. The word is about richness of output and abundance of generation.

"Fed up" means you are so tired, annoyed, or frustrated with something that you cannot tolerate it anymore. You have reached your limit. You have had enough. You don't want to deal with it any longer.
A system of government in which power is divided between a central government and regional governments, such as states or provinces, each with its own protected areas of authority.
A fedora is a type of hat. But it's not just any hat — it has a very specific look that sets it apart, and over time it has also picked up a cultural meaning beyond the physical object.

Feeble means so weak that it clearly falls short of what is needed or expected. The word is not just about ordinary weakness — it describes a weakness that is striking, noticeable, and often disappointing or pitiful.

Feebleminded describes someone — or something — that shows a serious lack of intelligence, mental sharpness, or sound judgment. The word combines "feeble" (weak) and "minded" (relating to the mind), so literally: having a weak mind.
Feedback is information you receive about something you did or produced, which tells you how well it worked, how it was received, or what effect it had.

To "feel it in one's bones" means to have a very strong inner sense or gut feeling that something is true or that something is about to happen — even when you have no logical proof or solid evidence to support it.

To feel sorry for oneself means to spend too much time pitying yourself over your own problems, bad luck, or suffering — often in a way that others (or even you yourself) consider excessive, unproductive, or self-indulgent.
To feel sorry for someone means to feel sadness, sympathy, or compassion in your heart because someone else is suffering, struggling, or in an unfortunate situation.

A feeling is something that happens inside you — in your mind, your body, or both. It is a private, inner experience. No one else can directly see or touch your feeling; only you can experience it from the inside.
To feign something means to pretend that you feel, experience, or have something — when you actually don't. You are creating a false impression in someone else's mind by putting on an act.

Feigned means deliberately pretended or consciously faked. When something is feigned, it is not real — but crucially, the person showing it knows it isn't real. They are putting on a performance, creating a false impression on purpose.
A feint is a deliberate, deceptive movement or action made to trick an opponent into thinking you are about to do one thing — so that you can actually do something else.
To feint means to make a fake move on purpose to trick someone, so that while they react to the fake, you do what you actually intended to do.
Feisty describes someone who is full of energy, spirit, and fight — someone who is bold, loud, and refuses to back down, especially when you might not expect it from them.
To felicitate someone means to congratulate them — to express joy and good wishes to a person on account of something happy or successful that has happened to them.
Felicitation means the act of congratulating someone, or the expression of joy and good wishes offered to a person on the occasion of something happy or successful in their life.
Felicitous means perfectly suited to the occasion — but with a special added flavor: not just "suitable," but pleasingly, elegantly, satisfyingly right.

Felicity doesn't just mean ordinary happiness — it means happiness of a full, complete, almost ideal kind. Think of the difference between feeling "okay" and feeling like everything in your life is exactly right. Felicity is the second one.
Feline means "of, relating to, or characteristic of a cat or the cat family."

"Fell" as an adjective means fierce, savage, cruel, and deadly. It describes something or someone that is ruthlessly destructive — not just dangerous, but terrifyingly so, with a quality of cold, merciless destruction.

"Fell" functions as a verb in two completely separate ways. They look identical but mean very different things. Mastering both will make you confident in virtually any context where you encounter this word.

Fellow feeling is the warm, empathetic understanding you feel for someone else when you recognise that they are going through — or have gone through — something similar to what you have experienced yourself.
A feeling of friendship and closeness among people who share interests or experiences. A fellowship is also a group of people with a shared purpose, or a paid research post at a university.
A felon is a person who has been officially found guilty by a court of law of committing a serious crime — specifically, a type of crime called a felony.

Felonious means relating to, involving, or having the character of a serious crime. When something is described as felonious, it means it is criminal in nature — and not just mildly criminal, but seriously, gravely criminal.

A felony is the most serious type of crime that a person can commit under the law. When a legal system looks at all the different crimes people can be charged with, it places them into categories based on how severe they are.
A fen is a type of wetland — a permanently wet, low-lying, flat piece of land that is waterlogged and soft underfoot.
To "fend for oneself" means to take care of yourself by your own efforts, without depending on anyone else's help.
"Fend off" is a phrasal verb that means to protect yourself from something or someone by pushing it away, blocking it, or stopping it from reaching you.

A fender is something that acts as a protective barrier — it fends off (pushes away or blocks) contact, damage, or danger. The word is used in several very specific, real-world contexts, each with this same underlying idea.

A fender-bender is a minor car accident. It is a collision between two vehicles — or between a vehicle and an object — where the damage is small and, most importantly, nobody is seriously hurt. Think of it as the least serious kind of car accident possible.

"Feral" describes a living thing — most often an animal, sometimes a person — that has broken free from human control and returned to a wild, untamed state. The word suggests something raw, unrestrained, driven by instinct rather than rules or training.

A fermata is a symbol used in written music (sheet music) that tells a performer to hold a note, a rest, or a pause longer than its normally written duration. It is both the symbol itself and the instruction it carries.
A state of excitement, unrest, or change in a society, as in "a time of political ferment." In science, it is a substance such as yeast that causes fermentation.
When food or drink ferments, yeast or bacteria break down its sugars, producing alcohol, gas, or acid. Figuratively, to ferment trouble means to stir it up.

Fermentation is a process in which tiny living organisms — most commonly yeast, bacteria, or fungi — break down sugars and other organic substances to produce energy for themselves, and as a side effect of doing so, they release byproducts like alcohol, gases, or acids.

The Fermi paradox is the puzzling contradiction between the very high likelihood that intelligent alien life exists somewhere in the universe, and the absolute silence we've heard from space so far — not a single confirmed signal, visit, or trace of anyone out there.
Ferocious means extremely fierce, violent, and dangerously powerful — in a wild, uncontrolled way that feels overwhelming or terrifying.
Ferociously means in a fierce, savage, or extremely intense way. It describes how something is done — with great force, aggression, or overwhelming intensity.
Ferocity is a noun that describes an extreme, intense, and overwhelming level of force, aggression, or energy — the kind that feels wild, powerful, and often frightening or unstoppable.
A ferret is a small, domesticated, meat-eating mammal that belongs to the weasel family — the same animal family that includes weasels, otters, badgers, and minks.

To ferret something out means to find or discover something that is hidden, secret, or difficult to uncover, through persistent and determined searching. It is almost always used as the phrasal verb "ferret out."
To ferret out something means to find or discover something that is hidden, secret, or difficult to locate — through a careful, determined, and persistent search.
To ferry something or someone means to carry or transport them from one place to another, typically by making repeated trips back and forth over the same route.
Fertile means capable of producing a lot, or capable of supporting new life and growth.
Fertility is the ability or capacity to produce new life, growth, or results in abundance. The word describes the power that something or someone has to create, reproduce, or generate.

Fervency is a noun that means the quality of feeling or expressing something with intense, burning passion and deep sincerity. It describes a state where your emotions aren't just warm — they're on fire.

Fervent describes a feeling or belief that is deeply intense, genuine, and almost burning with sincerity. When someone is fervent about something, they don't just care about it — they care about it deeply, with real fire inside them.

When you do something fervently, you do it with deep, intense, and completely sincere feeling — with your whole heart, not just your head. It is an adverb, which means it describes how an action is performed.

"Fervid" means intensely passionate, enthusiastic, or zealous — but with one quality that sets it apart from simply being "very passionate": the intensity feels like a kind of burning heat. Think of it as emotion so strong it seems to glow from the inside.
Fervor means a very strong, deeply felt, burning passion or enthusiasm for something you believe in, care about, or feel devoted to.
Festal is an adjective that means relating to, characteristic of, or fitting for a feast, festival, or celebration.

To fester means to become worse over time because something negative is left unaddressed. The single most important thing to understand about this word is its built-in logic: neglect + time = worsening.
Festive means relating to, suited for, or full of the spirit of a celebration or special occasion.

Festivity means joyful celebration. It refers to the feeling, spirit, and activity of celebrating something together — the happiness, liveliness, and cheerfulness that fill the air when people come together to mark a special occasion.
To festoon something means to decorate it by hanging or draping things on it, typically in a flowing, looping, or curving way.
Fetch means to go somewhere, get something, and bring it back — all as one complete action.
"Fetching" means pleasantly and charmingly attractive — the kind of attractive that catches your eye and draws you in with a light, lively, delightful quality.

A fete is a large, lively, festive celebration — typically held outdoors — that brings a community of people together for fun, entertainment, and socializing. Think of it as a grand, joyful public party or fair, often with a warm, communal atmosphere.
To fete someone means to celebrate and honor a person in a grand, festive, and admiring way — usually through a special event, party, or public ceremony organized specifically in their honor.
Fetid means having an extremely strong, deeply offensive, and nauseating smell — specifically the kind that comes from organic decay, rot, or stagnation.
An unusual sexual attraction to a particular object, body part, or activity. It can also mean an excessive devotion to something, or an object believed to have magical power.

To fetishize something means to treat it with an obsessive, irrational, and exaggerated level of importance, desire, or admiration — as if it has a magical, almost supernatural power or value that it doesn't actually possess.
A fetter is something that holds you back. More specifically, it is a chain or shackle locked around a prisoner's ankle — a physical device of restraint.

To fetter something or someone means to restrain them — to hold them back so tightly that they cannot move, act, or grow freely. Imagine putting chains around someone's ankles. They can't run, they can't escape, they can barely move.

Fettle means the condition or state that someone or something is in — particularly how well, healthy, or fit they are at a given moment. Think of it as a word that answers the question: "How is this person or thing doing right now?"

A feud is a long-lasting, bitter conflict between two people, two families, or two groups — where both sides strongly dislike each other and keep clashing, often over a long period of time, sometimes for years or even generations.
Relating to feudalism, the medieval European system in which people held land from a lord in return for service and loyalty. Figuratively, old-fashioned and rigidly hierarchical.

Feudalism is a system for organizing an entire society — its politics, economy, and social classes — around a single deal: land in exchange for loyalty and service. The most powerful person at the top (a king) owns all the land.
A feuilleton is a piece of writing — usually short, light, and entertaining — published in a newspaper or magazine, typically covering arts, culture, literature, criticism, or human interest topics.
"Fever pitch" means the highest possible level of excitement, intensity, or emotion — a state so extreme that it feels almost out of control, like a raging, burning fire.

To understand "feverish," start with what you already know: a fever. When someone has a fever, their body temperature is abnormally high. They feel hot, restless, and agitated. Their mind might race. They might toss and turn.
"Few and far between" means that something is rare, uncommon, or happens very infrequently.
Having a strange, otherworldly, or magical quality, as if touched by fairies. In older use, it meant fated to die, or showing a strange excitement thought to come before death.
A fez is a type of hat worn on the head. But it is not just any hat — it has a very specific, distinctive shape and look that makes it instantly recognisable.
A fiancée is a woman who has agreed to marry someone and is currently in that in-between stage — after the proposal, but before the wedding.
A fiasco is a complete, embarrassing, and often ridiculous failure — usually of something that was expected to go well.
A fiat is an authoritative command, order, or declaration that makes something happen — or makes something officially real — simply because someone powerful enough to say it has said it.
A fibber is a person who tells fibs — that is, someone who tells small, minor, harmless lies on a regular or habitual basis.

"Fibrous" describes something that contains fibers, is made of fibers, or has the qualities and texture of fibers. That's the entire idea. Everything else is just this idea appearing in different places.
Fickle means likely to change suddenly and for no clear reason, making someone or something unreliable.
Fickleness is the quality of changing your mind, feelings, opinions, or loyalties frequently, easily, and without a strong or consistent reason.
Fiction is anything that is invented — created by imagination rather than drawn from reality.
Fictitious means not real — something that has been made up or invented, and does not actually exist.
Fictive means belonging to, created by, or relating to imagination rather than reality. If something is fictive, it was invented — it does not exist in the real world, only in the mind or in a story.
To "fiddle while Rome burns" means to do something trivial or unimportant while a serious problem or disaster is happening around you.
Faithfulness and loyalty to a person, partner, or cause. It can also mean how accurately something is copied or reproduced, as in "high-fidelity sound."

To fidget means to make small, repeated, restless physical movements — especially when you are sitting still or supposed to be still. These movements are driven by an inner feeling of nervousness, boredom, impatience, anxiety, or discomfort.
Fidgety describes a person who cannot keep their body still and keeps making small, repeated, restless physical movements — often without even fully realizing it.

When something is described as fiduciary, it means it belongs to a special kind of relationship where one person is legally and morally required to act entirely in someone else's best interest — not their own.

A fiefdom is a territory, organization, domain, or area of activity that one person controls with near-total authority — often in a way that is self-serving, possessive, and resistant to outside interference.
The word field is remarkably versatile. It always carries the same underlying idea: a defined area or space — physical, mental, or abstract — within which something exists, happens, or acts.

A fiend is something or someone that has crossed a line — gone beyond what is normal — into a place of extreme intensity. That extreme intensity can be extreme evil, or, in a more modern and casual sense, extreme obsession.
Extremely cruel or wicked. It can also mean extremely clever or difficult, as in "a fiendish puzzle."
Extremely, especially in a difficult or clever way, as in "fiendishly difficult." It can also mean in a wickedly cruel way.
"Fierce" describes something or someone with a raw, overwhelming intensity — a power that feels almost impossible to stop, ignore, or stand against.
Burning or glowing like fire. Figuratively, passionate and quick-tempered, as in "a fiery speech," or, of food, very spicy.
A fiesta is a joyful, lively celebration — a festive event full of energy, people, music, food, and fun.
A fife is a small, simple musical instrument — specifically, a tiny flute.
A fifth column is a group of people who are secretly working against the very group they appear to belong to — by helping that group's enemy from the inside.
"A fifth wheel" refers to a person (or sometimes a thing) that is unnecessary, unwanted, or out of place in a situation.
When someone says "fight fire with fire," they mean that you should use the same methods, tactics, or weapons against someone that they are using against you.
To "fight shy of" something means to deliberately avoid it, usually because it makes you uncomfortable, nervous, or uneasy.

To "fight tooth and nail" means to try as hard as possible to do something or to oppose something with every bit of effort you have. It describes a struggle where someone refuses to give up, using every resource, energy, and determination available to them.
A figment is something that exists only in someone's mind — not in the real world. It is an idea, image, belief, or story that the imagination has invented, with no basis in reality whatsoever.
Figmental means existing only in someone's imagination and not in reality at all.
The adjective figurative describes language — words, phrases, or expressions — that are not meant to be taken at face value.

When you say something figuratively, you are using language in an imaginative, non-literal way — not to describe exact reality, but to paint a picture, express an emotion, or make an idea more vivid and powerful.
A figure is something that has a clear, recognizable form — something you can count, see, identify, or point to.

A figure of speech is a word, phrase, or expression that is used in a way that goes beyond its plain, literal meaning — on purpose — to create a stronger, more vivid, more interesting, or more persuasive effect on the listener or reader.
"Figure out" is a phrasal verb that means to understand, solve, or discover something through thinking and mental effort.
A figurehead is a person who appears to be the leader of a country, organization, or group — but who holds little or no real power.

A figurine is a small, three-dimensional object shaped to look like a person, an animal, a mythical creature, or a character. It is a miniature solid figure — something you can hold in your hand, place on a shelf, or display in a cabinet.
A filament is a very thin, long, thread-like strand or fiber. Think of it like a single thread pulled from a piece of fabric — extremely thin, but with noticeable length.
To filch something means to steal it in a sneaky, quiet, and casual way — usually something small and of low value. It is not bold, dramatic, or violent theft.
Filial means of, relating to, or appropriate for a son or daughter.

A filibuster is a tactic used by a politician — most commonly a senator — to delay or completely block a proposed law from being voted on, by talking for an extremely long time or using other procedural tricks to eat up time.

To filibuster means to deliberately talk for an extremely long time — or use other delaying tricks — inside a law-making body (like a country's Senate or Parliament) in order to block or slow down a vote on a law or decision.
Filigree is a form of delicate, handcrafted ornamental artwork — specifically, a type of fine metalwork.
A document officially submitted to an authority, such as a court or tax office. It can also mean the act of organizing documents, or the small particles removed by a metal file.
To fill someone in means to give a person the information they are missing about a situation — to update them, explain what happened, or bring them up to date on something they don't know yet.
Something that gives a boost or stimulus to something else, as in "the tax cut gave a fillip to the economy." Literally, a flick of the finger.
"Filmy" is built on the word film, which means a very thin layer of something — like the thin layer of oil you see floating on water, or the thin coating that forms on cold soup.
Filth means dirt or waste that is so extreme, so revolting, that it triggers a deep feeling of disgust — not just mild discomfort, but genuine revulsion.

"Filthy lucre" means money, but said with a sense of moral disgust — the idea being that money is dirty, corrupt, or shameful, especially when it is earned through dishonest, greedy, or unethical means.
To finagle means to get something, or to make something happen, through clever and slightly sneaky or dishonest means — rather than through honest, straightforward effort.

A finale is the last part of something — but not just any ordinary ending. It's the kind of ending that feels complete, significant, and often impressive. Think of it as the closing chapter that wraps everything up, often in a memorable way.
Finality means the quality or state of something being completely over, settled, or decided — in a way that cannot be changed, reversed, or undone.
Finance is the management of money — specifically, how money is raised, saved, spent, and invested, especially when the amounts are large or the decisions carry serious consequences.
A financier is a person who deals in money at a large scale — not just saving or spending it, but deploying it strategically to generate more wealth.

When we say there is "a fine line" between two things, we mean that the difference between those two things is very small, thin, or hard to notice — so small that it is easy to accidentally cross from one into the other.

As an idiom, "the fine print" means the hidden, less obvious, or deliberately obscured details, conditions, or limitations of any agreement, offer, deal, or situation — details that can significantly affect you, but which someone may not want you to notice easily.
Made of very small particles, as in "fine-grained sand." Figuratively, very detailed or precise, as in "a fine-grained analysis."
To fine-tune something means to make small, careful, precise adjustments to something that is already working well, in order to make it work even better — closer to perfect.
Finery refers to fine, showy, and often expensive clothing, jewelry, or accessories — especially the kind worn on special occasions to look one's very best or to impress others.
Finesse means the ability to handle something difficult in a way that is skillful, smooth, subtle, and elegant — all at the same time. It's not just about being good at something.

A finial is a decorative ornament placed at the very tip, top, or end of an object — its job is to "finish off" that object in a visually elegant way. Think of it as a crown or a full stop, but in physical, three-dimensional form.
Finicky means being extremely particular, hard to please, or overly fussy about small details — often to a degree that other people find excessive or even annoying.
Finish means to reach the end of something — to take something all the way to its completion, so that nothing more needs to be done.

Finished describes something that has reached its final state. But what that "final state" looks like varies — and this word actually carries three distinct, important meanings (plus one specialized one).
Finite means having a limit. Something finite has a definite end, a definite boundary, or a definite amount. It does not go on forever. It is not unlimited.

"Finito" is an adjective meaning completely finished, done, or over — with a strong sense of finality. When something is finito, it has ended, and there is nothing more to be done or said about it. It is over, full stop.

Finitude means the state or condition of being finite — that is, the quality of having limits, boundaries, or an end. If something has finitude, it means it is not limitless. It cannot go on forever, cannot hold everything, cannot do or know everything.
A person who is passionately committed to a cause and stirs up others to act, often in a provocative way. Literally, a piece of burning wood.
Firepower means the total destructive force or capability that someone — or something — can deliver. Think of it as a measure of how hard and how much someone can hit.
An extremely intense fire that creates its own powerful winds. Figuratively, a sudden outburst of anger or controversy, as in "a firestorm of criticism."

Firmament means the sky — but not in the flat, casual way we say "look at the sky." It refers to the sky as a vast, grand, sweeping expanse above us, especially when imagined as a great dome or canopy arching over the entire Earth.
"Firmly" describes how something is done — specifically, in a way that is strong, stable, and not weak or uncertain.
Permanent software built into a device's hardware that controls how the device works, sitting between physical hardware and changeable software.
"First and foremost" means "most importantly" or "above everything else."
Used to say that the most important thing should be done before anything else.
When something is described as first-hand, it means it comes directly from the original source — with no one in the middle passing it along, filtering it, or interpreting it for you.

Fiscal simply means "relating to money, especially the management of it." More specifically, it almost always refers to the money of an organized system — a government, a company, an institution — rather than your personal pocket money.

When you call a person "a fish out of water," you mean that they are in a situation, place, or group where they feel deeply uncomfortable, out of place, and unable to function well — because it is completely different from what they are used to.

Fissile means capable of being split. That's the single thread connecting everything about this word. But where it gets interesting — and where real precision matters — is how something splits, and what is doing the splitting.
Fission means the act of splitting or dividing something into two or more separate parts.

Fissiparous describes something that has a strong, inherent tendency to split or break apart into separate, smaller pieces. That tendency — that pull toward fragmentation — is the heart of the word. It works in two contexts: one scientific, one general.
A fissure is a long, narrow crack or opening in something — one that forms when a surface or material splits open or breaks apart.

Fisticuffs means a fight between people using their fists — that is, punching each other with their hands. It refers to physical combat where people hit one another with their closed hands (fists). Simple as that.
