Hasten means to make something happen faster, or to move/act quickly yourself. Think of it as adding speed — either to your own actions, or to a process or event in the world.
Hastily means doing something very quickly, often in a rushed way that leaves little room for care, thought, or proper attention.
Hasty means doing something too quickly, without enough thought, care, or preparation — and because of that speed, something important gets sacrificed: quality, accuracy, safety, or good judgment.

A hatch is a small opening or doorway — one that is built into a flat surface like a floor, a ceiling, a wall, or the deck of a ship — and that usually has a cover or door that you can open and close over it.
When a baby animal (like a chick, a turtle, a fish, or a snake) grows inside an egg and finally breaks through the shell to come out into the world, we say it hatches.
A hatchet is a small, lightweight tool used for chopping. Think of it as a miniature version of an axe — one you can hold and swing comfortably with just one hand.

A hatchet job is a piece of writing, a speech, or a broadcast that attacks a person, organization, book, film, or idea in a way that is deliberately cruel, one-sided, and designed to destroy their reputation — not to inform or critique fairly.
A hatchling is a very young animal that has just come out of an egg — or one that came out of an egg very recently and is still in the earliest stage of its life.
"Hats off to someone" means you deeply admire, respect, or praise a person for something impressive, difficult, or admirable they have done.

Haughtiness is the quality of acting as though you are far more important, superior, or better than the people around you — and showing that feeling through a cold, dismissive, contemptuous attitude toward them.

Haughty describes a person who believes they are superior to others — more important, more worthy, more refined — and who openly shows that feeling through the way they behave, speak, and carry themselves. It's not about silently thinking highly of yourself.
A haul is a collection of things gathered or obtained through a single effort or trip. Think of it as the result of going out and bringing back a bunch of things.
To haul means to pull or drag something with significant effort, usually moving it from one place to another. The two key ideas baked into the word are: force/effort and movement across a distance.
To haul someone over the coals means to scold, reprimand, or criticize someone very harshly because they did something wrong.

A haunch is the area of the body — human or animal — that includes the hip, the buttock, and the upper thigh, all considered as one region. Think of it as the fleshy "corner" where your leg connects to your torso at the back and side.

A haunt is a place where someone — or something — goes back to again and again. It is a place of return, a place tied to habit, memory, or strong presence. The word carries a feeling of atmosphere and depth. It is not just any ordinary place you visit.
When a ghost, spirit, or supernatural presence is said to haunt a place, it means that ghost repeatedly appears there, making the place feel frightening and disturbed.
When something is described as "haunting," it means it leaves such a deep impression on you that it stays in your mind long after the moment has passed.

Haute couture is the absolute highest level of fashion design — clothing that is made entirely by hand, crafted specifically for one single person, using the finest materials in the world, by a team of master artisans. It is not a brand or a style.

Hauteur means a cold, superior attitude that someone displays when they believe they are better than the people around them. It's not just feeling superior inside — it's the way that belief shows in how they carry themselves, speak, and treat others.

When something "has a bearing on" something else, it means it influences, affects, or is relevant to that thing. It tells you that the two things are connected — and that one of them matters to, or has an impact on, the other.
To "have a beef" with someone means to have a complaint, grievance, or conflict with them. It means you are angry or unhappy about something they did, and you feel that a wrong has been done to you.
To "have a change of heart" means to change your feelings, opinion, or decision about something — especially after you had already made up your mind.
When someone "has a field day," it means they are getting a great opportunity to do something they enjoy — and they are taking full advantage of it with a lot of excitement and enthusiasm.

"Have a go at something" means to try something or to make an attempt at it. When you "have a go" at something, you are willing to give it a try — even if you are not sure you can do it well, even if it is new to you, or even if it looks difficult.

To have a hankering for something means to feel a strong, persistent desire or craving for something — something you really, really want, often at a specific moment. It is more than just a passing "I want this."

To "have a shot at something" means to have a chance or opportunity to try something, usually with the hope of succeeding. It is used when someone gets the opportunity to attempt something — especially something challenging, competitive, or important.
Have a soft spot for someone
To have a soft spot for someone means to feel a special, warm, tender affection for that person. It is a feeling that is deeper and more emotional than just liking someone casually.

To have a spat with someone means to have a small, brief argument with them — a petty quarrel that is usually over something minor or unimportant. The key word here is small. A spat is not a serious fight.
To "have a way with" something or someone means to have a natural, special talent or skill for dealing with that thing or person — in a way that gets good results, often effortlessly.
"Have at it" means go ahead and do it — usually with energy, freedom, and no hesitation.

To "have it in for someone" means to be deliberately hostile toward a person and to look for opportunities to hurt them, cause them trouble, or treat them unfairly — usually because of personal dislike or past resentment.

When you "have it out with someone," it means you confront that person directly and openly about a problem, conflict, or grievance — usually in a heated, blunt, and emotionally charged way — with the goal of settling the matter once and for all.
Have one's heart set on something

To have one's heart set on something means to want something very strongly and deeply — so much so that you are completely focused on it and would feel truly disappointed or heartbroken if you didn't get it or achieve it.

When you say someone "has their work cut out for them," it means they are facing a task that is very difficult and will require a lot of effort. It is a way of saying: "This is going to be tough. You're up against a real challenge."

When you have second thoughts about something, it means you feel doubt or uncertainty about a decision you already made — or are about to make. You start questioning whether your original choice was the right one.
To do the decent or polite thing that a situation requires, especially when it is awkward or uncomfortable, as in "she had the good grace to apologize."
To "have the upper hand" means to be in a position of power, control, or advantage over someone else.
A haven is a place — real or imaginary — where someone feels safe, peaceful, and protected from whatever is difficult, dangerous, or overwhelming in the outside world.

"The haves and have-nots" is a phrase used to describe the two broad groups that exist in any society, community, or even a workplace: The haves — people who have wealth, power, resources, opportunities, or advantages.
Havoc means widespread destruction, chaos, or disorder — especially on a large scale, and especially when it is difficult to control or fix. It is not just "some damage."
Hawkish means favoring strength, aggression, and force over diplomacy, negotiation, or compromise — especially in politics, foreign policy, or economics.
A hawser is a very large, very thick rope or cable used on ships.
When something goes haywire, it means it has gone completely out of control, is behaving erratically and unpredictably, or has stopped working properly in a chaotic, messy way.
A hazard is anything that has the potential to cause harm, injury, damage, or loss.
To risk saying something, especially a guess, as in "hazard a guess." It can also mean to put something at risk, as in "hazarding his life."
If something is hazardous, it is capable of causing harm, injury, illness, damage, or death. The word describes anything that poses a threat to your safety, health, or well-being.
A thin mist of dust, smoke, or moisture in the air that makes things look blurred and unclear. Figuratively, a state of mental confusion, as in "a haze of tiredness."
"Hazy" describes something that is unclear, blurry, or not sharp — either in the physical world you can see, or inside your mind. Think of it as the opposite of clear and crisp.
To take action to prevent something bad from happening, as in "heading off a crisis." Literally, to get ahead of someone or something and block its path.

"Head over heels" most commonly means being so deeply and completely in love with someone that you feel overwhelmed, dizzy, and out of control — like you've lost your footing and are tumbling through the air.
A head start is an advantage you have at the very beginning of something — before others get going, or compared to where others are starting from.
Directly and firmly, without avoiding a problem, as in "tackle the issue head-on." Literally, with the fronts of two things meeting directly, as in "the cars collided head-on."

A headbutt is a forceful strike delivered using the head — specifically the forehead (the hard, bony front part of your skull) — as the weapon. It is the act of driving your head into someone or something with force and intent.
When you do something headfirst, your head leads — it goes before the rest of your body. That is the root image locked inside this word.
A heading is a short piece of text placed at the top of a page, section, chapter, document, email, or any block of content. Think of it as a signpost.
"Headlong" describes something — most often a movement, action, or process — happening with great speed, uncontrolled force, and a complete absence of caution. It is the opposite of slow and careful.
It describes doing something at reckless speed, with your head (and the rest of you) fully committed, whether you're ready or not.

If someone is headstrong, it means they are strongly determined to do things their own way, and they resist being controlled, guided, or told what to do by others — even when those others might be right.
Progress towards a goal, especially when it is slow or difficult, as in "to make headway." Literally, the forward movement of a ship.
When used about a smell, a drink, or the air around you, "heady" means so strong and rich that it almost overwhelms you — in a way that feels dizzying, pleasurable, and powerful all at once.

"Healthful" describes something that is good for your health — something that actively helps your body or mind stay well, grow stronger, or function better. In other words, if something is healthful, it has the quality of promoting or supporting good health.
Healthy means in a good state — not damaged, not broken, not sick, but working well and thriving. That one idea stretches across many different uses.
To heap praise on someone means to give someone a very large amount of praise, compliments, and admiration — generously, enthusiastically, and sometimes even excessively.
Hearken means to listen carefully and attentively — but with genuine intention and open-mindedness. It is not passive hearing (the way you might hear a car passing outside).
When something is described as hearsay, it means the information comes from what someone else said — not from what you personally saw, heard, or experienced yourself.
Hearsay is information that you have heard from someone else, but which you cannot confirm to be true because you did not see, hear, or experience it yourself.
A hearse is a specially designed vehicle used to carry a dead person's body — usually placed inside a coffin or casket — from one place to another. It is the vehicle you see at funerals.
Something heart-rending causes such deep, intense sadness or grief that it feels almost physically painful — like your heart is being violently torn apart. It goes far beyond ordinary sadness.

A heart-to-heart is a deep, honest, and personal conversation between people — usually two people — where both sides openly share their real feelings, thoughts, worries, or truths without hiding anything.
Heartache is a deep, lasting emotional pain that sits inside you — the kind of pain you feel not in your body, but somewhere in your chest, in the very center of who you are.

"Heartbreaking" describes something that causes a very deep, intense sadness — the kind of sadness that is so powerful, it feels like your heart is being broken or crushed inside your chest. Your heart is the traditional symbol of your emotions and love.
Heartbroken means feeling an extremely deep and painful sadness — the kind that comes when something you cared about very much is suddenly lost or destroyed.

To hearten someone means to make them feel more encouraged, hopeful, or confident — especially when they were feeling low, uncertain, or discouraged before. When you hearten someone, you give their spirit a lift.
Something is heartening when it makes you feel hopeful, encouraged, or more confident — especially after a period of worry, difficulty, or uncertainty.

"Heartfelt" describes something that is deeply and genuinely felt. When you call something heartfelt, you are saying it comes from the truest, most honest part of a person's emotions. It is not polite. It is not automatic. It is real and it runs deep.

A hearth is the flat, solid floor at the base of a fireplace — the area where the fire actually sits and burns. It is the bottom surface inside (and just in front of) a fireplace, typically built from brick, stone, tile, or marble.

"Heartily" means doing something with your whole heart — with genuine, full, and energetic enthusiasm. It is the opposite of doing something halfheartedly (which means weakly, or without real feeling). When you do something heartily, you hold nothing back.
When we describe someone or something as heartless, we mean they show absolutely no kindness, sympathy, or care for other people's feelings or suffering.

When something is heartwarming, it gives you a gentle, tender feeling of warmth and happiness deep inside your chest — as if your heart is being physically warmed up, like cold hands held near a fire.
Warm, enthusiastic, and sincere, as in "a hearty welcome." Of food, filling and substantial. Of a person, loud, cheerful, and energetic.

The idiom "in the heat of the moment" means doing or saying something impulsively, without thinking, because you are overwhelmed by a strong emotion at that exact time — like anger, excitement, fear, or passion.
Full of angry, passionate feelings, as in "a heated argument." Literally, made warm or hot, as in "a heated pool."
When you do something heatedly, you do it with strong, intense emotion — usually anger, frustration, or passionate disagreement. The emotion is so strong that it's hard to hold back.

A heath is a wide, open stretch of wild land covered mostly with low, shrubby plants — with few or no trees. It is not a forest, not a farm, not a meadow. It is a rough, exposed, often windswept landscape that feels untamed and remote.

When you use "heathen" as an adjective, you are describing something or someone as belonging to, connected with, or characteristic of people who do not follow one of the major Abrahamic religions — that is, Christianity, Islam, or Judaism.
A heathen is a person who does not follow one of the main, widely recognized religions — particularly Christianity, Judaism, or Islam.
To lift, pull, or throw something heavy with great effort. It can also mean to rise and fall heavily, to let out a sigh, or to retch as if about to vomit.
To "heave a sigh of relief" means to feel a deep, powerful sense of relief after a stressful, worrying, or frightening situation has finally passed or turned out well.

When something is "heavy going," it means it is difficult, slow, tiring, or hard to get through. It describes the feeling of struggling to make progress — as if every step forward costs a great deal of effort.

When something is described as heavy-duty, it means it is stronger, tougher, or more powerful than the standard version, and it is specifically designed or suited for demanding, difficult, or intense conditions.

Heavy-handed means using too much force, pressure, or emphasis — far more than the situation actually needs. The image the word paints is simple: instead of a careful, measured touch, someone is pressing down too hard. They've gone too far.
A person or organization with great influence, importance, or ability, as in "a political heavyweight." Literally, a boxer or wrestler in the heaviest weight class.
Hebdomadal simply means weekly — something that happens once every seven days, or something that belongs to or relates to a single week.
Hebetude means a state of mental dullness, sluggishness, or bluntness of mind. It describes a condition where the mind feels heavy, slow, and unresponsive — like it has lost its sharpness and edge.

To heckle someone means to interrupt and disturb a speaker or performer in public by shouting rude remarks, awkward questions, or taunting comments — with the goal of embarrassing them, throwing them off, or expressing strong disapproval.
A heckler is a person in an audience who rudely interrupts, shouts at, or taunts someone who is speaking or performing in public — usually to embarrass them, annoy them, or throw them off.
When something is hectic, it means it is full of a lot of activity, busyness, and rushing — often to the point of feeling chaotic, stressful, or out of control. It is not just "busy."
To hector someone means to bully or intimidate them through aggressive, overbearing talk — to pressure or dominate them using threatening or bossy language rather than reason or persuasion.

When someone hedges, they speak or answer in a careful, vague, or roundabout way — deliberately avoiding a clear, direct statement — usually because they want to protect themselves from being wrong, being held accountable, or offending someone.
To hedge one's bets means to protect yourself from loss or failure by trying more than one option at the same time, so that if one thing doesn't work out, another one will.

Hedonism is the idea that pleasure is the most important thing in life, and that seeking pleasure while avoiding pain is the ultimate purpose of human existence. A person who lives by this idea — or is described as living by it — is called a hedonist.
A hedonist is a person who believes — at their core — that pleasure is the most important thing in life, and who actively shapes their life around seeking pleasure and avoiding pain or discomfort.
Hedonistic describes a person, lifestyle, attitude, or choice that is centered on seeking pleasure and avoiding pain — and treating that as the most important thing in life.

"The heebie-jeebies" is an informal phrase that describes a feeling of nervousness, unease, or creepiness — that uncomfortable, crawly sensation you get when something disturbs or unsettles you. It sits somewhere between mild anxiety and outright fear.
Heed, as a noun, means careful, serious attention given to something — especially to a warning, advice, or something that truly matters.
To heed something means to pay careful attention to it and take it seriously enough to act on it.
"Heedful" means paying careful, deliberate attention to something — and letting that attention guide how you act. It is not just passively noticing something in the background.
Carelessly failing to pay attention to a warning, danger, or consequence, as in "heedless of the risks."
Heft means the weight of something — specifically, the weight you feel when you hold or lift it.
To heft something means to lift it or hold it up, especially to feel or judge how heavy it is.

Hefty means impressively large, heavy, or powerful — often more so than you might expect or feel comfortable with. Think of it as a word that signals something is notably big in some way. That "notably" part is important.
Hegemonic describes something — a country, culture, idea, group, or system — that holds such overwhelming dominance over others that it doesn't just lead the pack, it shapes the entire game.

Hegemony means the dominance, leadership, or authority that one entity — a country, a social class, or a culture — holds over others. But what makes this word special, and worth learning carefully, is that hegemony is not simply about force or raw power.

A hegira is a journey or flight made to escape danger, persecution, or an unbearable situation — a departure that is urgent, often forced, and usually marks a turning point in someone's life or history.

A heifer is a young female cattle animal — specifically, one that has not yet given birth to a calf (a baby cow). The moment she gives birth for the first time, she crosses over from being called a heifer and is now called a cow.

To heighten something means to make a quality, feeling, or experience stronger, more intense, or more noticeable than it already was. Think of it like a dial that controls the strength of something — when you heighten it, you turn the dial up.

Heightened means more intense, stronger, or sharper than normal. When something is heightened, it has moved beyond its usual, everyday level to a higher degree. Think of it like a dial that has been turned up past its regular setting.
Heinous means extremely and shockingly evil or morally wrong — so deeply wicked that it outrages and disgusts anyone who hears about it.
An heir is a person who is legally or rightfully entitled to receive someone else's property, money, title, or position after that person dies.

An heir apparent is a person who is guaranteed to inherit something — a throne, a title, a position, or an estate — from someone who currently holds it, as long as that person simply stays alive longer than the current holder.
An heiress is a woman or girl who is legally entitled to receive someone else's wealth, property, or title when that person dies. She is the designated receiver of everything a person leaves behind.

An heirloom is a special object that is passed down from one generation of a family to the next, usually over a long period of time, and is treated with great care because of its sentimental or monetary value.
A heist is a robbery — but not just any robbery. It is a carefully planned, cleverly executed theft of something very valuable, usually from a place that is well-protected or heavily secured.

Hell-bent means being so intensely determined to do something that you will not stop for anything — not warnings, not obstacles, not common sense, and not the people around you telling you to slow down.
Extremely unpleasant, difficult, or painful, as in "a hellish journey." It can also mean evil or devilish, like hell itself.
A position of leadership or control, as in "at the helm of the company." Literally, the wheel or handle used to steer a ship. In old use, a helm was also a helmet.
A helot is a person who is completely subjugated — trapped in a condition somewhere between a slave and a serf, with almost no freedom, no rights, and no real power over their own life.
A helping hand means assistance or support given to someone who needs it.
A helpmeet is a close companion — almost always a spouse — who actively helps and supports their partner in life. The word doesn't just mean helper and it doesn't just mean companion.
When you describe something as helter-skelter, you are saying it is happening in a way that is fast, disorganized, and out of control — all at the same time.
A hem is the finished, folded edge at the border of a piece of fabric or clothing — most commonly found at the bottom of trousers, skirts, dresses, shirts, curtains, or tablecloths.
When you hem something, you fold the raw edge of a piece of cloth over and sew it down neatly so that it doesn't fray or unravel. Tailors and seamstresses do this all the time.
To hem in means to surround something or someone on all sides so tightly that they cannot move freely or escape.
One half of a sphere. It usually refers to one half of the Earth, such as the Northern or Southern Hemisphere, or one of the two halves of the brain.
The word hemlock actually refers to two entirely different things in English — a plant and a tree. They share the same name but are unrelated to each other.
When a piece of fabric has its raw, rough edge folded over and stitched down to create a clean, neat border — that fabric is said to be hemmed.

A hemorrhage is a severe, significant loss of blood caused by a ruptured or damaged blood vessel. Think of it as bleeding, but at a serious, dangerous, and often hard-to-control level. It is not the tiny trickle from a paper cut.
To hemorrhage means to bleed severely, rapidly, and in a way that is very difficult or impossible to stop.
A hen is a female bird — but in everyday speech, it almost always means a female chicken specifically.

"Hence" is a word you use to show that what you just said is the reason for what you are about to say. It signals a cause-and-effect relationship — something happened, and because of that, something else is true.
Henceforth means "from this point in time onward."

A henchman is a person who loyally and obediently follows a powerful — and usually evil, criminal, or corrupt — person, and carries out that person's orders. The key idea is that a henchman does the dirty work for someone more powerful than them.

To henpeck someone means to constantly nag, criticize, or boss them around — especially about small, everyday matters — in a way that is persistent, controlling, and wears the other person down over time.

Hepatic means of, relating to, or affecting the liver. Whenever you see the word "hepatic," it's pointing you to the liver — either something that belongs to it, connects to it, happens inside it, or has something to do with it.

In its oldest and most literal sense, a herald is an official messenger — someone whose job is to deliver important news or proclamations on behalf of a powerful authority, like a king, queen, or government.
To herald something means to be a clear sign or signal that something significant is coming, or to publicly announce and celebrate something or someone with great praise.

"Heraldic" is an adjective that means relating to heraldry. Think of it the same way "musical" relates to music, or "historical" relates to history — "heraldic" simply means "of or belonging to heraldry."
"Herbaceous" is an adjective used mainly in botany (the study of plants) and gardening. It means: soft-stemmed and non-woody.
A herbicide is a chemical substance used to kill or control the growth of unwanted plants.

An animal is described as herbivorous when it eats only plants — and nothing but plants. No meat, no fish, no insects. Its entire diet comes from the plant world: grasses, leaves, fruits, seeds, roots, bark, flowers, and similar plant material.
"Herculean" describes something that requires a truly extraordinary amount of strength, effort, or determination — far beyond what an ordinary person can handle with ease.
A herd is a group of animals of the same kind that live together, move together, or feed together.
To herd means to gather a group and move them together in a particular direction, usually by guiding, pushing, or controlling them from behind or from the sides.
When someone uses "hereafter," they are pointing forward, saying: from this point on, things will be a certain way.
Hereby means "by means of this" — specifically, "by means of this very statement, document, or action that is happening right now."

Something is hereditary if it passes — or is capable of passing — from one generation to the next through family lines. The thing travels from parents to children, and potentially from those children to their children, and so on across generations.
Herein is a formal adverb. It means "in this" — more completely, "inside this" or "within this." The key question is: inside what?

Heresy is a belief or opinion that directly contradicts the official, accepted teachings of a religion, organization, or group — especially when that contradiction is seen as dangerous, offensive, or unacceptable by that group.

A heretic is a person who holds beliefs that go against the officially accepted teachings of a religion, institution, or powerful group — and who refuses to give up those beliefs, even when pressured to do so.

Something is heretical when it goes against the officially accepted beliefs of a group — whether that group is a religion, an institution, a culture, or any system of thought that holds certain ideas as sacred or beyond questioning.
Heretofore means "before this point in time" or "up until now."

Hereupon is a formal adverb that means "immediately after this" or "as a direct result of this." It points to a tight, immediate connection between something that just happened and what follows next — like a chain where one link pulls the next.
Heritage means anything — objects, places, customs, values, or ideas — that has been passed down from the past to the present. Think of it as a gift across time.

When something is described as hermeneutic, it means it relates to the act of interpreting meaning — especially the meaning found in texts, symbols, laws, or language that requires deeper thought to truly understand.
Sealed so completely that no air or liquid can get in or out, as in "hermetically sealed." It can also mean cut off from outside influence, or relating to ancient mystical and occult writings.
Hermetically means in a way that is completely and perfectly airtight — sealed so tightly that no air, gas, moisture, or any other substance can pass in or out.

A hermit is a person who deliberately chooses to live alone, cut off from other people and from mainstream society. The key word here is deliberately — a hermit is not lonely by accident or by force. It is a conscious, personal choice.

A hermitage is a place — typically small, simple, and isolated — where a person (or sometimes a small group) lives completely apart from the rest of society. Think of it as a private refuge deliberately chosen to be far from towns, cities, noise, and people.

"Heroics" refers to acts or behavior that are dramatic, bold, or daring — things done in a way that goes above and beyond the ordinary, often involving great risk or effort. The word is always used in its plural form.
A heroine is a woman who is deeply admired — either for her bravery and good deeds in real life, or as the main female character in a story.

Heroism means the quality of showing great courage, selflessness, and willingness to make a sacrifice — especially when facing danger, difficulty, or opposition — for the benefit of others or for a cause that is bigger than oneself.
A heron is a large bird that lives near water. Think of it as the patient, still hunter of the bird world — a creature built around the art of waiting.
A herpetologist is a scientist who studies reptiles and amphibians — two distinct groups of cold-blooded animals.

Herpetology is a noun. It is the branch of science that is devoted to the study of reptiles and amphibians — two groups of animals that, while different from each other, have historically been studied together by scientists.
A herring is a type of small, silvery fish. It lives in the cold ocean waters of the North Atlantic and North Pacific.
Hesitancy is the state or quality of being uncertain, unsure, or unwilling — in a way that causes you to pause, hold back, or move slowly before doing or saying something.

Hesitant describes a person (or their action, voice, movement, or manner) that is slow, uncertain, or unwilling to act because something is holding them back from the inside — doubt, fear, nervousness, awkwardness, or simply not being sure what to do.
When someone does something hesitantly, they do it with pausing, doubt, or uncertainty. They are not fully confident, not fully ready, and not fully comfortable — but they still do it.
To hesitate means to pause before doing or saying something, usually because you are unsure, nervous, or unwilling.
A hetaera (plural: hetaerae) was a specific kind of woman in ancient Greece — particularly in Athens — who existed in a completely unique social category that has no perfect modern equivalent.
If something is heteroclite, it deviates from the normal, expected rules of its category — it is irregular, anomalous, or doesn't behave the way things of its kind are supposed to.
A heteroclite is something — most often a word — that deviates from the expected norm or standard form. It doesn't fit neatly into the category it appears to belong to.

Heterodox describes a belief, idea, opinion, or person that goes against what is officially accepted, traditionally established, or widely approved within a particular field, institution, or community.
Made up of parts, elements, or members that are different from each other in kind, type, or nature.

When something is described as heuristic, it means it works by using practical experience, good judgment, and rough rules of thumb to reach a satisfactory answer — rather than following a guaranteed, step-by-step process that is certain to produce a perfect result.

A heuristic is a practical mental shortcut, rule of thumb, or problem-solving strategy that helps you arrive at a good-enough answer quickly — especially when finding the perfect answer is too difficult, too slow, or simply impossible.
"Hew" means to cut or chop something forcefully using a heavy, sharp tool — typically an axe, a pickaxe, or a chisel.
The word "heyday" means the period in which someone or something was at its absolute best — the peak era, the golden chapter, the time of greatest success, popularity, power, or energy.
A hiatus is a noticeable gap, pause, or break in something that was previously happening or ongoing. Think of it as a hole in time — something was flowing along, and then, for a period, it stopped.
A hibernaculum (plural: hibernacula) is a sheltered place where a living thing — usually an animal — retreats to survive winter by staying still, staying warm, and barely functioning.
Hibernal means of, relating to, or characteristic of winter. If something is hibernal, it belongs to winter, happens in winter, or carries the qualities and feel of winter.
To hibernate means to go into a long, deep state of sleep or stillness — usually to survive a difficult period, especially winter.

Hibernation is a prolonged state of deep, sleep-like inactivity that certain animals enter — most commonly in winter — as a survival strategy to endure a period when food is scarce and conditions are too harsh for normal life.
A small, temporary problem or setback, as in "a minor hiccup." Literally, a sudden involuntary spasm of the diaphragm that makes a short "hic" sound.

When you use "hiccup" as a verb, you are describing either a physical action your body does or a small, temporary disruption that something experiences. These two meanings are closely connected — the second one grows naturally out of the first.
A hidden agenda is a secret purpose or goal that someone has in mind — one they deliberately conceal from others while pretending to have a different, more acceptable reason for their actions.
To hide means to put something — or yourself — in a place where others cannot see it or find it easily. The basic goal is always the same: to make something unavailable to view or discovery.
To use something as an excuse or cover to avoid responsibility or criticism, as in "hiding behind the rules." Literally, to stay out of sight behind something.
"Hidebound" describes a person, institution, or way of thinking that is so rigidly stuck in old customs, traditions, or established beliefs that it refuses to accept new ideas or change.
Hideous means so extremely unpleasant, ugly, or morally offensive that it causes a strong feeling of shock, disgust, or horror.

A hideout is a secret place where a person — or a group of people — goes to stay hidden from others who are trying to find them. The key idea is that it is deliberately chosen because it is difficult for outsiders to discover.

Hierarchical is an adjective that describes anything — a system, a structure, an organization, a relationship — that is arranged in levels or ranks, where some things are above others, and where those at the top hold more power, authority, or importance than those below.

A hierarchy is a system in which people, things, or ideas are arranged in ranked levels — from the most powerful, important, or authoritative at the top, down to the least powerful, important, or authoritative at the bottom.
A major unsolved puzzle in physics: why gravity is so astonishingly weak compared to the other forces, and why the mass of the Higgs boson is so much smaller than theory suggests it should be.

Hieratic means belonging to or characteristic of priests and sacred ritual — and everything that comes with that: formal, solemn, stylized, elevated above ordinary life, and governed by strict convention rather than personal expression or natural feeling.

A hieroglyph is a single picture-symbol used as a unit of writing — where a drawn image of something (a bird, an eye, a hand, a wavy line) stands for a word, a sound, or an idea, instead of a letter of an alphabet.
A hieroglyphic is a single written character — a picture or symbol — that belongs to a system of writing where pictures stand in for words, sounds, or ideas, instead of using a regular alphabet.

When something happens or is arranged higgledy-piggledy, it happens in a completely disordered, jumbled, and confused way — with absolutely no system, plan, or pattern whatsoever. Think of it as the opposite of "neatly" or "in an orderly way."

Nearly every meaning of "high" as an adjective comes from one simple idea — being above a reference point. That reference point could be the ground, a normal level, an average, a rank, or a sober state of mind.
To be "left high and dry" means to be abandoned in a helpless situation, usually without the support, resources, or help you were counting on — and with no easy way out.
"High and low" means everywhere — every single place you can possibly think of, leaving no spot unchecked.

When someone is "on their high horse," they are acting as if they are morally superior to others. They behave in a self-righteous, arrogant, or preachy way — as if their values, opinions, or judgment are better than everyone else's.
The high seas are the parts of the world's oceans that lie beyond the legal boundaries of any country's authority. They are international waters — open to all nations and belonging to none.

"High-end" describes something that sits at the top of a range — in terms of quality, price, and refinement. When you call something high-end, you are saying it is among the finest, most carefully made, and most expensive options available in its category.
High-flown describes ideas or ambitions that are unrealistically grand, impractical, or far removed from the ground realities.
Extremely successful and ambitious, as in "a high-flying career." Literally, flying at a great height.
High-handed describes a way of behaving where someone uses their power, authority, or position in an arrogant, bossy, and dismissive way — without caring about what others think, feel, or deserve.

When you call someone high-minded, you are saying that they have strong moral principles and noble ideals — that they genuinely care about doing what is right, good, and ethical, often even when it is difficult or costly for them personally.
High-powered simply means having a very large amount of power — whether that power is physical (like in a machine) or personal (like in a person's career or influence).

When something or someone is described as high-profile, it means they attract a large amount of public attention. They are widely noticed, widely talked about, and widely covered — especially in the news and media.
High-ranking means holding a position near or at the top of a structured group, organization, or system.
A high-rise is a very tall building with many floors, built upward rather than outward, and equipped with elevators so people can move between floors without climbing endless stairs.

High-strung describes a person who is very nervous, tense, and easily stressed or upset. A high-strung person has emotional and mental sensitivity that is turned up very high — they react intensely to things that other people might brush off or barely notice.
When something is described as highbrow, it means it is intellectual, serious, and culturally sophisticated — the kind of thing associated with deep thinking, high education, and refined taste.
When you call something highfalutin, you are saying it is trying too hard to seem grand, impressive, or important — but in a way that feels fake, overdone, or unnecessary.
To highlight something means to draw special attention to it — to pull it out from everything around it and say, "Look at this. This matters."
In everyday English, hijab refers to the headscarf worn by many Muslim women — a piece of fabric that covers the hair, ears, and neck, while leaving the face fully visible.

To hijack something means to forcefully take control of something that is already in motion or already underway, without permission, and redirect it toward your own purpose — against the will of whoever was rightfully in charge of it.
A sudden, large increase, as in "a price hike" or "a tax hike." It is also a long walk in the countryside or mountains.

When you hike, you walk a long distance — usually through mountains, forests, hills, or countryside. It is not just any walk. It carries the sense of physical effort, distance, and being in an outdoor, natural setting.
Hilarious means extremely funny — so funny that it makes you laugh hard, loudly, or even uncontrollably. It is not just "a little funny" or "mildly amusing."

Hilarity means a state of great, often loud and uncontrollable laughter and amusement — usually shared among a group of people. It is not just "being happy" or "finding something a little funny." It is the peak of amusement.
A hillock is a small hill — a gentle, rounded rise of land that is noticeably higher than the ground around it, but clearly too small and modest to be called a proper hill or a mountain.
A hilt is the handle of a sword, dagger, or knife — the part that you hold in your hand when using the weapon.

To hinder someone or something means to make it harder for them to do something, move forward, or make progress. It puts obstacles, difficulty, or delay in the way — but it does not necessarily mean stopping something completely.
Hindmost means furthest to the back — the one positioned at the very rear of a group, line, or series, behind everyone or everything else.

A hindrance is anything — a person, a thing, a situation, or even an internal quality like a habit or a feeling — that makes something harder to do, slows you down, or gets in the way of your progress toward a goal.
Hindsight is the ability to look back at something that already happened and understand it clearly — often more clearly than you did when it was actually happening.
To depend entirely on one crucial thing, as in "the case hinges on one witness."
"Hint at" means to suggest something indirectly, without saying it openly or clearly.
"Hinterland" means the land that lies behind or beyond a main center — behind a coast, behind a city, behind a port — the areas that are further away, less developed, and often quieter or more rural.
If someone or something is hip, it means they are cool, fashionable, and aware of what's current in culture — music, art, fashion, ideas, or lifestyle. Being hip is not just about following trends.

A hippie is a person who rejects the normal, accepted way of living in mainstream society and instead chooses to live by a very different set of values — centered on peace, love, freedom, and closeness to nature, rather than on money, status, rules, or authority.
A hipster is a person — usually a young adult — who deliberately avoids mainstream, popular culture and instead seeks out things that feel underground, indie, obscure, or alternative.

A hireling is a person who works for someone — or does someone's bidding — purely for money or personal gain, with absolutely no real loyalty, genuine belief in the cause, or personal commitment to the work.

Hirsute simply means very hairy — but it's not just any kind of hairy. It specifically describes something or someone covered in a noticeably large amount of hair, or hair that is thick, coarse, and rough to the touch.
A hiss is a sharp, continuous sound that resembles a drawn-out "ssssss." It is thin, high, and piercing — not loud like a bang or deep like a rumble, but cutting in a very specific way.

To hiss means to make a sharp, continuous "sssss" sound — the kind of sound the letter S makes when you stretch it out. It is a high, thin, rushing sound produced when air or gas is forced through a very narrow space.
Histology is the scientific study of the microscopic structure of tissues in living organisms — particularly in humans and animals. A person who specializes in this field is called a histologist.
Something is historic when it is so important and significant that it deserves to be remembered in history — or already is. The word does not simply mean "old" or "from the past."
Historical means "of, relating to, or connected with history or the past."
When viewed through history, or as history shows, as in "historically, wars have been fought over land." It can also mean in a way that relates to history, as in "historically accurate."
"Histrionic" describes behavior, reactions, speech, or a person that is excessively and artificially dramatic — dramatic in a way that feels performed and staged rather than genuine.

Histrionics refers to exaggerated, theatrical, over-the-top emotional behavior — the kind that seems far too dramatic for the situation at hand. When someone engages in histrionics, they are putting on a show of emotion.
To "hit a nerve" means to say or do something that causes a strong, sudden emotional reaction in someone — especially a reaction involving discomfort, anger, embarrassment, or hurt feelings.
When something hits home, it means it is deeply felt, fully understood, or personally meaningful to someone — often in a powerful or emotional way.
"To hit it off" means to immediately like each other and get along well with someone the first time you meet them.
"Hit rock bottom" means to reach the lowest possible point in a situation — a point so low that things simply cannot get any worse.
Hit someone like a ton of bricks
When something hits you like a ton of bricks, it means something came suddenly and with great force — not physically, but emotionally or mentally.
"Hit the ground running" means to start something quickly and energetically, with full effort, from the very beginning — without needing time to warm up, learn, or settle in.
Hit the nail on the head
When someone hits the nail on the head, it means they have said or identified something exactly right. Not approximately right. Not almost right. Perfectly, precisely, completely right.
"Hit the roof" means to become extremely angry very suddenly.

When something is described as hit-and-miss, it means that it sometimes works well (a "hit") and sometimes doesn't (a "miss"), with no reliable way of knowing which outcome to expect before it happens.

When you call something hit-and-run, you are describing a situation where someone does something and then immediately runs away — without stopping, without taking responsibility, and without dealing with the consequences of what they did.
A hitch is an unexpected problem, delay, or obstacle — something that stops a plan from going completely smoothly. It's not usually a disaster; it's more like a snag. A bump in the road.
Hither means "to this place" — that is, toward the speaker, or toward the place being talked about.
Hitherto means "up until now" or "until this point in time."
A hive is the structure where a colony of honeybees lives together — their home, their nursery, and their food storage all in one place.
A place full of busy, energetic activity, with lots of people doing things at once — like bees in a beehive.
To separate a part of something from the larger whole it belongs to, usually to make that part stand on its own.
A hoard is a large collection of something — usually valuable, useful, or important — that has been gathered and stored away privately, often secretly, and often over a long period of time.
To hoard means to collect and store large amounts of something — and then keep it hidden away, guarded, or unused, often out of fear, greed, or obsession.

Hoarding is the act of collecting and keeping large quantities of things — far more than what a person actually needs — and being unable or unwilling to throw any of it away, even when the things are useless, broken, or worthless.

Hoarfrost is a coating of white, feathery ice crystals that forms naturally on outdoor surfaces — like grass, tree branches, leaves, spider webs, fences, and rooftops — during cold winter nights and early mornings.

When you describe a voice as hoarse, you are saying it sounds rough, scratchy, raspy, and strained — almost as if there is gravel or sand caught in the person's throat. A hoarse voice has lost its normal smoothness and clarity.

Hoarsely means in a rough, raspy, and strained way — used to describe how someone speaks or makes a sound when their voice is not smooth or clear, but instead sounds scratchy, low, and forced, as if something is wrong with their throat.
Very old and over-familiar; stale and overused, as in "a hoary old joke." Literally, white or grey with age, as in "a hoary beard."
A hoax is a deliberate, carefully constructed lie that is designed to make people believe something false is actually true. It is not a simple, casual lie — it is a built deception.

A hobbit is a fictional creature invented by the English author J.R.R. Tolkien. Hobbits appear in his famous books The Hobbit (1937) and The Lord of the Rings (1954–1955), as well as in the popular film adaptations directed by Peter Jackson.
When something hobbles, it moves or functions in a way that is awkward, restricted, and struggling — not smooth, not free. That one idea sits at the heart of every use of this word.
To hobnob with someone means to socialize with them in a friendly, relaxed, and informal way — chatting, mingling, eating, drinking, laughing — essentially spending enjoyable social time together.

A hobo is a person who has no permanent home and wanders from place to place — but who is willing to work to earn money or food along the way. That last part is important. A hobo is not simply lazy or idle.

The hock is a specific joint found in the hind leg of hoofed or four-legged animals — horses, cows, dogs, pigs, and similar creatures. Think of it as the animal's "ankle," but located further up the leg than you might expect.
A hodgepodge is a messy, random mix of different things that don't really belong together or go well together in any organized or unified way.

A hoe is a simple, handheld farming and gardening tool. Picture a long stick (the handle) with a flat, thin metal blade attached to one end at an angle — almost like the letter "L" but slightly tilted.
To hog something means to take far more than your fair share of it, selfishly, and often at the expense of others.
To hog the limelight means to selfishly take all the attention for yourself, leaving little or no attention for others around you.

A hogan is a traditional home built and lived in by the Navajo people — one of the largest Native American nations in the United States, living primarily in the desert Southwest (today's Arizona, New Mexico, Utah, and Colorado).
A hogshead is a very large wooden barrel — the kind used to store and transport liquids like wine, beer, whisky, rum, cider, or even tobacco. Think of it as the giant of the barrel world.
Hogwash means something that is complete nonsense — a statement, claim, argument, or idea that is so wrong, so foolish, or so untrue that it is not even worth taking seriously.

Hoi polloi means ordinary people — the general public, the masses, the common crowd. It refers to the large majority of people in society who are not wealthy, powerful, famous, or part of any elite group.
To hoist something means to lift it upward, usually with effort, and often using a rope, chain, pulley, crane, or some other mechanical tool.

Something is hokey when it feels fake, cheap, or embarrassingly oversimplified — especially when it's trying to seem meaningful, impressive, or emotional, but falls flat because it's too obvious, too clichéd, or too poorly put together to be convincing.
Hold means to keep something in place — to prevent it from falling, escaping, changing, or going away. This one idea runs through almost every use of the word.
To "hold at bay" means to keep something dangerous, threatening, or unwanted at a safe distance so that it cannot reach you, harm you, or get worse.
To be surrounded by a group of admirers or listeners and be the centre of attention, as in "she held court at the bar." Literally, said of a monarch receiving visitors.
To manage to keep a job for some time, as in "he can't hold down a job." It can also mean to keep something low, such as prices, or to physically press something in place.
To hold forth means to talk at length about a topic, usually in a confident, opinionated, and often self-important way.
When you "hold off" doing something, you deliberately wait before doing it. You have the ability to act, but you choose — or are asked — to pause.

To hold one's ground means to refuse to change your position, opinion, or decision when someone is pressuring you to do so. It means you stay firm and strong, even when things get tough or someone is pushing back against you.

To "hold one's own" means to perform competently or survive successfully in a difficult or competitive situation, without being defeated, overwhelmed, or outshone — even when the odds are not in your favor.
To hold one's tongue means to stay silent on purpose, especially when you really want to say something but choose not to. It is about deliberate, conscious self-control over your speech.
To resist or refuse to give in, as in "holding out for a better offer." It can also mean to last, as in "supplies won't hold out," or to hold something out to someone.
"Hold out for" means to refuse to accept something until you get exactly what you want.

"Hold sway" means to have strong power, control, or influence over someone or something. When a person, idea, belief, or force "holds sway," it dominates — it shapes how people think, feel, or behave in a powerful and often widespread way.

"Hold the fort" means to take care of things and keep a situation stable while someone else is temporarily away. It is used when one person leaves a place or a responsibility in someone else's hands, trusting that person to manage things until they return.

When something "holds true," it means that a statement, rule, fact, belief, or principle remains valid, accurate, and applicable — even when the situation changes, time passes, or new circumstances arise.
To delay someone or something, as in "the traffic held us up." It also means to support something, to stay strong, to raise something up, or to rob someone at gunpoint.

When something holds water, it means it is logically sound, believable, and able to withstand scrutiny — meaning that when you look at it closely and test it, it still makes sense. It still checks out. There are no holes or flaws in it.
A hold-up is a type of robbery where a criminal directly confronts a victim face-to-face, usually with a gun or another weapon, and forces them to hand over money or valuables on the spot.
"Hole up" means to hide in a place, or to stay in a place for shelter and safety, usually to avoid something dangerous, uncomfortable, or unpleasant outside.
"Holier-than-thou" describes the attitude of a person who behaves as though they are morally better, more virtuous, or more righteous than the people around them.

Holistic means looking at, treating, or understanding something as a complete whole — considering all of its parts together, along with how those parts connect and affect each other — rather than focusing on just one piece at a time in isolation.

To holler means to shout or yell very loudly, usually to get someone's attention, to express a strong feeling, or to make yourself heard across a distance. It is an informal, everyday word used mostly in spoken American English.
Empty inside, as in "a hollow tree." Figuratively, without real value, meaning, or sincerity, as in "a hollow victory" or "hollow promises." Of a sound, dull and echoing.
To hollow something means to remove the inside of it, creating an empty space within, while keeping the outer shape or structure mostly intact.
"Hollow out" is a phrasal verb. It means to make something hollow — that is, to remove or destroy the inside of something, leaving only the outer shell or surface.
The Holocaust was the mass murder of six million Jews and millions of others by Nazi Germany during the Second World War. In general, a holocaust is destruction or slaughter on a massive scale.
A hologram is a special kind of three-dimensional image — one that appears to have real depth and volume, even though it's recorded on a flat surface.

A holograph is a document written completely in the handwriting of the person who authored it — not typed, not dictated to someone else, not partially handwritten. Every single word, from beginning to end, must be in the author's own hand.
Relating to or produced by holography, a technique that creates three-dimensional images using light.
A theory in physics that all the information inside a three-dimensional region of space can be fully described by information on its two-dimensional boundary, like a hologram.

A holster is a shaped holder or case designed to carry a handgun (a pistol or revolver) securely on a person's body, so that their hands stay free while the gun remains accessible and ready to draw quickly when needed.
To holster something means to put a weapon — almost always a handgun — back into its holster after you have taken it out.
Something extremely desirable that people seek eagerly but that is very hard to find or achieve. Originally, the legendary cup that Jesus drank from at the Last Supper.

Homage is a deliberate, conscious act of showing deep respect and honor to someone or something you consider great, important, or worthy of admiration. It is not a casual "thank you" or everyday politeness.
"Home in on" means to move toward a target or goal with great focus and precision, getting closer and closer until you reach it.

A home truth is an honest, accurate statement about a person — usually about their character, behavior, or a situation involving them — that is unpleasant, uncomfortable, or even painful for that person to hear, but is undeniably true.
A homebody is a person who genuinely prefers staying at home over going out.
Homegrown means originating, developing, or being produced in one's own home, local community, or country — rather than being brought in, imported, or sourced from somewhere external or foreign.
A homeland is the country, region, or place that a person — or a group of people — originally comes from and feels a deep, natural sense of belonging to. It is the place where your roots are.
In British English, simple, cosy, and comfortable, like a home. In American English, plain-looking or unattractive.
Homeopathy is a system of alternative medicine based on the belief that the body can heal itself, and that extremely diluted substances can stimulate that healing process.

Homeostasis is the automatic process by which a system — most commonly a living organism — continuously monitors and adjusts its own internal conditions to keep them stable and balanced, even when the outside world is constantly changing.
In American baseball, a homer is a home run — the best possible hit a batter can get.
The word homespun describes something that is simple, plain, and unpolished — but in a genuine, honest, and unpretentious way. It is the opposite of fancy, sophisticated, or artificially refined.

A homestead is a piece of property — made up of a house, the land around it, and any supporting structures on that land (like a barn, a shed, or a stable) — that serves as someone's permanent home, especially in a rural or semi-rural setting.
Homicide means the killing of one human being by another human being. Simple.
A homie is a person you are very close to — someone you trust deeply, feel comfortable around, and consider a genuine friend. The word carries a strong sense of loyalty, familiarity, and belonging.

A homily is a talk or speech given by a religious leader — such as a priest, pastor, minister, or bishop — during a religious service, where they explain the meaning of a passage from a holy scripture (like the Bible) and connect its lessons to the everyday lives of the people listening.
Hominy is dried corn that has been soaked and cooked in a special alkaline (basic) liquid, which transforms it into something quite different from regular corn — in texture, flavor, and nutrition.
Homogeneity is the quality of being made up of the same kind of things throughout — of being uniform, consistent, and without meaningful internal variation.
Homogeneous describes something that is uniform throughout — meaning all its parts, members, or components are of the same kind, nature, or composition.
To homogenize something means to make it uniform — to process or blend something so that all of its parts become the same throughout, with no visible differences, clumps, or uneven spots.

When two or more things are described as homologous, it means they correspond to each other in a deep, fundamental way — they share the same underlying nature, position, or origin, even if on the surface they look different, are called something different, or even do something different.
A homonym is a word that shares the same spelling, the same sound, or both — with another word — but carries a completely different meaning.
Homophobia refers to negative feelings, attitudes, beliefs, or behaviors directed toward people who are gay, lesbian, or bisexual — or toward anyone perceived to be so.
A homophone is a word that sounds exactly like another word when spoken aloud, but is spelled differently and has a completely different meaning.

A honcho is a person who is in charge — a leader, a boss, or the most powerful person in a group, organization, team, or situation. When you call someone a honcho, you are saying that they are the one who holds authority, makes decisions, and calls the shots.
To hone something means to refine and perfect it through focused, deliberate effort — until it becomes sharp, precise, and highly effective.
Honest describes someone or something that is free from lies, deception, and pretense.
Honey is a sweet, thick, sticky liquid made by bees. It is one of the oldest natural foods known to humans, and it has been used for thousands of years.

A honeymoon period is the early phase of something new — a new job, a new relationship, a new government, a new product, a new agreement — during which everything feels unusually smooth, positive, and free of real problems.

To honk means to produce a short, loud, abrupt sound — the kind that cuts sharply through background noise and demands attention. The word itself imitates the sound it describes (this is called onomatopoeia).

Honor is about deep, moral respect — but it works in two directions at once: the respect that other people give you because of your good character, and the respect you give yourself by choosing to live rightly.

To honor something or someone means to treat it as genuinely important and to show that importance through your actions. It is not just a feeling inside your heart — it is something you do. Honoring is always expressed outwardly, in the real world.
Honorable describes someone or something that deserves respect because it is morally good, honest, and ethically sound.

An honorarium is a sum of money given to someone as a thank-you and a sign of respect for a professional service they provided — when there was no legal obligation or formal contract requiring them to be paid in the first place.

When something is described as honorary, it means it is given to someone purely as a sign of respect or recognition — not because they went through the normal process, met the usual requirements, or did the usual work to earn it.

Honored means one of two closely related things: Feeling a deep sense of privilege, respect, and gratitude because of something meaningful done for you or said to you. Being treated with special respect and high regard by others.
"Honorific" describes anything whose purpose is to show respect, reverence, or high regard toward a person.

An honorific is a special word or title that you attach to a person's name — or use in place of their name — to show respect, politeness, or to acknowledge something important about them, like their profession, social rank, gender, age, or relationship to you.
A hoodlum is a person who regularly behaves in a rough, violent, or criminal way — someone who causes trouble, intimidates people, or commits street-level crimes.

To hoodwink someone means to deliberately trick or deceive them, usually by feeding them false information or creating a false impression — so that they believe something that is not true, and you (or someone else) benefit from their belief.
Hooey means nonsense — words, ideas, claims, or beliefs that are completely false, foolish, or without any real basis in truth or fact.
A hoof is the hard, tough covering on the foot of certain animals. Think of it as a natural "shoe" that the animal is born with and carries its entire life.
To connect a machine or device to a supply or system. Informally, to meet up with someone, or to have a casual sexual encounter.

"Hook, line, and sinker" means completely, totally, and without any doubt. It is used to describe a situation where someone believes or is tricked by something entirely — not just a little bit, but one hundred percent.
Addicted to something or extremely enthusiastic about it, as in "she's hooked on crime novels." It can also mean curved like a hook, as in "a hooked nose."
Hookey means an unjustifiable absence from school or work.
A casual sexual encounter (informal). A hookup is also a connection to a supply of electricity, water, or gas, or a link between broadcasting stations.

A hooligan is a person who behaves in a rough, violent, or wildly disruptive way — especially in public. They cause trouble, pick fights, damage property, disturb the peace, and show little or no respect for people around them or for rules.
To a very great and helpless degree, as in "hopelessly lost" or "hopelessly in love." It can also mean in a way that has no hope of success.
"Hopper" is a noun with several distinct meanings. They can be grouped into two broad families: things that hop, and things shaped like a funnel or chute.

A horde is a large group of people, animals, or creatures — but the word is far more powerful than just "a large group." It carries a strong sense of being overwhelming, chaotic, noisy, and sometimes threatening.
The line where the earth or sea seems to meet the sky. Figuratively, the limit of a person's knowledge, experience, or interests, as in "travel broadens your horizons."
Hormonal is an adjective that means relating to, caused by, or involving hormones. That's its precise, one-line definition.

A horn is a hard, pointed growth that sticks out from the head of certain animals. Think of a bull, a goat, a rhinoceros, or a buffalo — the rigid, tapering spike or pair of spikes on their heads. That is the original, most fundamental meaning of the word.
A hornet is a large, flying insect — a type of stinging bug that belongs to the same family as wasps. Think of it as a bigger, more powerful cousin of the common wasp.
A situation full of trouble, anger, and conflict, especially one caused by stirring up a sensitive issue, as in "to stir up a hornet's nest."

A horoscope is a prediction or forecast about a person's personality, life, and future, based on the positions of the Sun, Moon, and planets — either at the time of that person's birth, or at a particular moment in time.

Horrendous means extremely and shockingly bad. It doesn't just describe something that is bad — it describes something so bad that it causes a strong feeling of shock, disgust, horror, or distress in the person experiencing or witnessing it.

"Horrible" describes something that is extremely bad, very unpleasant, or deeply shocking — something that causes a strong, immediate negative reaction in you, whether that's fear, disgust, sadness, or simply a sense that something is terribly wrong.
"Horrid" describes something that causes a strong feeling of displeasure, disgust, shock, or fear — something deeply unpleasant in a way that affects you strongly.

When you call something horrific, you are saying it causes horror — an intense feeling of shock, terror, and deep disturbance. It describes something so terrible that it overwhelms a person emotionally, makes their stomach turn, and is very hard to forget.

When someone is horrified, they are experiencing a sudden, intense mix of shock and a powerful negative reaction — either deep fear, strong disgust, or both — caused by something they have seen, heard, witnessed, or learned about that is extremely bad, disturbing, or morally wrong.

To horrify someone means to cause them to feel a sudden and overwhelming sense of horror — a powerful mixture of shock, fear, or disgust. When something horrifies you, it doesn't just make you uncomfortable or slightly upset. It hits you hard and deeply.
Something is horrifying if it causes horror in anyone who sees it, hears it, or learns about it. It describes the thing that creates that reaction — not the person experiencing it.
Horripilation is the formal medical and scientific term for goosebumps — those tiny raised bumps that briefly appear all over your skin, often accompanied by your body hair standing up straight.
Horror is an intense, overwhelming feeling that combines fear, shock, and disgust all at once. It is not just being scared.

An hors d'oeuvre is a small, bite-sized food item served before the main meal begins. Think of it as a little snack or taster that guests eat while waiting for the actual dinner or lunch to be served.
Horse-trading means tough, clever bargaining where both sides push hard for what they want and each side gives something up in order to get something in return.
Horseplay means rough, noisy, and physically wild behavior done in a playful — but not always safe — way.
Hortatory describes language, speech, or writing that is meant to strongly urge, encourage, or push someone toward action or a particular way of behaving.
Horticultural means "relating to or involving horticulture" — where horticulture is the skilled practice of growing plants, especially in gardens, orchards, greenhouses, and nurseries.

Horticulture is the science and art of growing plants — specifically fruits, vegetables, flowers, herbs, and ornamental (decorative) plants — in a careful, skilled, and often managed way, for the benefit of people.
Socks, stockings, and tights, considered together as a category of clothing.

A hospice is a place or a program of care designed specifically for people who are dying — people who have a terminal illness, meaning a serious illness that cannot be cured and will end their life, typically within months.

Hospitable describes someone — or something — that is warm, welcoming, and generous toward guests or strangers. It means making others feel comfortable, at ease, and genuinely cared for, especially when they are visitors in your home, city, or country.

Hospitality is the warm, generous, and welcoming treatment that you give to a guest, a visitor, or even a stranger. It is the quality of making people feel comfortable, valued, and at home — especially when they are in a place that is not their own.
A hostage is a person who is held captive — kept against their will — by someone who uses that person's safety as a tool to force others into doing something.
A hostel is a place where travelers pay to sleep and stay for a short period, usually at a very low price. Think of it as budget accommodation — a much cheaper alternative to a hotel.

A hostelry is a place where travelers can pay to sleep for the night, and usually also eat and drink. Think of it as a building that serves two basic needs of someone on a journey: a bed and a meal. It is an inn or a tavern with rooms.

"Hostile" means showing strong unfriendliness, opposition, or aggression toward someone or something. It is the opposite of welcoming — but much stronger than just "not welcoming." A hostile person, place, or force is not merely cold or indifferent.
Hostilities is the plural form of the noun hostility, which means a strong feeling of unfriendliness, opposition, or ill will toward someone or something.

Hostility means an unfriendly, aggressive, or deeply opposed feeling, attitude, or behavior toward someone or something. It is not just a mild dislike — it carries a sharp edge of antagonism, resistance, or even the desire to harm.

"Hot air" refers to talk that sounds confident and impressive on the surface but has no real value, truth, or substance behind it. It is empty, hollow speech — words that are loud and big but mean nothing in the end.
"Hot on the heels of" means following very closely behind something or someone, or coming very soon after something else.

A "hot potato" is a situation, topic, or problem that is controversial, sensitive, or difficult to deal with — so much so that people try to avoid it or pass it to someone else as quickly as possible.

A hot seat is a position or situation in which a person faces intense pressure, difficult questioning, harsh criticism, or serious scrutiny — usually from others, and usually in front of an audience or group.
An informal phrase for someone or something very impressive, exciting or attractive ("He thinks he's hot stuff").

"Hot under the collar" means to feel angry, irritated, or annoyed about something. When someone is "hot under the collar," they are upset — often because they feel something is unfair, disrespectful, or frustrating.

When you call someone hot-headed, you mean they get angry very quickly, very easily, and without much reason — and when they do get angry, they often act or speak immediately, without stopping to think first.
A place or environment where something, especially something harmful, develops quickly and thrives, as in "a hotbed of crime." Literally, a heated bed of soil for growing plants.
A hothead is a person who gets angry very quickly — almost at the drop of a hat — and who tends to act on that anger without stopping to think first.
A hothouse is a heated glass building used for growing plants.
When people do something hotly, they do it with deep feeling — usually strong disagreement, fierce competition, or heated emotion. There is nothing lukewarm or calm about it.

A hound is, first and foremost, a type of dog bred and trained for hunting. Not every dog is a hound — a hound is a specific kind of dog that helps humans chase and track animals like foxes, rabbits, deer, or wild boar.

To hound someone means to pursue them persistently and relentlessly — to keep going after them, again and again, without giving them rest or peace. It is not a single action. It is a continuous, repeated pressure that doesn't stop.
When someone is described as hounded, it means they are being relentlessly and persistently chased, pressured, or harassed — to the point where they feel they cannot escape.
The "hour of reckoning" refers to the critical moment when a person, group, or organization is finally forced to face the consequences of their past actions, decisions, or behavior.

When you use "house" as a verb, it means to provide a place for someone or something to stay, live, or be kept. Think of it as the action of giving something a home — whether that's a person, an animal, or even an object.
House arrest is a legal punishment or restriction in which a person is ordered — by a court or a government authority — to stay inside their home instead of going to prison.
A plan, system, or organization that looks impressive but is so fragile that one small problem could bring the whole thing crashing down.
A household name is a person, brand, company, or product that is so widely and commonly known that almost anyone — from any background, age group, or walk of life — has heard of it.
A hovel is a home that is so small, dirty, and falling apart that it is barely fit for a human being to live in.

To hover means to stay in one place — suspended, without landing, without leaving, and without moving much. The thing that is hovering is present but not settled. It is there, but it has not fully committed to being there.
A howl is a long, loud, raw cry or sound — one that rises up powerfully and lingers in the air. It is not a quick yelp or a sharp scream. It is drawn out, full-throated, and impossible to ignore.

To howl means to make a long, loud, continuous cry or sound that rises and falls in pitch — a raw, uncontrolled sound that seems to come from a place of deep feeling or wild force. The key word here is long. A howl is never a quick, sharp sound.

A hoyden is a girl or young woman who is loud, boisterous, rough, and wildly energetic — someone who behaves in a bold, carefree, unruly way that was traditionally considered unbecoming or improper for a girl.
A hub means the central point of something, from which everything else spreads out or connects.

"Hubba hubba" is an exclamation — a short burst of words you say out loud to express a feeling, like "Wow!" or "Oh yeah!" Specifically, it is used to express approval, excitement, or enthusiasm, usually about how attractive or impressive someone looks.
A hubbub is a loud, confused mixture of sounds and activity created by a crowd of people or things all at once.

Hubris means dangerous, excessive pride — the kind of arrogance that makes a person feel they are above limits, above consequences, or above everyone else around them. It is not just being proud or confident.
A huckster is a person who tries to sell you something — a product, a service, or even an idea — using dishonest, exaggerated, or manipulative methods.
To crowd closely together, usually for warmth, safety, or privacy. It can also mean to curl your body up tightly, or to get together for a private discussion.
