Something is irreplaceable when there is nothing else in the world that can take its place and serve the same role, hold the same value, or fill the same gap. If it is lost, damaged, or gone, it cannot be substituted or recovered — not fully, not truly.
Something or someone irrepressible is so powerful, lively, or strong that it simply cannot be held back, stopped, or suppressed — no matter how much force or effort is applied.
Irreproachable means so good, so correct, and so proper in behavior or character that absolutely no one can criticize it, blame it, or find any fault with it whatsoever.
Something is irresistible when it is so powerful, so attractive, or so overwhelming that you simply cannot say no to it — no matter how much you try.
Irresolute describes a person who is unable to make up their mind or commit firmly to a decision or course of action.
Irresolution means the state of being unable to make up your mind, commit to a decision, or settle on a clear course of action.
"Irrespective of" something means without taking it into account, as in "open to everyone, irrespective of age."
Irresponsible means not caring enough about the consequences of your actions, or not doing the duties that are expected of you.

Something irretrievable is something that is gone, lost, or broken in a way that is completely and permanently beyond recovery. There is no fixing it, no undoing it, no getting it back — not now, not ever, no matter what you do or how hard you try.

Irreverence is the attitude or behavior of treating something — or someone — that is widely considered important, sacred, or serious as though it is not deserving of that respect. It is the opposite of reverence.
Irreverent means showing a lack of respect toward something — but not just anything. This is a crucial detail.
When something is irreversible, it cannot be undone, taken back, or returned to the way it was before. The change is final and permanent — there is no going back, ever.
Irrevocable means permanently final — impossible to undo, cancel, reverse, or take back.

When something happens irrevocably, it creates a permanent change. The world before that moment and the world after it are different — and no action in the future can close that gap or restore what existed before.
To irrigate something means to deliberately supply water to it through a controlled system, rather than relying on rain or natural water sources.

Irrigation is the process of deliberately supplying water to an area — most commonly farmland or soil — through human-made systems, so that plants can grow even when natural rainfall is not enough or not reliable.

Irritability is the quality or state of being easily annoyed, frustrated, or angered — often by things that most people would not find particularly upsetting. Think of it as a low tolerance for anything bothersome.
If someone is irritable, it means they are easily annoyed or upset, often over small or minor things.
An irritant is anything — a substance, a person, a situation, or an event — that causes discomfort, annoyance, or a mild harmful reaction.

When you irritate someone emotionally, you cause them a nagging, uncomfortable feeling — not deep anger, but a steady, building impatience. The person doesn't explode; they quietly feel bothered or frustrated.
When someone is irritated, they are feeling a mild form of anger or annoyance. Something is bothering them — getting on their nerves, making them feel impatient, unsettled, or slightly upset.
Irritation means a state of being bothered, disturbed, or made uncomfortable — either in your mind (emotionally) or in your body (physically).
To irrupt means to break or burst INTO something suddenly, forcefully, and often in large numbers.
Irruption is the act of something suddenly and forcefully breaking into or bursting into a place — an abrupt, powerful entry from the outside, into somewhere it wasn't before.
An island is a piece of land that is completely surrounded by water on all sides.

An isle is a piece of land that is completely surrounded by water on all sides. In other words, it is an island. If you stand on an isle and look in any direction, you will see water all around you — no connection to any larger landmass.
An islet is a very small island — so small that it barely qualifies as land worth naming or living on. Think of it as a tiny patch of land poking out of the water, surrounded on all sides.
To isolate something or someone means to separate it completely from everything around it, so that it stands alone — with no connection, contact, or interaction with its surroundings.
Isolated means separated from everything else — cut off, alone, or apart.
Isolation means the state of being separated from everything else — people, places, groups, or things — with little or no connection to them.

Isolationism is a country's deliberate policy of staying out of the affairs of other countries — their wars, their conflicts, their alliances, and their political disagreements — and instead focusing almost entirely on what is happening within its own borders.

An isolationist is a person who believes that their country should stay out of the business of other countries — their wars, their politics, their conflicts — and instead focus all of its energy inward, on its own people and its own problems.
An isotope is one of two or more forms of the same chemical element, where each form has the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons in its nucleus.
Issuance means the act of officially putting something out into the world — releasing it, distributing it, or making it formally available to people.

An important topic or problem for discussion, as in "environmental issues." It can also mean a particular edition of a magazine or newspaper, the act of officially giving something out, or, in law, a person's children.
When something is issued, it is formally and officially sent out, given out, or put out — usually by a person or organization that has the authority to do so.
An isthmus is a narrow strip of land that connects two larger landmasses, with water running along both of its sides.

"It goes without saying" means that something is so obvious, so well-known, or so universally understood that there is no real need to say it out loud — yet you are saying it anyway, usually to stress its importance or to be clear.
A way of saying something amuses or delights you, as in "it tickles me that he still wears that hat."
A humorous admission that you have been caught doing something wrong and deserve it (British).
To italicize something means to write, type, or print a word (or a group of words) in a special slanted style, where the letters lean to the right instead of standing straight up.
An itch is an uncomfortable, irritating sensation that you feel on the surface of your skin. It is not pain — but it is distinctly unpleasant in its own way.

To itch means to experience — or to produce — an uncomfortable, irritating sensation on the skin that makes you feel a powerful urge to scratch that spot. The key feeling here is that it is hard to resist. When something itches, you almost have to scratch it.
When someone is itching to do something, it means they have a very strong, restless desire to do it — and they want to do it right now, or as soon as possible.
Item means a single, individual thing that belongs to a group, list, or collection.
To itemize something means to list every individual part of it separately, one by one, with specific details about each part.
To iterate means to repeat a process — usually multiple times — often with the goal of improving or refining something with each repetition.
Iteration means the act of repeating a process, or one single cycle within a repeated process.

Iterative describes something that works by repeating a process — but not in a mindless, going-in-circles kind of way. Each time you repeat the process, you use what you learned from the last round to improve the result.
Itinerancy means the practice or condition of regularly traveling from place to place, especially as a way of doing one's work or fulfilling a role, rather than being based in one permanent location.

Itinerant describes a person — or a lifestyle — that involves regularly traveling from place to place, especially as a central part of how someone works or lives, rather than being based in one fixed location.
An itinerary is a detailed, written plan for a trip or journey. It tells you — in order — where you're going, what you'll do, and when you'll do it.

Ivory is a hard, smooth, creamy-white natural material that comes from the tusks or teeth of certain animals. Think of it as a biological substance — somewhat like bone, but denser, heavier, and far more beautiful in appearance.

When someone lives in an ivory tower, it means they are cut off from the real world — living inside a comfortable bubble of ideas, privilege, or theory, while being completely out of touch with how ordinary people actually live and with the practical problems of everyday life.
Ivy is a plant. More specifically, it is a type of climbing or creeping plant — meaning it doesn't just stand upright like a tree or a flower. Instead, it travels.

To jab means to push or poke something into — or at — a person or object with a quick, sharp, sudden thrust. The motion is fast and forceful, not slow or gentle. Think of it as a short, snappy stabbing action.

Jabber means fast, excited, and unclear talk that is difficult to understand. It is not just talking — it is talking in a way that comes out so quickly, so mixed up, or so confusingly that the listener struggles to follow it or make sense of it.

To jabber means to talk very fast, in a way that is hard to understand or follow. When someone jabbers, they speak quickly and continuously — pouring out words in a rush — and the result is speech that sounds unclear, confused, or difficult to make sense of.

Jabberwocky means language, speech, or writing that sounds meaningful and important but is actually nonsense — words and sentences that give the impression of saying something without actually saying anything real.
A jabot is a decorative piece of fabric — typically made of lace, silk, or fine cloth — that hangs down the front center of a person's chest, attached near the neckline or collar.
A jack of all trades is someone with a wide range of skills and knowledge across many different areas, but without deep expertise or mastery in any particular one.
To raise something sharply, especially prices, as in "they jacked up the rent." Literally, to lift a heavy object, such as a car, with a jack.

A jackalope is a fictional creature from American folklore — specifically, an imaginary animal that looks like a large rabbit but has the antlers of a deer or an antelope growing out of its head. It does not exist in real life.

A jackanapes is a person — most often a young man or boy — who combines two irritating qualities at once: impertinence (being rude and cheeky, especially toward someone older or of higher standing) and conceit (having an inflated, unwarranted opinion of oneself).
A jackboot is a specific type of tall, heavy, hard-leather military boot that rises up to the knee — or sometimes even above it. It is thick, stiff, and rigid, built for soldiers.
Very muscular, with large, well-defined muscles (informal). It can also mean very excited or energetic, or, in slang, stolen.
Jactitation means making a false, loud, public claim about something — essentially bragging about something that isn't true, or publicly asserting a right or status that you don't actually have.

A jacuzzi is a large bathtub or small pool that has powerful water jets built into its walls (and sometimes its floor). These jets shoot out warm water and air in strong, swirling streams that bubble and churn around your body.
Jade is a hard, smooth, semi-precious stone that is highly valued for its beauty and has been treasured by humans for thousands of years.
Jaded describes a person who has experienced something so much, or for so long, that they have completely lost their excitement, wonder, or ability to enjoy it.

Jagged describes something that has a rough, uneven edge or surface covered with sharp, irregular points or notches — points that are unpredictable, like they could cut or hurt you. The key ideas packed into this one word are: sharp + uneven + irregular.
A jalopy is an old car that is in very bad condition — one that is worn out, falling apart, unreliable, and looks like it could break down at any moment.
Jam is a thick, sweet food made by cooking crushed or chopped fruit with sugar until the mixture becomes soft, sticky, and spreadable. You put it on bread, toast, or biscuits.
A jamb is either of the two vertical side pieces that form the frame of a door, window, or fireplace opening.
A jamboree is a large, lively, and festive gathering of people that is full of energy, excitement, and fun.
Janet's Law was created in memory of Janet Zilinski, an 11-year-old girl from Warren Township, New Jersey, who tragically died during cheerleading practice in 2006.

To jangle means to make a harsh, clashing, metallic sound — the kind produced when multiple hard or metallic objects strike against each other repeatedly or all at once. It is not a clean, clear, pleasant sound.
"Janus-faced" is an adjective that describes something — or someone — that has two contrasting, opposing faces or sides that coexist at the same time.

A jape is a joke or jest — but not just any joke. It's a joke that has a playful, mocking, or teasing edge to it. Think of it as a witty, sometimes cheeky remark or action made at someone's expense, though usually without serious malice behind it.
To have an unpleasant or disturbing effect, especially by clashing with something, as in "the bright colours jarred with the calm room." It can also mean to jolt or shake something painfully.
Jargon is the specialized vocabulary that belongs to a particular group of people — such as a profession, hobby, industry, or community.
Something is jarring when it creates a sudden, sharp feeling that something is wrong, out of place, or deeply uncomfortable. It's not a slow or mild discomfort — it hits you immediately, like a jolt.

To jaunce means to prance — to move with a lively, bouncing, high-stepping energy. Think of the way a spirited horse lifts its legs with flair and bounces forward, or the way a person might strut about with a spring in their step.
Jaundice is a medical condition in which a person's skin, the whites of their eyes, and the inner lining of their mouth turn noticeably yellow.
Bitter, cynical, and distrustful, especially as a result of bad experience, as in "a jaundiced view of politics." Literally, having jaundice, which makes the skin yellow.

A jaunt is a short trip or outing taken purely for pleasure. Not a long, tiring journey — just a brief, cheerful excursion that you do because you want to enjoy yourself, not because you have to go somewhere.
Jauntiness is the quality of being lively, cheerful, and casually self-confident — all at the same time.
Jaunty means having a lively, cheerful, and breezy self-confidence that is clearly visible from the outside — in the way someone moves, carries themselves, or presents themselves to the world.
A javelin is a long, thin, pointed spear-like stick — lightweight enough to be thrown through the air by hand over a long distance.
To jaywalk means to cross a road in a way that breaks traffic rules — either by crossing in the wrong place, or crossing at the wrong time.
Jazz has one rich, central meaning — a genre of music — and a few informal meanings that grew out of it over time.
"Jazz up" means to make something more exciting, lively, attractive, or interesting — especially something that was previously plain, dull, or boring.
"Je ne sais quoi" describes a quality that is real, positive, and powerfully felt — but utterly impossible to name or explain.

A jeer is a rude, mocking remark or sound that people direct at someone to show contempt, disapproval, or ridicule. It is a way of publicly laughing at someone — not with them — in a harsh, dismissive, or belittling way.
To jeer means to shout or call out at someone in a mocking, scornful, and disrespectful way — usually loudly, and usually in front of others.
Jejune means empty of substance. Think of it as the opposite of rich, deep, or nourishing — whether we're talking about ideas, writing, or a person's thinking.
To jeopardize something means to put it in danger of being lost, damaged, ruined, or taken away — especially something valuable or important that was previously safe or secure.
Jeopardy means serious danger — specifically, the danger that something important might be lost, destroyed, harmed, or go badly wrong.

A jeremiad is a long, gloomy, deeply serious complaint — usually about how bad society is, how far people have fallen from good values, or how the world is headed in the wrong direction. It is not a quick grumble.
A sudden, sharp pull or movement; also an informal insult for a rude, selfish or unpleasant person.
A jerkin is a type of short, close-fitting jacket — typically sleeveless or with very short sleeves — that was a common item of clothing in Europe, especially during the 1500s and 1600s.
Jerky is meat that has been preserved by removing almost all its moisture, leaving behind tough, chewy, intensely flavored strips that can be stored for a long time without refrigerating.

Jerry-built means cheaply and hastily constructed using poor materials and careless workmanship, in a way that looks functional on the surface but is actually flimsy, unreliable, and unlikely to last.

A jersey is a soft, stretchy, knitted fabric. Unlike woven fabrics (where threads cross over and under each other in a rigid grid), jersey is made by looping threads together in a way that creates a natural stretch and bounce-back quality.
A jest is something you say or do that is meant to be funny or playful — not serious. In its simplest form, it is a joke or a witty remark.
To jest means to say something in a playful, humorous, or light-hearted way — not seriously. When you jest, you are joking around, being witty, or making a funny remark on purpose.

A jester is a person whose job is to entertain others by being funny — through jokes, silly behavior, clowning around, comic performances, and witty remarks. Think of a jester as a professional funny person.
Using clever but misleading or overly subtle arguments to justify something. Literally, relating to the Jesuits, a Catholic religious order.
Jetsam is a noun from the world of maritime (sea-related) law and seafaring.

To jettison something means to deliberately throw it away or get rid of it — especially when holding onto it is becoming a burden, a danger, or a problem. The act is always intentional, often feels necessary, and is usually permanent.

A jeu d'esprit is a short, clever, witty piece of writing — or sometimes speech — that is playful and light-hearted, and whose whole point is to show off the writer's sharpness of mind and sense of humour.

To jib at something means to refuse to do it, or to show strong reluctance and resistance toward it — especially because you find it unpleasant, unfair, too costly, morally wrong, or simply too much to accept.
Jibber-jabber means rapid, meaningless, or hard-to-understand talk — a lot of words that add up to very little, if anything at all.
A mocking or insulting remark, as in "a cheap jibe at his expense." In sailing, a jibe is a turn that swings the sail across from one side to the other.

When two things jibe, it means they are consistent with each other — they line up, they match, they don't contradict one another. When things don't jibe, it means there is a mismatch or a conflict between them.
"To jibe with" means to agree with, match, or be consistent with something. When two things "jibe with" each other, they fit together smoothly — they don't contradict each other. They are in harmony.
Jiggery-pokery means dishonest, sneaky, or underhand tricks and scheming — the kind of clever but deceptive behavior someone uses to manipulate a situation or fool others, often for personal gain.
To jilt someone means to suddenly and cruelly end a romantic relationship with them — especially after making them believe the relationship was serious, promising, or heading toward commitment.
To jimmy something means to force it open using a prying tool, usually by wedging the tool into a small gap and using leverage to break or push past the lock or latch.
To jingle means to make — or to cause to make — a light, gentle, high-pitched, repeating sound, like small metal objects repeatedly hitting against each other.

Jingoism means an extreme, aggressive form of nationalism — a blind, passionate belief that your own country is superior to all others, combined with a strong desire to show that superiority through military force, threats, or an openly hostile attitude toward other nations.

A jingoist is a person who believes their own country is the greatest in the world — and, crucially, is ready and eager to use military force, aggression, or threats against other countries to prove it or protect it.

Jingoistic describes a person, attitude, speech, policy, or piece of writing that combines extreme pride in one's country with an aggressive desire for that country to dominate or threaten others, especially through military power.
A jinx is a person, object, or invisible force that is believed to bring bad luck — not just once, but repeatedly, in a way that feels like more than coincidence.
To jinx something or someone means to bring bad luck to it, or to cause something to go wrong, usually without meaning to.
Jitters means a feeling of nervousness, anxiety, or unease — the kind you feel right before something important, challenging, or unfamiliar happens.

Jittery means feeling nervous, anxious, and restless — often in a way that shows up physically in your body. When you are jittery, your mind feels uneasy and on edge, and your body seems to reflect that unease too.
When two things jive, they match, fit together, or make sense together. When they don't jive, they contradict or conflict with each other.

Jobbery means the corrupt practice of using a position of public trust or official power to secretly serve private interests — your own, or those of your friends, allies, or financial backers — instead of serving the public good you were supposed to serve.
To compete cleverly and persistently for an advantage, as in "jockeying for position." It can also mean to skilfully manoeuvre something into a tight space.
To jockey for position means to try to get yourself into the most favorable or advantageous spot — compared to others who are trying to do the exact same thing at the same time.

Jocose means playfully humorous and fond of joking. When you call someone or something jocose, you are saying that humor and lighthearted wit come naturally and habitually to them — it is not just a single joke, but a characteristic way of being.
Playful, joking humour, or a fondness for making witty remarks. A jocosity can also be a single joke or playful remark.
Jocular means playfully humorous — it describes a person who loves to joke around, or a tone/manner of speaking that is light-hearted, witty, and full of good-natured fun.

Jocularity is the quality of being playful, lighthearted, and fond of joking around. It describes a cheerful, fun-loving manner — the kind of easy warmth a person radiates when they're in the mood to laugh, tease gently, and keep things breezy and fun.

Jocund means cheerful, lively, and light-hearted — in a way that feels airy, bright, and full of easy joy. It describes the kind of happiness that isn't just felt quietly on the inside, but that seems to radiate outward.
Jocundity is the quality or state of being cheerful, merry, and full of light-hearted happiness.
Jodhpurs are a special type of full-length trousers designed primarily for horse riding.
To jog someone's memory means to help a person remember something they have forgotten or cannot recall at that moment.

Joie de vivre means a deep, radiant joy of being alive. It is the feeling of being genuinely thrilled to exist — a bubbling, enthusiastic delight in life itself, not just in one moment or one good thing, but in the very act of living.
"Join forces" means to come together with someone else to work toward a shared goal.
A joist is a long, horizontal beam that forms part of the hidden skeleton of a building — the structural framework inside floors and ceilings that you never see but always rely on.
Jollity is the noun that describes a lively, cheerful, festive happiness — the kind that is loud, expressive, and shared with other people. It is not quiet, private contentment.

A jolt is something sudden, sharp, and forceful that hits you — physically, emotionally, or as a strong dose of something. Think of it as a quick, powerful "punch" of an experience. It is never gradual. It never builds up slowly.
To move or shake something suddenly and roughly, as in "the train jolted to a stop." It can also mean to shock someone suddenly into action or awareness.

To jostle means to push, bump into, or knock against someone — usually repeatedly — in a rough or careless way. It almost always happens when people are in a tight space and are either competing for room or simply caught in a crowd.
A jot means the smallest possible amount of something — so tiny that it's almost nothing at all. Think of it as the absolute minimum unit of something, so small it barely exists.
"Jot down" means to write something quickly, briefly, and informally — usually so you don't forget it.
A jounce is a sudden, sharp, bouncing jolt — the kind that physically shakes or bumps you around in a rough, jarring way.
To jounce means to move up and down in a rough, jolting, bouncy way — or to cause something or someone to move in that way.
A notebook in which a person regularly writes down their thoughts and experiences. It is also a serious magazine on a particular subject, especially an academic one, or a newspaper.
Journalese is a word used to describe a bad style of writing that is typical of low-quality or lazy newspaper and news reporting.
A journey is the act of traveling from one place to another. But it is not just any movement — it usually involves a meaningful distance, a noticeable amount of time, or a significant experience.

A journeyman is someone who has fully learned a skill or trade, is competent and experienced enough to get paid work, but has not yet reached the top level of their field. They are past being a beginner, but not quite a master or a star.

A joust is a one-on-one combat contest between two knights on horseback, where each rider charges toward the other at full speed and tries to knock the opponent off their horse using a long pole called a lance.
To joust means to fight against someone on horseback using a long pole called a lance, in a competitive contest.
Jovial describes a person who is cheerful, warm, and full of hearty good humor — someone who radiates friendliness and makes the people around them feel good simply by being there.
Joviality is the quality or state of being warm, cheerful, friendly, and full of good humor — expressed openly and in a way that makes the people around you feel good too.
Relating to the planet Jupiter, as in "the Jovian moons." In mythology, relating to the Roman god Jupiter, or showing his majestic power.

A jowl is the soft, fleshy part of your lower cheek and jaw area — the thick, meaty part of your face near the sides of your chin. Think of it as the lower, outer region of your face where your cheek meets your jaw.
Jowly is an adjective used to describe a face — or a person — that has heavy, fleshy, and drooping skin around the lower cheeks and jaw area.
Joyless means completely without joy — empty of happiness, warmth, delight, or pleasure.
Jubilant means feeling or showing great joy and happiness because of a success, victory, or very good news.

When someone does something jubilantly, they do it with a feeling of intense, overflowing joy — the kind of happiness that bursts out of you when something wonderful happens, especially after a victory, success, or long-awaited good news.

Jubilation is a feeling of tremendous, overflowing happiness and triumph — the kind you feel when something absolutely wonderful happens, especially after a long wait, hard work, or a tough challenge. It is not quiet or private happiness.
A jubilee is a time of special, joyful celebration — one that marks a significant anniversary, a moment of freedom, or a period of deep renewal. It is never an ordinary occasion.
To judder means to shake or vibrate rapidly and with force, in a way that feels uneven, jerky, and hard to control.
To judge means to carefully look at something, think about it, and then reach a conclusion or opinion about it.
The ability to make good, wise decisions, as in "trust your judgement." It can also mean an opinion, or an official decision made by a judge or court.

A judgment call is a decision you have to make using your own personal assessment, experience, and reasoning — because no clear rule, formula, or guaranteed right answer exists to make the decision for you.

When we describe a person as judgemental, we mean they have a habit of forming strong, critical opinions about other people — their choices, their behaviour, their lifestyle, or their character — quickly, harshly, and usually without a full or fair understanding of that person's situation.
The word judicial simply means relating to courts of law, judges, or the legal process of deciding justice.

Judicial review is the power of a court — usually the highest court in a country — to examine a law, a government action, or an official decision and ask one fundamental question: Does this comply with the constitution?
The judiciary is the entire system of courts and judges in a country (or state) that is responsible for interpreting laws, settling disputes, and delivering justice.

Judicious means having and showing good judgment — making decisions that are wise, careful, and well thought out, especially in situations where you need to choose the right amount, the right approach, or the right moment.

When you do something judiciously, you do it with careful, wise, and well-reasoned judgment. It means you thought it through properly — you considered the situation, weighed your options, and made a smart, sensible choice — not a rushed or reckless one.
Common liquids kept in a jug: water, juice, milk, lemonade, wine, beer, syrup, or cream.

A juggernaut is something — a force, a machine, an organization, a movement — that is so enormously powerful and unstoppable that it crushes or overwhelms everything in its path, almost as if nothing can slow it down or get in its way.
To juggle means to keep several things going at the same time — and to do so with constant, careful attention so nothing gets dropped or ignored.
Trickery, deception, or manipulation, especially of facts or figures, as in "statistical jugglery." Literally, the art of juggling.

The adjective jugular means of, relating to, or located in the neck or throat. When you use it to describe something, you are pointing to that thing as belonging to — or being connected with — the neck region of the body.
The jugular is a large, important vein located in your neck. More completely, it is called the jugular vein, and you actually have more than one — a pair on each side of your neck (left and right).
Full of juice, as in "a juicy peach." Informally, of news or gossip, interesting and often scandalous, as in "juicy details." It can also mean attractive and rewarding, as in "a juicy contract."
A jukebox is a machine that plays music automatically when you put money into it and select the song you want to hear.
A julienne is a set of thin, uniform, matchstick-shaped strips cut from a food item — most often a vegetable, but sometimes meat, cheese, or fruit.

To jumble something means to mix it up in a confused, disordered, and random way — so that the result is a messy, chaotic mixture where nothing is in its right place and nothing is easy to make sense of.

A jumble sale is an event where people sell their old, unwanted, second-hand belongings at very cheap prices, usually to raise money for a good cause like a charity, a school, or a local community group.

To "jump down someone's throat" means to suddenly and harshly criticize or scold someone, often in an angry, aggressive, and over-the-top way — and usually before they have even finished speaking or had a chance to explain themselves.
To "jump on the bandwagon" means to start supporting or doing something simply because it has become popular, not because you truly believe in it or thought it through carefully.
To suddenly leave a job, organization, or cause, especially to join a rival, as in "she jumped ship to a competitor." Originally, for a sailor to desert their ship.

To jump the gun means to start something too early, before the right time, or before you have enough information to act wisely. It describes the act of rushing into something prematurely — often with the result that things go wrong or have to be redone.
To "jump through hoops" means to go through many difficult, complicated, annoying, or unnecessary steps in order to get something done or to satisfy someone's demands.

To jump-start something means to give it a quick, powerful push to get it going — especially when it is stuck, slow, or not working at all. Think of it as forcing something to wake up and move when it otherwise wouldn't.

"Jumped-up" describes a person who has recently risen to a higher position or status — in terms of wealth, power, or rank — and, as a result, behaves with an arrogance or self-importance that others feel is completely undeserved.

When a person (or animal) is described as jumpy, it means they are in a state of nervous anxiety so strong that even small, unexpected things — a sudden loud noise, someone tapping them on the shoulder, a door slamming — cause them to react with a startled, physical jolt.
A juncture is essentially a significant point — either a point in time or a point in space where things come together.
A junket is a trip — often to a nice place — where the person traveling does not pay for it themselves. Someone else foots the bill: a government, a company, a lobbyist, or some other organization.
A junta is a small group of military officers who seize control of a country's government by force and then rule that country together. It is not a government that was voted in by the people.
Juridical means of or relating to law, legal proceedings, or the administration of justice. When something is described as "juridical," it belongs to — or is recognized by — the formal legal system.

Jurisdiction means the official power or authority that a person, court, or government body has to make decisions, create rules, and enforce laws — and the defined boundaries within which that power applies.
Relating to the official power of a court or authority to make legal decisions, and the limits of that power, as in "a jurisdictional dispute."
Jurisprudence is a noun that means the philosophical and theoretical study of law. Not the practice of law — but deep, careful thinking about law.

A jurist is a person who possesses deep, expert knowledge of the law. Think of it as the highest tier of legal expertise — not just someone who practices law, but someone who masters it at a scholarly or authoritative level.
A member of a jury, the group of ordinary citizens who hear the evidence in a court case and decide whether someone is guilty or not guilty.
A final decision, conclusion, or judgment has not yet been reached. The matter is still uncertain, and people are still debating or waiting for more information.

Jury-rigged describes something that has been quickly put together or repaired using whatever materials happen to be available at the time, because the proper parts, tools, or resources aren't on hand.
"Just deserts" means getting exactly what you deserve — usually a punishment that fits a wrongdoing.
When you say something is "just what the doctor ordered," you mean it is exactly what was needed — perfectly suited to solve a problem, satisfy a need, or improve a situation.
Justice means giving people what they rightfully deserve — no more, no less.
Justifiable describes something — an action, decision, feeling, or belief — that can be proven to be right, reasonable, or acceptable using valid, logical reasons.

A justification is a reason — or a set of reasons — given to show that something is right, fair, acceptable, or necessary. It is the act of defending something, and the word refers to the defense itself.
To justify something means to show that it is right, reasonable, or acceptable — usually by giving reasons or evidence.

When something juts, it sticks out sharply and noticeably from a surface or a line, extending into the space around it. Think of it as something "pushing itself forward" or "poking outward" in a way that is sudden, definite, and easy to notice.
"Jut out" means to stick out or extend beyond a surface or edge — further than the things around it.
The word juvenile essentially means "of, relating to, or suited to young people" — specifically children and teenagers. Think of it as a more formal, precise way of saying "young" or "youth-related."
A juvenile is simply a young person or young animal that has not yet fully grown up or reached adulthood.
Illegal or antisocial behaviour by young people who are not yet legally adults.

Juvenilia refers to the early creative works that a writer, artist, or composer produced during their youth — before they had fully grown into their mature style or reached the peak of their abilities.

To juxtapose two things means to place them side by side — in the real world, in a piece of writing, in a photograph, or even in an argument — so that the contrast or comparison between them becomes clearer and more powerful than it would be if you looked at each thing separately.

When two things are juxtaposed, they are placed side by side — physically, visually, or mentally — so that their differences (or sometimes their similarities) become more vivid and striking than they would be on their own.
Juxtaposition is the placement of two things side by side so that their differences (or similarities) become more striking and clear than they would be if the two things were seen separately.
Describing a nightmarishly complex, absurd, and oppressive situation, especially involving bureaucracy, that is impossible to escape or make sense of — like those in the stories of Franz Kafka.
Kairos means the right moment — not just any moment in time, but the perfect, critical, fleeting window when conditions align and the time to act, speak, or decide is exactly now.
A kaleidoscope is a tube-shaped toy or instrument that you hold up to one eye and look through. The other end of the tube is usually capped with a transparent or semi-transparent cover.

When something is visually kaleidoscopic, it looks like a kaleidoscope — it is full of many bright colors, intricate shifting patterns, and a dazzling, almost overwhelming variety of visual elements all at once.
In a way that is constantly shifting, richly varied, and dazzlingly complex — just like the patterns inside a kaleidoscope.
A kameez is a long shirt or tunic that is a core piece of traditional clothing in South Asia — worn widely across India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan, among other countries.

A kamikaze is a person who deliberately sacrifices their own life in order to destroy a target — most often by using themselves, their body, or their vehicle as the weapon. The death is not accidental. It is fully intentional and chosen.

When something is kaput, it means it is completely broken, finished, or no longer working — and usually in a way that feels total and final. It doesn't describe something that's a little damaged or slightly off.

Karma is the principle that every intentional action has a consequence — and that consequence will eventually return to the person who performed that action. Think of it as a moral law of cause and effect.
A katydid is a type of insect — a living creature with six legs, a hard outer covering, and wings.
Katzenjammer captures a specific kind of misery — the wretched, foggy, disorienting suffering that follows a night of heavy drinking.

A kayak is a small, narrow boat built for one or two people. The person sitting inside it uses a double-bladed paddle — a paddle with a flat blade on each end — to push the boat through water, alternating strokes from side to side.

To kedge is to move a boat or ship by using a special trick involving a small anchor. Instead of using wind, sails, or an engine to push the vessel forward, the crew pulls it forward using an anchor they have dropped ahead of the vessel.
Kedgeree is a warm, cooked dish made primarily from rice and fish. Think of it as a soft, lightly spiced, all-in-one rice dish that brings together several ingredients into a single, satisfying meal.
Just as your spine is the central support your entire body is built around, the keel is the foundational structure that the entire frame of a ship is built upon.
"Keel over" is a phrasal verb that means to fall down suddenly — usually because of fainting, illness, exhaustion, or death. The defining quality of this phrase is suddenness.
To keelhaul someone means to punish or reprimand them severely — to drag them through a painful, humiliating ordeal, either literally or figuratively.
Eager and enthusiastic, as in "keen to learn." It can also mean sharp, as in "a keen blade," highly developed, as in "keen eyesight," or intense, as in "keen competition."

A keen is a loud, mournful cry or wail made in grief — specifically, a cry of sorrow performed over someone who has just died. It is not ordinary crying. It is a deep, raw, almost musical outpouring of grief that comes from a place of intense loss.
To keen means to wail loudly and bitterly in grief — to cry out in a raw, piercing, unrestrained way because of deep sorrow, especially over someone who has just died.
A sharp, highly developed understanding or perception of something, as in "a keen awareness of the risks."

Keening is a loud, raw, sustained wail of grief — a kind of crying that is far more intense and piercing than ordinary tears. It is specifically the sound a person makes when they are overwhelmed by sorrow, most often when someone they love has died.

Keenly is simply the adverb form of keen. It means doing something, feeling something, or being aware of something with great intensity, sharpness, and full force — nothing held back, nothing mild or halfway.
"Keep abreast of" means to stay up-to-date with something — to continuously follow new information, changes, or developments about a topic so that you are never behind or left out.

To keep something or someone at bay means to prevent them from coming closer, causing harm, or overwhelming you. You are holding a threat, danger, or unwanted thing at a safe distance — not letting it take over or get to you.
Keep one's ear to the ground
To "keep one's ear to the ground" means to stay alert and informed about what is happening around you — especially about the latest news, rumors, trends, or changes in a situation.
To keep tabs on someone or something means to watch, monitor, or track them carefully and continuously over a period of time.
Keep the wolf from the door

To "keep the wolf from the door" means to earn or have just enough money, food, or resources to survive — to prevent serious hardship, hunger, or poverty from affecting you. It does not mean comfort or prosperity. It means bare survival.

To "keep up appearances" means to behave in public as if everything in your life is perfectly fine, normal, or good — even when, in reality, things are going wrong, falling apart, or are not what they seem.
When something is in someone's keeping, it has been entrusted to them. They are responsible for protecting it, managing it, or looking after it.

A keepsake is a physical object that you hold onto — not because it is valuable or useful — but because it reminds you of someone you love, a place that mattered to you, or a meaningful moment in your life. Its value is entirely emotional, not monetary.
A state of dreamy, pleasant relaxation, as in "an afternoon of kef." It is also a powdered form of cannabis smoked in North Africa that brings on this state.
A person's buttocks or backside (informal, humorous American slang). In older slang, a keister was a suitcase or safe.
Kelp is a type of large, brown seaweed — more precisely, a giant marine alga — that grows in the ocean.
A kelpie is a supernatural creature that comes from the traditional folklore of Scotland. Think of it as a monster hiding in the water.

Kempt means neat, tidy, and well-groomed in appearance. When someone or something is described as kempt, it means they look properly maintained and carefully put together — nothing is messy, disheveled, or out of place.
Ken means the range or scope of what a person can know, understand, or perceive — essentially, how far your mind can reach.

A kennel is a shelter made specifically for a dog. Think of it as a dog's own personal house — a small, enclosed structure where a dog sleeps, rests, and stays safe from rain, cold, or harsh sun. It is almost always placed outdoors, in a yard or garden.
A kenning is a creative, compound descriptive phrase that substitutes for a simple, ordinary word — most commonly a noun.
A kepi is a type of military cap — a hat worn by soldiers. That is its single, essential identity: it is a soldier's hat with a very specific and recognizable shape.

Keratin is a protein. More specifically, it is a structural protein, meaning its entire purpose is to provide strength, toughness, and physical protection — not to carry messages through the body or speed up chemical reactions, like other proteins do.
"Keratinous" is an adjective that describes something made of, consisting of, or relating to a substance called keratin.

A kerchief is a piece of cloth — usually square or rectangular — that a person wears on their head or around their neck. Think of it as a simple fabric covering, not a hat or a full scarf, but something in between: light, flat, and flexible.
A kerf is the slot or groove that a cutting tool leaves behind in a material after making a cut.
A kerfuffle is a situation where there is a lot of noise, confusion, arguing, or fuss — but usually over something that is not very serious or important.
A kernel is always the innermost, most essential part of something — the thing at the very center that everything else surrounds or depends on.

Kerosene is a thin, flammable liquid fuel made from petroleum — the crude oil that is pumped out of the earth. It is usually clear or very pale yellow in color, and it has a sharp, distinct smell that immediately signals "fuel."

Kerygma is a word used in Christian theology and biblical studies to mean the essential, foundational proclamation of the Christian Gospel — the irreducible core message about Jesus Christ that the early apostles publicly announced to the world.

A kestrel is a small bird of prey — meaning it is a bird that hunts and eats other animals. More specifically, it belongs to the falcon family, which is a group of fast, sharp-eyed hunting birds with pointed wings and hooked beaks.
"A pretty kettle of fish" means an awkward or difficult situation. "A different kettle of fish" means something completely different from what was mentioned before.
The main idea or theme of something, as in "the keynote of his speech." A keynote speech is the main talk at a conference. In music, the keynote is the first note of a scale.
As a noun, "khaki" has three closely connected meanings — a color, a fabric, and a type of clothing — and they build on each other naturally.
Kibble refers to small, dry, hard pieces or pellets of processed food — most commonly food made for pets.
A kibbutz is a collective community found in Israel, where a group of people choose to live together, work together, and share everything they produce as one unified group.
To watch others, especially playing cards or chess, and give unwanted advice. It can also mean to chat or joke idly.
A kibitzer is a person who watches what someone else is doing and then jumps in with their own opinions, advice, or comments — even though nobody asked them to.
"Kibosh" as a noun refers to a decisive, final stop placed on something — one that completely halts, crushes, or kills a plan, idea, activity, or hope so thoroughly that it cannot continue.
"A kick in the teeth" means a sudden, cruel disappointment or setback — especially one that feels deeply unfair, humiliating, or hurtful.
"Kick something off" is a phrasal verb that means to start or begin something — usually an event, a project, a campaign, a meeting, a season, or any organized activity.
"Kick the bucket" simply means to die. That's its core meaning. It's used to say that a person — or sometimes an animal, or even an object — has died or stopped working permanently.
Kick the can down the road

When someone "kicks the can down the road," they are deliberately avoiding or delaying a problem instead of solving it right now. They push the problem into the future, where someone else — or a future version of themselves — will have to deal with it.
"Kick the habit" means to stop doing something that you do regularly, especially something that is bad for you or hard to stop.
To kick up a fuss means to complain loudly, protest strongly, or make a big scene about something — often in a way that seems excessive or unnecessary to the people around you.

To "kick yourself" means to feel deep frustration, regret, or anger directed at yourself because you made a mistake, missed an opportunity, or did something foolish that you clearly could have avoided.
An illegal payment secretly given to someone in return for helping arrange a deal or contract. It can also mean a sudden backward recoil, as of a gun.
To kidnap someone means to take a person away by force, threat, or trickery — against their will — and hold them captive, usually to demand something in return for releasing them.
A kill switch is a mechanism — a button, lever, feature, or system — that is specifically designed to immediately and completely shut something down, usually in an emergency or as a safety measure.

A killjoy is a person who spoils or ruins the fun, happiness, or excitement that others are experiencing. When people around them are enjoying themselves, a killjoy does or says something that brings that good feeling down — like popping a balloon at a party.
A kiln is a special type of extremely high-temperature oven — not for cooking food, but for transforming raw materials (like clay or stone) into something harder, stronger, or chemically different.
Kilter is a noun that means the proper, balanced, working condition of something — the state where everything is as it should be, functioning correctly, well-ordered, and in harmony.
A kimono is a traditional Japanese garment — essentially a long, wraparound robe that has been worn in Japan for centuries. It is one of the most recognizable symbols of Japanese culture.
Kin means your relatives — the people connected to you by family ties, especially by blood. Your parents, siblings, grandparents, aunts, uncles, and cousins are all your kin.
To kindle something means to cause something to start and begin to grow — whether that is a fire or a feeling inside a person.
Kindling is small, thin, dry pieces of material — most commonly sticks, twigs, or strips of wood — that are used to start a fire.

When you say something is kindred, you mean it is deeply similar in nature, character, or spirit to something else — not just alike on the surface, but connected at a fundamental level, as if the two things naturally belong together.
Kinematics is a branch of physics — a field of scientific study — that is devoted entirely to describing how objects move.
Kinesiology is the scientific study of human body movement.

Kinetic means relating to, involving, or caused by movement or motion. If something is kinetic, it either moves, is caused by movement, or produces movement. That's the anchor. Everything else about this word flows from that single idea.

"Kinetically" means in a way that involves, relates to, or is driven by motion and movement. Whenever you see this word, your brain should immediately connect it to the idea of things moving, and the energy that comes from that movement.
Kinetics is a noun that refers to the scientific study of motion and change — specifically, the causes, forces, and rates behind them.

Kinfolk means your relatives — the people you are connected to by blood or by marriage. In plain terms, it refers to your family: your parents, siblings, grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousins, and anyone else you are related to.
A kingdom is a place, area, or domain that is under the rule or control of one supreme authority — most classically, a king or queen.
"Kingdom come" is an old English expression that refers to the afterlife — the world that comes after death, often imagined as heaven or God's eternal kingdom.
A kingfisher is a type of bird — and not just any bird.

When we say something is kingly, we mean it has the qualities, appearance, or character that we would expect from a great king — not just any king, but an ideal one. Think of the image of a powerful, dignified, generous ruler sitting on a throne.
A kingmaker is a person who has the power to decide who gets to be the leader — but chooses not to be the leader themselves.
A kingpin is the single most critical element in a system — the one thing (or person) that everything else depends on. Remove it, and the whole system weakens, falls apart, or stops working.
A peculiar or unusual sexual preference. It can also mean a sharp twist or bend in a hose or wire, a muscle cramp, or a flaw or problem in a plan, as in "work out the kinks."
Kinship means a close connection or relationship between people.
A kinsman is a male relative — a man who is connected to you through family. If a man shares a family bond with you, he is your kinsman.

A kiosk is a small, standalone structure or unit set up in a public place to serve a specific, limited purpose — such as selling something, providing information, or letting you complete a task on your own.
In British, Irish, and Australian everyday speech, a kip simply means a sleep — often a short one, like a nap.

Kirsch is a strong, clear alcoholic spirit made by fermenting and then distilling whole morello cherries — a type of small, dark, sour cherry. It is sometimes also called "kirschwasser," which simply means "cherry water" in German.

A kirtle is a long garment — essentially a type of dress or tunic — worn in medieval and Renaissance Europe, roughly between the years 1000 and 1600. Think of it as an item of everyday clothing from a world long before modern fashion existed.
Kismet means fate — the belief that everything that happens in your life was already decided in advance, and that no matter what you do, certain things were always going to happen to you.
A kitchenette is a very small, basic cooking area — essentially a "mini kitchen" squeezed into a tight space.
Kith refers to your friends, neighbors, and acquaintances — the people you know and are familiar with, but who are not your blood relatives.

Kitsch is the name for a specific kind of object, artwork, or style that looks meaningful, beautiful, or emotionally touching on the surface — but is actually shallow, hollow, and fake underneath. It gives you a warm, easy feeling without earning it.

Kitschy describes something that looks or feels cheap, overly flashy, sentimental, or in poor taste — yet does so in such an exaggerated, over-the-top way that it becomes oddly charming, fun, or entertaining, at least to some people.
When a person — most often a woman or girl — behaves in a playful, lively, and flirtatious way, especially in a soft, charming, and slightly teasing manner, they are being kittenish.
A klaxon is a loud, electrically-powered horn or alarm — a device built specifically to make a sharp, blaring, impossible-to-ignore sound that signals urgency or danger.

A kleptocracy is a system of government in which the leaders use their political power to steal from the country and its people — and get away with it, because they are the ones in power. The word itself literally points to rule by thieves.
A kleptocrat is a political ruler or government leader who uses their power primarily to steal — to systematically loot their own country for personal enrichment.
Kleptocratic is an adjective. You use it to describe a government, a leader, a system, or a practice that is defined by rulers stealing from the very country or people they are supposed to govern.

Kleptomania is a recognized mental health disorder in which a person experiences powerful, uncontrollable urges to steal things — even things they don't actually need, don't particularly want, and could easily afford to buy.

A kleptomaniac is a person who has an uncontrollable urge to steal things — not because they are poor, greedy, or actually want what they are taking, but because of a powerful, irrational compulsion that their mind cannot resist.
Relating to kleptomania, an uncontrollable urge to steal, often things that are not needed.
A kludge is a solution to a problem that actually works — but works in a clumsy, messy, or poorly-built way.

A klutz is a person who is physically clumsy — someone who regularly trips, stumbles, bumps into things, drops objects, or generally lacks smooth, graceful control over their own body movements. The word refers to a person, not an action.
A knack is a special ability to do a particular thing with natural ease and skill — something you do noticeably well, often better than most people, and in a way that looks almost effortless.
Knackered is an informal word that means extremely tired or completely worn out. It is used in everyday speech, mainly in British, Irish, Australian, and New Zealand English.
A knapsack is a bag that you wear on your back. It has two straps — one for each shoulder — so the bag sits against your back while both your hands remain completely free.
A knave is a dishonest, deceitful, and cunning man — someone who tricks, cheats, or manipulates others for personal gain. Think of a swindler, a schemer, or a con artist.

Knavery is the behavior of someone who is deliberately dishonest, deceitful, and morally corrupt — especially when that person uses clever tricks, scheming, and cunning manipulation to cheat or exploit others for personal gain.
Knavish describes someone — or something someone does — that is dishonest, sneaky, and unscrupulous in a sly, cunning way. A knavish person is not just a liar; they are a crafty liar.

To do something knavishly means to do it in a way that is dishonest, deceitful, and cunningly self-serving — like a trickster or a cheat who deliberately misleads others for personal gain, often with a sly, sneaky quality to it.

To knead means to repeatedly press, push, fold, and stretch a soft material — usually with your hands — to work it into a smooth, uniform mass. Think of it as "working" a substance with firm, rhythmic pressure until it changes in texture or consistency.

When you describe something as knee-jerk, you mean it happened automatically, instantly, and without any real thought — like a snap reaction driven by habit, emotion, or a fixed mindset, rather than by careful reasoning.

When used as a verb, to kneecap someone or something means to deliberately cripple, weaken, or sabotage it — to damage it in a targeted way that stops it from functioning properly, especially while leaving it technically still alive or existing.

To kneel means to go down on one or both knees and rest your body's weight on them, rather than standing or sitting. When you kneel, your knee (or knees) touch the ground or floor, and you are supporting yourself on that part of your leg just below the thigh.
A knell is the slow, deep, mournful sound of a bell being rung solemnly — specifically the kind of bell that is rung to announce that someone has died, or to mark a funeral.
A knickknack is a small decorative object — something you keep and display mainly because it looks nice or has sentimental value, not because it does anything useful.

A knight-errant is a knight from the medieval era who travels from place to place, alone or with a small companion, in search of adventure. The word "errant" here simply means wandering or roaming — so a knight-errant is a wandering knight.
A knish is a savory filled pastry — a soft or crispy dough pocket stuffed with a filling, then either baked or deep-fried until cooked through.

To knit means to create fabric or a garment by interlocking loops of yarn using long, thin needles. You hold two knitting needles, wrap yarn around them in a specific pattern, and pull loops through other loops — row by row, again and again.
Knobbly describes a surface or object that has several small, hard, rounded lumps sticking out from it in an uneven, irregular way.

"Knock it off" is an informal English expression that means "stop doing what you are doing right now." It is almost always used when the thing someone is doing is annoying, bothering, or irritating another person.
This idiom has two meanings, and understanding both is important.

A knock-on effect is an indirect consequence that happens as a result of something else that happened first. In other words, it is what occurs not immediately from an event, but because of what that event caused.
The adjective "knockout" describes something so powerful, striking, or impressive that it overwhelms you — it figuratively knocks you out (stuns you into disbelief or admiration).
A blow that knocks a fighter unconscious and ends the match; also a person or thing that is stunningly impressive or attractive.
A knockout punch is a single, powerful blow that immediately ends a fight by putting the opponent completely out of action — leaving them with no ability to fight back or recover.
A knoll is a small, gently rounded hill. It's a natural rise in the ground — soft, low, and with a smooth, curved top rather than a sharp peak.
A knot is a fastening or lump formed by tying or looping a flexible material — like rope, string, cord, or thread — in such a way that the strands grip each other and hold together.
Difficult and complicated, as in "a knotty problem." Literally, full of knots, as in "knotty pine."
A knout is a specific type of heavy, brutal whip that was used in Russia to inflict severe physical punishment on people.
"Know better" means that a person has enough knowledge, experience, or maturity to understand that something is wrong, foolish, or harmful — and therefore should avoid it (or should have avoided it).

When you say you know something "just on an intellectual level," it means you understand it in your head — through thinking, reasoning, and logic — but you have not felt it emotionally or experienced it personally.
Know-how means practical knowledge — the kind of knowledge that actually allows you to do something, not just understand it in theory.

A know-it-all is a person who behaves as if they know everything about every topic — and, importantly, makes sure that everyone around them is aware of it. It is a word used to describe not just what a person knows, but how they act about it.
Deliberately, with full awareness, as in "she knowingly broke the rules." It can also mean in a way that shows you know something secret, as in "he smiled knowingly."
Knowledge is the state of genuinely holding something true in your mind, with good reason to believe it.
"Knuckle under" means to give in, submit, or surrender — especially when someone forces you to, or when pressure becomes too great to resist.
To knuckle down means to start working seriously, with full focus and strong effort, especially on a task that is difficult or demanding.

Knurled describes a surface that has been intentionally covered with a pattern of tiny, repeated ridges or bumps. The purpose is almost always the same: to give your fingers something to grip onto so the object doesn't slip.

A koan is a short question, statement, or story used in Zen Buddhism as a tool for meditation. It is specifically designed to be something your logical, rational mind cannot solve — and that's the entire point.
A kobold is a type of supernatural creature — a spirit or goblin-like being — that comes from old German and broader European folklore.

Kohl is a dark substance — almost always black or very dark grey — that people apply around their eyes as a cosmetic. Think of it as the ancient world's eye makeup: part eyeliner, part eye shadow, all in one.
A kohlrabi is a vegetable. More specifically, it is a plant whose swollen, round stem is the main edible part.

A kookaburra is a type of bird native to Australia and New Guinea. It is the largest member of the kingfisher family — a group of birds traditionally known for fishing — though the kookaburra is famous for being a kingfisher that doesn't really need to fish.

Kooky means slightly crazy, strange, or eccentric in a harmless and often charming way. When you call something or someone kooky, you are saying they are a little odd, unusual, or unpredictable — but not in a scary or seriously worrying way.
Of food, prepared according to Jewish religious law. Informally, genuine, legitimate, or acceptable, as in "the deal didn't seem quite kosher."

To kowtow means to act in an overly submissive way toward someone — essentially to do whatever they want, agree with everything they say, and bend to their every wish, even if it means losing your own dignity or going against what you truly believe.

A kraal is a word used in southern Africa — most commonly in countries like South Africa, Zimbabwe, and Botswana — and it refers to two closely related things: a livestock enclosure, and a traditional village.

A kraken is a legendary, gigantic sea monster from old Scandinavian folklore — imagined as an enormous creature resembling a squid or octopus, so impossibly large that it could destroy entire ships and drag them to the bottom of the ocean.
Kremlinology is the art of figuring out what is really happening inside a secretive, powerful government or organization — not by being told directly, but by carefully reading tiny, indirect clues.

A kris is a type of dagger — a short, sharp blade — that comes from Southeast Asia, most famously from the island of Java in Indonesia. It is one of the most culturally important objects ever made in that part of the world.
Kudos means praise, honor, or admiration given to someone because of something impressive they have achieved or done.

A kudu is a large, wild antelope — a type of graceful, deer-like animal — that lives in Africa. It is one of the most striking and recognizable animals on the continent, famous above all for the breathtaking twisted horns that the males carry.
Kudzu is a plant — specifically, a vine. A vine is a plant that doesn't stand up straight on its own like a tree or a bush.

A kulak was a peasant farmer in Russia who was wealthier than his neighbors. Not rich in the way a nobleman or businessman was rich — just modestly better off than the average rural person around him.
A kumquat is a tiny, oval-shaped fruit that belongs to the citrus family — the same family as oranges, lemons, and limes. It is, in fact, the smallest citrus fruit in the world.

A kurta is a long, loose-fitting garment — essentially a tunic or an oversized shirt — that is traditionally worn across South Asia, including countries like India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, and Sri Lanka.

To kvell means to feel and express an overflowing, beaming sense of pride and joy — usually about someone you love dearly, and usually because of something wonderful they did or something wonderful they simply are.
To kvetch means to complain — but not just complain once or twice. It means to complain repeatedly, persistently, and often about small or petty things, in a whiny, grumbling way.

A kyrie is a short, ancient prayer of mercy used in Christian worship. It is a plea — a person (or a congregation) calling out to God and asking for His mercy. The full traditional form of the prayer is "Kyrie eleison," which translates to "Lord, have mercy."
Labile means easily and readily changed, shifted, or altered — often unstably so.
"A labor of love" describes work that someone does out of pure passion or deep personal care — not for money, not because they are forced to, but because they genuinely love doing it.
When you call something labored, you mean it shows too much effort — and that effort is visible, obvious, and unnatural. The struggle is right there on the surface, where it shouldn't be.

Laborious means requiring a great deal of hard work, time, and effort. When something is laborious, it is slow, demanding, and tiring to do — not because it is impossible, but because it takes so much out of you to get through it.
A labyrinth is something that is so complex, so winding, and so full of twisting paths that it is very easy to get lost in — whether physically or mentally.
Extremely complicated and winding, like a maze, as in "labyrinthine corridors" or "labyrinthine rules."
Lace is a type of fabric — but unlike ordinary fabric (which is a solid sheet of woven threads), lace is open and full of holes. The holes aren't flaws; they are the design itself.

To lacerate means to tear, cut, or wound flesh or skin in a rough, jagged, irregular way. Think of it not as a clean, neat cut — the kind a surgeon makes — but as a violent, messy tear that leaves the skin or flesh ragged and uneven.
A laceration is a wound — specifically, a tear or a cut in the skin or body tissue. Think of it as the result of skin being ripped, slashed, or split open by something sharp or forceful.
Tearful and easily moved to tears. It can also mean causing tears or sadness, as in "a lachrymose film."
When you describe someone or something as lackadaisical, you are saying that they show a careless lack of effort, energy, or enthusiasm — especially when effort is expected or needed.
A lackey is a person who blindly obeys and serves a more powerful person — doing whatever that person says, without question, without pushing back, and often without any dignity.

When something is lackluster, it is dull, unimpressive, and fails to excite or inspire anyone. It has no spark, no energy, no brilliance — it's just flat and forgettable. Think of it as the opposite of something that makes you go "wow."
Someone or something laconic uses very few words — often far fewer than you'd expect — but still gets the point across.
When someone speaks or responds laconically, they cut away everything extra: no filler, no over-explaining, no unnecessary pleasantness. Only the essential remains.
Lacquer is a liquid substance that you apply onto a surface — like wood, metal, or even fingernails — and once it dries, it forms a hard, smooth, glossy shell on top of that surface.
Lacrosse is a team sport where two competing teams use long-handled sticks to catch, carry, pass, and shoot a small rubber ball into the opposing team's goal. The team that scores more goals wins.
Lactation is the process by which a female mammal's body produces and releases milk from her mammary glands (the biological structures inside the breasts or udders) to feed her newborn offspring.

A lacuna is a gap — but a very specific kind of gap. It means a missing piece where something should exist but doesn't. Think of it as a meaningful absence, a blank space that makes something incomplete.
To understand lacy, you first need to picture lace — the material it comes from.
Laden means heavily loaded or weighed down — either with a physical weight, or with something abstract like an emotion, a quality, or an atmosphere.

"Lady" is a polite and respectful word for a woman. Think of it as the more formal, gentler version of the word woman. When you choose to say "lady" instead of "woman," you are usually adding a tone of courtesy, respect, or refinement.

The word ladyfinger (also written as lady finger or lady's finger) is a noun with two distinct meanings — one refers to a vegetable, and the other to a type of biscuit. Both are named after the same idea: they look like a slender, elegant human finger.
A lag is a gap in time — specifically, the stretch of time in which something falls behind where it is expected to be, or the interval between two connected events where one trails the other.

To lag means to move, progress, or develop more slowly than others, or more slowly than expected, so that a gap — a distance or a difference — opens up between you and whoever or whatever you are being compared to.
A laggard is a person — or sometimes a thing like a company, country, or industry — that is slow to act, slow to progress, or consistently falls behind others in a group.

A lagniappe is a small, unexpected extra — something you receive beyond what you paid for, asked for, or were promised. It's the little bonus that wasn't part of the deal but shows up anyway, as an act of generosity or goodwill.
A lagoon is a calm, shallow body of water that is either fully or partially separated from a larger body of water — usually an ocean or sea — by a natural barrier standing between them.

A lair is a place where a wild animal rests, sleeps, and takes shelter. Think of it as the animal's private home — but not a cozy, open home. A lair is typically hidden, tucked away, and difficult for outsiders to find or enter.

If something is described as laissez-faire, it means it is characterized by a deliberate, conscious choice to not interfere — to step back, leave things alone, and let them run on their own without rules, restrictions, or control.
Laissez-faire means a policy or doctrine of deliberate non-interference — the conscious decision by a government (or any authority) to keep its hands off and let things operate freely on their own.
Ordinary members of a religious community, as opposed to the clergy. It can also mean ordinary people as opposed to experts in a particular field.

Lambaste means to criticize someone — or something — very harshly, forcefully, and with clear anger or strong disapproval. It is not a gentle word. When someone is lambasted, they are not given soft feedback or a quiet word of correction.
Of light or flame, glowing softly and flickering gently. Of wit or humour, light, playful, and brilliant.

When you call something lambic, you are saying it belongs to, relates to, or shares the defining qualities of a very specific, ancient style of beer from Belgium — a beer that is sour, complex, and made using wild yeast from the open air rather than yeast added by a brewer.

In its older, literal sense, lame describes a person or animal — most often an animal — that walks with difficulty because of an injury, pain, or weakness in a leg or foot. The inability to move properly is the core idea here.

A lament is a deep, heartfelt expression of sadness, grief, or sorrow — spoken, written, sung, or cried out, usually about something painful that has happened or been lost. It is not quiet, private sadness sitting inside you.
To lament something means to express deep sadness, grief, or regret about it — openly and with feeling. The word describes not just the emotion itself, but the act of giving that emotion a voice.
"Lamentable" describes something that is so bad, so inadequate, or so unfortunate that it deserves deep disappointment, grief, or pity.
A lamentation is a deep, heartfelt, outward expression of grief, sorrow, or regret. The key word here is outward — a lamentation is not just the feeling of sadness sitting quietly inside you.
When we say something is laminate, we mean it is made of multiple thin, flat layers that have been bonded together into one solid structure.
A laminate is a material made by permanently bonding two or more layers of material on top of each other — pressed and fused together — to create a single, unified product.
To laminate something means to bond or fuse layers of material together — either by covering something with a thin protective layer, or by joining multiple thin sheets into one unified object.
A piece of writing, a cartoon, or a sketch that mocks a person, group, or institution in a sharp, humorous, and exaggerated way to make them look foolish.

To lampoon someone or something means to publicly mock or ridicule them in a sharp, exaggerated, and cleverly humorous way — typically through writing, art, cartoons, comedy sketches, films, or performances.

A lanai is a covered, open-air porch or veranda that is attached to a house or building. Think of it as a transitional space — it's not fully indoors (it doesn't have walls all around it), and it's not fully outdoors either (it has a roof over it).
The most familiar meaning of "lance" is a long pole with a sharp metal tip, used as a weapon by soldiers fighting on horseback.

When you lance something, you cut into it with a sharp, pointed instrument to release what is trapped inside. Think of it as a precise, deliberate puncture — not a random stab, but a controlled, purposeful cut made to let something out.
A lancet is a word with two distinct meanings — one from medicine and surgery, and one from architecture. Both share a common thread: something small, sharp, and pointed.

A land mine is a hidden explosive device that is buried just under the surface of the ground. It is designed to explode when something heavy — a person stepping on it, or a vehicle driving over it — presses down on it.

A landfill is a large, specially prepared area of land where garbage and waste are permanently disposed of — primarily by burying it in the ground or stacking it in carefully managed layers on the ground.
A landlady is a woman who owns a property — such as a house, a flat, or a set of rooms — and allows other people to live in it in exchange for regular payments called rent.
A landlord is a person (or a company) who owns a property and allows someone else to live in it or use it — in exchange for regular payments of money.

A landlubber is a person who has little or no experience with the sea, ships, or sailing. In short, it's someone who has spent their life on land and is therefore unfamiliar with — and usually clumsy or uncomfortable in — the world of ships and seafaring.

A landmark is something that stands out from everything around it and carries significance — either to help you locate yourself in the world, or to mark an important moment in history, whether physical or figurative.
A landscape is everything you see when you look out across a wide stretch of land. Imagine standing on a hill and gazing into the distance.

To landscape means to deliberately plan, change, and improve the appearance of an outdoor area — usually the land around a house, building, park, or any open space — by adding, arranging, or modifying natural and decorative elements.

Languid means slow, weak, and lacking energy or enthusiasm — but in a relaxed, dreamy way rather than a sick or broken-down way. It is the feeling of having no desire to move, rush, or exert yourself, often because of heat, tiredness, or a deep sense of calm.
