Passion means an extremely strong, intense feeling — one that goes far beyond simple liking or interest. When you feel passion, the feeling is so powerful that it drives your actions, fills your thoughts, and often feels difficult to control.
When someone is passionate, they feel something very strongly and deeply — so strongly that it shows in everything they do or say about it. It is not just liking something or being interested in it.
Passionately means doing something with very strong, deep, and genuine feeling.
Passive means not doing, not acting, not resisting — but instead receiving, accepting, or allowing.
A passport is a small official booklet issued by your country's government that proves two things about you: who you are and which country you belong to.

"Passé" describes something that was once fashionable, popular, or modern — but no longer is. It sat at the peak of cool or relevance at some point, but that moment has passed, and now it feels dated, behind the times, or out of style.

Every single use of "paste" as a noun comes from this core image. The word describes a form or consistency, not one specific thing — which is why it appears across cooking, crafts, jewellery, and more.
A pastel is a small, stick-shaped tool used by artists for drawing and painting. It looks somewhat like a crayon or a piece of chalk, but it is neither.
A pastiche is a creative work — a novel, a film, a painting, a piece of music — that deliberately imitates the style of another artist, era, or genre.
A pastime is an activity that you enjoy doing in your free time — something you choose to do for pleasure, relaxation, or fun, not because you have to.

Pastis is a strong, anise-flavored spirit and aperitif predominantly produced in the south of France. It typically has an alcohol content of 40–45% ABV and contains less than 100 grams of sugar per liter.
Relating to peaceful, idealized countryside life, as in "a pastoral scene." It can also mean relating to the spiritual guidance and care that a priest or teacher gives to people.

Pastrami is a type of prepared beef that has been cured, coated in spices, smoked, and steamed — resulting in a tender, flavorful meat with a dark spiced crust on the outside and a pink interior. It is most famously eaten in sandwiches at delicatessens.
A dough made of flour, fat, and water, used for pies and tarts. A pastry is also a small baked cake or sweet item made with this dough.

A pasture is a piece of land — usually a field — covered with grass and other low-growing plants, which is specifically set aside so that farm animals can eat the vegetation growing there by walking around and grazing freely.
A "pat on the back" means praise, appreciation, or recognition given to someone for doing something good.
"Patella" is the medical/scientific name for your kneecap — the hard, flat bone you can feel at the front of your knee.
When "patent" is used as an adjective in general language, it means something that is so completely and plainly obvious that it cannot be missed, hidden, or denied.
A patent is an official, government-granted right that gives an inventor exclusive control over their invention for a limited period of time.
Patently means "in a way that is completely and undeniably obvious."

A paterfamilias is the male head of a family or household — the one person who holds the highest authority over everyone living under his roof. Think of him as the "ruler" of the family unit, whose word is final on all matters.

Paternal means "of, relating to, or characteristic of a father." Think of it as the adjective version of the word "father." Whenever you see the word paternal, your brain should immediately connect it to the idea of fatherhood.

Paternalism is when one person, group, or institution restricts or overrides another person's choices — not to protect someone else, but supposedly for the benefit of the very person being restricted.
Treating people the way an overbearing father treats children, by controlling their choices and deciding what is best for them without asking.
Paternity means the state or fact of being a father — specifically, the relationship that exists between a father and his child.
Pathetic describes something or someone that is so weak, helpless, or inadequate that it makes you feel either pity or contempt — or sometimes both at once.
A pathogen is any living organism or agent that enters your body and causes disease or illness.

"Pathological" means relating to, caused by, or resembling disease or abnormality. Think of it as a word that signals something has gone deeply, fundamentally wrong — not just a little off, but wrong in the way that a sick organ or a disordered mind is wrong.
Grief that does not heal over time but becomes prolonged, frozen, or distorted, preventing a person from accepting the loss and moving on with life.
A pathologist is a medical doctor who specializes in understanding and diagnosing disease by examining the body's tissues, cells, fluids, and organs in a laboratory.
Pathology is the study of disease — what disease is, what causes it, how it develops inside the body, and what effects it produces.

Pathos is the quality in something — a story, a speech, a film, a situation, a piece of music, or even a single image — that makes you feel a deep, tender emotion. Usually that emotion is sadness, pity, or sympathy.
Patience is the ability to wait for something — or to endure something difficult — calmly and without complaint.
A patina is a thin layer that slowly forms on the surface of an object over time, changing how it looks — usually its color, texture, or sheen. It is not something anyone puts there on purpose.
A regional or local form of a language that differs from the standard, especially one considered rough or informal. In Jamaica, Patois is the local creole language.

A patriarch is a man who holds the highest authority and is the dominant figure in a family, group, religion, or society. Think of him as "the man at the top of the ladder" — the one everyone looks up to, respects, and often obeys.
"Patriarchal" is an adjective that describes any system, society, family, institution, attitude, or set of values that is organized around male authority and male dominance.

A patriarchy is a society, system, or group in which men hold the most power — over families, institutions, governments, and culture — and in which this male dominance is treated as the natural, normal, or right way of things.
When you call something or someone patrician, you mean they belong to — or strongly give the impression of belonging to — the highest class of society: the old, established aristocracy.

A patrician is a person who belongs to the highest level of society — someone of noble birth, great wealth, and refined manners who is seen as naturally superior to ordinary people, either by law, tradition, or social standing.
Patricide means the act of killing one's own father. It is a specific type of killing — not just any murder, but the murder of one's own biological or legal father, committed by his own child.
Patrimony means something valuable that has been passed down to you from those who came before you — especially from your father, your ancestors, or from a long-standing institution.
A patriot is a person who deeply loves their country and feels a strong sense of loyalty, pride, and devotion toward it.
Patriotic describes someone — or something — that shows deep love, loyalty, and pride toward their own country.
A patrol is the act of moving through or around an area repeatedly and purposefully in order to watch over it, guard it, or make sure everything is safe and in order.

A patron is someone who gives support — financial, social, or spiritual — to a person, a group, or a cause. That support can take several different forms depending on the context, and each of those forms is a legitimate, important meaning of this word.

Patronage means support, help, or power given by someone who is in a stronger position to someone who needs it. Think of it as a one-way flow from the powerful to the less powerful — whether that's money, business, jobs, or influence.
When you patronize someone, you speak to them or behave toward them in a way that quietly signals that you consider yourself smarter, more important, or more capable than them.

When you call someone or something patronizing, you mean that the person is treating someone else as if they are less intelligent, less capable, or less important than they really are — often while pretending to be helpful, kind, or polite about it.

When something patters, it doesn't make one loud bang or one heavy thud. Instead, it makes many small sounds in rapid succession — tap tap tap tap tap — each sound light and gentle on its own, but together creating a kind of rhythm.

Patulous means wide open, spread out, or expanding outward. It describes something that has opened up or spread widely — almost like it's stretching itself out into the space around it, rather than staying closed or compact.
A patzer is a weak, unskilled chess player — someone who plays chess poorly, makes careless mistakes, and generally has a low level of understanding of the game.
Paucity means a very small amount of something — so small that it is not enough.
No two identical particles of a certain type can be in the exact same quantum state at the same time.
If someone is paunchy, they have a noticeably large, round, protruding belly — a stomach that sticks out prominently in front of them.

A pauper is a person who is extremely poor — so poor that they essentially have nothing and cannot support themselves through their own means. We're not talking about someone who is simply "a bit short on money."
To pave means to cover a surface with a hard, flat material so that it becomes smooth, firm, and easy to use.

When you call a surface paved, you mean it has been deliberately covered with a hard, flat, solid material — such as asphalt, concrete, brick, or stone — so that it becomes firm, smooth, and easy to walk or drive on.
A pavilion is a special-purpose structure — a building, a large tent, or a part of a building — that is set apart from ordinary surroundings for a particular use.

In the game of chess, a pawn is the smallest and most common piece on the board. Each player starts with eight pawns — more than any other piece. They stand in a row at the front, like foot soldiers guarding the more powerful pieces behind them.
To pawn something means to hand over a personal item you own to a special kind of shop called a pawnshop, in exchange for a cash loan. You are not selling the item permanently.
When someone is called "a pawn in the game," it means they are being used and controlled by someone more powerful, without having any real say or power themselves.

A pawnbroker is a person (or business) who lends money to people in exchange for a valuable item that the borrower leaves behind as security. If the borrower repays the loan — usually with added interest — within an agreed time, they get their item back.
Pay cable is a type of cable television service that you have to pay extra for, on top of whatever you already pay for basic TV, in order to watch a specific set of premium channels.
A payday is the specific day on which a worker receives their wages or salary — the day money lands in your hands (or your bank account) as payment for the work you have done.
A payout is a sum of money that someone receives — usually a significant or notable amount — as a result of a specific event, condition, or entitlement being met.
Peaceable means having a natural tendency or desire to avoid conflict, arguments, and violence.
Fine and satisfactory; excellent (informal, often used sarcastically), as in "everything's just peachy." Literally, like a peach in colour or texture.
A peacoat is a type of short, heavy overcoat that was originally designed for sailors and naval officers but is now a popular everyday fashion item worn by people all around the world.
To show off in a flashy, proud way to attract attention, especially romantic attention, like a peacock spreading its tail.
Looking pale, thin, and unwell, as in "you look a bit peaked." It can also mean having a point or peak, as in "a peaked cap" or "a peaked roof."
To peal means to ring out loudly, fully, and resonantly — producing a rich, powerful sound that spreads through the air and seems to fill the entire space around it.
A peasant is a poor, low-class person who works the land — farming, growing crops, and raising animals — typically in a rural area.

A pebble is a small, smooth, rounded piece of rock or stone. It is small enough to hold in your hand — roughly the size of a grape, a marble, or a large coin — though some pebbles can be slightly smaller or slightly larger than this.

Peccable means capable of sinning or doing wrong. If someone is peccable, it means they can make moral mistakes, yield to temptation, or act wrongly. It describes a being who is not morally perfect — someone who has the potential to err, sin, or behave badly.

A peccadillo is a small, minor wrongdoing or fault — something a person does that is slightly bad or morally questionable, but causes little or no real harm, and is generally easy to forgive or overlook.

Peckish means slightly hungry — not starving, not really hungry, just a mild, gentle nudge from your stomach saying it wouldn't mind a little something to eat. Think of it as sitting somewhere between "completely full" and "genuinely hungry."
To peculate means to steal money or property that was entrusted to you — especially public money or funds belonging to an employer or organization.
Peculation means the theft or dishonest misuse of money or property that someone was officially trusted to manage — especially public money, or funds belonging to an organization or employer.
Strange or unusual, especially in a way that is hard to explain, as in "a peculiar smell." Peculiar to someone or something means belonging only to them, as in "a custom peculiar to the region."

The word pecuniary means "relating to or involving money." Whenever something has a direct monetary dimension — a gain, a loss, a benefit, a penalty, or a financial stake — the word pecuniary describes it.

Pedagogical means relating to the art, science, or practice of teaching. When something is described as pedagogical, it has to do with how a teacher teaches — their methods, strategies, approaches, and goals when helping someone learn.
A teacher, especially one who is strict, pedantic, or dogmatic. In neutral, academic use, simply an educator.

Pedagogy means the art, science, and practice of teaching. More specifically, it refers to the thoughtful, structured approach a teacher takes to help someone learn — not just what is taught, but how, why, and for whom it is taught.
A pedant is a person who is obsessively focused on minor rules, small details, or technical correctness — often in a way that is irritating, unhelpful, or completely misses the bigger point.

Pedantic describes a person, behavior, or attitude that is excessively focused on minor details, technical rules, or correctness — especially in a way that feels annoying, unnecessary, or unhelpful in the moment.
Pedantry is an excessive, unhelpful obsession with minor details, rules, or the display of knowledge — in a way that is more irritating than useful, and that often misses the bigger picture entirely.

To peddle means to sell something, but not just in any ordinary way. It specifically suggests going out of your way — often moving from place to place, or actively pushing something onto people — to sell or spread it.
A peddler is a person who sells goods, but in a very specific way: they go to their customers rather than waiting for customers to come to them.
A pedestal is a raised base or support structure that something is placed on top of — usually to hold it up, display it, and make it stand out.

When pedestrian is used as an adjective, it means ordinary, dull, and completely lacking in imagination or originality. It describes something that is so plain and unremarkable that it fails to interest, inspire, or impress anyone.
A pedestrian is simply a person who is traveling on foot — someone who is walking from one place to another, rather than riding in or on any kind of vehicle.

Pediatric means relating to the medical care of children. When something is described as "pediatric," it belongs to, is designed for, or is connected with the health and medical treatment of children — as opposed to adults.

A pediatrician is a doctor who specializes in the health and medical care of children — from the moment a baby is born all the way through adolescence (typically up to age 18, though some pediatricians continue treating patients until age 21).
Pedigree means a recorded line of ancestors — a documented family history that traces where someone or something came from, going back through multiple generations.
A wide, low triangular section at the top of the front of a building, especially above columns in classical Greek and Roman architecture.
A peek is a quick, brief look at something — especially one that is secret, sneaky, or cautious. It is not a long, open stare.
To peek means to look at something quickly, secretly, or partially — usually from a hidden position, through a small opening, or when you are not entirely supposed to be looking.
A quick, secret look ("a peep through the keyhole"); or a short, high, weak sound, like a young bird's cry.
The term "peeping Tom" is used to describe a person who derives some sort of enjoyment — usually sexual — from secretly watching people during their most intimate moments.
The word peeps is an informal, casual way of saying "people" — but it carries a warmer, more personal feeling than just "people."

A peer is someone who stands at the same level as you in some important way — the same age, the same rank, the same job, the same social position, or the same skill level. Think of it as someone you are "on equal footing" with.
To peer means to look at something very carefully and with effort, especially when it is hard to see. It is not a casual glance. It is not a relaxed stare.
The evaluation of a piece of work, especially a scientific paper, by other experts in the same field before it is published.
Peerless means having no equal — so superior to everything else that nothing can even be compared to it.
To peeve someone means to mildly irritate, annoy, or bother them — to get under their skin in a low-level, nagging way.
Peevish means being easily annoyed and irritated — especially by small, trivial things — in a childish, sulky, or whiny way.

Peevishness is the state of being easily and repeatedly irritated or annoyed — especially by small, unimportant things — and showing that irritation through complaining, sulking, or making sharp, cross remarks.

A peg is a small, solid object — usually shaped like a pin, spike, or knob — that is used to fasten, hold, hang, mark, or fix something in place. Think of it as a physical anchor point, or a fixed reference point.
When you describe a word, phrase, or expression as pejorative, you mean that it carries a built-in sense of disrespect, disapproval, or belittling toward the person or thing it refers to.
Pelagic means "of, relating to, or living in the open ocean" — specifically the free, open body of water that stretches away from the coast and above the seafloor.

Pelf means money or wealth — but not just any money. It specifically refers to money that is viewed with moral disgust. Think of it as "dirty money." It's the kind of wealth associated with greed, dishonesty, corruption, or shameless self-interest.
A pelicanry is a place where pelicans gather specifically to breed — to court, mate, nest, lay eggs, and raise their young.
When something happens pell-mell, it happens in a rushed, headlong, and completely disorganized way — all at once, with no order or control.

A pellet gun is a type of air-powered weapon that shoots small, non-explosive projectiles called pellets. Unlike real firearms (like pistols or rifles), a pellet gun does not use gunpowder or a chemical explosion to fire.

Pellucid means so perfectly clear that nothing is hidden, blocked, or confused. It describes a kind of clarity that is almost effortless to perceive — whether you're looking through something with your eyes, or understanding something with your mind.
When you pelt someone or something, you throw things at them repeatedly, quickly, and with force. It's not a gentle toss. It's aggressive, rapid, and usually relentless — like an attack of throwing.

The pelvis is a large, bowl-shaped bony structure located at the very bottom of your torso — right where your trunk (the main body) ends and your legs begin. Think of it as the body's central hub: a sturdy ring of bone that connects your spine to your legs.
A pen is a tool you use to write or draw, and it works by releasing ink onto a surface (usually paper).
Penal means relating to punishment — specifically, punishment given by law for doing something wrong or criminal.

A penalty is a punishment or negative consequence that is officially given to someone because they broke a rule, violated a law, failed to meet an agreement, or did something they were not supposed to do.
Penance is an act of voluntary suffering, hardship, or sacrifice that someone performs to show they are truly sorry for something wrong they have done.
A penchant is a strong, natural, and habitual liking for something — a recurring pull toward a specific thing that feels like a defining part of who you are.
The word pendant always carries the idea of something that hangs or is suspended from something else. That single idea — hanging down — is the thread connecting all its meanings.
A pendent is an object — most often an ornamental one — that hangs suspended from something above it. The defining feature is that it hangs downward, attached at the top and free at the bottom.

When something is pending, it means it is waiting to be completed, decided, or dealt with. It exists in a kind of middle zone — it has already begun or been submitted, but it has not yet reached its conclusion. Nothing has been finalized.
When "pending" is used as a preposition, it means "while waiting for something" or "during the period before something happens or is decided."

If something is pendulous, it hangs loosely downward — and often sways gently under its own weight, the way a pendulum does. Think of it as the adjective version of a pendulum: heavy, hanging freely, and subject to the pull of gravity.
A pendulum is an object that hangs from a fixed point above it and swings freely back and forth. Think of a weight hanging on a string — when you push it to one side and let go, it doesn't just fall.
"Penetrate" means to go into or through something — especially something that has resistance, a surface, or a barrier. It is a more forceful, more specific version of "enter" or "pass through."

A peninsula is a piece of land that sticks out into a body of water and is almost entirely surrounded by water, but is still physically connected to a much larger piece of land (like a continent or a large island) on one side.
Penitence is the deep, sincere feeling of sorrow for something wrong you have done — paired with a genuine wish that you had not done it and a desire to make things right.
If someone is penitent, they feel genuine, sincere sorrow for something wrong they have done — and they wish they could undo it or make it right. It is not just being sad.

Penitential means relating to, expressing, or showing deep sorrow and regret for having done something morally wrong — and crucially, doing so with a genuine desire to make amends or seek forgiveness.
A pennant is a type of flag — but with a very specific, distinctive shape. Unlike a regular flag, which is rectangular, a pennant is long, narrow, and triangular.
The single-sentence core: Pennate means shaped or arranged like a feather.
A penny is the name of the smallest coin in a currency system — the coin with the least value. Think of it as the lowest rung on the ladder of money.
Penology is the scientific study of how societies punish people who commit crimes — what those punishments look like, why we use them, and whether they actually work.
A pension is a sum of money that is paid to a person on a regular basis — typically every month — after they have stopped working, usually because of old age or, in some cases, disability.
Pensive describes a person who is deep in quiet, serious thought — but with a gentle shadow of sadness or worry mixed in.
"Pent-up" describes something — almost always a feeling, emotion, or energy — that has been held inside, not allowed to come out, for a period of time, so that it builds up like pressure.

When you speak, some syllables come out heavier (louder, longer) than others. Say the word "banana" aloud — you naturally say it as ba-NA-na, with the middle syllable carrying more weight. That heavier syllable is called a stressed syllable.
Penultimate means second to last — the one that comes directly before the final one in any sequence or series.
An area of partial shadow around the edge of a full shadow, such as during an eclipse. Figuratively, a vague, uncertain area at the edge of something, as in "the penumbra of the law."
Extremely unwilling to spend money; stingy. It can also mean extremely poor.

Penury means a state of extreme, severe poverty — not just being short on cash or "struggling financially," but being so desperately poor that a person barely has enough (or has absolutely nothing) to survive.

A peon is a person who occupies the lowest level in a hierarchy — someone with little to no power, status, or authority, who is expected to do basic, unglamorous, or exhausting work, often under the control of someone more powerful.
A people pleaser is a person who has a strong, often uncontrollable need to make others happy, keep them comfortable, and earn their approval — even when doing so causes harm to themselves.
A pep talk is a short, encouraging speech given to someone to boost their confidence, energy, or motivation — especially before a challenging task or after a setback.

Peppy means full of bright, lively energy and cheerful enthusiasm. When you call someone or something peppy, you're saying it radiates an upbeat, bouncy, active quality — the kind that feels a little infectious and impossible to ignore.
"Per se" means "by itself," "in itself," or "on its own."

To perambulate means to walk through or around a place, usually in a slow, relaxed, and unhurried way. Think of it as walking about a space — not rushing to a destination, but moving through an area in a wandering, exploratory, or leisurely manner.
A baby's pram (formal or old-fashioned). It can also mean a person who walks about, or a wheel used for measuring distances.
Perceptible describes something that can be noticed or detected — either by your senses (sight, hearing, touch, smell, taste) or by your mind (as in, you become aware of it mentally).
Perceptibly means in a way that can be noticed or detected.
Perception is the way you notice, interpret, and make sense of the world — both through your senses and through your mind.

To be perceptive means to have a sharp, accurate ability to notice things — especially things that are subtle, hidden beneath the surface, or not immediately obvious — and to correctly understand what those things mean.
When someone does something perceptively, they do it with sharp, deep insight — noticing things that most people would miss, and understanding what those things really mean beneath the surface.
A perch is fundamentally a raised, narrow resting spot — a place where something or someone sits up high, balancing or settled.
"Perchance" means perhaps or possibly — you use it when you think something might be true or might happen, but you are not certain. It expresses a possibility, not a fact.

"Percipient" describes someone whose mind is sharp enough not just to notice things, but to immediately understand their deeper meaning — especially things that are subtle, beneath the surface, or easily missed by others.
Percolate means to move slowly through something that has tiny holes or gaps, filtering as it goes.
Musical instruments that are played by being struck or shaken, such as drums and cymbals. In medicine, percussion is tapping on the body to find out about the organs underneath.

Perdition means total, permanent, and irreversible ruin — the kind from which there is no return, no rescue, and no hope of recovery. That sense of absolute finality is the beating heart of this word, no matter how it is used.

To peregrinate means to travel from place to place, especially over a long distance or through foreign lands — often in a slow, wandering, exploratory way, rather than rushing straight to a single fixed destination.

Peregrination means a long, wandering journey through many places — especially through foreign or unfamiliar lands. Think of it as the opposite of a quick, straight trip from Point A to Point B. A peregrination is slow, expansive, and winding.

When someone speaks or acts in a peremptory way, they issue a command or make a statement that they expect to be followed immediately and without any argument, question, or refusal. It's not a request. It's not open for discussion.
Lasting for a very long time or recurring again and again, as in "a perennial problem." In gardening, a perennial plant lives for several years.

Having no faults or flaws; as good as it can possibly be. It can also mean complete or absolute, as in "a perfect stranger." In grammar, the perfect tense describes completed actions, as in "I have eaten."
A perfectionist is a person who is never satisfied with anything less than perfect — or what they believe is perfect.

Perfervid means intensely and almost overwhelmingly passionate or enthusiastic — but with a key twist: the intensity is so extreme that it can feel excessive, burning, or even a little out of control.
Perfidious means deliberately and deceitfully betraying someone who trusted you.
Perfidy means a deliberate act of betrayal — specifically, breaking a promise, a trust, or a bond of loyalty in a sneaky and dishonest way.
To perforate something means to make one or more holes that pass completely through it — from one side all the way to the other side.
Something is perforated when it has one or more holes that go completely through it — from one side to the other.
Perforce means "by necessity; because circumstances make it unavoidable."

When you do something perfunctorily, you do it just to get it done — with the bare minimum of care, attention, or interest. You're going through the motions. The task gets a tick mark, but your heart, mind, and effort were never really in it.
When something is perfunctory, it is done with the bare minimum of effort, care, or attention — just enough to technically get it done, without any real interest or sincerity behind it.

A pergola is an outdoor structure, typically built in a garden, backyard, patio, or walkway, that consists of vertical posts or pillars supporting a roof-like framework of horizontal beams and open, cross-hatched rafters overhead.
Perigee is the point in an orbit around Earth where the orbiting object — such as the Moon or a satellite — is at its closest distance to Earth.
Peril means serious, significant danger — a situation where something harmful, damaging, or destructive is very likely to happen. It is not just a small worry or a minor inconvenience.
Perilous means full of serious danger — the kind of danger that could cause great harm, injury, or even death. When something is perilous, it is not just a little risky.
Dangerously, especially close to disaster, as in "perilously close to the edge."
Perimeter means the total length of the outer boundary of a flat (two-dimensional) shape or area.

Periodic describes something that happens at intervals — it doesn't go on constantly or non-stop, but it keeps coming back again and again, with gaps in between. Think of it as a rhythm or a pattern: it appears, disappears, then reappears.
A periodical is any publication that comes out repeatedly, on a fixed schedule, over an indefinite period of time.

"Peripatetic" describes a person, a lifestyle, a career, or a way of doing something that is constantly moving from place to place — especially as a regular, defining feature rather than an occasional occurrence.

Of secondary or minor importance, as in "peripheral issues." It can also mean relating to the edge of something, as in "peripheral vision." In computing, a peripheral is a device connected to a computer, such as a printer.
The periphery of something is its outer edge, outer boundary, or outer zone — the part that is farthest from the center.

A periscope is a device that lets you see things that are not directly in front of your eyes — things that are hidden behind a wall, above a barrier, or around a corner — without you having to move your body or expose yourself to see them.
Perish means to die or to be completely destroyed — but it carries a specific weight and flavour that the plain word "die" does not.
A peristyle is a row — or rows — of columns arranged to completely surround either a building or an open courtyard, forming a covered walkway that runs all the way around on every side.

To perjure means to deliberately lie while you are under oath. Almost without exception, this verb is used reflexively — meaning the subject does it to themselves. The natural, correct form is: to perjure oneself
Perjury is the crime of deliberately lying under oath in an official legal setting.
A perk is an extra benefit or advantage that you get on top of something main — something pleasant that comes to you in addition to what you were already going to receive.

If someone is perky, they are cheerful, lively, and full of bright energy — in a way that is very noticeable and upbeat. Think of a person who bounces into a room with a big smile, an enthusiastic voice, and an almost electric positivity.

Permafrost is ground — whether soil, rock, or sediment — that stays frozen at or below 0°C (32°F) for at least two years in a row. That's the precise scientific definition. It doesn't have to be frozen for just one winter and thaw the next.
Permanence is the quality of lasting forever, or at least lasting so long and so unchanged that it cannot easily — or ever — be undone, ended, or altered.
Permeable describes a material or surface that allows liquids, gases, or other substances to pass through it.
To permeate something means to spread through every single part of it — completely, thoroughly, and often gradually. When something permeates, it doesn't just sit on the surface or affect one corner.
Permission is the act of someone in authority allowing another person to do something.
Permissive describes something or someone that allows a lot of freedom — that does not impose many rules, restrictions, or controls, and tends to say "yes" rather than "no."
To permit something means to allow it to happen — but with an important layer: the person or thing permitting has the authority or power to say yes or no in the first place.
A permutation is a specific arrangement of things in a particular order.

Something is pernicious when it causes serious harm — but does so in a slow, subtle, and often hidden way. It doesn't announce itself. It quietly works against you, and by the time you notice the damage, it may already be severe or even irreversible.

To perorate means to speak at great length in a grand, formal, or pompous way — often to the point where the listener feels the speaker is going on far too long and enjoying the sound of their own voice a little too much.

A peroration is the concluding section of a formal speech — the powerful ending where a speaker wraps everything up, reminds the audience of their key points, and makes one final push to move, persuade, or inspire them.

"Perp" is simply a short, informal form of the word "perpetrator." A perpetrator is a person who commits a crime or does something seriously wrong or harmful. So a perp is, in plain terms, the person who did it — the one who carried out the bad act.
To perpetrate something means to carry out or commit an act — almost always one that is wrong, harmful, illegal, or morally bad.
A perpetrator is a person who commits a harmful, wrong, or illegal act. In the simplest terms: if something bad happened, the perpetrator is the one who did it.
Perpetual means continuing or lasting forever, or for so long that it seems like it will never stop.
A frowning expression that never seems to leave someone's face, suggesting they are always unhappy, worried, or disapproving.
Perpetually means in a way that never stops, never ends, and goes on continuously — either forever or for such a long, unbroken stretch that it seems like forever.

To perpetuate something means to actively cause it to continue — especially for a very long time, or indefinitely. When you perpetuate something, you are the reason it keeps going. You are feeding it, keeping it alive, ensuring it doesn't die out on its own.

Perpetuation is the act of making something continue to exist, keep happening, or go on — often for a long time, sometimes indefinitely. It is the noun form of the verb "perpetuate," which means to keep something alive, going, or in motion.

Perpetuity means the state of lasting forever, or for an endless amount of time. When something exists in perpetuity, it never stops, never expires, and has no endpoint — it simply continues on and on, without any finish line.

To perplex someone means to fill their mind with a deep, tangled confusion — the kind where they genuinely cannot figure something out, no matter how hard they try. It's not just a passing "I don't get it" moment.

When you are perplexed, you are confused — but not just any kind of confused. It is the specific feeling of being puzzled by something that you cannot figure out, no matter how hard you try to make sense of it.

A perquisite is something extra that you receive — a benefit, a privilege, or an advantage — that comes to you because of your job, your role, or your status, rather than being something you directly earn through pay.
To persecute someone means to treat them in a cruel, unjust, and relentless way — specifically because of who they are or what they believe.

Persecution means the sustained, cruel, and unjust mistreatment of a person or group — carried out repeatedly and deliberately, usually by someone in a position of power, and almost always because of who the victims are rather than anything specific they have done wrong.
Perseverance is the quality of continuing to work toward a goal — steadily and consistently — even when things are hard, slow, frustrating, or seemingly impossible.

To persevere means to keep going with something difficult, even when you want to stop. It means you face obstacles, failure, pain, or discouragement — and you continue anyway, steadily, without giving up.

Persiflage is light, breezy, witty talk or writing that is playful and teasing on the surface — but notably lacks any real seriousness, depth, or substance underneath. Think of it as conversation that glitters but doesn't go anywhere.

A persimmon is a fruit — sweet, smooth, and typically bright orange or deep red-orange in color when ripe. It grows on trees and looks a little like a tomato at first glance: roundish, glossy, and orange.
Persist means to keep going despite pressure to stop — either a thing keeps existing when you expect it to end, or a person keeps trying when it would be easy to quit.
Persistence means continuing to do something, or continuing to exist, even when there is difficulty, resistance, or the simple passage of time trying to stop it.
Continuing firmly in a course of action despite difficulty, as in "a persistent salesperson." It can also mean continuing for a long time or happening again and again, as in "a persistent cough."
Persnickety means overly focused on small, often unimportant details — to a degree that most people would find excessive or unnecessary.
A persona is the version of yourself — or a character — that is deliberately presented to the world. Think of it as a "face" someone puts on.
A person who is not welcome somewhere, as in "after the scandal, he was persona non grata at the club." In diplomacy, a foreign diplomat who is officially no longer accepted by the host country.
When you call someone personable, you are saying that they are pleasant to be around — both in the way they look and in the way they behave and talk to people.
A personage is a person who is important, distinguished, or of high rank — someone who stands out from ordinary people because of their status, fame, power, or remarkable qualities.
Personal means "relating to, belonging to, or directly concerning one specific individual — and not others."
Your personality is the complete, unique set of qualities, traits, thoughts, feelings, and ways of behaving that together define who you are as a person — the total psychological picture of you.
To personify something means to give it a human face — either literally in your imagination or writing, or figuratively by treating a real person as the living, breathing form of an abstract idea.

"Personnel" means all the people who work for an organization — a company, a government body, a military unit, a hospital, a school, or any institution. It refers to the entire group of workers considered together as a unit.
Perspective means the particular way someone sees, understands, or thinks about something — shaped by who they are, where they stand in life, and what they've experienced.
Perspicacious means having a sharp, keen ability to notice and understand things that most other people would miss — or take much longer to figure out.

Perspicacity is the ability to understand things quickly, deeply, and accurately — especially things that are not obvious, hidden beneath the surface, or difficult to figure out. It is a sharpness of the mind.
Perspicuity is the quality of being expressed so clearly and plainly that it is easy to understand.

Perspicuous describes something — most commonly a piece of writing, a speech, an argument, or an explanation — that is so clearly and precisely expressed that its meaning comes through without any effort or confusion on the reader's part.
To perspire means to release sweat through the skin. Your body has millions of tiny openings in your skin called pores.
To persuade someone means to successfully get a person to believe something or do something — by working on their mind through reasons, arguments, evidence, or appeals to their emotions.

Persuasion is the process of convincing someone — through words, arguments, emotions, or reasoning — to believe something, feel something, or do something they weren't already inclined to believe, feel, or do.

When something — or someone — is persuasive, it means they are good at making you change your mind, believe something, or do something, through the power of reasoning, argument, emotion, or evidence — not through force, threats, or orders.
Bold and cheeky in a lively way, as in "a pert reply." Of a body part, small, firm, and attractively shaped, as in "a pert nose."
Pertain means to be connected to, related to, or concerned with something. When something pertains to a topic or subject, it belongs to that world — it has a relevant link or connection to it.

Pertinacious means holding firmly to a belief, goal, or course of action with such stubborn, unyielding persistence that almost nothing can shake you from it — not failure, not opposition, not even clear evidence that you might be wrong.

Pertinacity is the quality of holding on to something — a goal, a belief, an opinion, or a plan of action — with a fierce, unyielding grip, even when the world around you pushes back, things get hard, or other people think you should let go.
Pertinent means directly and meaningfully related to the specific topic, situation, or matter being discussed or considered.

To perturb means to make someone feel mentally or emotionally disturbed, unsettled, or anxious — often suddenly, and often in a way that is hard to shake off. It can also mean to throw a system, process, or state of order into disruption.
Perturbation means a disturbance or disruption to something that was otherwise in a calm, stable, or expected state. Think of it as something that throws a system — or a person — off balance.

When someone is perturbed, they are in a state of inner mental unease — unsettled, quietly agitated, and troubled by something. Picture your mind as still water. When something perturbs you, it drops a stone into that water and your calm breaks into ripples.
A perusal is the act of reading something.
To peruse something means to read or examine it carefully, slowly, and with close attention to detail.
To pervade something means to spread through every single part of it, completely and thoroughly.

Pervasive describes something that has spread so thoroughly throughout a place, situation, or group of people that it is difficult — or even impossible — to avoid or escape. It is everywhere, in every corner, affecting every part of something.
"Perverse" describes something or someone that goes against what is reasonable, right, or expected — and does so in a way that feels willful, stubborn, or deliberately contrary.

"Perversion" means the act of twisting, distorting, or corrupting something away from what it should rightfully be — turning something that was correct, good, or natural into something wrong, harmful, or unacceptable.

Perversity is the quality of deliberately choosing to go against what is reasonable, right, expected, or good — not because you are confused or ignorant, but often knowing full well that you're doing so.

A pervert is a person whose sexual desires, thoughts, or behaviors are considered deeply wrong, abnormal, or disgusting by the standards of society — especially when those desires involve harm, exploitation, or things that most people find morally offensive.

To pervert something means to take something that is good, correct, pure, or functioning as it should — and twist, corrupt, or distort it into something harmful, wrong, or completely unlike what it was originally meant to be.
Pervious means allowing something — usually a liquid or gas — to pass through.
Pesky describes something — or sometimes someone — that is annoying, irritating, or troublesome, but in a small, mild, and non-serious way.
Pessimism is a way of thinking in which a person expects the worst to happen in any situation.

A pessimist is a person who tends to expect the worst outcome in any situation. When faced with uncertainty — a job interview, a medical test, a new plan, the future in general — a pessimist's first instinct is to think: this will probably go badly.
To pester someone means to repeatedly bother or annoy them — usually by constantly asking for something, making demands, or interrupting them — in a way they find irritating and unwelcome.

Pestering is the act of repeatedly bothering or annoying someone — usually by asking for something over and over again, or by constantly interrupting them — in a way that makes them feel frustrated and worn out.
A pesticide is any substance — chemical or biological — that is used to kill, repel, control, or prevent organisms that are considered harmful or unwanted in a particular situation.
A pestilence is a deadly, highly contagious disease that spreads rapidly and kills enormous numbers of people across a wide area.
Pestilent means dangerously harmful — something that spreads harm, corruption, or destruction the way a deadly plague spreads through a population. That's the spirit the word carries.
Pestilential describes the air as if it were carrying disease — deadly, contaminating, spreading harm.
A pestle is a heavy, rounded stick used to crush and grind things.
A pet peeve is a small, specific thing that annoys you personally — something that bothers you more than it bothers most other people, and it bothers you every single time it happens.

A pet project is a project, idea, or task that someone feels a strong personal attachment to. It is something they care about deeply — not because they have to, but because they want to. It brings them a special kind of joy, pride, or satisfaction.
A petition is a formal, written request made by one or more people to someone who has the authority or power to act on it — asking that person or body to do something specific.
When you petition someone, you make a formal, serious request to a person or group who has power or authority over something — asking them to take a specific action or make a specific decision.

A petri dish is a small, shallow, round, flat container — like a tiny, wide lid — used in science laboratories to grow living microscopic organisms such as bacteria, fungi, or other cells so that scientists can study them.
Petrichor is the pleasant, earthy smell that rises from the ground when rain falls on dry soil or rock. It's that fresh, comforting scent you notice right when rain begins after a long dry period.
"Petrified" almost always appears in one of these forms: petrified of something → "She is petrified of heights." (This is the most common construction.
To make someone so frightened that they cannot move, as in "she was petrified of spiders." Literally, to turn something into stone over a long period of time, as with fossils.

A petroglyph is an image or symbol that ancient people carved, chipped, or scratched directly into the surface of a rock. The key idea is that the image is cut into the rock — not painted on top of it.
To pettifog means to deliberately get lost in tiny, unimportant details — or to use sneaky, dishonest tricks in an argument — especially as a way of avoiding the real, bigger issue at hand.
A pettifogger is a lawyer — but a particularly bad and dishonest kind. Not bad in the sense of incompetent (though that's often true too), but bad in character.
Focusing on tiny, unimportant details, especially in a petty or deceptive way, as in "pettifogging objections."
Pettish means being childishly sulky, irritable, or bad-tempered — especially over something small, trivial, or unimportant.
Of little importance; trivial, as in "petty details" or "petty theft." Of a person, overly concerned with minor matters, or small-minded and spiteful, as in "a petty revenge."
Petulance is the behavior of someone who gets easily annoyed, sulky, or rude about small, unimportant things — and who shows that displeasure in a childish, unreasonable way.
Petulant describes someone who is acting in a childishly irritable, sulky, or rude way — especially because they didn't get what they wanted or because something didn't go their way.
When someone does something petulantly, they do it in a way that shows childish, sulky displeasure — usually because they didn't get what they wanted, or because something minor didn't go their way.
A pew is a long, fixed bench with a back, found inside a church, where people sit during religious services such as Sunday worship, weddings, or funerals.

A phagocyte is a cell in your body whose job is to find, swallow, and destroy threats — things like bacteria, viruses, fungi, dead cells, and other harmful debris. Think of it as your body's built-in security guard and cleanup crew rolled into one.

A large group of people or things standing close together, especially for a shared purpose, as in "a phalanx of photographers." Originally, a tight formation of ancient Greek soldiers. In anatomy, a bone of a finger or toe.

A phantasm is something that seems real — that appears before you or takes shape in your mind — but has no actual, solid existence. It lives in the uneasy space between what is real and what is imagined, feared, or falsely believed.
A rapidly changing sequence of strange, dreamlike images or scenes, real or imagined, as in "a phantasmagoria of colours and sounds."

When you call something phantasmagoric, you are saying it feels like a waking dream — a strange, constantly shifting, visually overwhelming experience where images, scenes, or ideas keep appearing, morphing, and disappearing in ways that feel unreal, bizarre, and almost impossible to pin down.
A phantom is something that seems to exist but doesn't really exist — or something that exists in appearance, sensation, or imagination, but not in solid, real, physical reality.
A pharaoh was the supreme ruler of ancient Egypt — simultaneously the country's king, its chief religious leader, and a living god.
Pharisaic is an adjective that describes a person — or their behavior, attitude, or words — that is hypocritically self-righteous.

Pharisaical means being obsessively focused on outward rules, rituals, or the appearance of moral or religious correctness — while completely missing the real spirit or deeper meaning behind those rules — and, crucially, looking down on others who don't follow the same standards.

A self-righteous, hypocritical person who cares more about appearing religious or moral than being genuinely so. Historically, a Pharisee was a member of an ancient Jewish group known for strict observance of religious law.
A pharmacy is a place where medicines are stored, prepared, and given or sold to people. Think of it as the final stop between a medicine and the person who needs it.
A phase is a distinct, recognizable stage or period that is part of a larger process, sequence, or cycle.
When you call something phatic, you're saying it's a form of communication whose primary purpose is social, not informational.
Phenomena refers to things that happen or exist in the world that can be observed, experienced, or perceived.
In common use, "phenomenal" means something is so impressively good, powerful, or remarkable that it stands far beyond the ordinary. It is not just "very good" or "great."

Phenomenology is a branch of philosophy that studies conscious experience itself — specifically, what the world looks and feels like from the inside, from the perspective of a living, thinking person going through it.
A phenomenon is any observable occurrence, event, or fact — something that exists or happens in the world and can be noticed, perceived, or experienced.

A phenothiazine is a specific chemical structure that forms the backbone of a whole family of medicines — most famously, medicines used to treat serious mental illnesses and to stop nausea and vomiting.

A pheromone is a chemical substance that one living creature produces and releases into its surroundings, which then causes a specific reaction — either a behaviour or a body change — in another creature of the same species.

A phial is a small bottle — typically made of glass — designed to hold a small amount of liquid. If you imagine a tiny glass container, narrow and sealed, holding just a few drops or a small dose of something, you're imagining a phial.

To philander means for a man to flirt with, seduce, or have casual romantic or sexual encounters with multiple women — not out of genuine love, but purely for pleasure or self-gratification — while showing little to no real emotional commitment to any of them.
A philanderer is a man who repeatedly pursues romantic or sexual relationships with multiple women — without any genuine intention of love, loyalty, or long-term commitment toward any of them.

"Philanthropic" describes a person, organization, action, or mindset that is genuinely devoted to helping other people or improving society — typically through the generous giving of money, time, or resources — with no expectation of personal gain in return.

A philanthropist is a person who actively works to improve the lives of other people or to benefit society as a whole, usually by giving away large amounts of their own money, time, or resources — and doing so without expecting anything in return.

Philanthropy is the act of willingly giving your time, money, or resources to help other people or to improve society — without expecting anything in return. The word is a noun, and its entire spirit rests on one idea: genuine care for fellow human beings.
A philatelist is a person who collects and studies postage stamps — and more broadly, anything connected to the history and materials of postal services.
When someone says "I went to hear the philharmonic last night," they mean they attended a concert by a large, professional orchestra that performs classical music.
A philippic is a fierce, passionate, and blistering verbal or written attack directed at a specific person, group, or cause.
A philistine is a person who has no appreciation for art, culture, literature, music, or ideas — and, crucially, is either proud of this or completely unbothered by it.
Philology is the scholarly study of language as it appears in written texts, especially old or ancient ones.
Philosophical is an adjective with two closely related meanings — one formal, one everyday. Understanding both will give you complete command of the word.

To philosophize means to think deeply, carefully, and seriously about the big, fundamental questions of life — questions like: Why do we exist? What is right and wrong, and why? What is real? Can we truly know anything for certain?
The word philosophy has two main layers of meaning — one everyday and personal, and one formal and academic. Both are widely used, and you'll encounter both regularly.

Phlegm is a thick, sticky, slippery fluid produced by the inner lining of your lungs and the airways that lead to them — the bronchial tubes and the passages running from your lungs up to your throat.

Phlegmatic describes a person who is naturally, deeply, and habitually calm — someone whose emotional temperature simply runs cool. They are not easily excited, not easily upset, not easily stirred into passion or enthusiasm.

A phobia is an intense, irrational, and persistent fear of a specific thing, situation, animal, or activity — a fear so extreme and overwhelming that it goes far beyond what the actual danger (if any) would justify.
When someone is phobic, it means they have an intense, excessive, and often irrational fear or aversion toward a specific thing, situation, or group.
Phobophobia is the fear of fear itself.
A phoenix is a legendary, magical bird that appears in the myths and stories of many ancient cultures. It is not a real animal — it exists only in mythology and imagination.
Phonetics is the scientific study of the sounds that humans produce when they speak.
A phonograph is a machine that can both record sound and play it back. Think of it as the great-great-grandparent of today's music speakers and streaming devices.

Phony means not real, not genuine, or not sincere — but deliberately made to look as if it is. The single most important thing about this word is that deception is built into it. Something phony isn't just wrong or mistaken by accident.
Phosphorescence is the ability of certain materials to absorb light and then slowly release it back as a soft glow — even after the source of light has been completely removed.

Phosphorescent describes something that glows in the dark — but not in just any way. It describes a very specific kind of glow: one that continues even after the light source that caused it has been removed or turned off.
A photon is the smallest possible, indivisible unit of light — and of all electromagnetic radiation. Think of it as a single, tiny packet of energy that travels through space.

Phraseology means the specific words, phrases, and expressions that are chosen and arranged to communicate something — with a focus on the particular style or pattern of that language, not just the meaning.
Phrenology is the now-discredited belief that the shape and bumps of a person's skull can reveal their personality, intelligence, and character.
In biology, a major group into which living things are classified, ranking below kingdom and above class, such as the phylum of animals with backbones.
A physicist is a scientist who studies physics — the branch of science that tries to understand the most fundamental rules of how the universe works.
Physics is the branch of science that studies the most fundamental aspects of the universe — matter, energy, space, time, and the forces that connect them all.
Physiognomy means one of two closely related things: either the face and its features, or the belief/practice of judging someone's character by looking at their face.
Physiological is an adjective that means "relating to the normal functioning of a living body."
The branch of biology that studies how living things and their parts function, such as how the heart pumps blood. It can also mean the way a particular organism or body part works.
Physique refers to the overall shape, structure, and appearance of a person's body — particularly how it looks from the outside in terms of size, build, and muscular development.
Describes a story that follows a clever, roguish hero of low birth who drifts from one adventure to the next and survives on cunning and charm rather than virtue.
When you call something picayune, you are saying it is trivially small, petty, or of so little importance that it barely deserves attention.
When people picket a place, they gather outside it — usually in a visible, public way — to protest against the people or organization inside, and to pressure them into doing something differently.

A picnic is an outdoor meal shared with other people, usually in a natural or open-air setting like a park, a beach, a meadow, a forest, or a garden. The food is prepared at home beforehand, packed up, and then carried to the chosen spot to be eaten there.

Something is picturesque when it is so visually beautiful, charming, and interesting that it looks like it belongs in a painting. Not just pretty — but the kind of scene that makes you stop, stare, and wish you had a camera or a paintbrush.

A pidgin is a simplified, mixed language that springs into existence when two or more groups of people who do not share a common language are brought together and need to communicate. No one is born speaking a pidgin — it is nobody's first or native language.

A pie is a baked dish made of a filling (the food inside) that is enclosed in, covered by, or sitting inside a layer of pastry, which is called the crust. The crust is a simple dough made from flour, fat (usually butter or lard), and a little water.

A pie chart is a type of graph — a visual tool used to show how something whole is divided into parts. It looks exactly like a circular pie (the food) that has been cut into slices. Each slice represents a portion, or share, of the total whole.

Piebald describes something — almost always an animal — that has large, irregular patches of two colors, where one of them is white. The patches don't blend into each other. They have sharp edges and appear in a random, unpredictable arrangement.

When something is described as piecemeal, it means it is done, built, or developed in separate, disconnected fragments — one small piece at a time — rather than as a complete, unified whole with a clear overall plan.
Piecework is a system of work where a person is paid based on how many individual units of work they complete, not on how many hours they spend doing it.
Pied means having two or more colors appearing in irregular patches or blotches.

A pier is a long, raised walkway or platform built out from the shoreline — of a sea, lake, or river — into the water. It is supported underneath by a row of pillars, posts, or columns that are driven into the ground below the water.

To pierce means to go into or through something by making a hole or opening in it — usually with something sharp, narrow, or pointed. The action is direct, focused, and forceful. Something goes into a surface that would otherwise resist it.
To understand "piercing," start with a simple image: a needle going through cloth. It doesn't push the cloth aside — it cuts straight through it, sharp and deep.
Pierogi are a type of stuffed dumpling — small, soft pockets of dough that are folded around a filling, sealed shut, and cooked. Think of them as little dough parcels with a surprise inside.
Piety is a deep, sincere, and active devotion toward something you hold sacred or consider worthy of the highest respect. It is not just a feeling — it is a feeling expressed through action.

Piffle means foolish, trivial, or meaningless talk, writing, or ideas — the kind of thing that sounds like it might mean something, but when you actually pay attention to it, it turns out to be empty, weak, or simply not worth taking seriously.
A pigment is a substance whose job is to give color to something else. It can come from nature or be made in a laboratory.

To pilfer means to steal, but not in a grand or dramatic way. It means to take small things, of little value, usually sneakily and often repeatedly. Think of it as petty theft — the quiet, opportunistic kind.

Pilferage is the act of repeatedly stealing small things, usually in tiny amounts, in a sneaky and gradual way. Think of it as petty theft done quietly and often — not a dramatic heist, but a slow, steady trickle of things going missing.
A pilgrim is a person who travels to a place that is sacred or holy — a place of deep religious or spiritual significance — out of faith and devotion.
A pilgrimage is a journey made to a place that holds deep sacred, spiritual, or special significance to the person travelling there. It is not an ordinary trip for leisure or business.
Pillage means the act of violently stealing goods, valuables, and belongings from a place — usually a town, village, or region — on a large, widespread scale. It is not a quiet, sneaky theft.
To pillage means to steal goods, valuables, or resources from a place — such as a town, village, or territory — using force or violence, especially during a war, invasion, or raid.

A pillory is a wooden punishment device from the past — specifically, a frame with holes cut into it designed to lock a person's head and wrists in place, leaving them completely unable to move while standing upright in a public space for all to see.
To pillory someone means to publicly criticize, ridicule, or attack them in a way that is harsh, humiliating, and very visible to others.
A person who flies an aircraft, or who guides ships into or out of a harbour. A pilot is also a trial episode of a TV series, or a small test project, as in "a pilot scheme."
To pilot something means to guide or steer it with skill and responsibility. You are in control of something — and you are carefully leading it through a process, a place, or a challenge.
To hold someone down so they cannot move, as in "pinned to the ground." It can also mean to fasten something with a pin, or to place blame or hope on someone, as in "they pinned the blame on him."

A pinafore is a type of garment — specifically a sleeveless garment worn over other clothing. Think of it as something you put on top of what you're already wearing, rather than as a standalone outfit.

A pince-nez is a type of eyeglasses — but with one very important difference from the glasses you know today. It has no earpieces. No arms stretching back over your ears. Nothing hooking around the sides of your head.
That's the soul of "pincer." Every meaning this word carries is a variation of that same idea.
A very small amount of something, as in "a pinch of salt." It is also the act of squeezing skin between finger and thumb. "In a pinch" means in a difficult situation or emergency.

To pinch means to press or squeeze something firmly between two points — almost always between your thumb and one or more fingers, or between any two surfaces that come together and trap something in between.

A pine is a type of tree — specifically, an evergreen tree that belongs to a large family of trees called Pinus. "Evergreen" means it stays green all year long, even through winter, because it never completely sheds its leaves the way most trees do in autumn.
To pine means to feel a deep, quiet, and lasting sadness because you want something — or someone — that you cannot have, or that is no longer with you. It is not just wanting something.
To pine after someone or something means to feel a deep, sad, and prolonged longing for something you cannot have or have lost.
To pine away means to slowly become weak, sad, and lifeless because of deep grief or intense longing for someone or something you have lost — or cannot have.
The word pinion has two completely separate, unrelated meanings — one from the world of birds, and one from the world of machines. Context always makes it clear which one is meant.
A pinnace is a small boat — and understanding it well means understanding when and why it existed, because this word belongs firmly to the world of ships and the sea.

A pinnacle is the very highest point of something — the absolute top, the peak, the supreme level. Nothing sits above it. Think of it as the tip of a pyramid: everything else is below it, and it marks the ultimate limit of how high something can go.
To pinpoint something means to identify, locate, or define it with complete and exact precision — no guessing, no approximation, no vagueness.
A pint is a unit of measurement used to express the volume or capacity of something — essentially, how much space a liquid (or sometimes a loose dry substance) takes up.
A pioneer is someone who goes first — into a place, an idea, or a field — where very few or no one has gone before, and in doing so, opens the way for others to follow.
To pioneer something means to be the first to do, develop, explore, or introduce it — in a way that opens the door for others to follow.
Pious describes someone who is sincerely and deeply devoted to their religion. A pious person doesn't just believe — they live their faith.
A pipette is a thin, narrow tube — usually made of glass or clear plastic — used in science laboratories to measure and transfer very small, precise amounts of liquid from one container to another.
A pipsqueak is a person who is small, unimportant, or insignificant — someone who doesn't have much power, authority, or status, yet often behaves as though they do.
Piquancy is the quality of being pleasantly sharp, stimulating, or excitingly interesting — in a way that wakes up your senses or your mind and makes you want more.
Pleasantly sharp or spicy in taste. Figuratively, pleasantly stimulating, exciting, or provocative, as in "a piquant detail."

Pique is a feeling of irritation or resentment that arises specifically when your pride has been hurt — when you feel slighted, overlooked, disrespected, or not given the recognition you believe you deserve.

When something piques your interest or curiosity, it sparks it — it wakes it up or stirs it into life. Something catches your attention from the outside, and as a result, you find yourself wanting to know more.
The crime of attacking and robbing ships at sea. It also means illegally copying and selling or sharing someone else's work, such as films, music, or software.

A pirate is a person who attacks and robs ships on the water, with no permission from any government, purely for their own personal gain. Think of a pirate as an armed robber — except instead of robbing people on land, they rob ships at sea.
When you use "pirate" as a verb, it means to illegally copy, reproduce, or distribute something that belongs to someone else — without their permission and without paying for it.

A pirouette is a complete spin of the body — a full rotation — performed while balancing on just one leg. The person spins on the very tip or the ball of one foot while their other leg is lifted off the ground.

Piscatorial means relating to fish, fishing, or fishermen. If something is piscatorial, it belongs to the world of fish and fishing — the creatures, the activity of catching them, and the people who do it.
A large hole in the ground; a hollow or small dent in a surface; or the hard stone inside fruits such as peaches and cherries.
Pita is a soft, round, flat bread that is baked and eaten widely across the Middle East, the Mediterranean region, and now the whole world. It is one of the oldest types of bread humans have made.
How high or low a sound is. A pitch is also a sports field, a persuasive sales talk, as in "a sales pitch," the degree of slope of a roof, or a dark sticky substance like tar.

Piteous is an adjective that describes something so sad, suffering, or helpless that it makes you feel deep sorrow and compassion when you see or hear it. In other words, something piteous moves you to feel pity.

A pitfall is a hidden danger, difficulty, or mistake that is easy to stumble into — especially when you are not paying close attention or don't have enough experience. Think of it as a trap waiting for you that you don't see coming.
"Pith" has two main families of meaning — one literal (physical), one figurative — plus an older, less common sense worth knowing. Understanding all three will give you the complete picture.
Pithy describes something that says a great deal in very few words — and says it powerfully.

"Pitiful" describes something or someone that triggers a strong emotional reaction in you — either deep sympathy or quiet contempt. These are its two distinct meanings, and understanding both is essential because they're used differently.
Pitiless means showing absolutely no pity, mercy, or sympathy — especially toward someone who is suffering, struggling, or in pain.
A pittance is a very small amount of money — so small that it feels unfair, insulting, or laughably inadequate compared to what was expected, deserved, or needed.
To pivot means to turn or rotate around a fixed central point.

Pivotal means so critically important that everything else depends on it, turns because of it, or is shaped by it. Something pivotal is not just important — it is the central point that determines the direction, outcome, or success of everything around it.

Pizzazz is a quality that makes a person, object, performance, or place feel exciting, glamorous, and impossible to ignore. It is that special "something" — a blend of energy, style, and flair — that lifts something from ordinary to extraordinary.

A placard is a flat piece of card, board, or stiff material that has writing, a message, or an image on it — and is meant to be seen by people. Think of it as a sign that communicates something to the public.
To placate someone means to calm down a person who is already angry, upset, or irritated — usually by doing or saying something that satisfies them, at least partially.
Placatory describes something that is meant to calm a person's anger, soothe their hurt feelings, or restore peace after a conflict or offense.

A placebo is a fake treatment — such as a sugar pill, a saline (salt-water) injection, or even a sham surgery — that contains no active medical ingredient and has no direct physical effect on the body.
Placid means calm, peaceful, and not easily disturbed or upset.
Placidity means the state or quality of being deeply, gently calm — undisturbed, untroubled, and at peace.
When someone or something acts placidly, they do it with a calm, peaceful, undisturbed quality — as if nothing in the world could bother or agitate them.
Plagiarism is the act of taking someone else's work, words, or ideas and presenting them as your own, without giving that person credit.
To plagiarize means to take someone else's words, ideas, or creative work and present them as your own — without giving credit to the original creator.

A plague is a disease — but not just any ordinary disease. It is a disease that spreads very fast, affects an enormous number of people across a wide area, kills many of those it infects, and feels almost impossible to stop or escape.
To plague someone or something means to cause continuous, serious trouble or suffering that is very hard to escape or get rid of.
A plaintiff is the person (or group, or organization) who starts a lawsuit against someone else because they believe they have been wronged.

Plaintive describes a sound, voice, expression, or tone that carries a quiet, aching sadness — the kind that makes you feel sympathy almost instantly. It is the sound of gentle sorrow, not of rage or despair.

Plaintively means doing something in a way that expresses gentle, mournful sadness or longing — often with a quiet, soft quality, as if the person (or creature, or sound) is expressing sorrow that is helpless, tender, and sometimes silently appealing for sympathy.
A plait is a single, rope-like length of something — most often hair — that has been made by weaving three or more strands over and under each other in a regular, repeating pattern.

A plan is a decision, made in advance, about what you are going to do and how you are going to do it. It lives in your mind or on paper before action begins. The moment you act, the plan starts becoming reality — or it doesn't, if things go sideways.
A plangent sound is one that is loud and resonant, and carries a deep sense of sadness or longing with it.
Plankton are living organisms — animals, plants, bacteria, and others — that live in water and drift wherever the current takes them, because they are either too small or too weak to swim against it.
The word plantain as a noun refers to two completely different things. They share the same name but have no connection to each other. Understanding both is essential to truly knowing this word.
A large estate where crops such as tea, coffee, cotton, or sugar are grown, historically often worked by enslaved people. It can also mean an area of planted trees.

A plaque is something flat that sits on or inside a surface — whether that surface is a wall, a tooth, or an artery. This idea of "a flat layer or patch clinging to something" connects all of its meanings.

Plaster is a thick, paste-like substance that is spread over walls, ceilings, and sometimes floors while it is still soft and wet. Once it dries, it becomes hard, smooth, and solid — almost like a thin shell of stone covering the surface underneath.
The word "plastic," as an adjective, has one powerful core idea, and almost everything else about the word flows from that idea.
Plasticity is the quality of being able to change shape, form, or structure permanently — and stay that way.
A plateau is something that is elevated and flat — raised above everything around it, but level on top rather than pointed or sloped.

A platform is a flat, raised surface that lifts something or someone above the surrounding level. Everything else this word means — and it means a lot — flows from this one simple image: something raised up, made stable, and ready to support.
A platitude is a statement that sounds meaningful or wise, but is actually hollow and overused — so worn out from repetition that it has lost any real impact or depth.

Platitudinous describes something — a statement, a speech, a piece of writing, or a person's communication style — that is full of dull, obvious, overused remarks presented as though they are wise, deep, or meaningful, when in reality they say nothing new, useful, or genuinely insightful.
Of a relationship, close and affectionate but not romantic or sexual, as in "platonic friendship." It can also mean relating to the philosophy of Plato.
