A resin is a thick, sticky substance that starts as a liquid or soft semi-solid and can harden into a tough, durable solid over time. Think of it as nature's version of glue or sealant — something that flows when fresh and sets firm when dry.
To resist something means to hold firm against a force that is trying to affect you, change you, overcome you, or pull you somewhere you don't want to go.

Resistance is a pushing back. Whenever a force tries to move, change, harm, or overcome something, resistance is the opposing force that pushes back against it — making that harder, slower, or even impossible.

When something is resistant, it means it is able to withstand, fight off, or not be easily affected by something — or, when talking about a person, it means they are unwilling to accept or go along with something.

If you are resolute, you have made up your mind about something, and nothing — no obstacle, no criticism, no difficulty, no pressure from others — can make you give up or change course. You are firm. You are decided. You will not waver.

When someone does something resolutely, they do it with firm, unwavering determination — having made a clear decision, they follow through on it completely, without hesitation, doubt, or backing down.
When you firmly decide to do something (or stop doing something) — not casually, but with real commitment — that decision is called a resolution.
Resolve means a deep, firm, and unshakeable decision to do something — especially something hard — and the inner strength to see it through no matter what.
To find a solution to a problem or settle a dispute, as in "resolve the conflict." It can also mean to make a firm decision to do something, as in "she resolved to quit."
Resonance means a powerful, amplified response that occurs when something receives energy in a way that perfectly matches its own natural tendency to vibrate or respond.
Of a sound, deep, clear, and continuing to echo, as in "a resonant voice." Figuratively, bringing to mind strong feelings, images, or memories, as in "a resonant phrase."
To strike a chord with someone, or to have a strong personal meaning for them, as in "her words resonated with the audience." Literally, to produce a deep, full sound that echoes or vibrates.
A resort is a place — usually a large hotel or a whole complex — that is specifically designed so that people can relax, have fun, and enjoy their free time.
To resort to something means to turn to a particular action or solution — especially when other, better options have failed, are unavailable, or are simply not enough.
To resound means to ring out loudly and powerfully — and especially to fill an entire space with sound, so the sound seems to vibrate all around you, coming from every direction at once.
Emphatic and unmistakable, as in "a resounding success" or "a resounding no." Literally, loud and echoing.
A resource is anything — a thing, a person, a quality, or a capability — that is available to you and can be used to get something done, meet a need, or solve a problem.

Resourceful means being very good at finding clever, practical solutions to problems — especially when you don't have much to work with. A resourceful person does not give up when things get difficult or when they are short on time, money, tools, or help.
Respect is an attitude of recognition — you see that someone or something has genuine worth, value, or importance, and that recognition shapes how you think about them and how you treat them.
Honest, decent and socially acceptable ("a respectable family"); or fairly good in amount or quality ("a respectable score").
Respectful describes a person, action, manner, or attitude that shows respect — meaning it recognizes someone's worth, dignity, or importance, and treats them accordingly.
"Respective" means "each one's own — applied separately to each person or thing already mentioned."
"Respectively" means "each one in the order that was just listed."

Respiration means the process of breathing — specifically, the complete cycle of drawing air into your body and then pushing it back out. One full cycle of breathing in (inhaling) and breathing out (exhaling) is one act of respiration.
"Respiratory" simply means: relating to, involving, or connected with breathing.
A respite is a temporary break or relief from something difficult, painful, unpleasant, or exhausting — a welcome pause before the hard thing continues.

Resplendence is the quality of being dazzlingly bright, visually magnificent, and gloriously impressive — all at once. When something has resplendence, it shines and dazzles so powerfully that it fills the people who see it with a feeling of awe and wonder.

Something that is resplendent is so visually magnificent, so rich and dazzling in its appearance, that it commands immediate admiration and awe. It describes a kind of beauty that is not quiet or subtle — it is bold, brilliant, and impossible to ignore.

To respond means to do or say something as a reaction to something that happened or was said. The key idea is that something always comes first — a question, a situation, an action, a stimulus — and your response comes after, because of it.

A respondent is simply a person who responds — someone who is formally placed in the position of giving an answer or a reply to something directed at them. That "something" is always official or structured in nature, not casual.
Responsibility means being in a position where you are expected to do something, take care of something, or answer for the consequences of something.
Having a duty to do or take care of something; being the cause of something ("Who is responsible for this mess?"); or reliable and sensible.
Responsive describes someone or something that reacts — and not just reacts, but reacts readily, appropriately, and in a useful way.
Responsiveness is the quality of being able and willing to react to something — quickly, suitably, and in a way that fits the situation.

Restitution means the act of giving something back, or making up for something that was taken, damaged, or lost — with the goal of restoring a person to the exact position they were in before the wrong was done to them.
Restive means unwilling to be controlled, impatient under restriction, or stubbornly resisting authority — and therefore difficult to manage.

Restless describes a state of being unable to stay still or be at peace — either physically, mentally, or emotionally. Something restless is in constant motion, or constantly unsettled, and cannot seem to stop or calm down.
Restoration means the act of bringing something back to the state it was in before — before it was damaged, lost, taken away, or broken down.

When you say something is restorative, you mean it has the power to bring something — your energy, your health, your emotional state, or even a physical thing — back to a good condition after it has been depleted, damaged, or lost.
To restore something means to bring it back to the condition, state, or position it was in before — before it was damaged, lost, taken away, or changed for the worse.
To restrain means to hold something or someone back, keep it under control, or prevent it from acting, moving, or growing freely.

A restraining order is an official legal command issued by a court of law that tells a specific person to stop doing something — most commonly, to stay away from another person or to stop contacting them.
Restraint is the act, quality, or force of holding something back from going further than it should.
To resume something means to start doing it again after a pause or interruption.
Resumption means the act of starting something again after it has been paused or interrupted.

Resurgent describes something that is rising, growing, or becoming powerful again — after a period of decline, weakness, or fading. The most important word in that sentence is again. Something resurgent is not growing for the first time.
To resurrect something means to bring it back to life, or back into existence, after it had completely died, ended, or disappeared.
To resuscitate someone or something means to bring it back to life, consciousness, or activity after it has stopped — or nearly stopped.
To retain means to keep something and not let it go away.
When you hire a professional — most commonly a lawyer, but also consultants, accountants, or PR agencies — you sometimes pay them a retainer upfront, before they even do any work for you.
To retaliate means to deliberately do something harmful or unpleasant to someone, because they did something harmful or unpleasant to you first.
Retaliation is the act of doing something harmful or unpleasant to someone because they first did something harmful or unpleasant to you.
To retard something means to slow it down or delay its progress — especially something that is naturally moving forward, growing, or developing.

A retelling is a new version of a story, event, or account that already exists and is already known. Someone takes a story — a myth, a folktale, a novel, a historical event, a religious text — and tells it again, but in a new way.
Retention means the act of keeping something, or the ability/state of holding onto something — without losing it, releasing it, or letting it leave.
Retentive means having the ability to hold onto something and not let it go — whether that "something" is information in the mind, moisture in the soil, or a substance in the body.

Reticence is the quality of being unwilling to speak freely or share information. It is the tendency to hold back your thoughts, feelings, or knowledge — to say less than you could, especially about things that are personal or sensitive.

If someone is reticent, they are unwilling to speak freely or openly — especially about their personal thoughts, feelings, or private information. A reticent person holds things back. They don't share much. They keep their cards close to their chest.

Reticulate describes anything that has a net-like pattern — a structure where lines, veins, fibers, cracks, or ridges crisscross and interconnect with each other, forming a mesh of enclosed spaces in between.

Reticulated means having a pattern that looks like a net — a surface or structure marked by intersecting lines that cross, branch, and connect to form a web of shapes or cells, just like the mesh of a fishing net.
A retinue is a group of people who regularly accompany, assist, and serve one important or powerful person — wherever that person goes.
"Retire" means to withdraw from something — to step back, step away, or stop being part of something, either permanently or temporarily. Everything else about this word grows from that root idea.

Retirement means the act of permanently leaving your job, career, or a role you have held — usually after many years of working — and not returning to it again. It also refers to the entire period of life that comes after you stop working.
When "retiring" is used as an adjective, it describes a person who is naturally shy, quiet, and modest — someone who genuinely prefers to stay in the background rather than be noticed.
A retort is a quick, sharp reply — the kind you give when someone has criticized you, insulted you, or said something to challenge or provoke you. It is not just any response. It has an edge to it.

To retort is to reply to someone in a sharp, quick, and often clever way — especially when that person has criticized you, accused you of something, insulted you, or said something challenging. It is not just any reply. It's a comeback. A fired-back response.

To retrace something means to go over something again that was already covered before — following the exact same path, sequence, or course a second time. The key idea is that you are going back along something that already existed, not creating something new.

Retract means to pull something back — either physically (an object moves back to where it came from) or figuratively (you take back something you said or offered). That image of pulling back is the single thread that connects every use of this word.

A retraction is the official act of taking back something that was previously said, written, published, or claimed — because it was wrong, false, misleading, or should not have been stated in the first place.
To retreat means to move back or pull away from something — usually from a place, a situation, a person, or even a position you held.
To retrench means to cut back — specifically to reduce spending, resources, or the size of a workforce in response to financial pressure or a need to become more economical.
Retrenchment means deliberately cutting back — reducing spending, resources, staff, or activities, usually because of financial pressure or a need to survive a difficult period.
Retribution means punishment that someone receives because of something bad they did — specifically, punishment that is seen as deserved and fair based on the harm they caused.
If something is retributive, it is meant to punish someone because they did something wrong. It's about making sure a wrongdoer "gets what they deserve."
To retrieve something means to go and get it back — especially when it was stored away, lost, thrown somewhere, or became hard to access — and bring it back to where it is needed.

Retroactive describes something that applies backwards in time — meaning it doesn't just take effect from now or the future, but reaches back to cover things that already happened in the past, even before the rule, law, or decision was made.

Retrograde means moving backward, going in the opposite direction from what is normal, or returning to an earlier and worse state. Think of it as the opposite of progress or forward movement — literal or figurative.
Retrospect means a look back at the past — specifically, the act of thinking about or reviewing something that has already happened.
The adjective retrospective means looking back at the past, or relating to things that already happened.
Retroussé is an adjective used almost exclusively to describe a specific type of nose — one whose tip is turned or tilted slightly upward, so that the nostrils are partially visible from the front.
Repeat bookings of a performer or speaker at a venue where they have appeared before, usually because they were popular the first time.

To revamp something means to improve it in a deep, sweeping way — to rework it so thoroughly that it comes out the other side noticeably better, more modern, or more effective than it was before. It is not about making tiny fixes.

Revanchism is a political belief or policy where a country, government, or group is so deeply bitter about something it has lost — usually territory, power, or national pride — that it becomes obsessed with getting it back.
To reveal something means to make something known or visible that was previously hidden, unknown, or kept secret.
Reveille is a signal — most commonly a short, brisk bugle call — sounded early in the morning to wake up soldiers and officially mark the start of the military day.
To revel means to take intense, open, and enthusiastic pleasure in something — or to celebrate in a loud, joyful, festive way. It's not quiet or subtle enjoyment.
A revelation is the act of making something known that was hidden, secret, or unknown before — or it is the piece of information itself that gets uncovered. Think of it like lifting a curtain.
Revelry means loud, lively, joyful celebration — the kind where a group of people is having an uproariously good time together, often with music, dancing, laughter, and usually drinks.

A revenant is a dead person — or sometimes a dead creature — who has come back from death and now exists among the living. The single most important thing to understand about this word is that the "coming back" is the whole point.
Revenge is the act of deliberately harming someone because they harmed you first. It is a response — specifically a harmful response — to something hurtful that was done to you.
Revenue is the total amount of money that flows into a person, business, or organization from their normal activities — counted before any expenses or costs are subtracted.
To reverberate means to bounce back and keep spreading, whether that's a sound echoing through a space, or the effects of an event continuing to be felt long after it happened.
In its most fundamental sense, reverberation is the persistence of sound in a space after the original source of that sound has stopped, caused by sound waves bouncing repeatedly off surfaces.
To revere someone or something means to feel a very deep, almost sacred level of respect and admiration for them — so deep that it borders on awe or worship.

When someone or something is described as revered, it means they are held in the deepest, most profound respect — a respect so strong that it borders on worship or devotion. It goes far beyond ordinary admiration.
Reverence is a feeling — a deep, solemn mixture of respect, awe, and admiration that you feel toward something or someone you consider truly great, sacred, or worthy of the highest honor.
A title of respect for a member of the clergy ("the Reverend John Smith"); also deserving deep respect.
Reverent describes a deep, sincere, almost sacred form of respect — the kind that comes straight from the heart and is mixed with a strong sense of awe and admiration.

Reverential means showing or expressing a feeling of very deep, humble respect mixed with a sense of awe — the kind of respect you feel not just in your mind, but that shows up in the way you speak, act, move, and carry yourself.
A reverie is a state of pleasant, dreamy thinking that you drift into while you are fully awake.
To reverse means to go against the current direction, order, or state of something — either by moving backward, flipping things around, or undoing what was done.
To revert means to go back to a state, condition, behavior, or topic that existed before.
To revile someone means to attack them with harsh, bitter, and deeply contemptuous words — to verbally tear into someone with anger and scorn. It is not a quiet complaint or a polite disagreement.

When something is described as revised, it means that it originally existed in one form, was then carefully looked at again, and was changed or corrected — to make it better, more accurate, or more up to date.
To revisit something means to go back to it — after a gap of time — and engage with it again.
To revitalize something means to bring it back to a state of energy, strength, and active life after it has become weak, tired, slow, or dull.
A revival is what happens when something that had faded away, stopped, or nearly died comes back to life again.
To revive means to bring something back to life, strength, activity, or awareness after it had weakened, stopped, or nearly disappeared.

To revivify something means to bring it back to life, energy, or vitality after it had grown weak, dull, lifeless, or inactive. Think of it as breathing fresh life and vigor into something that had lost its spark.
Revocation is the official act of taking back, canceling, or withdrawing something that was previously granted, issued, or put into force. When something is revoked, it is no longer valid.

To revoke something means to officially cancel or take it back — especially something that was given, granted, or decided in the past, and that had been giving someone a right, a power, or a permission.
A revolt is when a group of people says "enough" — and then does something about it.
To rise up against a ruler or authority, as in "the people revolted." It can also mean to make someone feel disgust, as in "the cruelty revolted her."
Revolting describes something that causes a strong, powerful feeling of disgust — the kind that makes you want to immediately back away, look away, or even feel physically sick.

The overthrow of a government by its people, often by force. It can also mean a dramatic and far-reaching change, as in "the digital revolution," or one complete turn around a central point, as of the Earth around the Sun.

A revolutionary is a person who actively works to bring about a revolution — a sudden, sweeping, and total change in society, almost always in its political system, its government, or its social order.

A revolver is most commonly a type of handgun — a firearm small enough to be held and fired with one hand. What makes a revolver unique and different from other handguns is one key feature: a rotating cylinder.
Revulsion is an intense, overwhelming feeling of disgust and loathing — so strong that it makes you want to recoil, back away, or turn away completely from whatever is causing it.
Rhapsodic means expressing overwhelming enthusiasm, joy, or admiration in an intensely passionate, almost uncontrollable way.

To rhapsodize means to talk or write about something with enormous, overflowing enthusiasm and admiration — often with so much passion and emotion that your words pour out almost uncontrollably. You are not just saying "I liked it."

"Rhapsody" always carries one central idea: a free-flowing, passionate outpouring of feeling — whether in words, music, or emotion. Something that is a rhapsody is not controlled, structured, or restrained.
Rhetoric is the skill and art of using language effectively to communicate, persuade, or move people. Think of language as a raw material — like wood or clay.

Relating to the skilful use of language to persuade or impress. A rhetorical question is one asked for effect, with no answer expected. It can also mean showy but empty, as in "mere rhetorical flourishes."
A rhetorician is a person who is highly skilled in the art of using language — especially spoken or written language — to persuade, influence, or move an audience.
Rheum refers to a thin, watery discharge that seeps naturally from the eyes, nose, or mouth — particularly the kind produced when you are sick, cold, or simply waking up from sleep.
Rheumatic means: of, relating to, or caused by rheumatism — or affected by rheumatism.
Rheumatism refers to pain, stiffness, swelling, or restricted movement in the joints, muscles, and the soft tissues surrounding them.
Describing eyes that are watery and moist, often because of old age or a cold.

Rhythmic is an adjective that describes something which has a regular, repeated pattern — especially in its timing, beats, or movements. When something is rhythmic, it doesn't happen randomly or chaotically.
"Rhythmically" means in a way that follows a regular, repeating pattern.

Rib-tickling means extremely funny — funny in a way that makes you laugh out loud, openly, and heartily. When you call something rib-tickling, you are saying it produces the kind of laughter that is real, strong, and hard to hold back.

Ribald describes something that deals with sex or the human body in a way that is crude, rude, and coarse — but also, crucially, meant to be funny. That last part is the heart of the word. Ribald humor is not dark or disturbing or harmful.

Ribaldry is crude, vulgar, or indecent humor — especially the kind that involves sex, bodily functions, or other "taboo" topics — delivered in a way that is meant to be funny, lively, and entertaining rather than genuinely harmful or serious.
Friendly, good-natured teasing, as in "he took a lot of ribbing from his friends." It is also a pattern of raised ridges in knitting or fabric.

If something is rickety, it is weak, unstable, and likely to break, fall apart, or collapse — especially because it is old, worn out, or badly made. The single most important idea locked inside this word is: it looks like it could give way at any moment.
A rickshaw is a small, lightweight vehicle designed to carry one or two passengers as paying customers, typically over short distances.
When something ricochets, it hits a hard surface and bounces off in a new direction, continuing to move rather than stopping.
A rictus is a wide, rigid, open-mouthed grin or grimace — one that is frozen on a person's (or animal's) face, and that looks unnatural, forced, or locked in place.
When you riddle something, you pierce it so many times that it ends up full of holes — like a sieve or a piece of Swiss cheese.

When something is riddled with something, it means that thing is completely full of it — spread throughout, in large amounts, and impossible to ignore. But there's an important twist: what it's full of is almost always something bad, harmful, or unwanted.
A person riding a horse, bicycle or motorbike; also an extra clause added to a document, law or agreement.

A ridge is a long, narrow, raised strip — something that runs lengthwise and sits higher than the surfaces on either side of it. Think of it like the spine of a book: raised in the middle, with flat or lower areas dropping away on both sides.
Ridicule is the act of making someone — or something — look foolish, stupid, or absurd, usually through mocking words, cruel jokes, or contemptuous laughter.
Something is ridiculous when it is so unreasonable, absurd, or extreme that it cannot be taken seriously.
A famous unsolved problem in mathematics, proposed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, about the pattern of zeros of a special function, which would reveal how prime numbers are distributed.

Rife means that something — almost always something bad or unwanted — is so common and widespread that it is hard to avoid or ignore. It describes a situation where a problem, danger, or negative thing is everywhere around you, present in large amounts.
Riffraff refers to a group of people who are seen as low-class, disreputable, rough, or simply undesirable — people that someone considers beneath them or not worth associating with.
To rifle through something means to search through it quickly, roughly, and carelessly — usually tossing items aside, creating disorder — in order to find something specific or steal valuables.
A rift is a crack, split, or gap that forms when something that was once whole or connected breaks apart.

The verb rig has two very different lives — one honest, one dishonest. They are connected by a shared idea: secretly or cleverly arranging something. Understanding both will give you full command of this word.
"Right as rain" means perfectly fine, in excellent condition, or fully recovered.

Righteous means morally right, just, and virtuous. A righteous person is someone who does what is genuinely good and fair — not just following rules because they have to, but because they have strong, deeply held moral principles and they live by them.

Righteousness is the quality of being morally good, fair, and just — not just once in a while, but as a deep, consistent part of who you are. It's about genuinely doing what is right, treating others fairly, and living with integrity.

When something belongs to you, or is owed to you, or is proper and appropriate for you — based on a genuine, recognized reason — it is rightful. That reason might come from law, morality, fairness, tradition, or a combination of these.
Rigid means unable to bend, change, or flex. Something rigid holds its shape, its position, or its way completely — it does not give way, it does not adapt, and it does not move from where it stands.
A rigmarole is something that is unnecessarily long, complicated, or confusing — and because of that, it is frustrating and tiresome.

Rigor means a quality of being extremely thorough, careful, precise, and uncompromising — whether in thinking, working, following rules, or enduring difficulty. Think of it as the opposite of being sloppy, careless, or half-hearted.

Rigor mortis is the stiffening of a dead body's muscles that occurs naturally after death. The word is used as a noun — you would say "rigor mortis has set in" or "the body was in a state of rigor mortis."
Extremely careful, thorough, and exact — with no shortcuts, no sloppiness, and no room for errors or loose ends.
To rile someone means to irritate, annoy, or anger them — to get on their nerves and stir up a feeling of frustration or agitation inside them.

"Rile up" is a phrasal verb (a verb + a particle working together as one unit of meaning). It means to make someone emotionally agitated — usually angry, irritated, or intensely worked up about something.
When someone is riled, they are annoyed, irritated, or agitated — their calm has been disturbed, and they feel a rising sense of frustration or anger inside. It is not a quiet, still emotion.

A rill is a very small, narrow stream of flowing water. Think of it as one of the tiniest forms of moving water you can find in nature — a thin trickle or gentle thread of water moving along the ground.

Rime is a coating of rough, white ice that forms on outdoor surfaces — tree branches, grass, fences, power lines, rocks, aircraft wings — when the air is foggy or misty and the temperature is at or below freezing.
A riot is a situation where a large group of people lose control in public — becoming violent, destructive, and impossible to manage. It is not just a crowd being loud or angry.

Riotous describes something that has completely broken free from normal limits — it is wilder, louder, funnier, or more intense than what is considered controlled or moderate. Think of it as "so much of something that it overflows."

Rip means to tear something with force and speed. But not just any tearing — ripping is raw, sudden, and rough. It leaves behind jagged, uneven edges, not clean ones. And it's almost always accompanied by that characteristic tearing sound.
Riparian means relating to, found on, or associated with the bank of a river or stream.
Ripe means fully developed and ready. It describes something that has reached its best, most complete state — not too early, not too late, but exactly at the right point.

A riposte is a swift, sharp counter-move made in direct response to an attack. That's the idea you should hold onto above everything else — it is always a response, never a first move, and it always strikes back.
Having a very muscular, well-defined body with little fat (informal). It can also mean torn, as in "ripped jeans," or, in slang, drunk or high.
To ripple means to move, flow, or spread in small, gentle, wave-like motions — or to cause something to do so. Think of a calm pond. You throw a small pebble into it.

Rise means the act or process of going upward, or an increase in something. Whether something moves physically higher, grows in number, or climbs in power — that movement or growth is a rise. Think of it as capturing the energy of going up.

Risible means so absurd, foolish, or ridiculous that it provokes laughter — specifically the kind of laughter you can't help but let out when something is just too stupid or unreasonable to take seriously.

Something risqué is slightly sexual, indecent, or improper in a way that pushes the boundary of what is considered acceptable — but without crossing all the way into being fully explicit, crude, or truly offensive.
A rite is a formal act or series of acts performed in a specific, set way — usually because of religious belief, cultural tradition, or social custom. It is not just any action.
A rite of passage is an event, ceremony, or experience that marks a significant change in a person's life — specifically, a move from one stage, role, or identity to another.
A ritual is a series of actions performed in a specific, fixed way — usually in the same order, at the same time or occasion — that carries a deeper meaning beyond the actions themselves.
A rival is a person, group, or thing that competes with another for the same goal — and is roughly equal in ability or strength, making the competition genuinely close and real.

To rival something means to be as good as it, or to come very close to matching it in a particular quality. It's a comparison word. When you say X rivals Y, you're saying: "X has reached the same impressive level as Y."
Something is rivalrous when one person using it, consuming it, or having it means there is less of it left for everyone else. The more people "compete" over it, the scarcer it gets.
To rive means to split, tear, or break something apart — usually with great, violent force.
Riven means split apart, torn open, or deeply divided — usually in a way that is violent, painful, and severe.
A rivet is a small, solid pin made of metal, used to permanently join two or more pieces of material together.
When someone is riveted, they are so completely and intensely focused on something that they cannot look away, move, or think about anything else.

When something is riveting, it grabs your attention so powerfully and completely that you find it almost impossible to look away, stop reading, stop listening, or stop watching. You are fully locked in.

A rivulet is a very small, thin stream of flowing liquid — most commonly water. Think of it as a tiny river. When you see a narrow line of water trickling slowly across a surface or down a slope, that is a rivulet.
A roadrunner is a real bird — and understanding it fully means knowing what it looks like, how it lives, and why it has that name.
To roam means to move around from place to place without a fixed destination or a specific plan.
Roan describes a specific coat color pattern seen mainly in animals — most famously horses, but also cattle and some dog breeds.

A robber is a person who takes something that belongs to someone else — usually money or valuable items — by using force, violence, or the threat of violence. The key idea is power over the victim. A robber doesn't sneak around quietly.
A robe is a long, loose garment that wraps around the entire body, typically from the shoulders down to the knees or ankles.
Robust means strong, healthy, and built to handle difficulty without breaking down or failing.
A "rock star" is someone who is not just good at what they do — they are exceptional, admired, and celebrated for it. The word carries a feeling of excitement, admiration, and awe.
Rococo means elaborately decorated to the point of excess.
A rodent is a type of mammal — a warm-blooded, usually furry animal that gives birth to live young and nurses them with milk.

Rodomontade is a type of speech or writing in which someone boasts about themselves in an empty, exaggerated, and theatrical way — talking very big about their own achievements, power, or greatness, but without any real substance to back it up.
Rogue describes something or someone that has broken away from the control, rules, or expected behavior of a system — and in doing so, has become unpredictable and often dangerous.

A rogue is a person who is dishonest, untrustworthy, or badly behaved — but with a twist. Unlike a cold-blooded villain, a rogue is often charming, clever, and even likable despite their bad behavior.
To make a liquid muddy or turbulent by stirring up sediment. Figuratively, to disturb or agitate something, or to make someone angry, as in "markets were roiled by the news."
Roiling describes something that is in a state of intense, violent, chaotic agitation — churning, swirling, and completely disturbed, with nothing settled or still.

To roister means to enjoy yourself in a loud, noisy, and unrestrained way — to have a wild, rowdy good time, often with others, often with drinking involved, and with little concern for being quiet or well-behaved.

Roko's Basilisk is a thought experiment proposing that a future all-powerful artificial intelligence might punish — by simulating and torturing them — the people who knew it could exist but chose not to help bring it into being.
A roller skate is a specially designed boot — similar to a regular shoe or ankle boot — that has small wheels fixed to its bottom.

To roller-skate means to move around or travel by wearing roller skates — special boots or shoes that have small wheels fixed to the bottom — and gliding smoothly across a surface by pushing off the ground with your feet.

Rollicking means full of lively, noisy, and carefree fun. When you call something rollicking, you are saying it is bursting with cheerful, uninhibited energy — the kind that sweeps you up in the moment and makes you want to join in.
"Rolling" as a noun names the act, process, or motion of something that rolls — meaning something that turns over and over, or rotates around an axis while moving.

A roman à clef is a novel — or sometimes a film, play, or other narrative — in which real people, real events, and real places are given fictional names and presented as invented, while actually being recognizable, thinly or heavily disguised accounts of things that truly happened.

To romanticize something means to think about it, talk about it, or portray it in a way that makes it seem far more beautiful, exciting, or ideal than it actually is — by mentally focusing on the appealing parts and filtering out or ignoring the flaws, hardships, and ugly realities.
To play roughly and energetically, as in "children romping in the garden." It can also mean to win easily, as in "they romped to victory."
A large crucifix, especially one set above the entrance to a church's choir; also an old unit of land, a quarter of an acre.

What it looks like: A rook is shaped like a small tower or castle turret — a flat-topped cylinder with notches cut into the top edge, like a medieval battlement. This is why people casually call it a "castle," though rook is the proper chess term.
A roost is a place where birds — and sometimes bats — go to sleep, rest, or take shelter, especially at night. Think of it as a bird's bedroom, or its regular sleeping spot.
A rooster is an adult male chicken. That is the heart of what the word means.

A root cellar is an underground (or partially underground) storage space — usually built beneath a house or dug into a hillside — where people store food, especially vegetables and fruits, to keep them fresh for a long time without electricity or refrigeration.
A rosary is a string of beads used by Catholics to count prayers as they repeat them in a specific order while meditating on scenes from the lives of Jesus and Mary.
Rose-coloured or pink, as in "a roseate dawn." Figuratively, overly hopeful or optimistic, as in "a roseate view of the future."
A rosette is anything that is arranged or shaped to look like a rose — specifically, like a rose viewed from above, with parts fanning outward in a circle from a central point.

A roster is an official list of people who belong to a group, team, or organization — often including extra details like their roles, assigned duties, or scheduled times. The simplest way to think of it: the official roll call of a group.
A rostrum is essentially any raised, elevated platform that lifts a person above the surrounding floor or ground level so they can be seen and heard by an audience.
Rot means decay — the slow breakdown and destruction of something, especially something that was once living or healthy.
Rotary means relating to, involving, or caused by rotation — that is, the spinning or turning of something around a fixed central point or axis.
To rotate means to turn around a central point or a central line, the way a wheel spins around its axle, or the way the Earth turns around an imaginary line running through its poles.
Rote means the practice of learning or memorizing something purely through repetition — saying it, reading it, or drilling it over and over again — without actually understanding what it means.
Roti is a soft, round, flat bread from South Asia — the kind eaten every day by hundreds of millions of people in India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, and neighboring countries.
Rotund means round and full — imagine a perfect circle or a ball. That roundness is the soul of this word. Everything else the word means flows from that single visual idea.
A rotunda is a large, circular room or building — and almost always, it has a dome above it. Those two things — the round shape and the domed ceiling — are what define a rotunda.
Rotundity simply means the quality or state of being round. When something has rotundity, it has a round, full, curved shape — like a sphere or a globe.
Rouge is a makeup product — a soft powder or cream that is reddish-pink in color — applied to the cheeks to give them a warm, rosy, flushed glow.
Having an uneven, bumpy surface; not gentle or careful; difficult and unpleasant ("a rough day"); or approximate ("a rough guess").
Almost every time you encounter "rough-edged" in real life, it is describing a person's character, a creative work, or a situation — not a physical object.

Roughhousing is loud, physical, energetic play where people wrestle, tumble, chase, shove, pin each other down, or generally get into each other's space in a wild and boisterous way — all in good fun, with no real intention to hurt anyone.

When something is roundabout, it is not direct. Instead of going straight to the point — whether physically or in words — it goes around, takes a longer path, or approaches things in an indirect way. Think of it as the opposite of a straight line.

A roundelay is a short, simple song — but one with a very specific and defining feature: a phrase or section that keeps coming back, again and again, throughout the song. This repeating part is called a refrain (or sometimes a "burden").

When something is rousing, it stirs up strong, positive feelings in people — excitement, enthusiasm, energy, or inspiration. It wakes something up inside you emotionally. It makes you feel fired up, alive, and ready.

A rout is not just a defeat. It is a total, crushing, chaotic defeat — the kind where the losing side doesn't just lose, but completely falls apart and flees in panic and disorder. Think of it as the most extreme point on a scale of losing.
To defeat someone completely and force them to retreat in disorder, as in "the army was routed." It can also mean to search through something, or to drive someone out of a place.
When routine is used as an adjective, it describes something that is ordinary, standard, and nothing out of the usual.
A routine is a fixed set of actions that you do repeatedly, usually in the same order, and often at the same time.
A roué is a man who has spent his life chasing pleasure — particularly sensual, morally questionable pleasure — with no shame and no restraint.

To rove means to move or travel freely across a wide area, without a fixed destination, a planned route, or a specific goal. It is deliberate movement — you are actively going somewhere — but where exactly is open. You follow no schedule and answer to no map.
"Rubbish" means something that has no value, is not wanted, or is not true. This one idea branches into three closely related meanings, all of which share the same spirit: worthlessness.

Rubble is a noun that refers to the broken, fragmented remains of a structure — most commonly a building, wall, bridge, or any construction made of hard materials like stone, brick, concrete, or mortar — after it has been destroyed, collapsed, or demolished.
A rube is a person who is naive, gullible, and easily fooled — someone who lacks the worldly experience and street-smarts to recognize when they're being tricked, manipulated, or taken advantage of.
Rubescent describes something that is turning red, becoming reddish, or taking on a red flush. The key idea locked inside this word is not just being red — it is the process or quality of reddening.
Rubicund is an adjective that means having a reddish or rosy complexion, especially in the face.
A rubric is a structured guide — something that provides a framework for organizing, classifying, or evaluating things. It tells you the rules of the game, or how to make sense of something.
A rucksack is a bag designed to be carried on your back. It attaches to your body using two straps — one strap goes over each shoulder — so both your hands stay completely free while you carry it.

A ruckus is a noisy, chaotic disturbance — a situation where there is a lot of loud noise, disorder, and general chaos, often caused by people arguing, fighting, or behaving in an unruly, out-of-control way.
A ruction is a noisy, disruptive commotion — a burst of disorder that disturbs the peace around it. Think of it as a storm of noise and conflict happening in one place at one time.
A rudder is a flat, movable blade used to steer a vessel — most commonly a ship, a boat, or an aircraft. It is the device that controls direction, not speed.

"Ruddy" is fundamentally a color word. It means a warm, rich shade of red — not a bright, fire-engine red, but a deeper, earthier, reddish tone. Think of the color of red bricks, autumn leaves, or the sky just as the sun is setting.
When we describe a person's behavior, words, or actions as rude, we mean they show a lack of respect, politeness, or consideration for others.
Rudimentary means basic, undeveloped, or existing only in the most simple and incomplete form.

To rue something means to feel deep regret and sorrow about a past action or decision — especially one that turned out badly for you. When you rue something, you look back at it and wish, painfully, that you had done things differently.
Rueful describes a feeling — or an expression of that feeling — that blends quiet sadness, regret, and a gentle, self-aware acceptance, all at once.

Ruefully means doing something in a way that shows quiet, mild regret or sorrow — especially when you're at least partly aware of what went wrong, and you're accepting it with a kind of soft, resigned sadness.
A ruffian is a violent, rough, and lawless person — someone who uses physical force, intimidation, or brutality as a way of dealing with the world.
To ruffle means to disturb something that was calm, smooth, or orderly — and leave it unsettled.

Rugged means tough, strong, and rough — not smooth, not soft, not gentle. That single idea runs through every use of this word, whether you're talking about a mountain, a person's face, a piece of equipment, or a way of life.
Rugose means covered with wrinkles, folds, or ridges — specifically describing the texture of a surface.

Ruin means total destruction — not minor damage, not something broken that can easily be fixed, but the complete collapse or loss of something that once had value, strength, or wholeness. Think of a sandcastle swallowed by a wave.
To ruin something means to damage it so badly that it is destroyed, made useless, or made significantly worse — often in a way that is permanent or very hard to fix.

Ruinous means causing complete destruction or devastation, or being in a state of complete collapse. The word carries a sense of severity and totality — not just damage, not just harm, but the kind that leads to total wreckage of something.
A rule of thumb is a simple, practical guideline based on experience or common sense that works well enough in most situations — even though it is not perfectly precise or scientifically exact.
Rumble means to make a deep, low, continuous, rolling sound — the kind of sound that feels heavy and powerful, almost like it vibrates the air around you.

Rumbustious means being so full of energy and liveliness that you become noisy, boisterous, and hard to keep in order — but in a wild, spirited way that often feels exciting rather than purely negative.
A ruminant is a hoofed, plant-eating mammal that digests its food through a unique two-stage chewing process.
To think deeply about something for a long time, often in a worried or brooding way. Literally, of cows and sheep, to chew food brought back up from the stomach.
The word rumination describes the act of going over something again and again — chewing on it repeatedly, either physically or mentally.

Ruminative describes a kind of thinking that is deep, slow, and repetitive — where a person keeps turning the same thought or problem over and over in their mind, like a mental loop that is hard to exit.
To rummage means to search through a place or a collection of things in a messy, disorganized way, usually because you are looking for something.

To rumple something means to make it wrinkled, creased, or untidy — usually by pressing against it, handling it carelessly, or disturbing it. The result is something that looks messy and disordered, but not completely destroyed.

Rumpled means wrinkled, creased, and loosely disordered in appearance — in a soft, irregular way — because something has been bent, bunched, handled, or pressed out of its smooth shape and hasn't been straightened back.
A rumpus is a noisy, chaotic disturbance — a burst of loud, disorderly activity that draws attention and disrupts the peace around it.
"Run in" is a phrasal verb (a verb + a preposition that together create a new meaning). It is also used as a noun ("a run-in").
To run something by someone means to tell someone about an idea, plan, or piece of information so that they can give their opinion, feedback, or approval.
A run-in describes an unwanted, unplanned meeting or clash with someone or something. The word carries a sense of friction — things bumping up against each other.

When you call something run-of-the-mill, you are saying it is completely ordinary — nothing special, nothing bad, just average. It is the kind of thing that is so standard and typical that it leaves no impression on you. It doesn't surprise you.
"Run-of-the-mill" means ordinary, average, and nothing special. It describes something — or someone — that is completely standard, unremarkable, and does not stand out from the crowd in any way.

The word runaway as an adjective captures one central idea: something that has broken free from control and cannot easily be stopped. Think of a horse that has bolted — it's moving on its own, faster than anyone intended, and nobody can rein it in.

A runaway is something or someone that has broken free from control and is now moving, acting, or existing outside the bounds of where it should be — often in a way that is hard or impossible to stop.
A rundown is a structured summary or overview of something — a clear, organized account of the main points, details, or facts about a topic, situation, or event.
A rune is a single character — a letter — from an ancient writing system used by Germanic and Norse peoples of Northern and Western Europe, primarily from around the 2nd century CE onward.
A rung is one of the horizontal bars on a ladder — the individual steps you place your feet on when climbing up or down.
"Runic" means of, relating to, or written in runes. It describes anything connected to runes — the ancient carved letters of Northern European peoples.

A runnel is a very small, narrow stream of flowing water. Think of it as one step above a mere trickle — water that is actually moving along a defined little path, but is too tiny and thin to be called a stream or a brook.

At the heart of nearly every adjective use of "running" is one simple image: something that keeps going without stopping. Like a river that never pauses, something "running" is continuous, uninterrupted, or in constant motion.
Runoff is what happens when a system reaches its limit and the excess spills over or flows away.
A rupture is a sudden, forceful break — the moment something that was whole, sealed, or connected tears apart or bursts open, often under pressure.

When something ruptures, it breaks open suddenly and forcefully — usually because internal pressure has built up to a point where the object can no longer hold itself together, or because an extreme external force causes it to give way.

"Rural" means of or relating to the countryside — areas that are away from cities and large towns, where you find open land, farms, forests, rivers, and very few buildings or people packed closely together. If a place is rural, it is the opposite of a city.

A ruse is a deliberately planned trick or deception — an action or scheme designed to make someone believe something false, so that you can achieve a goal they would not allow if they knew what you were really doing.
Rustic means simple, rough, and natural in a way that reminds you of the countryside or old-fashioned rural life — the opposite of modern, polished, or city-like.
When someone rusticates, they leave the city behind and go to live in — or spend a significant period of time in — the countryside.
Rusticity means the quality or state of being rustic — that is, having the character, feel, or qualities of simple, rural, countryside life.
To rustle means to make (or cause) a soft, dry, whispery, shuffling sound — the kind produced when lightweight, slightly stiff things rub against or brush past each other with gentle movement.
"Rustling" describes something that is making — or is associated with — a soft, dry, whispery sound produced when light, thin things brush or slide against each other with gentle movement.
A rut is fundamentally about something being worn deep through repetition — a groove that gets deeper every time something passes through it, until it becomes a kind of trap.
Ruthless describes someone who is completely without mercy, pity, or compassion — especially when they are trying to achieve a goal.

A sabaton is a piece of armour that covers and protects the foot. Specifically, it is the foot-armour worn by knights and soldiers during the age of plate armour — roughly the 14th through the 16th centuries in Europe.

A sabbatical is an extended, planned break from your regular job or responsibilities — typically lasting several weeks to a full year — during which you step away to rest, grow, create, or pursue something that your everyday work life doesn't allow.
A small, dark-furred animal of northern Asia prized for its soft fur; also a poetic word for the colour black.
Sabotage is the deliberate act of damaging, destroying, or disrupting something — so that it fails, weakens, or stops working properly.
To sabotage something means to deliberately damage, weaken, or ruin it so that it fails — and usually to do so in a hidden or sneaky way.

A saboteur is a person who deliberately damages, disrupts, or destroys something — not by accident, but on purpose — in order to prevent it from working, succeeding, or continuing. The key word here is deliberately.

Saccharine means excessively and artificially sweet — but almost always in a non-physical sense. It is used to describe something that pretends to be warm, kind, or pleasant, but is so overdone that it feels fake, hollow, or even irritating.
Sacerdotal is an adjective that means "of, relating to, or characteristic of priests or the priesthood."
A sack is a large, flexible bag — typically made of rough, sturdy material like cloth, burlap (jute fabric), or heavy paper — used to hold and carry bulk goods.
When a person has been told to leave their job by their employer — against their own wish — they can be described as "sacked."
A sacrament is a sacred religious ritual or ceremony in which a physical, visible action is believed to carry a spiritual reality — either symbolising God's grace, delivering it directly, or both.

When something is called sacred, it means it belongs to a higher level of existence — one that is set apart from the ordinary, everyday world. It is connected to something greater: God, a divine power, a religion, or a deeply revered value.

In Hinduism, the cow is a holy animal. It is not to be harmed, slaughtered, or even forcibly moved. Even if a cow stands in the middle of a busy road blocking traffic, people work around it — because it is sacred.

A sacrifice is the act of giving up something you value — something that genuinely costs you — for the sake of something else you consider more important. The key idea is voluntary loss with purpose. You are not robbed of something.
Sacrilege means the act of treating something sacred, holy, or deeply revered with disrespect, misuse, or violation.
Something is sacrilegious when it shows deep disrespect toward — or actively violates — something that people consider sacred.

A sacristy is a room inside or directly attached to a church. It is a private, working room — not part of the main hall where worshippers sit. Think of it as a combination of a storage room and a dressing room, but exclusively for sacred religious purposes.
If something is sacrosanct, it means it is considered so important, so respected, or so special that it must never be questioned, criticized, interfered with, or changed.

A saddle is a shaped seat — traditionally made of leather, padded on the inside — that is strapped onto the back of a horse (or a donkey, mule, or camel) so that a rider can sit on the animal comfortably and safely.
To get ready for a challenge or task, as in "saddle up, team." Literally, to put a saddle on a horse before riding.

Sadistic describes someone — or something — that involves getting pleasure, enjoyment, or satisfaction from causing pain, suffering, or humiliation to others. The absolute heart of this word is not just causing harm, but enjoying it.
A safari is a trip made into the wild for the purpose of observing animals living freely in their natural environment.
A costly golden spice made from the dried threads of a crocus flower; also its deep orange-yellow colour.

A saga is a long, complex, and weighty story — one that spans a great deal of time, involves many events (often dramatic or difficult ones), and usually features many people whose lives are intertwined.

Sagacious means having or showing an exceptional ability to understand situations clearly, judge them wisely, and make smart decisions — especially in complex, difficult, or tricky circumstances. It goes far beyond simply being "smart" or knowledgeable.
When someone does something sagaciously, they do it with sharp, practical wisdom and keen judgment — especially in situations where most people would struggle to see things clearly.
Sagacity is the quality of being exceptionally wise, perceptive, and sound in judgment — especially in practical, real-world situations.

When you call something or someone sage, you mean they show deep, calm, and trustworthy wisdom — the kind that comes not just from being smart, but from careful thinking, long experience, and a genuine understanding of how the world works.
A deeply wise person, especially an old one, respected for their wisdom. Sage is also a fragrant herb with greyish-green leaves, used in cooking.

A sahib is a person of authority, rank, or high social standing who is treated with great respect and deference — specifically, in the South Asian context, it most strongly refers to a European (and especially British) man during the colonial era in India.
Salacious describes something that deals with sex or sexual matters in a way that is indecent, crude, or shamelessly inappropriate — and is often designed to shock, excite, or titillate people.
Salient means most noticeable, most important, or most prominent — the thing that rises above everything else and demands your attention.
Saline means containing salt, consisting of salt, or relating to salt.
Salinization is the process by which salts build up in soil or water over time, eventually reaching levels that are harmful to plants, ecosystems, and human use.
To salivate means to produce saliva — the watery liquid that your mouth naturally makes. Your salivary glands (small organs inside your mouth and jaw) release this liquid.
Sallow describes a skin color that is a dull, pale, yellowish or yellowish-brown tone — the kind that makes a person look unhealthy, tired, or unwell.
A witty or clever remark. It can also mean a sudden charge out of a besieged place to attack the enemy, or a short trip or excursion.
To sally means to rush out or burst out suddenly from a place — especially a place where you were staying, resting, hiding, or being held back — and move forward with energy, boldness, or purpose.

Salmonella refers to a group of microscopic, single-celled living organisms called bacteria. More specifically, it is a genus of bacteria — meaning it is a family name that covers hundreds of related types under one umbrella.

Saltation means a leap, jump, or bound — a sudden movement from one point to another, skipping over the space in between. Think of it as the opposite of a slow, smooth, continuous slide. Instead, it's a sharp, abrupt jump.

Salubrious means conducive to good health or well-being — in other words, something that is good for you, promotes health, or creates a pleasant and wholesome condition. Think of it as a single, elegant word that captures the idea of "healthy and beneficial."

Salutary describes something that produces a genuinely good, beneficial effect — especially when it helps correct a mistake, improve a bad situation, or lead someone (or something) toward a better outcome.
A salutation is a greeting — any word, phrase, gesture, or formal act used to acknowledge and welcome another person, almost always at the beginning of an interaction or written communication.
A salutatory is an opening speech that welcomes an audience at a formal ceremony — most commonly, a graduation ceremony (called a commencement).

To salute means to show respect or honor to someone through a gesture or action. It is a deliberate, conscious act — you are not just noticing someone, you are actively acknowledging them with a sense of respect.
Salvage means something saved or rescued from damage, destruction, or total loss — and also the act of saving it.
To salvage something means to save it from a situation where it was being lost, destroyed, or ruined — and to make it useful again, even if it is not perfect.

Salvation means being saved — rescued — from something harmful, destructive, or beyond your ability to escape on your own. The key idea is that you are in serious trouble, and something or someone pulls you out of it.

A salve is something that soothes and heals. That one idea — soothing relief — is the thread running through every use of this word, whether you're talking about something physical or something emotional.
A salver is a flat, rigid tray — typically made of silver, gold, or another polished metal — used to carry and present objects to someone.

Salvia is the scientific name for a very large group — or genus — of flowering plants. A genus is simply a category in science used to group together plants (or animals) that are closely related to each other.
A salvo is a sudden burst of many things delivered together, all at once or in very rapid succession. Think of it as "a concentrated flood of things hitting at the same moment."
A person who helps others in need, especially strangers, as in "a good Samaritan." Historically, a person from the ancient region of Samaria.

A samosa is a small, savory fried pastry — a type of food. It has a stiff, thin outer crust made from dough, and it is filled with a spiced mixture on the inside. The whole thing is then deep-fried in oil until it turns golden-brown and crispy.
A samovar is a large, decorated metal container designed specifically to heat water and keep it hot for a long time.
A samurai is a highly trained warrior from Japan who lived during a specific period of history — roughly from the 10th century to the late 1800s.
To sanctify something means to make it holy, pure, or set apart for a sacred and special purpose.
Sanctimonious describes a person who acts as though they are morally better than everyone else — and makes sure everyone around them knows it. It is not just about having high moral standards.
Sanctimony is the act of performing moral goodness rather than actually living it — while simultaneously making others feel inferior for not being as "good" as you.
A penalty imposed on a country to make it obey international law, especially a trade ban, as in "economic sanctions." Confusingly, it can also mean official approval or permission.
To give official permission for something, as in "the government sanctioned the deal." Confusingly, it can also mean to impose a penalty on someone.

"Sanctioned" can mean two almost opposite things. This is not a mistake or an accident. The word genuinely carries both meanings, and your ability to use and understand it correctly depends entirely on recognizing which one is being used in a given sentence.
Sanctity means the quality of being so deeply important, pure, or sacred that it must be treated with the highest possible respect — and must never be violated, harmed, or taken lightly.

"Sanctuary" means a place where someone or something is safe, protected, and at peace — a place where the outside world, with all its dangers and troubles, cannot easily reach. Think of it as a protective bubble.
A sanctum is a place that is set apart from the rest of the world — a space that is either sacred and holy, or deeply private and personal. The defining quality is that not everyone can enter.

Sand is a loose, natural material made up of countless tiny grains — small, hard bits of broken rock, minerals, or shells. The grains are neither as fine as powder nor as large as pebbles; they sit in between.

Sangfroid means the quality of staying perfectly calm, composed, and in full control of yourself when you are under enormous pressure — in a dangerous, frightening, or extremely stressful situation that would make most people panic, fall apart, or lose their head.
"Sanguinary" means involving a great deal of blood and killing.
Sanguine means optimistic — specifically, feeling cheerfully confident that things will turn out well, even when the situation is uncertain or difficult.

A sanitarium is a type of medical institution — a live-in facility — where people with serious, long-lasting illnesses were admitted to stay for weeks, months, or even years to rest, follow a structured routine, and hopefully recover, all under medical supervision.
Sanitary means clean and safe in a way that protects people from disease and illness.
To sanitize something means to make it safe or acceptable by removing whatever is harmful, dangerous, or unwanted from it.
Sanity means the state of having a healthy, sound, and normally functioning mind.
To sap something means to slowly and gradually drain it of its strength, energy, or power — leaving it weaker than before.

Sapid means having a strong, noticeable, and pleasing quality — something that is rich, full, and satisfying rather than weak, dull, or flat. Think of the opposite of bland. That's the spirit of sapid.
Sapience is the quality of being deeply wise — not just smart, not just knowledgeable, but profoundly wise, in a reflective and almost philosophical sense.
Sapient means wise — but in a deep, full sense of the word.
Sapiential means "of, relating to, or characterized by wisdom."

A sapling is a young tree — one that has started growing and is clearly a tree, but has not yet grown into its full adult size and strength. Think of it as a tree in its "childhood" or "teenage" years.

"Sappy" most commonly describes something — or someone — that is excessively sentimental or emotional, in a way that feels overdone, unrealistically sweet, or embarrassingly soft. The key word is excessively.

Sarcasm is when someone says the opposite of what they actually mean, using a sharp or mocking tone, to express frustration, contempt, humor, or criticism. The words themselves sound like one thing, but the real message is the complete reverse.
When someone is sarcastic, they say the opposite of what they actually mean — but they do it on purpose, and they usually expect you to know they don't mean it literally.
A sarcophagus is a large, rigid container — most often made of stone — that was used to hold a dead person's body. Think of it as a very grand, very permanent coffin carved out of solid stone.

Sardonic describes a kind of expression — a smile, a laugh, a remark, a tone — that is darkly mocking and laced with cold contempt. When someone is sardonic, they are not just making fun of something.

A sari is a traditional garment — specifically, a single, long piece of cloth that a woman wraps and drapes around her body to wear as an outfit. It is not stitched or cut into the shape of a garment the way a shirt or dress is.
Sartorial is an adjective that means relating to clothing, dress, or the way a person is dressed. More specifically, it can also relate to the craft of tailoring — the skilled making of clothes.
A long strip of cloth worn around the waist or over one shoulder; also a window frame that slides up and down.
A window made of one or more sliding frames holding glass, which open by being pushed up or down rather than swinging out.

To sashay means to walk or move in a confident, showy, and graceful way — typically with your hips swaying and a light, gliding quality to your steps. The person doing it knows they are being watched, and they love it.

A Sasquatch is a large, mysterious, ape-like creature that many people believe lives hidden in the wild forests of North America, especially in the Pacific Northwest — places like the dense woodlands of Washington State, Oregon, and British Columbia in Canada.

"Sassy" describes a person (or their behavior, words, or style) that is boldly confident, cheeky, and a little bit disrespectful — but in a way that is charming, witty, and entertaining rather than truly offensive.

A satchel is a type of bag designed to be carried over one shoulder. Its most recognizable feature is a flap — a wide fold of material that comes down over the opening of the bag and fastens shut, usually with a buckle or clasp.

To sate means to satisfy a desire, craving, or appetite so thoroughly and completely that nothing is left wanting — the desire is fully used up. You've had enough, and then some. The desire doesn't just get met; it gets extinguished.

An object in space that orbits a planet, such as the Moon, or a machine sent into orbit to send back information. Figuratively, something that depends on or is controlled by a larger body, as in "a satellite town."

To satiate something means to completely and thoroughly fulfill a desire, hunger, craving, or need — so fully that nothing is left wanting. Think of it as filling a cup until it doesn't just reach the brim, but overflows.
Satiated means having a desire, appetite, or need so completely and fully satisfied that you no longer want any more of something — at least not for now.

Satiety is the feeling of being so completely full or satisfied that you don't want any more of something. It is the state you reach when a need, hunger, or desire has been fully met — and you are content to stop.

Satire is a piece of writing, art, film, cartoon, or performance that criticizes something — a person, a group, a government, an institution, or society itself — by using humor, irony, or exaggeration rather than direct, serious complaint.
Something is satirical when it uses humor, mockery, or exaggeration to criticize people, ideas, or society — not just to make you laugh, but to make you think.

Satisfaction is the feeling — or the act — of having something fulfilled. That "something" could be a desire, a need, an expectation, or a requirement. When it is properly met, the result is satisfaction.

When you are satisfied, it means you have received or experienced exactly what you needed or wanted — and now you feel that it is enough. You are not looking for more. There is a quiet sense of "yes, this is complete."

A satrap is a governor — a powerful official who rules over a region or province on behalf of a higher authority (usually a king or emperor). The satrap controls the day-to-day running of that region, but he himself is not the ultimate ruler.
To saturate something means to fill it so completely with something that it cannot hold, absorb, or contain any more of it.
A saturnalia is a period of wild, unrestrained celebration where the normal rules of behavior are completely thrown out the window.
Saturnine describes a person who is deeply and persistently gloomy, slow-moving in spirit, cold in manner, and brooding in nature.
A satyr is primarily a creature from ancient Greek mythology — but the word has also taken on a figurative meaning in everyday English, and even a scientific one in zoology.

Sauciness is the quality of being playfully bold, a little cheeky, and mildly disrespectful — but in a fun, spirited way, not a mean or harmful one. Think of it as the sweet spot between being perfectly polite and being outright rude.
Cheeky and slightly rude in a playful way ("a saucy reply"); or mildly sexy ("a saucy postcard").

Sauerkraut is a food made from finely shredded raw cabbage that has been preserved and transformed through a natural process called fermentation. The end result is a soft, tangy, sour-tasting food with a distinctive sharp smell.
To saunter means to walk slowly, casually, and without any hurry — as if you have all the time in the world and not a single worry in your mind.
A sausage is a food made from ground (finely chopped) meat that is seasoned with salt, spices, and other flavorings, and then packed tightly into a tube-like wrapping called a casing.
To sauté means to cook food quickly in a small amount of fat — like oil or butter — over high heat, while keeping the food in motion (stirring, tossing, or flipping it) so it cooks evenly.

Savage describes something that is fierce, violent, and completely without mercy or gentleness. Think of it as the extreme end of the scale — not just harsh, not just rough, but brutally and shockingly intense.
A savage is a person who is seen as wild, brutal, or completely without the rules and restraints that society expects people to follow.

Savagery means extreme, brutal, or merciless behavior — the kind that goes so far beyond normal human decency that it shocks or horrifies people. It is not just cruelty. It is cruelty at its rawest, most uncontrolled, most ruthless extreme.
A savanna is a large, open landscape dominated by grass, with trees scattered across it here and there — but not so many trees that they block the sunlight or form a forest.
A savannah is a large, open landscape covered mostly in grass, with trees scattered here and there — but those trees are spread far apart, never packed together like in a forest.
A savant is a person who has a remarkable, almost superhuman level of ability or knowledge — usually in one very specific area.
Savant syndrome is a condition where someone demonstrates exceptional aptitude in one specific domain — such as art or mathematics — despite significant social or intellectual impairment.

To save face means to protect your reputation, dignity, or self-respect in front of others — especially in a situation where you could have been embarrassed, humiliated, or made to look foolish or weak.

A savior is a person — or sometimes a thing — that rescues someone or something from serious danger, harm, failure, or total destruction. The word carries weight: it isn't used for small, everyday help.
Savoir-faire is a noun that means the ability to always know the right thing to do or say in any situation — and then to actually do or say it with ease, confidence, and grace.
A savor is the distinctive quality — most often a taste or a smell — that something has, which makes it recognizable, special, or pleasurable.
To savor something means to enjoy it slowly, deeply, and with full attention — deliberately taking your time so you can appreciate every small detail of it, rather than rushing through it.
When something is described as savored, it means it was enjoyed slowly, deliberately, and with complete attention — treated as something precious, not rushed through.
Of food, salty or spicy rather than sweet. It can also mean pleasant-tasting and appetizing, or, of a person or behaviour, morally acceptable, as in "a less than savory character."
When you call someone savvy, you are saying they have sharp, practical knowledge about how something really works — not just on paper, but in the real world.
Savvy means practical knowledge and sharp judgment that helps a person understand how things really work — and use that understanding skillfully to get things done.
A pattern of slow, steady rises followed by sudden sharp drops, repeating over and over like the teeth of a saw.

A saying is a short, familiar phrase or sentence that expresses a general truth, a piece of wisdom, or a common observation about life. It is something many people know, repeat, and pass down — often across generations.
The hard crust that forms over a healing wound; also an insult for a worker who keeps working during a strike.
A scabbard is a protective case or sheath that holds the blade of a sword, dagger, or knife when it is not being used.
Indecent or offensive, especially sexually, as in "scabrous jokes." It can also mean rough and scaly to the touch, or difficult to deal with.

A scad is a small, silvery saltwater fish found mostly in warm, tropical, and subtropical ocean waters around the world. Scads are slender, swim in large schools (groups), and are related to the jack and trevally family of fish.
A scaffold is a temporary supporting structure — something built not as a permanent fixture, but to serve a specific purpose, and removed once that purpose is fulfilled.
Something is scalable if it can grow larger (or shrink smaller) without breaking down, losing quality, or becoming unworkably complicated in the process.
A mischievous person or rascal; historically, a white Southerner who supported Reconstruction after the American Civil War.
To scald means to burn or injure skin using very hot liquid or steam. It is specifically about wet heat — boiling water, hot soup, steam from a kettle, hot oil — not flames or dry surfaces.
Scalding describes something — usually a liquid or steam — that is so intensely hot that it can burn and injure your skin the moment it touches you.

The size or extent of something, as in "on a large scale." A scale is also a series of musical notes, a range of levels or numbers for measuring, a weighing device, or one of the thin plates on a fish's skin.
To scale something means to adjust its size, amount, or capacity in a controlled, proportional way while keeping its essential structure intact. The clearest way to grasp this is through maps.
"Scalene" describes something whose parts — most often sides or lengths — are all unequal to each other. Not just "some are different," but none of them are the same.

A scallop is a type of shellfish — a living animal that lives in the ocean, protected inside a hard shell. More precisely, it is a bivalve, meaning its body is enclosed between two shells (called valves) that are hinged together at one end.
Having an edge shaped like a row of curved half-circles, like a scallop shell; or (of food) baked in a creamy sauce.
A scalpel is a small, extremely sharp surgical knife used to make precise cuts in the human body during medical operations or in biological specimens during scientific study.
To scamper means to run or move quickly with small, light, rapid steps — in a way that feels lively, energetic, and often a little playful.

A scandal is an event or situation where someone — usually a person in a position of power, trust, or public visibility — does something widely considered wrong, immoral, dishonest, or corrupt, and this becomes publicly known, causing widespread shock and moral outrage.
Causing public shock and outrage because it is morally wrong or improper, as in "a scandalous affair." It can also mean shockingly bad, as in "a scandalous waste of money."
Scant means barely enough — or not even that.

"Scanty" means barely enough — or, more often, less than enough. When something is scanty, it is not completely absent, but it exists in such a small amount that it fails to satisfy the need or meet the expectation. The heart of the word is inadequacy.
