A scapegoat is a person — or a group of people — who is blamed for something that is not entirely, or not at all, their fault. The blame they receive is unfair.
A scapegrace is a person — very often a young man or a boy — who is habitually reckless, mischievous, and morally undisciplined.
Something is scarce when it exists in such small amounts or numbers that there is not enough of it to meet the need or demand for it.
"Scarcely" means "almost not at all" or "only just barely."
Scarcity means there is not enough of something to satisfy everyone who wants or needs it. It is the gap between how much of something exists and how much people desire.

To scarify means to make shallow cuts, scratches, or scrapes on a surface — deliberately, and usually for a specific purpose. The key word here is shallow: you're not slashing deep into something, you're just breaking or roughening its outer surface.

To scathe means to harm, hurt, or damage — and to do so in a way that is serious, not minor. Think of it as a verb that describes a striking, cutting, burning kind of damage. It's not a scratch. It's the kind of harm that leaves a real mark.
If something is scathing, it is harshly and powerfully critical — so critical that it cuts deep, like a blade. A scathing comment, review, or remark doesn't just point out a flaw.
"Scatter" means to cause things to separate and go in many different directions at once, ending up spread out rather than gathered together in one place.

If someone is scatterbrained, their mind works in a scattered, unfocused, disorganized way. Think of the word "scatter" — like how you scatter seeds, throwing them in many random directions with no pattern.
Scattered means: spread out over a large area or space, with gaps in between, in no particular order or pattern — not grouped together, not concentrated in one place.
Scattershot means random, unfocused, and spreading in too many directions at once — without a clear aim or a coherent plan.
To scavenge means to search through things that are discarded, leftover, or no longer wanted, in order to find something useful.
A scavenger is a person, animal, or thing that searches through what others have left behind — things that are dead, discarded, leftover, or unwanted — in order to find something useful or edible.
A scenario is a description of a situation — real, imagined, or possible — that gives you a picture of who is involved, what is happening, and how things might unfold.
A scene is a specific place, moment, or stretch of action that you can picture in your mind — almost like a photograph or a short video clip.

Scenery refers to everything you can see around you in a place — especially the natural features of a landscape like mountains, forests, rivers, valleys, fields, and coastlines — when you look at them and find them visually impressive or beautiful.
A scenester is a person who makes being part of a particular social or cultural scene — such as a music scene, art scene, or fashion scene — a central part of their identity and lifestyle.
"Scenic" describes a place, view, or route that is visually beautiful — especially because of its natural surroundings.
A scent is a smell — the invisible quality that something gives off and that you detect with your nose.
To detect or track something by smell, as in "the dog scented a fox." Figuratively, to sense that something is coming, as in "scenting victory." It can also mean to give something a pleasant smell.

A scepter is an ornamental rod or staff — usually short enough to hold in one hand — that a monarch (a king, queen, emperor, or empress) carries as a physical symbol of their royal power and authority.

Schadenfreude is the feeling of pleasure, satisfaction, or even quiet delight that you get when something bad happens to someone else. Not just any pleasure — specifically the pleasure that comes from their misfortune.

The word schematic describes something that has been deliberately stripped down to show only its essential structure — like a skeleton that reveals how the parts connect, without the flesh, color, or texture of the real thing.

A secret or dishonest plan, as in "a get-rich-quick scheme." In British English, it often means simply an official plan or programme, as in "a pension scheme." It can also mean an arrangement, as in "a colour scheme."
To scheme means to secretly make a clever, cunning plan — usually to get something you want or to harm someone — in a way that involves deception, manipulation, or hidden motives.

When you call someone scheming, you are saying that this person habitually makes secret, clever, and self-serving plans — usually to get something they want, often by deceiving or manipulating others.
A schism is a serious, deep split or division within a group of people who were once united — caused by strong disagreements over beliefs, values, or principles. It is not a small argument.
Schizophrenia is a serious, long-term mental illness that disrupts how a person thinks, perceives reality, feels emotions, and behaves.
Relating to schizophrenia, a serious mental illness that distorts thinking and perception; informally (and insensitively), wildly inconsistent.
To schlep something means to carry or drag it from one place to another — but not just any carrying.

To schmooze means to chat in a friendly, warm, and charming way with people — especially with people who are important, powerful, or useful to you — with the hidden (or not-so-hidden) goal of building a good impression, making connections, or gaining some future advantage.

A schmuck is a stupid, foolish, or contemptible person — someone who behaves in a way that makes others think less of them, either because they did something dumb, acted selfishly, or were just generally unpleasant and objectionable.
A scholar is a person who studies a subject very seriously, deeply, and systematically — usually over a long period of time — and who develops expert-level knowledge in that area.
Showing the deep knowledge, careful study, and discipline of a serious student or academic, as in "a scholarly book."
A scholarship is money given to a student to help pay for their education, and — crucially — this money does not need to be paid back. It is a gift, not a loan.

"Scholastic" means relating to schools, education, or formal academic learning. When you call something scholastic, you're placing it squarely in the world of classrooms, textbooks, exams, and institutions of learning.
A sailing ship with two or more masts; also a large glass for beer or sherry.

A thought experiment by physicist Erwin Schrödinger, in which a cat in a sealed box is, according to quantum theory, both alive and dead until someone looks. It was designed to show how absurd some views of quantum mechanics are.

Science fiction is a genre of storytelling — found in books, films, television shows, comics, video games, and other media — that tells imaginative stories grounded in science and technology. It asks the fundamental question: "What if?"

A scintilla is an extremely tiny amount of something — so tiny it barely exists at all. Not "a little." Not "a small amount." We're talking about the most microscopic, almost-nothing trace you can imagine.

To scintillate means to flash or sparkle with rapid bursts of light — like a spark flying off a fire, or a star twinkling in the night sky. Think of tiny, quick flickers of brightness appearing and disappearing in rapid succession.
Brilliantly clever, lively, or exciting, as in "scintillating conversation." Literally, sparkling or giving off flashes of light.

Sciolism is the practice of pretending to know more than you actually do — specifically, displaying a shallow, surface-level knowledge of a subject while giving the impression that your understanding is deep and expert.
A scion is a child, grandchild, or direct descendant of a family that is powerful, wealthy, aristocratic, or historically important.
Sclerosis means the abnormal hardening or stiffening of a tissue or organ in the body.
Rigid and unable to adapt or change, as in "a sclerotic bureaucracy." In medicine, of body tissue such as arteries, abnormally hardened.
To scoff means to mock, dismiss, or speak about something with open contempt and disbelief — treating it as if it is stupid, ridiculous, or not worth taking seriously.
Scoliosis is a medical condition in which the spine curves sideways in an abnormal way.

A sconce is a light fixture that is attached directly to a wall. It is not a floor lamp, not a ceiling light, not a table lamp — it lives on the wall and sticks out from it. Think of it as a bracket or arm that is fixed to the wall, holding a source of light.

A scone is a small, baked item made from flour, butter, a little sugar, a rising agent, and milk or cream. It sits somewhere between bread and cake — not as sweet or soft as a cake, but richer and slightly tender compared to plain bread.

"Scope out" means to carefully look at or examine something — usually before taking action. The purpose is to get information, check if something is safe or suitable, or simply understand a situation better.
To scorch something means to burn its surface with intense heat — but not burn it all the way through. The damage is real, but it stops at the outer layer.
At the heart of "scorching" is one simple idea: so intensely hot that it burns, or feels like it burns.
The score is the number of points each side has earned in a game, match, exam, or any kind of contest.
Scorn is a strong feeling of disrespect and contempt for someone or something you believe is deeply unworthy, foolish, or beneath you.

To scorn someone or something means to treat them as completely unworthy of your respect, time, or serious attention — because you believe they are beneath you, worthless, or deeply inferior. It is not simply disliking something.

Scornful means feeling or showing scorn — a powerful mix of contempt and superiority directed at someone or something you see as worthless, foolish, or beneath you. A scornful person doesn't just dislike something.
To scotch something means to put a firm, decisive stop to it — to crush it, suppress it, or block it before it can go any further.
A scoundrel is a person who is deeply dishonest, selfish, and morally bad — someone who cheats, deceives, or takes advantage of others, and feels little to no guilt about it.
To search a place thoroughly, as in "police scoured the area." It can also mean to clean something by scrubbing it hard, or of water, to wear away the ground.

A scourge is something — or sometimes someone — that causes great, widespread suffering and is very hard to escape or defeat. Think of it as a powerful force of misery that affects large numbers of people.

To scourge something or someone means to cause severe suffering, punishment, or destruction upon them — often repeatedly and mercilessly. Think of it as an extreme, relentless form of harm or torment, either physical or figurative.
A person sent ahead to gather information, especially about an enemy. A scout is also someone who looks for talented people, such as athletes or actors, or a member of the Scouts youth movement.
To scout means to go somewhere ahead of time to look around, gather information, and report back — so that you or someone else can make a better decision later.

A scowl is a facial expression. Specifically, it is the look on someone's face when they are angry, deeply displeased, or disapproving of something. It is not a subtle or mild expression — a scowl is strong, visible, and hard to miss.

To scowl means to make an angry, disapproving, or threatening facial expression — specifically by pulling your eyebrows down and together, wrinkling your forehead, and tightening your face into a look that clearly signals you are upset, angry, or displeased with something or someone.

To scrabble means to scratch, scrape, or claw at something with your fingers — quickly, repeatedly, and in a somewhat frantic or disorganized way. Picture a person who has dropped their keys into a dark corner of the room.

Scraggly means looking thin, uneven, rough, and untidy in a way that suggests poor growth, neglect, or a general lack of fullness and neatness. When something is scraggly, it looks like it should be fuller, neater, or more regular — but it isn't.
The sudden emergency shutdown of a nuclear reactor, usually by rapidly inserting control rods.

Scramble always carries the feeling of disorder + urgency. Something is either moving in a hurried, clumsy way, or things are being mixed up and disordered. Every meaning of this word connects back to that feeling.
A small piece or amount of something, as in "a scrap of paper." It also means waste metal or materials, especially for recycling. Informally, a scrap is a short fight or quarrel.
To abandon or get rid of something completely, as in "the plan was scrapped." Informally, it also means to fight or quarrel.
When something is scraped up, it means it has multiple scrapes, scratches, or rough surface damage on it — caused by rubbing or dragging against something hard or rough.
Determined, feisty, and willing to fight, especially against the odds. It can also mean disorganized or untidy, as in "a scrappy game."
To scrawl means to write something in a messy, careless way that is hard to read.
Scrawny means unpleasantly and unhealthily thin — so thin that the person or animal looks weak, frail, or as if they haven't been eating enough.

A scream is a loud, sharp, high-pitched cry that comes out of a person's (or animal's) mouth. It is the kind of sound that cuts through the air, grabs your attention immediately, and is very hard to ignore.

Scree is a collection of loose, broken rock fragments scattered across a steep mountain or cliff face, or piled up at the bottom of one. Think of it as the rubble that nature chips away from rocky mountainsides over time.

A screech is a sharp, high-pitched, harsh sound — the kind that is unpleasant to hear and seems to stab right into your ears. Think of the sound when someone drags fingernails across a blackboard, or when a car slams on its brakes suddenly.

To screech means to make a loud, sharp, high-pitched sound that is harsh and unpleasant to the ear. Think of it as a sound that feels like it stabs through the air — it is not just loud, it is also piercing and grating.
A screed is a long, rambling, and usually angry or bitter piece of writing or speech — one that goes on and on, often complaining about something or ranting against someone.

A screen is almost always something that stands between two things. It might divide, protect, hide, filter, or display — but in every case, it sits in the middle, doing a job because of where it is positioned.
When a film, documentary, or video is "screened," it is shown to an audience — in a cinema, on television, at a festival, or in any viewing setting.
To scribble means to write or draw something quickly and carelessly, in a way that looks messy, rushed, or hard to read. It's the opposite of writing neatly and thoughtfully.
At its most literal, a scribbler is someone who scribbles — someone who writes in a rushed, messy, hard-to-read way. The focus here is on the act of writing, not on the quality of the content.
A scribe is a person whose job or role involves writing — specifically, writing things down carefully and precisely on behalf of others, or copying existing written material by hand.
A scrim is a type of loosely woven, open-mesh fabric or material — meaning it has tiny gaps or holes running through it, almost like a very fine net or gauze.
A scrimmage is a practice game — a game that looks and feels like the real thing, but officially doesn't count.
To scrimp means to spend as little money as possible, or to use as little of something as possible — usually because money is tight, or because you're working hard toward a financial goal.
Scripture means sacred writing — text that a group of religious believers considers holy, divinely inspired, and carrying the highest spiritual authority. It is not just any old religious book.

To scrounge means to get something you need — not by working for it, buying it, or earning it in the normal way, but by searching, begging, borrowing, or finding things wherever you can, often in a crafty or slightly shameless manner.

To scrub means to clean something by rubbing it hard and repeatedly, usually with a brush, rough cloth, or an abrasive pad. The key element is force and friction — you are not just wiping gently, you are working against stubborn dirt, stains, or grime.

In the sport of rugby, a scrum is a structured, physical contest between the two opposing teams, used to restart play after certain minor rule violations — such as when a player accidentally knocks the ball forward, or an illegal pass is made.

Scrumptious means extremely delicious and deeply appealing, almost always used to describe food that gives you a strong feeling of pleasure and satisfaction just by tasting it, smelling it, or even looking at it.
To crush or squeeze something into a small, wrinkled shape, as in "she scrunched the paper into a ball." It can also mean to screw up your face or eyes, or to make a crunching sound.
A scrunchie is a hair accessory — specifically, a soft, fabric-covered elastic band that people use to tie their hair.
A scruple is a feeling of moral doubt or hesitation that holds you back from doing something — because a part of you suspects it might be wrong, unfair, or dishonest.
Extremely careful and thorough, as in "scrupulous attention to detail." It can also mean very concerned to do what is morally right and honest.
Scrupulously means doing something with extreme care, complete honesty, and strict attention to every detail — in a way that is totally beyond question or criticism.
To scrutinise something means to examine it very carefully, slowly, and in great detail — usually because you want to find something, check something, or make sure nothing is wrong or hidden.

To scrutinize something means to examine it very carefully, closely, and thoroughly — paying sharp attention to every single detail — often because you want to check if something is correct, find a flaw or problem, or truly understand what is going on.
Scrutiny means a close, careful, and thorough examination of something — looking at it with full attention, often to check it, evaluate it, question it, or find any flaws or problems in it.
To scud means to move very fast and smoothly across an open space, usually driven or swept along by an outside force — most often the wind.

To scuff means to lightly scrape or rub a surface in a way that damages or marks it. The key idea is surface-level damage — not a deep scratch, not a break, but a dull, rough, or discolored patch left behind from friction.

A scuffle is a short, messy, disorganized physical struggle between two or more people. Think of it as a minor physical confrontation — people grabbing, pushing, shoving, or wrestling with each other briefly, in a confused and clumsy way.
To scuffle means to fight with someone in a rough, messy, and unorganized way — usually involving grabbing, pushing, shoving, and wrestling rather than clean, deliberate punches.

A scullery is a small, separate room built next to the main kitchen of a house, used for the dirtiest, most water-heavy chores that happen around food and cooking — primarily washing dishes, pots, and pans, but also cleaning vegetables, scrubbing floors, and storing cleaning supplies.

A scullion is the absolute lowest-ranking servant in a kitchen — the person at the very bottom of the pecking order, assigned the dirtiest, most exhausting, and most thankless work that everyone above them refused to do.
To sculpt something means to deliberately shape a material into a three-dimensional form — a form that has height, width, and depth, meaning you can walk around it and see it from all sides.

When you call something sculpted, you are saying that it has a sharply defined, clean, and beautifully precise shape — as if a skilled artist carefully carved or shaped it, rather than it being soft, vague, or unformed.
A sculptor is an artist who creates sculptures — works of art that exist in three dimensions (they have height, width, and depth).

To scupper something means to ruin it, destroy it, or prevent it from succeeding — usually suddenly, completely, and often deliberately. The thing being scuppered is typically a plan, a deal, an effort, or any goal that someone was working toward.

If someone says something scurrilous about a person, they are making a vicious, unfair, and often vulgar attack on that person's character or reputation — usually through words, and usually in a way that is meant to humiliate, damage, or destroy how others see that person.

To scurry means to move quickly using many small, rapid steps, usually because you are in a hurry, frightened, or trying to get somewhere fast. It is not just fast movement — it is fast movement that looks busy, light, and slightly rushed or flustered.
Scurvy is a serious disease caused by not getting enough vitamin C in your diet over a long period of time.
To deliberately ruin a plan or proposal, as in "the deal was scuttled." It can also mean to sink your own ship on purpose, or to run with short, quick steps, like a crab.
Rumour or gossip (informal). Originally, a water barrel on the deck of a ship, where sailors gathered to chat.
A scythe is a large, hand-held cutting tool that was traditionally used to cut grass, wheat, and other crops growing close to the ground.

A sea star is a marine animal that lives in the ocean. You may know it better by its older, more common name — starfish — but "sea star" is actually the preferred name used by scientists today, because this creature is not a fish at all.
A sea mammal with flippers and a sleek body; or a stamp, wax mark or closure that fixes something shut or shows it is genuine.
A seam is a line formed where two things meet, join, or are held together. Think of it as the visible "meeting point" or "junction" between two separate parts.
Smooth and continuous, with no visible joins or interruptions, as in "a seamless transition."

A seamstress is a woman who sews — professionally, as a craft, or as a skilled occupation. She uses needle and thread (or a sewing machine) to stitch pieces of fabric together to make or repair clothing and other textile items.
Seamy means sordid, morally unpleasant, and corrupt — the kind of dark, dirty, or shameful side of something that most people prefer not to look at or talk about openly.

To sear means to burn or scorch a surface with sudden, intense heat. The key idea is always the same: something very hot hits a surface fast and powerfully, changing it — browning it, hardening it, damaging it, or leaving a permanent mark.

The adjective searing describes something that is so intensely hot, sharp, painful, or powerful that it feels like it burns — as if it is scorching whatever it touches. Think of placing your hand on a hot iron pan.

A season is a distinct, recurring period of time that has a recognizable character — defined by weather, nature, an activity, or a cultural pattern. It's a "window" in the year that you can identify and name.
The word seasonable means fitting or appropriate to the time — either to the current season of the year, or more broadly, to the present moment or circumstances.
The adjective seasonal means of, relating to, depending on, or varying with the seasons of the year.

When "seasoned" describes a person, it means they have a great deal of experience in something — and more importantly, that experience has shaped them deeply. It has made them wise, calm, reliable, and highly capable.

To seat means to cause someone (or something) to be placed into a sitting position or into a fixed position. Notice the word cause — this is the key. When you "seat" something or someone, you are doing the action to them, not doing the action yourself.
Sebaceous is an adjective that means relating to oil or grease, specifically the natural oil that your own skin produces.

To secede means to formally and officially break away from a larger group, organization, or country — usually to become independent or to join or form something separate. It is always a deliberate, conscious act done by a group, not an individual.

Secession is the formal, deliberate act of a group — most often a region, state, or political community — officially breaking away from a larger organization or country it currently belongs to, in order to become separate.
To seclude means to deliberately keep someone — or yourself — away from other people, the noise of the world, and public life.

When we say a place is secluded, we mean it is tucked away from the rest of the world — quiet, private, and not easily found or reached by other people. It is a place that feels cut off, in a gentle way, from the noise, crowds, and busyness of everyday life.

Seclusion means the state of being separated from other people or from the outside world. It is the condition of being away, hidden, shut off, or kept apart — whether by your own choice or by someone else's.
Second means coming right after the first — it names the position, place, or rank of number two in any ordered sequence.

To second-guess means to question or doubt a decision — one you made yourself, one someone else made, or one someone is about to make. Think of it as looking at a decision a second time from a position of doubt, criticism, or foresight.
Secondary means coming after something else in rank, order, or importance. Whenever you see this word, your brain should immediately ask: "Second after what?"
Secondhand means: not coming to you directly or originally — something that has passed through someone else first.
To produce and release a substance, as glands release saliva or sweat; or to hide something away secretly.

When you describe someone or something as secretive, you mean that they deliberately hide information, thoughts, plans, or activities from others — and they do this as a habit or pattern, not just once.

A sect is a group of people who share a specific set of beliefs or practices — and whose shared beliefs set them apart from a larger, more established group they originally came from or exist in contrast to.
Relating to divisions or hostility between religious or political groups, as in "sectarian violence." It can also mean narrow-minded and intolerant of other groups' beliefs.
Secular means "of the ordinary world, not of religion." Think of life as being divided into two zones. One zone belongs to religion — churches, temples, mosques, scripture, priests, worship.
A person who is not a member of the clergy; a layperson. As an adjective, "secular" means not connected with religion.

"Secure" means free from danger, doubt, or the risk of something going wrong. Whether you're talking about a building, a physical object, a job, or a feeling inside a person — when something is secure, it is safe, stable, and not easily threatened or lost.

To succeed in getting something, especially with effort, as in "secure a contract." It also means to fasten something firmly, to make a place safe from attack, or to guarantee a loan against property.
A sedan is a specific style of passenger car. It is probably the most common and "standard" type of car you see on roads.

Sedate means calm, quiet, and unhurried — with a sense of controlled dignity. When something or someone is sedate, they are not rushed, not excitable, not noisy, and not dramatic. Everything moves and happens at a slow, steady, composed pace.
To sedate someone means to give them a drug that makes them calm, drowsy, or unconscious. That drug is called a sedative.
A sedative is a substance — almost always a drug or medication — that slows down the activity of the brain and nervous system.

Sedentary describes something or someone that involves very little physical movement — mostly sitting, staying still, or not being active. If something is sedentary, there is a strong pattern of not moving much.
Sediment is solid material that has settled at the bottom of a liquid, or that has been carried and deposited somewhere by water, wind, or ice.

Sedition is the act of encouraging or stirring up other people to violently rebel against, overthrow, or undermine their own government or ruling authority — usually through speech, writing, or organized action.

Something is "seditious" when it is designed to encourage people to rise up against, resist, or overthrow the government or those in power — usually through words, writing, speeches, or organized action.
To seduce someone means to attract, tempt, or lure them into doing something — particularly something they were hesitant about, resistant to, or wouldn't normally do on their own.
When something is seductive, it is so attractive or appealing that it pulls you toward it — often so powerfully that it's difficult to resist, even when a part of you knows you should resist.

Sedulous means showing careful, persistent, and devoted effort in doing something — working hard not just with energy, but with steady attention and dedication over time, without slacking off or losing focus.

To "see eye to eye" with someone means to agree with them — to share the same opinion, feeling, or view on something. When two people see eye to eye, they think alike about a particular topic. They understand each other and are on the same side of an idea.
To go with someone to the place they are leaving from and say goodbye, as in "she saw him off at the airport." It can also mean to chase off an intruder, or to defeat an opponent.
To see someone through something means to support and help a person during a difficult time or experience until it is completely over.
A seed is a small object produced by a plant, from which a new plant of the same kind can grow.
"Seedy" describes something — a place, a person, an atmosphere, or a situation — that feels dirty, run-down, and morally questionable all at once. It is not just about being physically messy or old.
"Seemingly" means "in a way that appears to be true or real, but may or may not actually be so."
"Seemly" describes behavior, actions, speech, or appearance that is proper, fitting, and appropriate — especially in a social or public setting.

To seep means to move slowly, quietly, and gradually through very small openings, cracks, pores, or gaps — almost as if the substance is squeezing itself through a surface that wasn't really designed to let it pass.
A seer is a person who sees things that ordinary people cannot see — specifically, things that are hidden, distant in time, or beyond the reach of normal human senses.
Seersucker is a type of cloth — specifically, a lightweight fabric known for its distinctive bumpy, crinkled surface texture.
To seethe means to be in a state of intense, turbulent, barely-contained agitation — like something that is violently churning and boiling on the inside.

When someone is seething, they are experiencing an intense, burning anger — but crucially, that anger is usually held inside, not erupting outward. Think of it as a fury that is churning within a person, barely under control.
A segment is a distinct part of something larger — a clearly defined piece that belongs to a whole, where the whole can be naturally or logically divided into such pieces.
To segregate means to separate someone or something from the rest of a group and keep them apart — usually based on a specific characteristic, category, or identity.
To segue means to move from one thing to another in a smooth, natural, uninterrupted way — so smoothly that the shift barely feels like a shift at all.
A seine is a large fishing net designed to catch fish by surrounding them, rather than by waiting for fish to swim into it on their own.
Seismic is an adjective that means "of or relating to earthquakes." If something is seismic in the literal sense, it has to do with the shaking, trembling, or vibration of the Earth.

"Seize" means to take something suddenly, firmly, and with force or decisiveness. It is the opposite of a slow, gentle, or hesitant action. When you seize something, you act fast, you act with purpose, and you take clear possession or control of it.
At the heart of every meaning of seizure is one simple idea: something is suddenly and forcefully taken or grabs hold.

Seldom means not often — something happens, but only a very small number of times. It is the opposite of "usually" or "always." When you say something happens seldom, you are saying it is a rare event. Not impossible, not zero — just very, very infrequent.

Selective means carefully choosing only certain things from a larger group, and leaving out the rest. A selective person or thing does not take, accept, or use everything available — it applies a filter, and only what meets a certain standard gets through.
Harming yourself, through behaviour such as drug misuse or neglect; also an old-fashioned word for masturbation.

Self-actualization is the process — and the ongoing state — of becoming the fullest, most complete version of yourself. It means realizing your true potential, living in alignment with your deepest values, and doing what you were uniquely built to do.

The word breaks apart neatly: self + conscious. To be conscious of something is to be aware of it. So to be self-conscious is to be aware of yourself — specifically, of how you look, what you're doing, or how you're coming across to others.
Self-control is the ability to manage your own thoughts, emotions, urges, and behavior — especially when a part of you wants to do something that your better judgment says you shouldn't.
A self-effacing person is someone who deliberately makes themselves seem smaller, less important, or less noticeable than they actually are.

Self-governance is the ability of a person, group, or community to manage and direct their own affairs — making their own rules, decisions, and choices — without being controlled by an outside authority.

A self-important person believes they are more significant, more authoritative, or more worthy of attention than they actually are — and they show this belief through the way they speak and behave. The key word is "important."

Self-indulgence means the act of freely giving yourself whatever you want — pleasure, comfort, or satisfaction — especially without holding back, without worrying about whether it's good for you, and often without caring much about consequences.
Self-mutilating describes something — most often a person, animal, or behavior — that involves deliberately causing serious physical damage, injury, or disfigurement to one's own body.
Self-pity is the feeling of being excessively sorry for yourself — dwelling on your own suffering, misfortune, or troubles in a way that goes beyond what the situation truly deserves.

When you possess something, you own it and have control over it. Self-possessed takes that idea and applies it to a person's own inner world — their emotions, reactions, and behavior. A self-possessed person, in a sense, owns themselves.
When someone is self-righteous, they are deeply convinced that they are morally good, morally correct, and morally superior — and they make sure other people feel it.
Self-sufficient means: able to provide for your own needs without depending on others.
Selfless describes a person who puts other people's needs, happiness, or well-being before their own — often at a personal cost to themselves.
To underestimate or fail to value someone or something properly, as in "don't sell yourself short." In finance, to sell borrowed shares hoping to buy them back later at a lower price.

Seltzer is simply plain water into which carbon dioxide (CO₂) gas has been dissolved under pressure. That dissolved gas is what creates the bubbles you see — and the fizzy, tingly feeling you experience when you drink it.
Semantic means relating to meaning — specifically, the meaning of words, phrases, sentences, or symbols.
Semblance means the outward appearance of something — especially when that appearance does not fully match the reality underneath.
A semicolon is a punctuation mark that looks like this: ;

When we call something seminal, we mean it was so original and powerful that it became the foundation for everything that came after it in its field. It didn't just matter — it shaped the future direction of an entire subject, genre, or area of thought.
A seminar is a focused learning session where a group of people come together — usually with a knowledgeable leader or expert — to study, discuss, or deeply explore a specific topic.
A seminary is a school — but not just any school. It is a specialized institution whose entire purpose is to train people to become religious leaders.
Semiotics is the systematic study of signs — what they are, how they work, and how human beings (and sometimes animals) use them to create and communicate meaning.

Sempiternal means existing across all of time — with no beginning and no end. It describes something that has always existed and will always exist, at every single moment, throughout infinite past and infinite future.
A senate is a formal governing body made up of a group of people — called senators — who have been given the authority to debate, create, and vote on laws.

Senescence is the gradual, natural process of deterioration that living things go through as they age — a slow biological decline in the ability to function, repair, and sustain life, which eventually leads toward death.

Senescent means in the process of growing old and declining. It describes a living thing — a person, an animal, a cell, an organism — that is aging and losing its former strength, vitality, or ability to function properly.

Senile describes a person — almost always an elderly one — who has experienced a serious and noticeable decline in their mental abilities due to old age or the deterioration of the brain that can come with aging.

Senility is the state of serious mental and physical decline that sometimes affects very old people. It is not just ordinary forgetfulness or slowing down — it is a significant breakdown in a person's ability to think, remember, and function in daily life.

"Senior" means higher, older, or more advanced than others within a system or group. It is always a word of comparison — it places one person or thing above another in terms of age, rank, experience, or stage.
Sensation is about experiencing something — either inside your own body and mind, or as a powerful impression on many people at once. These two broad areas give the word its different meanings.
Extremely good or impressive, as in "a sensational performance." It can also mean causing great excitement, or presenting news in a deliberately shocking way to attract attention.

Sensationalism is the practice of presenting information — most commonly news, stories, or events — in a way that is deliberately exaggerated, dramatic, or shocking, with the main goal of triggering a strong emotional reaction in the audience.

When you sense something, you become aware of it — not because someone told you, and often not because you consciously saw or heard it clearly, but because something inside you picked it up. It's a kind of quiet, internal knowing.
A sense of belonging is the feeling that you are a valued, accepted, and welcome member of a group or place — that you genuinely fit in there, not just physically, but emotionally and socially.
Sensibility is a person's deep inner capacity to feel, perceive, and respond to the world — especially its emotional, moral, and aesthetic dimensions.

"Sensible" means showing good, practical judgment. A sensible person thinks clearly before deciding, avoids unnecessary risks, and does what is genuinely realistic and appropriate — not just what sounds exciting or clever.

"Sensitive" describes something or someone that reacts easily — often to things that others might not even notice, or that require careful handling. Think of it as having a low threshold. It doesn't take much to produce a reaction.
At the heart of every use of this word lies one idea: sensitivity is the quality of reacting to, detecting, or being affected by something — and the degree to which that happens.

Sensitization means the process by which something — a person, an organism, or a system — becomes more sensitive or reactive to something it previously wasn't sensitive to, or was only mildly sensitive to.
The adjective sensory simply means relating to the senses — or more precisely, relating to how living beings receive and experience information from the world through their body.

Sensual describes something that gives deep pleasure to the physical senses — touch, taste, smell, sight, and sound. It is about the body's experience of the world — the richness, the warmth, the indulgence of physical feeling.

"Sensuous" describes something that gives pleasure through the five physical senses — sight, sound, touch, taste, or smell — in a rich, deep, and absorbing way. When something is sensuous, it doesn't just register on a sense; it envelops you.
A group of words that expresses a complete thought, usually including a subject and a verb. In law, a sentence is the punishment given by a court to someone found guilty.
To officially state the punishment that a person found guilty of a crime will receive, as in "sentenced to five years in prison."

If someone is sententious, they love to make grand, wise-sounding moral statements — often in a preachy, self-important way, as if they alone have figured out the secrets of life and virtue, and feel a duty to share them with everyone, repeatedly.
Sentience is the capacity to feel — to have inner, lived experiences.
If something is sentient, it means it is capable of feeling and experiencing things — such as pain, pleasure, warmth, cold, happiness, fear, or suffering — from a first-person perspective.
A sentiment is a feeling or emotion that is shaped by your thoughts, values, memories, or experiences — not just a sudden, raw gut reaction, but something more reflective and emotionally rich.

When something is sentimental, it means it is deeply tied to emotions — specifically warm, tender, nostalgic feelings like love, longing, or fond memory. Think of it as the emotional glow that surrounds certain things, people, or moments in your life.

Sentimentality is the quality of having or expressing feelings — especially tender, warm, nostalgic, or tearful feelings — in a way that is excessive, exaggerated, or simply not fully justified by the actual situation.
A sentinel is a person — or sometimes a thing — whose entire purpose is to watch, guard, and warn.
A sentry is a person — almost always a soldier or an armed guard — who is officially placed at a specific spot to keep watch, protect a location, and control who is allowed to pass through or enter.
Infected with harmful bacteria, as in "the wound went septic." It can also relate to sewage disposal, as in "a septic tank."
A septuagenarian is a person who is in their seventies — that is, someone who is at least 70 years old but has not yet reached their 80th birthday.

A septum is a thin wall or partition that divides a space into two separate sections. Think of it as an internal divider — like a fence that runs through the middle of a space to keep two sides separate from each other.
A sepulcher is a tomb — a place where a dead person's body is placed and sealed, usually permanently. But it's not just any burial spot.
Gloomy, dark, and deathly, like a tomb, as in "a sepulchral voice" or "sepulchral silence." Literally, relating to a tomb or burial.

A sequel is a work — such as a book, film, TV show, or video game — that continues the story of an earlier work. It picks up where the previous one left off and follows the same world, characters, or events forward in time.
A sequela is a medical condition or health problem that is the direct, lasting consequence of a previous disease, injury, or medical event.
A sequence is a group of things arranged in a specific order, where each item comes after the previous one, and where that order itself is meaningful.
To sequester means to isolate or separate something (or someone) from the rest, and keep it apart — usually for a specific purpose or by force.

Sequestration means the act of separating, isolating, or setting something aside — keeping it away from where it normally exists or belongs. Think of it as deliberately putting something "in a box" and locking it away from everything else.
A sequin is a tiny, flat, round, shiny disc used as decoration on clothing and accessories. Think of it as a miniature, glittering coin — but made for fashion, not for spending.
A conclusion or statement that follows logically from what came before. The word is best known in "non sequitur," a remark that does not follow logically from what was said.

A sequoia is a type of enormous, ancient, cone-bearing tree native to the western United States, especially California. These are not just large trees — they are among the most massive and oldest living things that have ever existed on Earth.
A seraph is a type of angel — not just any angel, but one of the most powerful, exalted, and holy beings in the angelic world, described in Abrahamic religions (Judaism, Christianity, and Islam).
Seraphic means having the qualities of an angel — specifically a quality of pure, radiant, blissful peace and beauty that seems to come from a place completely untouched by the troubles of the world.

Sere means completely dried out and withered — drained of all moisture, freshness, and life. It describes something that was once living and full of vitality, but has now become dry, brittle, and lifeless.
To serenade means to perform music — singing or playing an instrument — for a specific person, as a personal gesture directed at them, usually to express love, admiration, or deep feeling.

Serendipitous describes something good, valuable, or fortunate that happened purely by accident — something you never planned, never expected, and never even tried to make happen, but it turned out to be a wonderful thing.
Serendipity is the experience of accidentally discovering something wonderful that you weren't even looking for.
Serene means calm, peaceful, and completely undisturbed — in a way that feels deep, stable, and almost beautiful.

Serenity is a noun that means a state of being completely calm, peaceful, and undisturbed — both in your mind and in your surroundings. When you experience serenity, there is no worry, no stress, no chaos, and no noise pulling at your attention.

A serf was a person who was legally tied to a piece of land and was forced to work it — not as a free worker who chose to be there, but because the law and the social system of the time gave them no choice. They could not simply pack up and leave.
Seriatim means one by one, in a fixed order, treating each item separately.
When something is serious, it carries real weight — it matters, it has consequences, it demands genuine attention. It is the opposite of anything light, playful, or trivial.

A sermon is a formal, spoken address — essentially a prepared speech — delivered by a religious leader to an audience, with the purpose of teaching, guiding, or inspiring people on matters of religion, faith, or morality.
Serotonin is a chemical messenger your body makes naturally that carries signals between nerve cells and influences how you feel, digest food, sleep, and much more.
Winding and twisting like a snake, as in "a serpentine road." It can also mean cunning and treacherous, like a serpent.
Serrated describes an edge that has a row of small, sharp, pointed teeth or notches cut into it, like the edge of a saw.
Of rows of people or things, standing close together in tight ranks, as in "serried ranks of soldiers."

When something "serves her well," it means that thing is very useful, helpful, or beneficial to her. It is doing its job for her in an excellent way — giving her a good result, an advantage, or a positive outcome.
Servile means being excessively, embarrassingly submissive and eager to please someone — to such a degree that you completely abandon your own dignity and self-respect in the process.

Servitude means the condition of being completely under another person's control, with little or no personal freedom — especially being forced to work for them or obey them, often with no choice in the matter.
Using long, complicated words, especially when simpler ones would do, as in "a sesquipedalian style." Of a word, very long.
A set square is a flat, rigid, triangular drawing tool used to draw perfectly straight lines at specific, precise angles.

A setback is something that delays, slows down, or partially reverses your progress toward a goal. It is a problem or unfortunate event that pushes you backward — or at least stops you from moving forward — when things were going reasonably well.
A settee is a piece of furniture — specifically, an upholstered seat large enough for two or more people to sit on together. It has a backrest, two armrests on either side, and cushioned seating.
Almost every meaning of "settle" shares one underlying idea: something that was moving, unsettled, or unresolved comes to a point of rest, stability, or finality.
To sever something means to cut it completely apart or to end something totally and cleanly, leaving no connection between the two sides.

Severance means the act of cutting something off or ending a connection completely. It comes from the verb "sever," which means to cut or separate, and the noun form captures that moment — or the result — of something being cut away from something else.
Severe means going well beyond what is normal, comfortable, or mild — in a way that is harsh, intense, or hard to bear.

When something is severed, it means it has been completely and cleanly cut off from something it was once connected to — so completely that the two parts are now fully separate, with no remaining link between them.

Severity is a noun that describes how serious, extreme, harsh, or intense something is. Think of it as a measure of "how bad" or "how strong" something is — especially when that thing is dangerous, painful, strict, or difficult.
When you describe something as sexist, you are saying that it reflects, expresses, or causes unfair treatment of a person — or an entire group of people — based solely on their sex or gender.

A sextant is a handheld navigational instrument used to measure the angle between a celestial object — such as the sun, the moon, or a star — and the horizon. That angle, once known, tells a navigator exactly where on Earth they are standing (or sailing).

Shabby describes something (or someone) that looks worn out, neglected, and in poor condition — the kind of appearance that comes from a long time of use, little care, or not enough money to maintain things properly.
A shack is a small, roughly built structure — a building that is simple, basic, and often put together carelessly or with cheap, leftover materials.
"Shack up with someone" means to live together with a romantic or sexual partner without being married.

A shackle is a metal device that locks, binds, or connects — something that holds things (or people) in place, usually by force or necessity. Every meaning of this word grows from this single root idea.
To shackle someone means to restrict their freedom so severely that they cannot move, act, or function as they normally would.
Shade is about something being blocked from light — or, by extension, about something being reduced, softened, or partially hidden.
Dark and full of shadows; hard to see clearly; or secretive and mysterious ("a shadowy figure", "a shadowy organisation").
Something long, narrow, and cylindrical — like a rod or a pole. Almost every meaning of "shaft" connects back to this core image.
Coarsely cut tobacco for rolling cigarettes. A shag is also a carpet with a long, thick pile, a type of seabird related to the cormorant, or, in British slang, an act of sex.
"Shake a leg" is a common English idiom that means to hurry up or to start moving quickly. When someone tells you to "shake a leg," they are asking you to stop being slow and get going — fast.

A shalwar is a garment — specifically, a pair of loose, baggy trousers worn on the lower body, from the waist down to the ankles. Think of it like regular trousers, but much more relaxed and flowing in fit.

When you call something sham, you are saying it looks real and genuine on the outside, but is actually fake and deceptive on the inside. A sham thing is built to fool people — it wears a disguise of authenticity, but underneath, it is hollow and dishonest.

A sham is something — or someone — that looks real, genuine, or valuable on the outside, but is actually false, hollow, or worthless on the inside. The defining feature of a sham is the gap between appearance and reality. It wears a disguise.

A shaman is a person who is believed to have the special ability to enter the spirit world — a hidden, invisible realm — and communicate with the beings there, in order to help people in the real world.

To shamble means to walk in a slow, awkward, shuffling way — dragging your feet along the ground instead of lifting them properly, with your body moving in a loose, uncoordinated, slightly clumsy manner.
A shambles is a situation, place, or thing that is in a state of complete disorder, confusion, or mess — so bad that it looks like everything has fallen apart or gone terribly wrong.
Shambolic means chaotic, completely disorganized, and badly managed — in a way that shows a clear lack of planning, competence, or control.

A shanty is a small, crude dwelling — a hut or shack put together quickly and cheaply, often using whatever materials are available, like scrap wood, corrugated metal sheets, cardboard, or salvaged scraps. It is not a proper, well-constructed house.

A shantytown is a poor, overcrowded settlement made up of makeshift homes that people have built themselves — usually from whatever cheap or discarded materials they could find, like scrap wood, corrugated metal sheets, plastic tarpaulins, cardboard, or mud bricks.

A shard is a sharp, jagged piece that has broken off from something hard and brittle. Think of a glass bottle hitting the floor and exploding into dozens of dangerous little pieces — each one of those pieces is a shard.
A sharecropper is a poor farmer who farms land that belongs to someone else, and instead of paying cash rent, pays the landowner with a portion — a share — of the crops they grow at harvest time.

The word sharp carries one powerful idea: the quality of cutting through something — cleanly, precisely, and intensely. A sharp knife cuts material. A sharp mind cuts through confusion. A sharp comment cuts through feelings.
Suddenly and by a large amount ("Prices rose sharply"); harshly ("She spoke sharply"); or clearly and distinctly.

To shatter means to break something suddenly, violently, and completely — into many small pieces, all at once. It is not a gentle break. It is not a crack. It is a total, explosive destruction that leaves something in fragments.
The act of removing hair with a razor; also a thin slice cut off wood or another material.

A sheaf is a bundle of similar things gathered and held (or tied) together as a single, neat unit. Whenever you see the same kind of object collected together into one tidy grouping, you are looking at a sheaf.

To cut the wool off a sheep. It also means to cut something off with shears, or, of a part, to break off under strain, as in "the bolt sheared off." To be shorn of something means to be stripped of it.

A sheath is a snug, close-fitting cover or casing that wraps around something to protect it or hold it in place. Think of it like a custom-made sleeve — shaped specifically for whatever it is meant to hold, fitting it closely rather than loosely.
To sheathe something means to slide it, fit it, or encase it into a close-fitting protective covering.

A shebang refers to a thing, situation, operation, or collection of related parts — treated as one whole unit. Think of it as a way to refer to "the entire setup" or "everything involved in something."
A shed is a simple, plain structure — essentially a small building — that is built for a practical purpose like storage or work, not for people to live in.

Shed means to let something fall away, come off, or be released from something — whether naturally, deliberately, or even accidentally. The thing being shed typically moves away from its source or is separated from it.

Sheen is a soft, smooth, gentle brightness that you see on the surface of something. It's not a strong, blinding flash of light — it's more like a quiet, calm glow that seems to live on the surface itself, as if the surface is quietly radiating a mild light.
A sheep is a medium-sized, four-legged animal that humans have kept and raised for thousands of years. It is one of the most common farm animals in the world.
"Sheepish" describes how a person looks, feels, or behaves when they are mildly embarrassed — specifically because they've done something wrong, silly, or foolish, and they are quietly aware of it.

When someone does something sheepishly, they do it with a mix of embarrassment, mild guilt, and awkward self-awareness — especially when they know they've done something wrong, silly, or foolish, and they can't hide that they know it.
When placed before an abstract noun, "sheer" means pure — utterly and completely that one thing, with nothing else mixed in. It is a word of emphasis and exclusivity. It says: "this and only this."

A sheik is a respected leader, elder, or authority figure in Arab and Muslim communities. Think of it as a title of honor — like calling someone "Chief" or "Elder" — but it carries much deeper meaning depending on the situation.
A shell is a hard, protective outer layer — something firm on the outside that covers, guards, or contains whatever is inside. Think of it as nature's version of armour or a container.
Shelter means protection from something harmful or unpleasant — and the word almost always refers to either the place that gives you that protection or the state of being protected.
Sheltered means protected from something harsh, dangerous, or difficult.
Shenanigans is an informal noun that describes two closely related types of behavior: harmless, playful mischief and sneaky, underhanded tricks.
A sweet frozen dessert made with fruit juice; in Britain, a fizzy sweet powder; in South Asia and the Middle East, a chilled sweet drink.

A Sheriff is an official who is responsible for keeping law and order in a particular area — most commonly a county — and who holds legal authority to enforce the law, carry out court orders, and protect the people living in that area.
A shibboleth is something — a word, phrase, custom, habit, or belief — that signals whether a person truly belongs to a particular group. Think of it as an invisible membership test.
"Shift" means to move something — or someone — from one position to another, or to change the state, direction, or focus of something.
Shiftless describes a person who is lazy, lacks ambition, and makes no real effort to work, improve their life, or take care of their own responsibilities.

When you call someone shifty, you are saying that they seem dishonest, untrustworthy, or sneaky — like they're hiding something or trying to deceive you. It's a feeling you get about a person before you can even prove anything is wrong.

A shill is a person who secretly works for — or is paid by — someone else, but pretends to be a completely independent, ordinary member of the public, in order to deceive other people into trusting, buying, or supporting something.

To shimmer means to shine with a soft, gentle, trembling light — a light that seems to move slightly or waver, as if it is quietly breathing. It is not a bold or powerful shine. It is delicate, subtle, and beautiful.
A shimmy is a rapid, repeated, side-to-side shaking or quivering motion — something that vibrates or wobbles quickly, either on purpose or by accident.
"Shimmy" captures a very specific quality of movement: small, rapid, quivering oscillations — a fast trembling or wobbling from side to side, or up and down, in tight little bursts.
Shine is about light and brightness — either giving off light, reflecting light, or standing out brilliantly.
A shingle is a thin, flat, rectangular piece of material — usually wood, asphalt, slate, or fiber cement — that is used to cover the outside of a roof or sometimes a wall.
When a ship is shipwrecked, it means the ship is completely destroyed — it crashes onto rocks, is torn apart by a violent storm, runs aground on a reef, or sinks due to some disaster.

To shirk means to deliberately avoid doing something that you are supposed to do — especially a duty, a responsibility, or a task that is expected of you — usually because it feels difficult, unpleasant, or requires effort you don't want to give.
A shirtwaist is a woman's top — specifically a blouse that is cut and styled to look like a man's dress shirt.

The most basic, literal meaning of shit is the solid waste your body pushes out when you go to the toilet — what you'd call feces in medical or polite language, or poop in everyday gentle speech. Every animal and human produces it as a byproduct of digestion.

A shitshow is a situation, event, or organization that is chaotic, deeply dysfunctional, and often embarrassingly out of control — usually because of poor management, gross incompetence, or simply too many things going wrong at once.

A shiver is a sudden, brief, involuntary trembling or shaking of your body — or a part of it. "Involuntary" here is key: it means your body does it on its own, without you deciding to. You don't choose to shiver; it just happens to you.
A shoal is a place in a sea, river, lake, or any body of water where the water is very shallow — so shallow that the ground underneath (the bed) comes dangerously close to the surface.

Shoddy means of poor quality, made without proper care, or done carelessly and without enough effort. When something is shoddy, it means whoever made it or did it cut corners — they didn't give it the skill, time, or attention it actually needed.
"Shoot" is about something being sent outward, fast — with force or intent.

"Shoot the breeze" means to have a casual, relaxed conversation with someone — the kind where you're not discussing anything serious or important. You're just talking for the fun of it, enjoying each other's company through light, friendly chatter.

A room or booth where people shoot at targets for practice or as a fairground game. In slang, it is also a place where drug users gather to inject drugs, or a situation in which people are easy targets for attack.
A shopper is a person who goes to a store, a market, a shopping mall, or a website with the purpose of looking at goods and possibly buying them.
Shorn means having been cut away or having had something removed by cutting.
To shortchange someone means to give them less than what they are owed, what they deserve, or what they were fairly promised.
A shortcoming is a fault or weakness — specifically, a way in which someone or something falls short of a standard, expectation, or ideal.
To shorten something means to make it less long than it currently is. If something has a certain length — in space, in time, or in content — and you reduce that length, you have shortened it.
Shorthand is a special system of fast writing where you replace normal words with quick symbols, squiggles, or abbreviations.
"Shorthanded" describes a situation where a person, team, business, or organization has fewer people available than it needs to function properly.

In medicine and everyday speech, shortsighted describes a person whose eyes can see nearby objects clearly but cannot see distant objects clearly. A shortsighted person can read a book held in their hands but struggles to read a signboard across the street.
"A shot in the dark" means a guess that is made with very little or no information — an attempt at something when you have almost no idea whether it will work or be correct.

When you shoulder something abstract — a responsibility, a cost, a burden, or blame — it means you accept it and take it upon yourself. You put that weight on your own shoulders and carry it forward, often even when it is heavy, difficult, or unfair.

A shout is a single, loud burst of sound made by a person using their voice. It is louder and more forceful than ordinary speech, and it usually comes out quickly — in one sharp release of air, not drawn out.
To shove means to push someone or something with force and roughness. It is never gentle. The action is quick, strong, and often careless or aggressive.
Show means to make something perceptible — to bring something from a state where it is hidden, unknown, or unnoticed into a state where it can be seen, understood, or felt.
To showcase something means to present or display it in a way that deliberately highlights its best, most impressive qualities — so that others notice, appreciate, or admire it.
Showmanship is the skill of presenting something — yourself, your talent, or your work — in a way that is exciting, dramatic, and entertaining.
Shrapnel is the jagged, sharp fragments of metal — and sometimes other hard materials — that fly outward at deadly speed when something explodes.
A bad-tempered, nagging woman (an old-fashioned, insulting term), as in "The Taming of the Shrew." Literally, a shrew is a tiny, mouse-like animal with a long pointed nose.
A shrewd person is someone who is practically clever in a sharp, perceptive way — especially when it comes to understanding people, situations, and how to get the best outcome for themselves.

When you do something shrewdly, you do it with sharp, practical intelligence — in a way that shows you clearly understand a situation, see what others might miss, and use that understanding to your advantage.
To shriek means to make a very loud, high-pitched, sharp cry or sound that bursts out suddenly and involuntarily.
Shrill describes a sound that is very high in pitch, sharp, and unpleasantly piercing — the kind that hits your ears in a way that makes you wince.
To shrive means to hear someone's confession of sins, give them a task of penance (something they must do to show true regret), and then formally forgive them — all as an act of religious authority.
To shrivel means to become — or to cause something to become — smaller, thinner, and wrinkled, because it is losing moisture or substance from inside.
Something that covers and hides, as in "a shroud of secrecy" or "a shroud of mist." Literally, a cloth used to wrap a dead body for burial.

To shroud something means to cover it completely, hiding it from view or keeping it from being understood. Think of it as wrapping something so thoroughly that it becomes invisible, unclear, or mysterious.
To shrug means to raise both your shoulders up briefly, then drop them back down. It is a quick, effortless movement — like your shoulders going up and coming back down in a fraction of a second.

A shuck is the outer covering that wraps around certain foods — the shell, husk, or pod that you peel away or crack open to get to the edible part inside. It is the packaging that nature puts around food.

To shudder means to shake or tremble suddenly and briefly, usually through the whole body or a large part of it, as a reaction to something — something frightening, disgusting, horrible, or deeply unpleasant.
To shuffle means to move things — or yourself — in a sliding, mixing, or rearranging way, without a clear order or smooth, deliberate motion.
To shun someone or something means to deliberately and persistently stay away from them — not by accident, not just once, but as a clear, conscious, and repeated choice.
A shunt is a diversion — something that redirects a flow away from its main path and into an alternative one. Think of it as a bypass.
To shunt means to push, redirect, or move something (or someone) away from the main path and into a different, often secondary, one.
When you shush someone, you are telling them to be quiet — to stop talking, to lower their voice, or to stop making noise. You are, in effect, commanding silence.
A shutter is something that covers, closes off, or controls the flow of light or access to a space — think of it as a barrier you can open and close on demand.

A shuttle is something that moves back and forth between two fixed points, repeatedly. Every meaning of this word connects to this idea of going and coming, going and coming — like a pendulum, or like your hand when you wave.
A shyster is a person — most often a lawyer, but sometimes a businessman or politician — who is deliberately dishonest and unscrupulous in the way they do their work.
Something is sibilant when it produces a hissing sound — specifically the kind of thin, airy, high-pitched hiss you hear in the letter "S" or "SH."
A sibling is a person who shares at least one parent with you. In other words, your sibling is your brother or your sister.
A sibyl is a woman believed to have the divine gift of prophecy — meaning she could receive messages from the gods and use them to predict the future or reveal hidden truths.

"Sibylline" describes something — a remark, a look, a piece of writing, a person's manner — that is cryptic, mysteriously ambiguous, and prophetic in quality, like a riddle spoken by an ancient oracle.
Sicken means to cause illness, or to feel or become ill — but it also extends powerfully into the emotional world, meaning to fill someone with deep disgust or horror.

"Sickening" describes something that produces such a strong, overwhelming reaction — of disgust, horror, or excess — that it feels like it is making you physically ill. The key idea is that the reaction isn't mild. It is gut-level, visceral, and intense.
A sickle is a simple, hand-held cutting tool used mainly in farming and gardening. Its entire purpose is to cut through plant stems — things like grain, grass, weeds, or crops — quickly and cleanly.

Often ill or in weak health, as in "a sickly child." It can also mean looking pale and unhealthy, causing a feeling of sickness, as in "a sickly smell," or excessively sentimental, as in "sickly sweet."
A short article or panel beside a main one, with extra information; also a side column on a web page, or a private talk between lawyers and a judge.

When something is sidelong, it is directed or angled to the side rather than straight ahead — and more importantly, it is done in an indirect, subtle, or secretive way rather than openly and directly.
Sidereal is an adjective that means "relating to, or measured with reference to, the distant fixed stars."
To sidestep something means to deliberately avoid it — either by physically moving out of its way, or by cleverly refusing to deal with it directly.
To sidetrack means to cause someone or something to move away from the main goal, topic, or task — and get pulled into something less important or unrelated instead.
To sidle means to move sideways in a slow, quiet, careful way — especially to approach or slip away without being noticed or without drawing attention to yourself.

A siege is a situation where one group of people completely surrounds a place — like a city, a castle, or a building — and blocks everything from going in or out, in order to force the people inside to give up.
A siesta is a short rest or sleep that a person takes in the early afternoon, usually right after the midday meal.
A sieve is a simple but clever tool: it is a frame — usually round — with a bottom made of wire mesh, a woven net, or a plate punched full of tiny holes. Its entire purpose is separation by size.
To examine something carefully in order to separate what is useful or important from the rest, as in "sifting through the evidence." Literally, to pass flour or sand through a sieve to remove lumps.
A sigh is a single, long, slow breath outward — much deeper and longer than your normal breathing — that makes a soft, audible sound. Think of the sound like "haaaah" or "hhhhh."

To sigh means to breathe out slowly, deeply, and audibly — in a way that expresses how you are feeling inside. The key word here is audibly, meaning people around you can actually hear it. It is not a normal, silent breath.
"A sight for sore eyes" is used to describe someone or something that you are very happy, relieved, or overjoyed to see — especially after a long time apart or after going through something hard.

In internet slang, a man who is admired for being independent, self-assured, and successful while living outside social hierarchies — a "lone wolf." It is often used ironically or as general praise meaning "cool."

A sign-off phrase is a short word, expression, or sentence placed at the very end of a communication — like an email, a formal letter, a text message, a speech, or even a television or radio broadcast — just before the sender's name or the program ends.
Signage means signs, considered as a collection, a system, or a category.

Significance is the quality or property that something has when it matters deeply or carries meaningful weight — either because it means something important, or because it has a noticeable impact or consequence.

"Significant" means important or large enough to deserve attention, to make a real difference, or to carry a meaningful message. When something is significant, it is not trivial, not minor, and not easily dismissed. It stands out because it genuinely matters.

To signify means to be a sign of something — to point toward, represent, or communicate a meaning. Think of it this way: when something "signifies," it is doing the job of a sign. It is telling you something without necessarily using plain, direct words.

A silhouette is the dark, solid shape of a person, animal, object, or scene that appears against a brighter background — one in which all internal detail is lost and only the outer shape remains visible.
"Silly" describes someone or something that shows a lack of seriousness, careful thinking, or common sense — but almost always in a small, harmless, and often funny or charming way.
When used as a noun, "silly" refers to a foolish, simple, or giddy person — someone who acts without much thought, says something absurd, or behaves in a childishly playful way.
A silo is a large, tall, cylindrical structure — imagine a giant tube standing upright, like a thick column — used to store bulk materials in large quantities.

Silt is a natural material made of extremely tiny particles — finer than sand but coarser than clay. These particles come from rocks and minerals that have been slowly ground down over long periods of time by water, wind, and ice.
A silver bullet is a single, simple, and highly effective solution that instantly solves a difficult or complex problem — almost like magic.

"Simian" means of, relating to, or resembling an ape or monkey. If something is described as simian, it has qualities, features, or characteristics that are typical of — or look like — an ape or monkey.
A simile is a figure of speech — a creative way of describing something — by directly comparing it to something else using the words "like" or "as."

Similitude means likeness — the quality or state of two or more things being similar to each other. When two things share characteristics that make them alike in a deep or meaningful way, there is a similitude between them.
To simmer means to stay at, or bring something to, a state of gentle, low-level activity — right at the edge of becoming more intense, but not quite there yet.
Simony is the act of buying or selling something sacred — most specifically, a position, role, or spiritual power within the Christian Church — in exchange for money or personal gain.

To simper means to smile in a way that looks silly, fake, or overly sweet — usually because the person is trying too hard to appear charming, innocent, or pleasing. It is not a genuine, natural smile.
To simplify something means to make it less complicated, easier to understand, or easier to use — by removing what is unnecessary, confusing, or overly complex, while keeping what is truly important.

Simplistic means so simple that it becomes wrong, misleading, or inadequate. It describes something that treats a complicated subject as if it were far easier than it really is — leaving out important details, nuances, or complications along the way.
An image or representation of something, especially one that imitates its appearance but lacks its real substance, as in "a simulacrum of democracy."

To simulate something means to artificially create or imitate the experience, behavior, conditions, or appearance of something real — usually so you can study it, practice with it, test it, or understand it — without using or experiencing the real thing itself.

A simulation is an artificial imitation of something real — a process, a system, a situation, or an event — that is created so it can be studied, tested, experienced, or practiced without engaging with the actual thing.
Simultaneous means happening at the same time. When two or more things are simultaneous, they occur together — not one before the other, not one after the other, but at the same moment.
Simultaneously means at the same time — not one after the other, but both (or all) happening at the exact same moment.
When you describe something as sincere, you are saying it is genuinely felt or genuinely meant — there is no pretending, no acting, and no hidden motive behind it.

Sincerity is the quality of being genuine — meaning what you say, feeling what you express, and intending what you claim to intend. When someone has sincerity, there is no gap between their inner reality and what they show on the outside.
When something is adjourned, suspended, or postponed sine die, it means it has been put off without any date being set for it to resume or continue.

A sinecure is a job, position, or role that pays you — or gives you some kind of benefit, status, or privilege — but asks almost nothing of you in return. You hold the title. You receive the reward. But you do little to no real work.

A sinew is a tough, strong, cord-like tissue inside your body that connects a muscle to a bone. The scientific word for it is a tendon, and sinew and tendon mean exactly the same thing — sinew is just the older, more literary word.
A sinew is a tendon — the tough, cord-like tissue inside your body that connects muscle to bone.
To singe something means to burn it very lightly on the surface — just enough to scorch the outermost layer, but not enough to set it on fire, burn it through, or destroy it.

"Singular" means relating to just one. Almost every meaning of this word grows from that single seed. Think of it as the opposite of "many" or "multiple." Whenever you see "singular," your brain should first think: one — standing apart from the rest.

A singularity is a point — a moment, a location, or a condition — that is so extreme, so utterly unlike everything around it, that normal rules stop working there. It is the one point where everything breaks.
"Sinister" describes something that is, or strongly appears to be, evil, threatening, or deeply wrong — especially in a dark, hidden, or secretive way.

A sinking feeling is a sudden, unpleasant physical sensation — felt mostly in your stomach or chest — that happens the moment you realize something is wrong, something bad is about to happen, or that a situation is worse than you hoped.
