Sinuosity means the quality or degree of having curves, bends, and winding turns. It describes how curvy or twisting something is — as opposed to being straight.

Sinuous means smoothly and gracefully curved — bending and curving repeatedly, like a snake. Something sinuous is never straight, never jagged or sharp. Instead, it flows through a series of long, smooth, gentle curves, one after the other.
To sip means to drink something in very small amounts, slowly, one tiny mouthful at a time — instead of taking a big mouthful or drinking quickly.

To siphon means to draw liquid out of a container and move it somewhere else through a tube or pipe, usually by creating suction or using gravity to get the flow going. Once the flow starts, the liquid keeps moving on its own.

A device that makes a loud, wailing warning sound, as on a police car or ambulance. In Greek mythology, the Sirens were creatures whose beautiful singing lured sailors to their deaths, so a siren is also a dangerously seductive woman.
A sirocco is a powerful, hot wind that blows out of the Sahara Desert in North Africa and travels northward across the Mediterranean Sea toward southern Europe.
A sitar is a large, plucked string instrument that is one of the most important and iconic musical instruments of North Indian classical music, also called Hindustani classical music.
A sitcom is a type of television (or radio) show built around a fixed group of characters who keep finding themselves in funny, awkward, or absurd situations.
Site means a specific place identified for a particular reason — whether that reason is what happened there, what is happening there now, or what will happen there in the future.
To situate something means to deliberately place it somewhere — either in a physical location or, more importantly, within a context, framework, or set of circumstances.
"Sizable" means large enough to be worth noticing or taking seriously. It describes something that is not just a little big — it is big in a way that clearly stands out and actually matters.
To size up something or someone means to carefully look at, assess, and form a judgment about them — usually so you know how to deal with them.
To skedaddle means to leave somewhere quickly, usually to avoid a person, a situation, or some kind of trouble. Think of it as a more colorful, energetic way of saying "run away" or "hurry off."
A loose coil of yarn or thread. It can also mean a flock of geese or ducks flying in a line, or a complicated tangle of things, as in "a skein of lies."
Relating to the skeleton; extremely thin, as if only bones remain; or reduced to the bare minimum ("a skeletal staff").
"A skeleton in the closet" means a dark, shameful, or embarrassing secret that someone — a person, family, company, or even a government — is hiding from the world.

A skeptic is a person who does not simply accept a claim, belief, or idea just because someone says it is true. Instead, a skeptic pauses, questions it, and asks: "What is the evidence for this? Does this actually make sense? Why should I believe it?"

When someone is skeptical, they are not easily convinced. They hear a claim, a story, or an idea — and instead of immediately believing it, they pause and think: "Really? Are you sure? Where's the proof?"
Skepticism is the philosophical position that questions whether we can truly know anything — or at least, whether we can be as certain about things as we think we are.
A rough, quick drawing. It can also mean a short humorous scene in a comedy show, or a brief description giving the main facts, as in "a sketch of his life."

When you sketch something, you draw it quickly and roughly. You are not trying to make a perfect, detailed picture. You are just trying to capture the basic shape and feel of something — the essential outline — without worrying about every little detail.
Seeming suspicious, dishonest, or unsafe (informal), as in "a sketchy neighbourhood." It can also mean incomplete or lacking detail, as in "a sketchy memory."

Skeuomorphism is the practice of designing something new so that it visually or functionally imitates the appearance of an older, physical thing it is replacing or representing — even when those imitated details are no longer necessary in the new version.
To make something inaccurate or biased, as in "the results were skewed." It also means to make something lopsided or to move at an angle.
Skewed means tilted, pulled, or distorted in one direction — away from what would be straight, balanced, or fair. Think of it as the opposite of "even" or "neutral."
To criticize or mock someone harshly and effectively, as in "the critics skewered the film." Literally, to pierce food with a long, thin stick for cooking.
When something skids, it slides suddenly and without control, usually sideways or in an unintended direction, because it has lost its grip on the surface beneath it.

A skiff is a small, simple, open boat — the kind a single person can easily handle on their own. Think of it as the most basic, no-frills boat you can imagine: no cabin, no roof, no fancy equipment. Just a lightweight vessel that gets you across the water.
A skill is the ability to do something well — an ability that you have developed through learning, practice, and experience.
When something lighter floats to the surface of a liquid, you can scoop it off with a spoon or ladle. That act is called skimming.

To skimp means to use less of something than is really needed or appropriate — less money, less material, less effort, less care — usually to save time or money, but in a way that hurts the quality of the result.

Skimpy means too little of something — not enough in size, amount, or coverage. It describes things that fall short of what is needed, expected, or proper. Think of it as the feeling you get when you expected more but received noticeably less.
Skin refers to the outermost covering or layer of something — whether a living body, a fruit, a liquid, or even a digital interface.

When "skin" is used as a verb, the central idea is almost always about removing or damaging an outer covering — whether that's the hide of an animal, the peel of a fruit, or the surface layer of your body.
"Skin and bones" means extremely thin or underweight — so thin that a person (or animal) looks like there is nothing on their body except skin covering their skeleton.

A skinflint is a person who is extremely unwilling to spend money — someone so stingy and tight-fisted that they will go to unreasonable lengths to avoid parting with even the smallest amount of cash. It is always used as an insult or a mockery.
A skirmish is a small, brief fight or conflict — one that is minor in size and short in duration, especially when compared to a larger battle, war, or dispute it might be part of.
To avoid dealing with a difficult subject, as in "she skirted the question." Literally, to go around the edge of something rather than through it, as in "the road skirts the village."

To skitter means to move quickly with light, short, and slightly irregular movements — often in a darting, unpredictable way. Think of a small creature that is in a hurry and a little nervous: it doesn't walk smoothly or run in a perfectly straight line.

Skittish describes something or someone that is easily frightened, nervously alert, and quick to react — usually by pulling back, flinching, or fleeing. The essential idea is excessive reactivity: the trigger is small, but the response is big.
An informal British word: to avoid work or school by staying away or slipping off ("He skived off the meeting").

Skulduggery means sneaky, dishonest, and underhanded behavior — especially the kind that involves scheming, tricking, or manipulating others behind the scenes to get what you want. It is the art of being cleverly crooked.
To skulk means to move around or hide somewhere in a secretive, sneaky way — usually because you don't want to be seen, and usually because you have a guilty, cowardly, or suspicious reason for it.

To skylark means to play around in a lively, carefree, and mischievous way — to fool around, joke, frolic, or engage in boisterous fun, often when you should be doing something more serious or productive.
Slack describes something that is less than it should be — less tight, less active, less careful, or less energetic than expected.

Slack means to ease up, loosen, or reduce intensity. Think of a taut rope — when you release some of its tension, it goes limp. That image of going from tight to loose, from active to less active, is the soul of this word.
Slacken means to become less tight, less fast, or less intense — or to cause something to become that way.
The waste left over when metal is extracted from ore; also offensive British slang for a woman, used as an insult.

Slake means to fully satisfy something that has been pressing and demanding — to give it exactly what it needs until it quiets down and is relieved. Think of it as answering a strong inner call so completely that the call goes silent.
Slander is a false spoken statement about a person that damages their reputation.
To slander someone means to make a false spoken statement about them that damages their reputation, while presenting it as if it were true.
Slanderous is an adjective that describes a statement, claim, or remark that is false, is spoken about a specific person, and causes serious damage to that person's reputation.
A slant is something that leans or tilts — it goes neither perfectly flat nor perfectly straight up, but somewhere in between, diagonally.

To slant means to go at an angle — not perfectly flat like a tabletop, and not perfectly upright like a wall, but somewhere in between, leaning or tilting in a particular direction. Everything else the word does grows from this central idea.

Slapdash describes something done too quickly and too carelessly, resulting in poor quality. When something is slapdash, the person who did it clearly didn't take enough time, didn't pay attention to detail, and didn't bother to check or improve the result.

When you describe something as slapstick, you mean it involves a type of humor that is loud, exaggerated, and based on physical actions — things like people falling down, getting hit by objects, bumping into walls, throwing pies at each other's faces, or stumbling over their own feet in ridiculous ways.

Slapstick is a style of comedy built entirely on exaggerated, over-the-top physical action — things like wild falls, collisions, pies thrown in faces, people running into walls, getting bonked on the head, slipping on banana peels, or accidentally dumping buckets of water on themselves.
To slash means to cut something with a fast, forceful, sweeping stroke — the kind of movement your arm makes when swinging widely through the air.
A slat is a thin, flat, narrow strip of hard material — most often wood, but sometimes metal or plastic. It is flat (not round, not hollow), narrow (much narrower than it is long), and rigid.
When something is slated, it means it has been officially planned, scheduled, or set to happen. Think of it as something being "lined up" or "put on the agenda."
To slather something means to spread or apply it over a surface thickly, generously, and somewhat carelessly — in a way that suggests abundance rather than precision.

A slattern is a woman who is habitually dirty, untidy, and slovenly — in both her personal appearance and her living environment. The word doesn't describe someone who had a messy week or forgot to do laundry.

Slatternly describes someone — or something belonging to someone — that is habitually dirty, messy, and carelessly untidy. The key word here is habitually. It doesn't mean a person is having a bad day or is temporarily disheveled.
"Slaughter" means the killing of a large number of living beings — either animals or people — in a way that is brutal, systematic, or completely one-sided. It is not a neutral word.

To slaughter means to kill. But it is not just any kind of killing. The word carries a sense of scale, brutality, and helplessness. The victims — whether animals or people — are essentially powerless. There is little or no resistance, no fair fight.

To slaver means to let saliva drip or flow uncontrollably from the mouth — in plain terms, to drool heavily. When a hungry dog sits in front of a piece of meat and saliva streams down its chin, it is slavering.
Slavish describes behavior that resembles how a slave was historically forced to act — with zero independence, zero original thinking, and total submission to something or someone else.
Sleazy describes something or someone that feels morally dirty, corrupt, and disgusting — cheap and low in a way that makes decent people uncomfortable or repulsed.
A sled is a simple vehicle designed to glide smoothly over snow or ice. Instead of wheels, it has runners — two long, narrow strips (usually made of metal or wood) fixed to the underside.
A sledge is a vehicle that has no wheels. Instead of wheels, it has flat strips of metal or wood on its underside — called runners — that allow it to glide smoothly over snow, ice, or rough ground.
Sleek means smooth, shiny, and elegantly shaped — in a way that looks polished, refined, and attractive.
The most direct meaning: a sleeper is simply someone who sleeps, especially when described by how they sleep.

Sleeping quarters refers to any place or area where a person sleeps or is meant to sleep. It is simply the space — a room, a section of a building, a compartment on a ship, or even a designated corner of a larger space — set aside for sleeping.
A sleigh is a vehicle designed to travel over snow and ice. The key thing that makes it a sleigh — and not a cart or a carriage — is that it has no wheels.

Sleight means a clever, deceptive skill — the kind of skillful trickery where someone does something so smoothly, quickly, or cleverly that you don't notice what's really happening. It's not just being good at something.
Slender means thin — but not just thin in any ordinary way. It means thin in a way that also feels graceful, elegant, or attractive.

A sleuth is a detective — someone who investigates mysteries, crimes, or secrets to find the truth. Think of it as a vivid, more characterful word for a person who digs, searches, and figures things out when answers are hidden.
A large number or amount of something, as in "a slew of complaints." Slew is also the past tense of "slay."
Slick = smoothness that removes all friction.

"Slight" means small in degree, not strong, not serious, or not substantial. The feeling it gives you is: this thing exists, but it's at the very low end of the scale. It's not zero — but it's not much, either.
To slight someone means to treat them as if they are unimportant, not worth your attention, or beneath your notice — especially when they deserved better from you.
"Slim" means pleasantly small in size or amount — either in width (how thin something is) or in degree (how little of something there is).

A medical sling is a triangular piece of cloth tied around your neck that acts like a small hammock for your arm. If you break your wrist or injure your shoulder, a doctor places your arm inside this cloth and loops it behind your neck.

"Sling" always implies a movement that is loose, casual, and lacking careful precision. Think of swinging your arm in a wide, relaxed arc and letting something fly — that sweeping, effortless motion is the soul of this word.
To slink means to move in a quiet, slow, and sneaky way — but not just any sneaky movement. What makes slink special is the reason behind it.
Slipshod describes something done carelessly, with little attention to quality, effort, or detail — in a way that is clearly below the standard it should have met.
To slither means to move along a surface in a smooth, twisting, sliding way — with the body close to or touching the surface. Think of a snake moving across the ground.
A sliver is a very thin, narrow, and usually long piece of something that has been cut, split, or broken away from a larger whole. Think of it as a kind of fragment — but with a very specific shape.
To slog means to do something that requires hard, sustained effort that is tiring, slow, or tedious — but you keep going anyway.

A slogan is a short, catchy phrase that is designed to stick in your memory and represent something bigger — like a brand, a movement, a political campaign, or an organization. Think of it as a tiny package carrying a big message.
Careless and lacking attention to detail, as in "sloppy work." It can also mean messy and untidy, too watery, as in "sloppy porridge," or overly sentimental.

At the heart of "slosh" is liquid moving in a messy, uncontrolled way — often with a splashing or swishing sound. Whenever a liquid doesn't stay still or move neatly, but instead wobbles, spills, splashes, or slaps around carelessly, that's sloshing.
Extreme, habitual laziness, one of the seven deadly sins in Christian tradition. A sloth is also a slow-moving animal that hangs upside down in the trees of Central and South American rainforests.
"Slothful" means extremely lazy — so lazy that a person consistently and habitually avoids work, effort, or responsibility as a fundamental way of life.

When you slouch, you let your body droop and collapse inward instead of holding it upright. Your back curves forward, your shoulders round and fall down, your chest caves in, and your head hangs forward.
To slough means to shed, peel away, or cast off something that has died, worn out, or is no longer needed — usually in the form of a layer.

A sloven is a person who is habitually dirty, untidy, and careless — in how they look, how they live, and often in how they work. If you call someone a sloven, you are saying that messiness and neglect are not accidents for them — they are a way of life.
Slovenly means untidy, dirty, and carelessly maintained — but with an important extra layer: it's not just about being messy once.
Sludge is a thick, soft, wet, and dirty semi-liquid substance — something that is too thick to flow like water but not solid enough to hold its shape like clay. It sits uncomfortably in between.
To slug means to strike someone with a powerful, heavy blow — almost always with a closed fist, though sometimes with a blunt object. It is not a light tap or a slap.

A sluggard is a person who is deeply and habitually lazy — someone who consistently avoids work, effort, and responsibility, and whose defining characteristic is an unwillingness to get up and do what needs to be done.

"Sluggish" describes something or someone that is moving, working, or responding more slowly than normal or expected — and usually with a sense of heaviness, low energy, or resistance pulling it back.
A sluice is a structure built to control the flow of water. Think of it as a "water door" — one that can be opened to let water rush through, or closed to hold it back.

To sluice something means to wash or clean it using a large, forceful rush of water — the kind of washing where water doesn't just trickle or drip, but floods over a surface with power and speed, sweeping everything in its path away.

Slumber means sleep — but not just any sleep. It refers to sleep that feels peaceful, gentle, and undisturbed. Think of the quiet stillness of a child tucked in at night, or the soft rest of an afternoon nap in a hammock.

To slumber means to sleep. But it is not just any kind of sleep — it is sleep that is gentle, calm, and peaceful. When someone slumbers, they are resting quietly, undisturbed, often in a soft and serene way.
A slump is a significant, noticeable fall or drop — in performance, numbers, energy, or activity — that lasts for a period of time. It is not a tiny dip. It is not a single bad moment.

To slump means to fall, sink, or drop in a heavy, limp, and lifeless way — as if all strength or support has suddenly been drained away. The key image behind this word is something giving way under its own weight, without control or energy.

A slur is a word, phrase, or remark that attacks or degrades a person or a group of people — usually based on something about their identity, such as their race, religion, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, or disability.
To speak unclearly, running words together, as when drunk or tired. It can also mean to make insulting remarks about someone to damage their reputation, or, in music, to play notes smoothly together.
To eat or drink noisily, with a loud sucking sound.
If someone is sly, they are clever in a hidden, secretive way — they get what they want through quiet tricks, secret plans, or subtle deception, without others noticing what they are really doing.
"Small fry" refers to a person — or a group of people — who are unimportant, low in power, or of little significance, especially when compared to those who hold real authority, influence, or status.

Small talk is light, casual conversation about unimportant topics that people have with each other — especially with people they don't know well, or in social situations where a deeper conversation would feel awkward or out of place.
Smarmy means excessively flattering, charming, or agreeable in a way that feels deeply fake and self-serving.
"Smart" means impressive in some way — whether that's in thinking, in appearance, in behavior, or even in technology. The exact impression it creates depends on the situation.
When "smart" is used as a verb, it means to feel a sharp, stinging pain — the kind that is sudden, intense, and tends to linger for a bit.
"Smarten up" is a phrasal verb that essentially means: improve yourself — your behavior, your thinking, or your appearance.
A smattering of something means a small, scattered, and incomplete amount of it. It is always used with "of."

A smear is something — a substance, a stain, or a damaging claim — that has been spread across something else, usually in a thin, messy, or deliberate way. The word almost always carries a sense of dirtiness, messiness, or harm, depending on the context.

"Smear" means to spread a soft, wet, or greasy substance across a surface by rubbing or sliding it. The key feeling of this word is messiness and imprecision — not neat, not careful, but a rough, sliding spread that covers something.
To extract metal from ore by heating and melting it; also an old past tense of "smell".
A smidgen is an extremely small, indefinite amount of something. When you say "a smidgen of something," you mean just barely a little — so little that it's almost nothing, but not quite nothing.

A smirk is a type of smile — but it is not a warm, kind, or happy smile. It is a smile that secretly communicates something negative, such as superiority, mockery, or self-satisfaction. Think of it as a smile with a hidden, unfriendly message inside it.
To smirk means to smile — but not in a warm, friendly, or innocent way.

Smite means to strike or hit something with great, powerful force — but it almost always implies more than just a simple punch or blow. When something is smited, it is hit decisively, overwhelmingly, often with the sense that the blow is final or crushing.

Smithereens means tiny, scattered fragments or broken pieces — the kind left behind when something is completely and violently destroyed. Think of an explosion, a sledgehammer smashing a plate, or a vase hitting a stone floor.
A smithy is a workshop — a physical place — where a blacksmith works. Think of it as a blacksmith's workplace, the same way a bakery is a baker's workplace or a studio is an artist's workplace.
When someone is smitten, they are powerfully and often helplessly attracted to someone or something — so much so that the feeling seems to have taken over them completely.

A smock is a loose, lightweight garment worn over your regular clothes — not instead of them. Its entire purpose is to protect your clothes underneath from getting dirty, stained, or damaged. Think of it as a shield for your outfit.
Smoggy describes a place, day, sky, or air that is filled with smog — a thick, dirty, hazy kind of air pollution that hangs visibly over an area, especially cities.
To smolder means to burn slowly, without a flame, while producing smoke. But it also means to feel a strong emotion deeply and quietly, without letting it fully out.
In its most literal sense, smoldering describes something that is burning this way: without visible flame, but with real, sustained heat and smoke underneath.
To smooch someone means to kiss them — usually in an affectionate, warm, or romantic way.
A smorgasbord is a large, varied mixture of things — a collection where there are many different types, all present together at once.

To smother means to cover something so completely and heavily that it cannot breathe, escape, survive, or be expressed. Think of a thick, heavy blanket dropped over something — whatever is underneath gets blocked off from the outside world entirely.

When you smudge something, you rub it, press on it, or accidentally brush against it in a way that creates a blurry, messy, or dirty mark. The result is not a sharp, clean stain — it is a spread-out, unclear, untidy mark.
If someone is smug, it means they are excessively pleased with themselves — and they show it in a way that other people find irritating or off-putting.
To smuggle something means to move it secretly from one place to another, while breaking a rule or law in the process.

A snafu is a situation that has gone wrong in a chaotic, confused, or disorganized way — typically because of poor planning, miscommunication, or a tangle of errors involving multiple people or systems.

A "snag" is a problem that suddenly appears and gets in the way of what you are doing — especially one you didn't see coming. It is a minor-to-moderate difficulty, not a total disaster, but enough to slow things down or make things complicated.

The verb "snag" always carries the idea of catching or being caught — like a hook suddenly gripping onto something. That single image — a hook catching — is the soul of this word. Every meaning of "snag" flows from it.
A long, legless reptile; also a disloyal, deceitful person ("a snake in the grass").
Snap always suggests something happening suddenly, sharply, and quickly. Often (but not always) with a brief, sharp sound. That feeling of abruptness is the soul of the word.

To be close behind someone and threatening to catch up with or overtake them, as in "rivals are snapping at our heels." It can also mean to keep annoying or harassing someone, like a small dog biting at their feet.
To snap out of something means to suddenly and quickly stop being in a negative or unproductive mental or emotional state.

A snare is a trap — specifically, one that works by catching and holding something, usually without the trapped thing realising what is happening until it is too late. Think of it as a hidden danger that grabs you the moment you step into it.
To snare something means to catch or trap it, usually through cleverness, a trick, or a carefully laid plan — so that the thing caught has little or no chance of escape.

Snark is a type of remark — or a general style of speaking — that is sharp, clever, and mocking, with a clear edge of contempt or dismissal. It's what happens when someone wraps criticism or scorn inside wit.

To snark means to say something in a mocking, sarcastic, or dismissive way — usually something sharp and clever — directed at a person, thing, or situation you find annoying, ridiculous, or beneath you. When you snark at someone, you're not just being rude.
If someone is snarky, they are being rude and sarcastic in a cleverly cutting way. Think of it as a mix of two things working together: a sharp, biting tone and a hint of wit or cleverness.
An angry, aggressive growl made with bared teeth, or a similar angry tone of voice. A snarl is also a tangle or a confused, complicated situation, as in "a traffic snarl."
To growl angrily with bared teeth, like an angry dog, or to say something in an angry, aggressive way. To snarl up means to tangle or become stuck, as in "traffic was snarled."

To snatch means to grab or take something quickly, suddenly, and often forcefully. The defining quality of this word is the combination of speed and abruptness — the action happens in a sharp, swift motion, often without warning.
Snazzy means attractively stylish, visually impressive, and eye-catching — usually in a fun, bold, or flashy way.

To sneak means to move, do, or take something quietly and secretly, so that no one notices you. The key feeling behind "sneak" is hiding — you are deliberately trying to avoid being seen, heard, or caught.
To sneak up on someone or something means to approach quietly and gradually, without being noticed — until it is too late to prepare or react.

If someone is sneaky, it means they do things in a hidden, quiet, and secretive way — usually because they know that if others noticed what they were doing, those others would disapprove, stop them, or catch them doing something wrong.
A contemptuous or mocking expression, smile, or remark that shows you think someone or something is beneath you.
To sneer means to show contempt toward someone or something — to make it obvious that you think they are stupid, worthless, inferior, or not worthy of your respect.
When you snicker, you laugh in a quiet, partly suppressed way — usually at someone or something, in a mocking or disrespectful manner. It's the laugh you try to hold back but can't quite kill.
When something is snide, it is indirectly cruel or mocking. A snide remark doesn't attack you openly and honestly — it stings you in a sneaky, sly way.
To sniffle means to repeatedly draw air up through your nose in small, short, quiet bursts — making a soft, slightly wet sound each time.

To snip means to cut something using scissors (or a similar sharp tool like shears or garden clippers) with a short, quick, single cutting motion. The cut is small and precise — not a long sweep, not a heavy chop, just a brief, clean snick of the blades.

To snipe means to attack from a hidden or safe position, with precision, in a way that is hard for the target to defend against or respond to. That idea — hidden, precise, one-sided — runs through every use of this word.

A sniper is a highly skilled shooter who fires at targets from a hidden position at a long distance, with extreme precision. The three pillars — concealment, distance, and accuracy — are what separate a sniper from an ordinary shooter.
A snippet is a small piece of something — specifically, a brief portion that has been taken or pulled out from something larger.

A snit is a state of irritation, agitation, or flustered annoyance — usually over something small or trivial. When someone is in a snit, they are worked up, flustered, and emotionally bothered, but not in a dramatic or deeply serious way.
To snivel means to cry, whimper, or complain in a weak, pathetic, and self-pitying way — usually with sniffling and a runny nose involved.
A snob is a person who believes — consciously or not — that they are better than others, and who makes this belief visible through the way they treat people.

"Snobbish" describes a person who believes they are better than others — and acts on that belief by looking down on people they consider inferior while eagerly admiring or trying to impress those they consider superior. It is always a negative word.
Snobby describes a person who believes they are better than others — and who actually shows this belief through the way they talk, act, or treat people.

Someone who is snooty believes they are better than other people — better in terms of wealth, social class, taste, or refinement — and they show this belief through cold, dismissive, or superior behavior toward others.
A snorkel is a breathing tube — a hollow, tube-shaped device that lets a person breathe air while their face is underwater.

A snort is a short, sharp, rough sound that comes out through the nose — sometimes through the nose and throat together — when air is forced out suddenly and forcefully. Think of it as a quick "blast" of air through the nose.

To snub someone means to deliberately treat them as if they don't matter — by ignoring them, dismissing them coldly, or refusing to acknowledge them — in a way that is meant to show disrespect, contempt, or a sense of superiority over them.
To put out a candle flame. Figuratively, to snuff out something means to end it abruptly, as in "snuffing out all hope." In slang, to snuff someone means to kill them.
A snuggery is a small, cozy, and private space — typically a room or a tucked-away corner — where a person can retreat to feel warm, comfortable, and peacefully cut off from the outside world.
"So much for [something]" is a phrase you use when something has failed, collapsed, or turned out to be useless — especially when you expected it to work or last.
Used to show doubt that a name or description is deserved ("the so-called expert"), or simply to introduce what something is commonly called.

Soak means to make something completely and thoroughly wet by keeping it in liquid — or to become completely wet yourself. The key idea is not just wetness, but deep, total saturation over time. Think of a dry sponge dropped into a bucket of water.
To soar means to rise or fly high up into the sky smoothly and effortlessly, staying up there with ease.
To sob means to cry in a deep, intense way where your breathing becomes uncontrollable and broken.

"Sober" always points to one central idea: the absence of excess. Whether it's the absence of alcohol, the absence of wild emotion, or the absence of flashy decoration — sober always means something is restrained, grounded, and clear.

When something is sobering, it makes you feel serious, grounded, and thoughtful — often by confronting you with a difficult, important, or uncomfortable truth. It pulls you away from a light, happy, or carefree mood and brings you face-to-face with reality.

Sobriety means being in a clear, controlled, and undisturbed state — free from anything that clouds your mind, throws you off balance, or leads you into excess. Think of it as the quality of being grounded and steady.
A sobriquet is a nickname — but a very specific, meaningful kind.

If someone is sociable, it means they genuinely enjoy being around other people, like talking to them, and feel comfortable and happy in social situations. A sociable person is friendly, easy to approach, and naturally makes others feel at ease.

A social convention is an unwritten rule that people in a group or society follow — not because a law forces them, and not necessarily because it's the "morally right" thing to do, but simply because everyone expects everyone else to follow it, and so they follow it too.
Social media is a collective term for internet-based platforms and apps that let people create, share, and exchange content — and interact with one another — in real time.
The division of a society into layers or classes based on wealth, power, and status, which is often passed down across generations.

A socialist is a person who believes that the economy — especially its most important parts, like major industries, natural resources, land, and banks — should be owned or controlled collectively, rather than by private individuals.

A socialite is a person — almost always wealthy — who is well-known and prominent within high society, and whose life largely revolves around attending and being seen at fashionable, exclusive social events like galas, parties, charity balls, fashion shows, and luxury gatherings.

When you socialize, you interact with other people — talking, laughing, sharing a meal, attending gatherings — simply for the pleasure of human connection. It's not about working together or achieving a goal. It's about being with people.
Societal means "relating to, affecting, or coming from society as a whole."

An important phrase — "under the sod": This is a poetic, slightly old-fashioned way of saying that someone has died and been buried. Since a buried body lies beneath the ground — beneath the sod — this phrase means "dead and in the grave."

Sodden means so completely soaked with liquid that nothing more can be absorbed. It describes something that is not just wet, but saturated all the way through — heavy, limp, and dripping because it is full of liquid.

A soffit is the underside — the bottom-facing surface — of a structural part of a building that hangs overhead. Think of it this way: whenever something architectural is above you and you look up at its underside, that surface you're looking at is a soffit.
When we say someone is soft-spoken, we mean they speak in a quiet, gentle, and calm voice. Their tone is smooth and mild — never harsh, sharp, or loud.
"Soften" means to make something less hard, less harsh, or less intense — or to become that way on its own.
Soggy describes something that has absorbed so much liquid — almost always water — that it has become thoroughly wet, soft, and heavy.
"Soi-disant" is an adjective placed before a noun to describe a person who has given themselves a particular label, title, or identity — and the speaker wants you to know they're not convinced by it.
A soiree is an evening social gathering — essentially a party — but one that is elegant, refined, and carefully put together. Think of it as a step above your typical casual get-together.

A sojourn is a temporary stay in a place — somewhere you are for a while, but not permanently. Think of it this way: if you live somewhere for the rest of your life, that's your home. If you stop somewhere for five minutes, that's just a stop.

To sojourn somewhere means to stay in a place temporarily — not forever, not just for a quick visit, but for a meaningful stretch of time with the clear understanding that you will eventually leave and return to where you belong, or move on somewhere else.
Solace means a feeling of comfort and relief that eases your pain, sadness, or worry — but without actually removing the painful situation itself.

To solace someone means to bring them comfort and relief during a time of deep sadness, grief, loss, or suffering. It is about gently easing someone's emotional pain — making a hurting person feel a little less alone, a little less broken.
Solar means "of, relating to, coming from, or powered by the Sun."

A solarium is a room — or an enclosed space — built specifically to let in as much natural sunlight as possible. The defining feature is glass: its walls, its ceiling, or both are made largely of glass, so sunlight floods in freely.

To solder means to permanently join two metal surfaces together by melting a special soft metal alloy — called solder — onto them, so that it flows into the joint, cools down, and hardens into a solid bond that holds the two pieces together.
Sole means one, and only one — with nothing else alongside it.
A solecism is a mistake that breaks an accepted rule — either a rule of correct language, or a rule of proper social behavior.

"Solely" means "only" — and nothing/no one else. When you use "solely," you are drawing a tight boundary around exactly one thing — one person, one reason, one cause, one purpose — and completely shutting everything else out.

Solemn describes something — or someone — that is deeply serious, dignified, and full of weight. It signals that a moment, a person's expression, a promise, or an atmosphere carries great importance and deserves full respect and quiet attention.

Solemnity is the quality of being deeply serious, grave, and dignified — especially in a way that feels weighty, ceremonial, or sacred. It is the feeling that something truly matters, and that everyone present understands and respects that.
Solemnly means doing or saying something with deep seriousness, genuine sincerity, and a strong sense that the moment truly matters — in a way that feels weighty, dignified, and fully intentional.
To solicit means to actively go out and ask someone for something — whether that's help, money, an opinion, a vote, business, or anything else you want or need.
In Britain, a lawyer who advises clients and prepares legal documents; in the US, a person who goes around selling things or asking for donations.

Solicitous means showing a deep, active, attentive kind of concern for someone's well-being, comfort, or happiness — the kind of concern that makes you go out of your way to make sure the other person is okay.
Solicitude is a deep, careful concern for someone's well-being, comfort, or safety — one that is warm and caring on the inside, but tinged with worry or anxiety on the outside.
Solidarity means a powerful sense of unity among a group of people — a feeling of "we are in this together" — along with the active support and loyalty that comes from that feeling.
To solidify something means to make it solid, firm, or stable — or for something to become solid, firm, or stable on its own.
To soliloquize means to speak your thoughts aloud to yourself — not to another person, but as a spoken expression of what is happening inside your own mind.

A soliloquy is when a character in a play speaks their private, inner thoughts out loud — alone on stage, or as though no one else is there — so that the audience can hear what is going on inside their mind, even though the other characters in the play cannot.
Solipsism is a philosophical idea — specifically a theory about reality and knowledge — that says: only your own mind can be known to truly exist.

When we describe someone or something as solipsistic, we mean they operate as if their own mind, perspective, and experience are the only things that are truly real — and that the inner lives, feelings, and realities of other people barely register, or don't fully compute.
Solitaire always refers to something that is alone, singular, or meant for one.

Solitary means completely alone — with no one else present, no company, no companion. But it does more than the plain word "alone." It carries a sense of striking, total aloneness — one person, one thing, standing entirely apart from everything else.
Solitude is the state of being alone — physically separated from other people, with no one around you.
When "solo" is used as an adverb, it means doing something completely alone — without any partner, helper, or companion.

A solstice is one of the two moments each year when the Sun reaches its extreme position in the sky — either the highest it ever gets (giving you the longest day) or the lowest it ever gets (giving you the shortest day).
Able to be dissolved in a liquid, especially water, as in "soluble aspirin." Of a problem, able to be solved.
Having enough money to pay all your debts, as in "the company remained solvent." In chemistry, a solvent is a liquid that dissolves other substances.
A solvent is a substance — almost always a liquid — that can dissolve another substance.
Somatic simply means "of or relating to the body."

Somber means dark, serious, and heavy with sadness or gravity. When something is somber, it carries a quiet but deep weight — not loud or dramatic, but thick with a heavy, gloomy feeling that you can almost sense in the air.

Somberly means in a way that is quietly serious, heavy, and dark in mood or tone. It describes how someone does something — specifically, with a feeling of deep gravity, sadness, or gloom that is calm and subdued rather than dramatic or loud.
A wide-brimmed hat with a tall crown, traditionally worn in Mexico to give shade from the sun.
A somersault is a movement in which a person rotates their entire body in a complete circle — head over heels — either along the ground or through the air.

The word somnambulant describes something or someone that resembles a sleepwalker — moving, functioning, or existing in a dreamlike, automatic, unaware state, as though the conscious mind has switched off but the body is still going through the motions.
A somnambulist is a person who sleepwalks — someone who gets up, moves around, and sometimes does other things while they are still asleep, completely unaware that any of this is happening.
Somniferous means causing sleep or tending to induce sleep or drowsiness. If something is somniferous, it makes you feel sleepy, heavy-eyed, or causes you to drift off.
Somnolence means a heavy, overpowering state of drowsiness or sleepiness — that deep, foggy pull toward sleep that is hard to resist, even when you are still technically awake.
Somnolent means drowsy — in a heavy, slow, deeply sleepy way. It describes that state where you are not quite asleep, but not fully awake either.

"Son of a gun" is a mild, old-fashioned exclamation used to express surprise, delight, admiration, mild frustration, or affection. It is also used to refer to a person — either fondly or with light disapproval.

Sonder is the sudden, quiet realization that every single person around you — a stranger walking past you on the street, a driver in a car you'll never see again, a face in a café window — is living a life that is just as rich, just as complicated, and just as real as yours.
Sonic means "of, relating to, or involving sound or sound waves."
A sonnet is a poem of exactly 14 lines, written according to a strict set of rules about rhythm and rhyme. It is one of the most structured, disciplined, and celebrated forms of poetry ever created.
A sonogram is an image — a picture — created by using sound waves to "see" inside something that you cannot see into with your eyes or ordinary light.
Sonority means the quality of sound that is rich, full, deep, and resonant — the kind of sound that seems to fill a space and linger in the air rather than just hitting your ears and disappearing.

When something is sonorous, it produces a sound that is deep, rich, full, and impressively resonant. It's not just loud — it has a certain weight and grandeur to it that fills the air and almost vibrates in your chest.
To soothe means to gently calm, comfort, or relieve someone — or something — that is in a state of pain, upset, or discomfort.
Something soothing gently takes away pain, discomfort, worry, or agitation — and replaces it with a feeling of calm, comfort, or relief.

A soothsayer is a person who claims — or is believed — to be able to predict the future. When you call someone a soothsayer, you are saying they have the ability to see, know, or tell what is going to happen before it actually happens.
A sophism is an argument that looks correct and logical on the surface, but is actually flawed and misleading underneath — and crucially, the person making it knows this.

A sophist is a person who uses clever, convincing-sounding arguments to win debates or persuade people — but without genuinely caring whether those arguments are true or honest. The cleverness is the whole point.

A sophisticate is a person who is polished, worldly, and deeply familiar with the finer and more complex sides of life — culture, art, fashion, society, ideas. They have been around. They have seen things.
Sophisticated means refined, complex, and highly developed — and the complexity is handled with skill and elegance, not messiness. It is almost always a compliment.
Sophistication is the quality of being developed, refined, and advanced — beyond something simple, basic, or naive.

Sophistry is the practice of using arguments that sound logical, intelligent, and convincing — but are actually flawed, misleading, or outright false. The goal of sophistry is never to find the truth.

Something that is soporific causes you to feel sleepy or makes you fall asleep. If a thing has a soporific quality, it has the power to bring on that specific heavy-eyed, can't-keep-my-eyes-open drowsiness.
Sordid means morally disgusting, shameful, and repulsive — especially when the bad behavior involves selfishness, greed, dishonesty, or sexual misconduct.
Sore describes a feeling of pain, tenderness, or discomfort — either in the body or in the mind.
A sore point is a topic, subject, or issue that makes a person feel upset, embarrassed, angry, or uncomfortable the moment it is mentioned.

"Sorely" means very much, greatly, or intensely — but not in a neutral or happy way. It carries a built-in sense of pain, hardship, difficulty, urgency, or deep emotional weight. That's what makes it different from simply saying "very."
The adjective sororal means "of, relating to, or characteristic of a sister or sisters." In plain words: if something is sororal, it has the quality of being sisterly.
A leafy plant with sour-tasting leaves, used in salads and soups; also a reddish-brown colour, especially of a horse.
Sorrow is a deep, heavy feeling of sadness that arises from losing something or someone important, from painful disappointment, or from witnessing suffering. It is not just "feeling a little sad."
To examine a number of things carefully in order to organize them or understand them, as in "sorting through old papers" or "sorting through her feelings."
A sortie is essentially a single, purposeful trip out — most commonly in a military context, but also in everyday informal use.

A sot is a person who drinks alcohol heavily and repeatedly — not just someone who got drunk at a party once, but someone for whom excessive drinking has become a defining, persistent habit. Think of it as a strong, old-fashioned word for a habitual drunkard.
In a quiet voice, so as not to be overheard, as in "he said sotto voce." In music, it means sung or played softly.

A sough is a soft, gentle, sighing or murmuring sound — the kind that seems to drift through the air quietly and continuously, without any sharp edges to it. Think of it as the voice of something moving slowly and naturally, whispering rather than speaking.
The spiritual part of a person, believed by many to live on after death; a person's deepest self and feelings; or a genre of African American music.

Soulful means full of deep, genuine, heartfelt emotion — the kind of feeling that seems to come from the very deepest place inside a person, and that reaches into the deepest place inside you when you experience it.

When you call a person soulless, you are saying they seem to lack genuine human feeling, empathy, warmth, or moral depth. They go through life — doing their work, saying the right words, performing the right actions — but there is nothing behind it.

A sound is anything you hear. The bark of a dog, a clap of thunder, the note from a piano, a baby's cry, the hum of a refrigerator — all of these are sounds. If your ears can detect it, it is a sound.
Deeply and peacefully ("slept soundly"); thoroughly ("soundly beaten"); or in a sensible, well-reasoned way.

A soupçon means an extremely tiny amount of something — so small that it barely exists, yet just enough to be noticeable. Think of it as the smallest possible trace of something: a whisper of a quantity, not even a little bit, but a hint of a bit.
The most fundamental meaning of sour describes a sharp, biting, acidic taste — the kind that makes your mouth water, your lips pucker, or your eyes squint slightly.
When "sour" works as a noun, it names a thing — not just a quality or taste. That thing is usually a drink, a type of candy, or the taste sensation itself treated as a category.

Sourdough is about fermentation. Fermentation, in simple terms, is what happens when tiny living organisms — yeast and bacteria — feed on something (like flour) and produce gases and acids as a result.
A sourpuss is a person who is consistently grumpy, sullen, and hard to please — someone who seems to carry a permanent scowl on their face and a bad mood in their heart.
A southpaw is a left-handed person — someone whose dominant hand is their left hand. That's the foundation of the word.
A souvenir is an object you keep in order to remember a particular place, time, person, or experience.

Sovereign means supreme — the highest there is, with no authority standing above it. When something is described as sovereign, it sits at the very top of a chain of power. It is not controlled, limited, or overruled by anything external to itself.
A sovereign is the supreme ruler of a land — the single person who sits at the very top of power and answers to no one above them. A king, a queen, an emperor, an empress — these are all sovereigns.
Sovereignty means the highest, final power to make decisions and rules in a given place or over a given group of people — with no outside force having the authority to overrule those decisions.
To sow means to scatter or place seeds in the ground so they can grow into plants. Picture a farmer walking across a field, dropping seeds into the soil — that act is sowing.
When someone is spaced-out, their mind is not fully in the present moment. They feel mentally distant — like they are floating somewhere far away while the world around them continues.
Spacious means having a lot of space — large, open, and roomy, with plenty of room to move around, breathe, or fit things in comfortably.
Span means the full reach or extent from one end to the other — like measuring "how far" or "how long" something stretches, whether in space or in time.
To span means to stretch across something from one end to the other, covering everything in between.
A spangle is a small, thin, flat, shiny disc or piece of glittering material. Its defining quality is that it catches light and throws it back brilliantly, creating a sparkling, eye-catching effect.

A spaniel is a type of dog — not a single specific breed, but a whole group of dog breeds that share certain physical features and personality traits. Think of it like how "terrier" or "hound" refers to a family of related dogs. A spaniel is one such family.
To spar means to engage in a fight or argument with someone — but in a controlled, non-deadly, back-and-forth way. It is not a real, all-out fight.
Extra, kept in reserve, or not being used, as in "a spare key" or "spare time." It can also mean plain and simple, without decoration, as in "a spare style," or, of a person, thin.

"Spare" as a verb always revolves around one idea: holding back, or choosing not to use something fully. That "something" can be your power to hurt someone, an unpleasant experience, or a resource you own.

Sparing means using something in a very small, careful, and deliberately restrained amount — only as much as is truly needed, and not a drop more. When you are sparing with something, you are consciously holding back.
A spark is fundamentally a tiny, brief flash of light and heat — a small, glowing particle that appears suddenly and disappears just as fast.
To cause something to begin, especially suddenly, as in "the decision sparked protests." Literally, to give off sparks.

When something sparkles, it produces many small, quick, bright flashes of light — not one steady beam, but countless tiny bursts of brilliance, appearing and disappearing rapidly. Think of a diamond under a lamp.
A sparrow is a small bird. More precisely, it is a small, seed-eating bird belonging to a group of birds known for being common, adaptable, and widespread across the world.
Sparse means thinly spread out — when something exists, but in such small amounts or at such wide intervals that it feels noticeably insufficient, scattered, or far from full.

When you call something or someone spartan, you mean it is stripped down to the absolute bare minimum — no comfort, no decoration, no luxury, no excess. Just what is strictly necessary, and nothing more.

A spasm is a sudden, involuntary contraction — a tight, forceful squeezing — of a muscle or group of muscles that happens on its own, without you choosing or wanting it to happen. Three words define every spasm: sudden, involuntary, and contraction.

Spasmodic is used in two closely related ways: 1. The literal, physical sense — describing actual bodily movements or sensations that resemble or are caused by muscle spasms. These are movements that are jerky, convulsive, and not under conscious control.
"Spastic" describes something that is stiff, jerky, and happening in uncontrolled spasms — particularly muscles and the movements they produce.

A spat is a brief, minor quarrel — the kind that flares up quickly and usually dies down just as fast. It's not a deep conflict or a serious fight. It's more like a small clash over something trivial.
Spate means a large number of similar things happening suddenly, one after another, within a short period of time.

Spatial means relating to space — but not outer space with stars and galaxies. It means the physical space that exists all around us every day: the area, distance, position, size, shape, and arrangement of things in the world.

A spatula is a hand-held tool with a flat, broad, thin blade fixed to a handle, designed for sliding under, lifting, flipping, spreading, or scraping things — especially in cooking, baking, or science labs.
Spawn means the eggs of a water-dwelling creature — specifically fish, frogs, shellfish, or similar animals. These creatures don't lay their eggs one by one the way a hen does.

Spawn means to produce or bring something into existence — but it's not just simple creation. It carries the sense of something emerging from a source and often appearing in large numbers or as a direct result of something else.
A speakeasy is a hidden, illegal bar — a secret place where people could go to buy and drink alcohol when doing so was against the law.
When you spear something, you drive something sharp and pointed into it — usually in one quick, forceful thrust. Think of a hunter pushing the tip of a spear weapon through a fish.
Something is specialized when it is designed, trained, or developed to focus on one specific thing — rather than being made for many different things.
A species is a group of living things so similar to one another — in their biology, genetics, and behavior — that they naturally mate with each other and produce healthy, fertile young.
"Specifically" means: in a precise, particular way — focused on one exact thing, and not anything else.
When you specify something, you state it in a clear, exact, and precise way — removing all vagueness, ambiguity, or guesswork.
A specimen is a single item — one thing taken from a larger group — that is kept, examined, or shown as a representative example of that entire group.
Specious describes something that looks correct, reasonable, or genuine on the surface — but is actually wrong, flawed, or misleading when you look more carefully.

A speck is something extremely, almost incomprehensibly small — either in size or in amount. It sits at the very bottom of the scale of smallness. Think of the tiniest thing you can picture, and a speck is right there at that level, or even smaller.

When you speckle something, you cover it with many small, tiny spots or dots of color — scattered randomly across a surface. Think of it as dotting something, but in a way that looks natural, irregular, and spread out rather than neat or deliberate.
Something is speckled when its surface is covered with many small spots, dots, or tiny marks of a color that stands out against a different background color.
Covered with many small, scattered spots or marks, as in "an egg speckled with brown."

A spectacle is something that is striking, remarkable, or dramatic to look at — something that makes you stop, stare, and pay attention. It's not just any ordinary sight. It has a quality of scale, intensity, or drama that sets it apart from everyday things.
Spectacular means something that is so dramatically impressive, visually striking, or overwhelming in scale that it instantly grabs your attention and fills you with awe or amazement.
A spectator is a person who watches something — an event, an activity, or a situation — without taking part in it. They are present, they observe, but they do not get involved.
A specter is something that cannot be fully seen, touched, or grasped — yet its presence is powerfully felt, and it fills you with a sense of dread or unease.
Ghostly, eerie, and faint, as in "a spectral figure." In science, it relates to a spectrum, especially the range of colours of light.

A spectrum is a continuous, ordered range of something — stretching from one extreme to another — where every point along the way gradually blends into the next, with no sudden jumps or sharp breaks in between.

"Specular" is an adjective that means mirror-like or of or relating to a mirror. When you call something specular, you are saying it reflects light (or other waves) the way a mirror does — cleanly, sharply, and in a single, predictable direction.

To speculate means to form an opinion, make a guess, or think about something when you don't have complete facts or certainty. You're not stating a proven truth — you're exploring what might be true, based on limited information and your own reasoning.

Speculation is the act of forming an opinion, theory, or guess about something when you don't have complete or certain knowledge to back it up. It lives in the space between "I know this for a fact" and "I have absolutely no idea."
Speculative means based on guessing, imagining, or theorizing — rather than on confirmed facts or solid evidence.

A speculator is a person who takes on significant financial risk by buying or selling something — most commonly stocks, land, currencies, commodities (like oil or gold), or other assets — with the primary goal of making a profit from changes in price.

Speechless means being temporarily unable to speak because an emotion is so strong and overwhelming that it has taken away your ability to find words. You open your mouth, but nothing comes out — or you simply don't even try, because no words feel adequate.
A spell is a set of words, phrases, gestures, or rituals believed to have magical power — power to make something happen through supernatural means.
The verb spell means to say or write the individual letters of a word in their correct order.

When something is spellbinding, it is so fascinating and captivating that it completely takes over your attention — as if you are under a magic spell and simply cannot look away, stop listening, or think about anything else.
When someone is spellbound, they are so completely fascinated and captivated by something that the rest of the world seems to disappear.
To spelunk means to explore caves, especially as a hobby or recreational activity.

A spendthrift is a person who spends money carelessly, wastefully, and without restraint — someone who throws money away freely, often spending far more than they can afford, and almost never thinking about the future.

Spent means completely used up, with nothing left over. It describes the state of something — a person, an object, or even a force — after it has given or used everything it had. The key word here is completely. "Spent" doesn't mean half-empty or running low.
To spew means to pour or push something out forcefully, rapidly, in a large and uncontrolled amount — usually from an opening of some kind, like a mouth, a pipe, a vent, or a machine.
A sphere is a perfectly round, three-dimensional shape in which every single point on its surface is exactly the same distance from the center. That fixed distance is called the radius.
Spherical simply means shaped like a sphere — that is, perfectly round in three dimensions, like a ball. If something is spherical, it has no flat sides, no corners, no edges.
A sphincter is a ring-shaped muscle that wraps around an opening or passage in the body, and whose job is to open and close that passage on cue — like a biological valve or drawstring.

A sphinx is a mythological creature — meaning it exists in ancient stories and legends, not in real life. The classic sphinx has the body of a lion and the head of a human. Depending on the culture and tradition, it may also have wings.

A spice is a natural substance — almost always from a plant — that you add to food to give it a distinctive flavor, smell, or color. Spices make food taste richer, more interesting, and more complex. Without them, most food would taste flat and forgettable.

When you use "spice" as a verb, you are talking about adding something that makes a thing more flavorful, lively, or interesting — whether that thing is actual food, or something more abstract like a story, a relationship, or a routine.

A spiel is a long, smooth, rehearsed speech that someone delivers — usually to persuade you, sell you something, or get you to agree with them. The defining quality of a spiel is that it feels practiced.
To spiel means to talk at length in a fast, smooth, and persuasive way — usually to sell something, convince someone, or impress them.
A spigot is a device that controls the flow of liquid — it lets you start, stop, or adjust how much liquid comes out of a pipe, a barrel, or any container holding fluid.
A spike is a sharp, pointed object — like a thick, heavy nail, or the sharp tip of a fence. It stabs. It goes in fast and hard. It sticks out sharply.

"Spiky" means having sharp points sticking outward. Think of a spike — a thin, rigid, sharply pointed object. When something is spiky, it has one or more of these sharp points, or it behaves like one.
At the heart of "spin" is one simple image: rotation. Something turning around and around a central point.
A spin class (also called indoor cycling) is a group exercise class where a group of people ride stationary bicycles together inside a gym or fitness studio, led by an instructor.
A thin rod that spins and winds thread when spinning by hand. It is also a rod or pin that turns in a machine, or one of the thin upright posts in a railing.
Spindly describes something that is long and thin in a way that looks weak, fragile, or unable to properly hold up its own weight.
Spindrift is the fine, wind-driven spray that is torn from the tops of ocean waves and swept low across the surface of the sea by a strong wind.

The backbone, the column of bones running down the middle of the back. Figuratively, courage and strength of character, as in "he has no spine." A spine is also a sharp spike on a plant or animal, or the back edge of a book.
The most common meaning of spineless (as an adjective) is: lacking the courage, strength, or willpower to stand firm in a difficult situation.
A spinster is a noun used to describe a woman who has never married and, importantly, is considered to be past the age when society typically expects women to get married.
A spiral is a curved line or path that winds around a central point, but — and this is the key — with each loop it moves farther and farther away from that center.
A spire is a tall, slender structure that tapers upward to a sharp point at the top — like an elongated, pointed cone or needle rising high into the air.

"Spirited" means full of life, energy, and strong feeling. A spirited person, animal, performance, or discussion is one that shows clear force, enthusiasm, or courage — not something dull, weak, or half-hearted.

"Spirited dialogue" means a conversation or discussion that is lively, passionate, and energetic — one where the people involved care deeply about what they are saying and are not afraid to express it with intensity and force.

Relating to the human spirit or soul rather than to physical things, as in "spiritual growth." It can also mean relating to religion. A spiritual is also a religious folk song first sung by African-Americans.

Spite is a feeling or desire to hurt, annoy, or upset someone — not for any practical gain, but simply because you want them to feel bad. It is a cold, deliberate kind of meanness rooted in ill will toward a specific person.

Spiteful describes a person, action, or remark that is deliberately meant to hurt, upset, or annoy someone — not by accident, but on purpose, and usually out of a feeling of anger, jealousy, or a desire for revenge.

A spitfire is a person — most often a woman or girl — who has an extremely fiery, intense, and passionate personality. They get angry quickly, speak their mind boldly, and are not afraid to fight back against anyone, no matter how powerful.
The most fundamental meaning. A splash is the event — and the sound — that happens when something falls into liquid, or when liquid is thrown against a surface.
"Splash out" means to spend a noticeably large amount of money on something, especially as a treat — for yourself or for someone else.

A splat is what happens — and what you see and hear — when something soft, wet, or liquid hits a hard surface suddenly and with enough force to spread out flat. It captures three things at once: the sound, the visual result, and the event itself.
To splay something means to spread it outward, wide apart, and often at an angle — usually in a way that feels stretched, flat, or ungainly.
A spleen is an organ inside the human (and animal) body. It sits in the upper-left part of your belly, tucked just behind your stomach, roughly the size of your fist.

Splendid means something is impressively excellent, beautiful, or magnificent — so good or striking that it fills you with admiration or delight. It describes something that truly stands out in a very positive way.

Splendiferous means extraordinarily magnificent, impressively grand, or dazzlingly wonderful — something so beautiful, impressive, or excellent that ordinary words like "nice" or even "great" feel completely inadequate to describe it.
Splendor means a kind of beauty or greatness that is so impressive, so grand, and so striking that it immediately fills you with a sense of awe and wonder. It's not quiet, soft, or subtle beauty.

If someone is splenetic, they are deeply, habitually bad-tempered, bitter, and prone to angry, sharp outbursts. Think of it as a kind of poisonous grumpiness — not a passing mood, but a persistent state of irritability mixed with spite and scorn.
To splice means to join two things together at their ends — in a way that makes them feel like one continuous, unbroken thing.

A splinter is a small, thin, sharp piece that has broken off or separated from a larger solid object. Think of it as a fragment — but not just any fragment. A splinter is specifically thin, needle-like, and usually pointed at one or both ends.
To splinter means to break — but not just any kind of break. It's a very specific, vivid kind of breaking where something hard and rigid shatters or cracks into thin, sharp, jagged fragments.

To split hairs means to focus on tiny, unimportant differences or details that don't really matter. It describes a situation where someone is being overly precise, picky, or fussy about something so small that it has no real practical value.

A splotch is a mark, patch, or blob of something — paint, ink, mud, blood, food, or any colored substance — that has landed or spread on a surface in an irregular, messy way. The defining quality of a splotch is its uneven, rough outline.
To splurge means to spend more money than you normally would, usually on something special, luxurious, or pleasurable — and to do so willingly and deliberately.

"Spoil" means to damage or ruin something — to take something that was good and make it worse, or even completely useless. Think of it as a word for when something goes from a good state to a bad one.
When you are spoiled for choice, you have so many good options available that it becomes hard to pick just one — not because the options are bad, but because too many of them are good.

A spoilsport is a person who ruins the fun or enjoyment that others are having — usually by refusing to join in, by complaining, by enforcing rules too strictly, or simply by being too serious in a moment meant for play and laughter.

When you are spoilt for choice, you have so many good options available that choosing just one becomes genuinely difficult. The "problem" you face is not a lack of good things — it is an abundance of them.
A spoke is one of the thin, straight rods or bars that connect the center of a wheel to its outer ring.
A spokesperson is a person who has been officially chosen to speak on behalf of someone else — another person, a group, a company, an organization, or a government.

Spoliation means the act of destroying, damaging, seizing, or suppressing something — usually something valuable — in a way that is wrongful, harmful, and often deliberate. Think of it as a step beyond ordinary theft. A thief takes something.
Spontaneity is the quality of doing something naturally, in the moment, without any planning or outside pressure.
Happening naturally and without planning, as in "spontaneous applause." Of a person, acting on impulse.
A funny imitation that mocks something ("a spoof of spy films"); or a trick or hoax meant to deceive.

A spoonerism is a phrase in which the beginning sounds of two words have been accidentally — or deliberately — swapped with each other, typically producing something funny, absurd, or unintentionally rude.
Spoor is the complete trail of physical clues left behind by a moving animal (or person), which reveals that it passed through a place and allows you to follow where it went.

Sporadic means something that happens occasionally, irregularly, and unpredictably — not following any fixed pattern, not happening all the time, and not something you can reliably expect or plan around.
The core meaning in one line: Something that happens sporadically happens at irregular, unpredictable intervals — with no fixed pattern, and usually not very often.

Sportive means playful, merry, and full of lighthearted fun. When you describe someone or something as sportive, you are saying they are in a mood of carefree, joyful play — full of energy, laughter, and a desire to frolic, not to be serious.
Sportsmanship is the quality of competing with fairness, respect, and integrity — winning without arrogance, losing without bitterness, and always treating everyone involved with dignity.
A spot is something small and specific — a small place, a small mark, or a small amount of something. That sense of smallness and specificity runs through almost every use of the word.
To spot means to notice or see something — but it carries a specific flavour that plain words like "see" or "notice" do not.
To talk at length about something, especially in a tiresome or unthinking way, as in "spouting nonsense." Literally, to send out a liquid in a strong stream, as a whale does.
Sprawl means to spread out in a loose, wide, and uncontrolled way — taking up a large amount of space without neatness, planning, or compactness.

When something is sprawling, it spreads out over a large area in an irregular, disorganized, or unplanned way — like it has grown outward in many directions without following any neat, controlled shape.
"Spray" describes something that is scattered or spread out in many small pieces — usually tiny drops of liquid flying through the air. Picture an ocean wave crashing against a rock.
When you spray something, you send out a liquid (or sometimes a fine powder) as a large number of tiny droplets scattered over an area, rather than as a single solid stream or mass.

A spree is a short burst of time during which a person does one particular thing repeatedly, intensely, and with very little restraint — often more than they normally would. Think of it as a temporary loss of control over a specific urge or behaviour.
Sprezzatura means the art of making something very difficult look completely effortless and natural.

A sprig is a small, slender stem or shoot taken from a plant — one that still has its leaves, flowers, or berries attached to it. Think of it as a tiny, neat little piece snipped or plucked from a larger plant.

Sprightly means full of energy, liveliness, and cheerfulness — in a way that feels light, quick, and bright. When you call someone or something sprightly, you are saying they have a kind of bubbly, active, upbeat quality.
In folklore, a sprite is a small, supernatural being — a kind of fairy or spirit that is believed to live in nature.
To spritz something means to spray it with a small amount of liquid in a fine, light mist. The action is quick, controlled, and gentle — you're not pouring, drenching, or splashing.

A sprocket is a wheel with teeth sticking out around its edge, designed to interlock with a chain (or any flexible material that has matching holes or links). The teeth slot into the gaps of the chain, and when one moves, it forces the other to move with it.
To sprout means to begin growing, or to produce something new that grows outward. The key feeling inside this word is: something that was not visible before is now pushing its way out and growing.

When you describe someone or something as spruce, you mean they look neat, clean, and smartly put-together. It's the kind of neatness that suggests effort and care — not just "not messy," but actively well-presented and trim in appearance.
A spruce is a type of tree — specifically, a tall, cone-bearing evergreen tree that belongs to the genus Picea.
To spruce up means to make something or someone look noticeably cleaner, neater, fresher, or more attractive — usually through small, careful improvements.
Spry means active, lively, and energetic in a light, quick, and effortless way — particularly when this energy is surprising given a person's age or physical condition.
Spume is the white, bubbly, frothy foam that forms on the surface of water — especially the sea — when it is violently disturbed or agitated.
Spunk means bold courage, lively spirit, and determined guts. A person who has spunk is feisty, spirited, and refuses to be pushed around or give up — even when the odds are against them.

Spunky describes a person (or animal, or character) who shows courage, energy, and determination — especially when facing something difficult, intimidating, or discouraging. A spunky person doesn't back down.
Something that encourages someone to act, as in "a spur to action." "On the spur of the moment" means suddenly and without planning. Literally, a spike on a rider's boot used to urge a horse forward.
To spur something or someone means to cause, encourage, or push something to happen — often faster, harder, or more strongly than it would have on its own.

Something spurious looks real, genuine, or valid on the surface — but is actually false, fake, or flawed underneath. The word carries a specific and important idea: the appearance of being legitimate.
To spurn someone or something means to reject it with contempt or scorn — not just to say "no," but to push it away with a sense of pride, disgust, or disdain.
A spurt of liquid is when a liquid shoots out suddenly, in a short burst, with some force — not a slow drip, and not a long steady flow, but a quick, forceful gush.

When something spurts, it shoots out suddenly, with force, in a quick, pressured stream. Think of pressing your thumb against a garden hose — the water doesn't just flow out gently; it shoots out in a fast, forceful burst. That's spurting.
To make a series of popping or spitting sounds, as a failing engine or flame does. It can also mean to speak in a quick, confused way, or for something to work unevenly and start to fail.
A spyglass is a small, handheld tube-shaped instrument that makes faraway objects appear much closer and larger when you look through it.
A squab is a baby pigeon — specifically one that is still in the nest and has not yet flown or learned to fly on its own. This typically means a pigeon chick that is roughly 25 to 30 days old.

A squabble is a small, noisy argument about something that is not very important. Think of it as a minor quarrel — it is real and heated in the moment, but it is too petty and trivial to be called a serious fight or conflict.
