A squad is a small, organized group of people who share a common purpose, task, or identity.
A squadron is an organized, structured group of military people and their vehicles — usually aircraft, ships, or cavalry horses — that operate together as a single unit under one commander.
Squalid describes something that is extremely dirty, neglected, and miserable — especially in a way that feels degrading or shameful.
To squall means to cry or scream very loudly, harshly, and without control. It describes a raw, sharp, piercing kind of wailing — the kind that cuts through the air and can't easily be ignored.
Squalor means a state of extreme, filthy, and degrading dirtiness — especially one that has built up over a long time through neglect. It is not just a messy room or ordinary dirt.
To squander something means to waste it in a careless, reckless, or foolish way — particularly something that was valuable and could have been used much better.

"Square away" means to organize, settle, or take care of something so that it is completely in order and ready. Think of it as tying up all the loose ends — making sure nothing is left messy, unfinished, or unsettled.
Square one means the very beginning — the starting point of a process, a plan, a task, or an effort, before any progress has been made.
Square peg in a round hole

A square peg in a round hole describes a person who does not fit into a situation, environment, group, or role they have been placed in — because their personality, skills, or nature are fundamentally incompatible with what that situation requires.
Directly and exactly, as in "hit squarely on the nose." It can also mean firmly and without avoiding the issue, as in "the blame lies squarely with them."
A vegetable of the gourd family, such as pumpkin or courgette; a racket sport played in a walled court; or a fruit drink diluted with water.
"Squash" means to apply force or pressure to something so that it is reduced — in shape, in size, in power, or in presence.

When squat is used as an adjective, it describes something — or someone — that is noticeably short in height but wide or thick in body. Think of it as something that looks "pushed down" or "compressed."
To squat means to lower your body by bending your knees deeply, so that your bottom moves close to the ground — but does not touch it — while your feet stay flat on the floor.

A squatter is a person who moves into and lives in a place — usually a building or a piece of land — that does not belong to them, without the owner's permission, without paying rent, and without any legal right to be there.

A squawk is a sudden, loud, harsh, and unpleasant noise — the kind that feels almost jarring to hear. Think of a parrot screaming, a hen that just got frightened, or a rusty door hinge. The sound is sharp, shrill, and decidedly not musical.
To squawk is to make — or say something in — a loud, harsh, sharp, and unpleasant cry or sound. Think of the noise a parrot, a seagull, or a frightened chicken makes.

To squeak means to produce a short, sharp, high-pitched sound — one that is thin and piercing in quality, but not very loud and not long-lasting. Think of the sound a mouse makes, or the sound of a door with a rusty hinge.
To make a long, high-pitched cry or noise, as a pig does or tyres do when braking hard. In slang, to squeal means to inform on someone to the police or authorities.

If someone is squeamish, they are easily made to feel sick, disgusted, uncomfortable, or faint when they encounter something unpleasant — especially something involving blood, injury, gore, bodily functions, or anything visually or physically disturbing.

"Squeeze" means to press something firmly from two or more sides at the same time, usually with your fingers, hands, or body. Think of holding an orange in your palm and pressing it tightly — that is squeezing.
To squelch something means to press down on it with enough force to crush or silence it completely — stopping it dead in its tracks, leaving no room for it to survive or continue.

When you partially close your eyelids — because a light is too bright, or because you're straining to make out something small or far away — the resulting look on your face is called a squint. It's the half-closed, scrunched-eye expression itself.

When you squint, you partially close your eyes — not completely shut, but narrowed down to a thin slit. Picture someone stepping outside into blazing sunlight: they don't shut their eyes, but they squeeze them almost closed.
In England, a country gentleman who owns the main estate in a village. Historically, a squire was a young man who served a knight as an assistant while training to become one.
To squirm means to twist and wriggle your body with small, restless movements, usually because you are uncomfortable, in pain, or trying to get free from something.
To squirrel something away means to save or store something — usually money, food, or supplies — carefully and quietly, so that you have it available for later when you might need it.

To squish something means to press, squeeze, or step on it in a way that forces it to change shape — usually because the thing is soft, wet, or easily deformable. The result is typically a flattening, a spreading out, or an oozing of the material.
Imagine the feeling of a sharp knife being thrust into your body — sudden, intense, piercing. That's the image "stabbing" brings when used as an adjective.

Stability means the state of being steady, secure, and unlikely to change, collapse, or be disrupted. When something has stability, it holds its position, its condition, or its functioning reliably over time — even when outside forces push against it.

When you call something stabilizing, you are saying that it actively works to bring about or maintain stability — meaning it reduces chaos, prevents things from getting worse, keeps wild swings in check, or holds a system in a balanced, controlled state.
Consisting of a series of short, sharp, separate sounds, as in "staccato gunfire" or "a staccato voice." In music, describing notes played crisply and detached from one another.

A stadium is a very large structure built specifically so that a huge number of people can gather to watch an event — most commonly a sports match, but sometimes a concert or a ceremony — in the same place, at the same time.
The "staff" of an organization refers to all the people who work for it — the employees, taken together as a group.

A stagecoach is a large, enclosed carriage pulled by horses that traveled on fixed routes between towns, carrying passengers, mail, and goods — operating much like a bus service does today, but in a much earlier era of history.
Stagecraft is the collection of technical skills and practical knowledge needed to create and run a theatrical production on stage.
Stagflation is when a country's economy is barely growing (or shrinking), unemployment is high, and prices are rising — all at the same time.

When someone staggers, they are trying to walk or stay upright, but their body keeps swaying, lurching, or nearly falling. They don't fall completely — but they clearly can't move in a straight, controlled way either.
When something is staggering, it means it is so extreme in size, amount, or degree that it almost shocks you — like it's hard to fully believe or take in, even when you know it's true.

Something stagnant is not moving, not flowing, not growing, and not changing — and because of this prolonged stillness, it has become unhealthy, unproductive, or worse than it was before. It is almost always a negative word.
To stagnate means to stop moving, growing, or progressing — and because of that stillness, to slowly become worse, weaker, or lifeless.
Stagnation is the state of something that has stopped moving, growing, or changing — and has stayed that way for a long time.
Staid describes a person, place, organization, or thing that is so settled, conventional, and serious that it comes across as dull, unadventurous, and resistant to anything fresh or exciting.

A stain is a mark left on a surface when a substance — usually a liquid — soaks into it and changes its color in a way that is difficult or impossible to remove. The critical thing that makes a stain a stain is that it does not just sit on top of a surface.
To stain means to leave a mark on something — a mark that goes deep into the surface and is very difficult, sometimes impossible, to completely remove.
A staircase is a complete, structured set of steps — along with everything built around and alongside those steps — that allows a person to walk from one level or floor of a building to another.
A stairway is a structure made up of a series of steps that connects one level or floor of a building to another. Its entire purpose is to let people walk up or down between different heights.

A stairwell is the enclosed vertical shaft — essentially a tall, hollow column of space — built inside a building specifically to house a staircase. Think of it as the "room" that the stairs live inside.
A strong pointed post driven into the ground; a share or interest in something ("a stake in the company"); or money risked on a bet.
Stale describes something that has lost its original freshness, quality, or interest — usually because too much time has passed, or because it has been used, repeated, or left unchanged for too long.
A stalemate is a situation where two opposing sides are so equally blocked, stuck, or evenly matched that neither one can move forward, win, or make any meaningful progress. Everything just... stops.

Stalinism is a brutal, totalitarian system of political rule built around one all-powerful leader, absolute state control over every corner of life, and the use of terror, fear, and force to crush anyone who questions that power.

When someone stalks another person, they follow them, watch them, or track their activities repeatedly — in a way that is unwanted, intrusive, and often frightening. The person doing it is called a stalker.
A stalker is a person who obsessively and repeatedly pursues, follows, watches, or contacts someone else — in a way that is unwanted, uninvited, and frightening to the other person.
At the heart of every use of "stall" is one idea: something that is supposed to keep moving or progressing has stopped — or is being stopped.

When you call something or someone stalwart, you are saying they are strongly built, deeply reliable, and completely unwavering — not just on a good day, but consistently, over time, even when it's hard.
Stamina is the ability to keep doing something demanding — physically or mentally — for a long time without giving up or becoming too tired to continue.

To stammer means to speak in a broken, interrupted way — where words don't come out smoothly but instead get stuck, repeated, or forced out with visible difficulty. Think of it as your speech getting "caught" before it reaches the listener.

Stamp means to bring something down with force and intention — usually a foot, or a tool, onto a surface. Think of it as an action that is deliberate, firm, and leaves a mark — either a physical one or a lasting impression.
"Stamp out" means to completely destroy or eliminate something, especially something harmful, unwanted, or negative.

A stampede is a sudden, wild, and uncontrolled rush of a large number of people or animals, all moving together in the same direction at the same time, usually driven by panic, fear, or sometimes intense excitement.

To stampede means to suddenly run — or to cause something to suddenly run — in a wild, panicked, uncontrolled rush, usually as part of a large group. The key idea is that control is lost. It is not a calm or planned movement.
A stance is a position — either a physical position of your body, or a mental position (your view, opinion, or attitude) on something. Both uses share the same underlying idea: where you stand.
To stanch something means to stop a flow — most often the flow of a liquid, and most often blood. Think of it as plugging a leak. When something is flowing out and you act to stop it, you stanch it.

A stanchion is a vertical upright post or bar — something that stands perfectly straight up — that is firm, sturdy, and built to either hold something up or create a boundary that guides or contains movement. Think of it as a "standing rod with a purpose."

The phrase "stand by" comes from a very simple physical image: imagine a soldier or a sailor standing beside their post, weapon, or station — not walking away, not sitting down, but staying right there, alert and ready.
To "stand up to someone" means to bravely face and resist a person who is more powerful, aggressive, or intimidating than you, and to refuse to let them control you, bully you, or treat you unfairly.
A person who takes someone else's place temporarily, especially an actor's place while lighting and cameras are set up, or a substitute.
Normal, usual, or regular, as in "standard practice." It can also mean widely accepted as a reference or authority, as in "a standard textbook," or, of language, generally considered correct.
A standard is something that is used as a reference point — a fixed measure, level, rule, or model against which other things are compared, judged, or built upon.
To standardize something means to make it conform to a fixed, agreed-upon model — so that it is consistent, uniform, and meets a set level of quality or follows a set format.
When something is standing, it means it was established once and continues to exist permanently — it doesn't expire after a single use or a single occasion.
"Standing" means your recognized position within a system — where you sit on the ladder of importance, respect, or rights in a group, society, institution, or the law.
If someone is standoffish, they are cold, distant, and unfriendly in the way they behave toward other people. They don't make you feel welcome. They don't show warmth.
A standstill is a situation where all movement or activity has completely stopped — nothing is going forward, nothing is progressing, everything is frozen in place.

A stanza is a group of lines in a poem that are arranged together and separated from other groups by a blank line. It is the basic building block of a poem, the way a brick is the basic building block of a wall.

When you call something a staple, you mean it is a fundamental, always-present, widely relied-upon part of something larger — not because it's the flashiest or most exciting thing, but because everything else is built around it. It is the backbone.
A main or basic item that is used regularly, especially an important food, as in "rice is a staple of their diet." A staple is also a small, U-shaped piece of wire used to fasten papers together.
Starboard means on the right side of a ship, boat, aircraft, or spacecraft — when you are facing forward (toward the front/nose of the vessel).
To starch something means to treat a piece of fabric or clothing with a substance called starch so that it becomes stiff, crisp, and firm.
Stardom is a noun that refers to the state or condition of being a famous, celebrated person — most commonly in entertainment, sports, or public life.
Harsh, plain, and bare in appearance, as in "a stark landscape." It can also mean unpleasantly clear and impossible to avoid, as in "a stark reminder," or complete, as in "stark madness."

A starling is a type of bird. More precisely, it is a medium-sized, highly social bird belonging to a large family of birds called Sturnidae, which contains over 100 different species spread across the world.
To start means to move from a state of not doing something into a state of doing it — or to cause something to go from not existing/happening into existing/happening.
To startle someone means to cause them to feel a sudden, sharp jolt of surprise and mild fear — because of something unexpected that their body was not prepared for.

To starve means to suffer severely, or to die, because of a lack of food over a long period of time. The key idea inside this word is painful deprivation — not just a little less than enough, but a serious, damaging absence of something essential.
To stash something means to put it away in a hidden or private place, usually so you can use it or find it later.

Stasis means a state of complete stillness — a condition in which things have stopped moving, changing, or developing. Think of it as a "freeze" or a "pause." Nothing is progressing. Nothing is evolving. Everything is locked in place, exactly as it is.

When something is stately, it has a calm, impressive grandeur that naturally commands respect and admiration. It looks or moves in a way that feels dignified, serious, and unhurried — not flashy or loud, but quietly powerful in its presence.
Not moving or changing, as in "prices remained static." It can also refer to static electricity, the crackling noise on a radio, or, in physics, objects at rest.
To station someone (or something) means to deliberately place them at a specific location so they can perform a duty or function there.
Stationary means not moving — remaining fixed in one place. If something is stationary, it is completely at rest, not traveling from one location to another.

Stationery refers to writing materials and the supplies you use to write, send letters, or do desk-based work. Think of everything you'd find at a shop that sells paper, pens, and notebooks — that whole category of items is called stationery.
"Statistical" means relating to, based on, or involving the collection, analysis, and interpretation of large amounts of numerical data to understand patterns, trends, and probabilities.
A statue is a solid, three-dimensional figure of a person, animal, god, or sometimes an imaginary or symbolic being, made by an artist from a hard or durable material.
Statuesque describes a person who has the kind of physical appearance that reminds you of a classical statue — tall, well-proportioned, graceful, and impressively dignified.
The importance and respect that someone has earned, as in "a scientist of international stature." It can also mean a person's natural height, as in "small in stature."
Status refers to the position that someone or something holds — either in relation to others (a rank or standing), or in terms of its present condition (the state something is in right now).
"Status quo" means the existing state of things — the way things currently are, right now.
A statute is a written law formally created and enacted by a legislative body — such as a parliament, a congress, or a state or national assembly.
Statutory means "created by, required by, or relating to a statute" — where a statute is a written law formally passed by a lawmaking body such as a parliament, congress, or legislature.
When you call someone staunch, you are saying they are deeply and unshakably loyal, committed, or supportive — and they stay that way no matter what.

Staunchly means in a way that is firmly, completely, and unwaveringly committed — to a belief, a cause, a person, or a position — especially when there is pressure, opposition, or difficulty involved.
"Stave off" means to hold back or delay something bad ("to stave off hunger"); "stave in" means to break or smash a hole in something.
"Stay put" means to remain exactly where you are, without moving.
Stead means the place, position, or role that someone or something holds — not a physical place like a room or a city, but a functional place: the slot a person or thing occupies in a situation.
To stead someone means to be of use, help, or benefit to them — to serve their interests in a practical way.
Steadfast means firmly and unwaveringly committed — to a person, a belief, a cause, or a decision — especially when there is pressure, difficulty, or temptation to give that up.
Firmly committed and completely unwilling to change — especially when under pressure, temptation, or difficulty.
Steadily means: in a way that is even, smooth, and continuous — without sudden changes, interruptions, or shakiness.
To steal a march on someone means to gain an advantage over a person or group by doing something before they do — often quietly, without them realizing it.
Stealth is the quality or practice of doing something in a way that is so quiet, careful, and hidden that nobody notices you doing it.
Stealthily means doing something in a way that is carefully designed to avoid being seen, heard, or detected.
Stealthy describes someone or something that moves, acts, or operates in a way that is careful not to be seen, heard, or noticed.
A steed is a horse. But saying it that way undersells the word entirely, because "steed" is not simply a synonym for horse — it carries a whole world of meaning packed into it.
When you call something or someone steely, you are saying that they remind you of steel — they carry those exact qualities: hardness, coldness, strength, and an unyielding, unshakeable nature.
Steep describes something that rises or falls sharply, at a large, dramatic angle — not gradually, not gently, but abruptly and significantly.
To steep something means to soak it in a liquid — usually hot — and leave it there for a period of time, so that something valuable transfers between the two.
A steeple is a tall, narrow tower that rises from the roof of a building — almost always a church — and ends in a sharp, pointed tip at the very top.
The cheapest passenger section of a ship, where poor emigrants once travelled; also the act of steering a vessel.
A stein is a large mug designed specifically for drinking beer. Think of it as a sturdy, oversized cup — but with a few special features that make it stand out from an ordinary mug.
An upright stone slab or pillar carved with inscriptions or pictures, put up in ancient times as a monument or grave marker. In botany, a stele is the central core of a plant's stem or root.
Excellent; outstanding, as in "a stellar performance." Literally, relating to the stars.
The stem is the main upright stalk of a plant — the central, tube-like structure that holds the plant above the ground. It connects the roots below to the leaves, flowers, and fruit above.
When something stems from something else, it means that other thing is its source, origin, or root cause. It answers the question: "Where does this come from?"
A stench is an extremely strong, deeply unpleasant smell — the kind so foul and powerful that it can make you gag, recoil, or feel physically sick. It is not just a bad smell.

A stenographer is a professional whose job is to listen to spoken words and write them down — accurately and in real time — as fast as people speak. The end goal is a written record of everything that was said.
Stentorian means extremely loud, powerful, and commanding — used almost always to describe a voice or the way someone speaks.
A steppe is a vast, flat or gently rolling plain covered mostly with grass and low plants — but with very few or no trees at all.

A stereotype is a fixed, oversimplified belief about an entire group of people — a mental "thumbnail image" that your brain stamps onto every single member of that group, whether or not it actually fits them.
When we say something is stereotyped, we mean it has been reduced to — or shaped by — such a fixed, oversimplified image, rather than being treated as genuinely complex, individual, or original.
"Sterile" means producing nothing, or preventing anything from growing or living.

To sterilize means to completely eliminate all life — or all possibility of life — from something. That "life" could be tiny microorganisms living on a surface, or the reproductive ability within a living being.

When you call something or someone sterling, you mean they are of genuinely excellent quality — deeply, thoroughly, and reliably good. Not just impressive on the surface, but the real thing, all the way through.

When someone is stern, they are serious, strict, and firm — especially about rules, behavior, or expectations. A stern person means business. They do not joke around, do not let things slide, and do not accept excuses.
The stern is the back end of a ship or boat — the rear part, the tail end, the section that faces away from the direction the vessel is heading.
Sternly means in a serious, firm, and strict manner — with no softness, warmth, or playfulness.
The sternum is a flat, narrow bone located right in the middle of your chest — the vertical bone you can feel when you press the center of your chest with your fingers.
Stertorous is an adjective that describes a very specific kind of breathing — breathing that is noisy, heavy, and makes a deep snoring or rattling sound.

A stethoscope is a medical instrument that doctors, nurses, and other healthcare professionals use to listen to sounds happening inside your body — particularly sounds made by your heart, lungs, and stomach — without cutting you open or using any technology that requires electricity.

A stew is a dish made by cooking ingredients — most often pieces of meat, vegetables, or both — slowly in a relatively small amount of liquid, usually water, broth, or stock. The cooking happens over gentle, low heat for a long time, often one to three hours.
To worry or be angry about something silently for a long time, as in "she left him to stew." Literally, to cook food slowly in liquid in a closed pot.
A steward is a person who is trusted to look after, manage, or take care of something — not for themselves, but on behalf of others, or for the benefit of a larger group.

Stewardship is the responsible management, care, and protection of something that has been entrusted to you — not as an owner, but as a caretaker — on behalf of others or for the benefit of future generations.
Stick = something becoming fixed, attached, or held in one place — either by force, by choice, or by circumstance.
A sticking point is a specific issue, topic, or problem that causes progress to stop or slow down significantly — something that people can't easily move past or agree on.
A stickler is a person who insists — very strongly and very strictly — on something being done the right way, with no shortcuts, no exceptions, and no compromises.
If someone says you are "on a sticky wicket", it means you are in a difficult, awkward, or tricky situation — one that is hard to handle and where any wrong move could make things worse.
Stiff means something that resists movement, bending, or flow. It describes things — and sometimes situations or people — that are firm, rigid, unyielding, or harder than expected.
To stiffen means to become stiff, or to make something stiff. It captures the process of going from flexible/loose/soft toward rigid/firm/hard.
To stifle something means to suppress it, hold it back, or stop it from happening — often by force or deliberate control. Think of it as putting a lid on something that wants to come out or grow.

Stifled describes something that has been held back, suppressed, or prevented from coming out or developing the way it naturally would. Think of it as something being smothered — it exists, it wants to emerge, but something is pushing it down or blocking it.
"Stifling" describes something so oppressive, so overwhelming in its restriction or heat, that it makes you feel like you cannot breathe — either literally, or metaphorically.
A stigma is a mark of shame or disgrace — not usually a physical mark, but a social and emotional one.
Stigmata are mysterious wounds or marks that appear on a living person's body, in the same places where Jesus Christ was wounded during his crucifixion.

To stigmatize someone means to treat them as shameful, disgraced, or inferior because of a particular characteristic they have — and to make that judgment publicly known in a way that sticks to them like a label.
A thin, very high heel on a woman's shoe, or a shoe with one; also a small dagger with a narrow, pointed blade.
Something is stilted when it is stiff, unnatural, and awkward in a way that makes it feel forced or artificial — like someone is struggling to do something that should come easily and naturally.
To stimulate something means to cause it to become more active, more energetic, or more likely to grow or develop.
A stimulus is anything that causes a reaction or a response. Think of it as a trigger — something that sets something else in motion.

If someone is stingy, it means they are unwilling to give, spend, or share — even when they can easily afford to. A stingy person holds on tightly to what they have and gives as little as possible to others.
To stink means to produce a strong, bad smell. When something stinks, it doesn't just smell a little — the smell is noticeable, unpleasant, and often hard to ignore or escape.
The most common meaning of stint is a fixed, temporary period of time that a person spends doing a particular job, playing a particular role, or being in a particular place.

To stint means to limit or restrict the supply of something — usually to a degree that feels too small, too tight, or not enough. When you stint on something, you are deliberately holding back, giving less than what is really needed, deserved, or expected.
A stipend is a fixed, regular sum of money given to a person — not as a wage for the hours they work, but as financial support so they can focus on a particular role, study, training, or service.
To stipple means to create shading, texture, or a pattern on a surface by applying many small, separate dots or tiny dabs — rather than using solid fills, smooth strokes, or continuous lines.
When you stipulate something, you are clearly and firmly stating it as a required condition — something that must happen or must be true, usually as part of an agreement, deal, contract, or rule.

A stipulation is a specific condition or requirement that someone insists on as part of an agreement. It is something one party demands must be accepted or fulfilled before they agree to a deal, arrangement, or contract.
"Stir" is about bringing movement to something that was still. That one idea runs through every use of this word, whether you're talking about cooking, sleeping, emotions, or human behavior.

When you describe something as stirring, you mean it is so powerful, impressive, or emotionally moving that it wakes up strong feelings deep inside you — feelings like excitement, inspiration, pride, or courage.

Something is stochastic if its outcome involves genuine randomness — but a structured kind of randomness governed by probability, so you can predict what's likely to happen even though you can never know with certainty what will happen.

When "stock" is used as an adjective, it describes something that is routine, standard, and ready-made — so commonly used or produced that it requires no original thought or customization. The easiest way to picture it: imagine a warehouse shelf.

A supply of goods kept for sale or use, as in "in stock." It also means shares in a company, farm animals, a liquid made by simmering bones or vegetables, or a person's ancestry, as in "of farming stock."

A stockade is a strong, tall fence or wall made by hammering thick wooden posts or stakes tightly into the ground, one right next to the other, in a continuous line — like a row of giant pencils standing upright, touching each other shoulder-to-shoulder, forming a solid wooden barrier.

Stockholm syndrome is a psychological phenomenon where a person who is being held captive, abused, or controlled begins to develop positive feelings — such as sympathy, trust, loyalty, or even love — toward the very person who is harming or controlling them.

A stockpile is a large amount of something that has been deliberately gathered together and stored away, so that it is ready and available when it is needed in the future — especially during times of shortage, emergency, or high demand.

To stockpile something means to deliberately collect and store a large amount of it over time, so you have a big supply ready for the future — especially for a time when that thing might become difficult or impossible to get.
Stocky describes a person (or animal) who has a short or medium height combined with a broad, solid, and compact body. Think of someone who is wide and dense rather than tall and thin.

Stodgy is an adjective with two closely related meanings — one for food and one for people, ideas, writing, and organizations. Both meanings share the same underlying feeling: something is heavy, dull, and unpleasant in a way that weighs you down.

If someone is stoic, it means they endure pain, hardship, or difficulty without complaining, without showing distress, and without being shaken by it. They remain calm, composed, and steady — even when life is being brutal to them.
A Stoic is a member of an ancient school of philosophy called Stoicism, which was founded in Greece around 300 BC by a thinker named Zeno of Citium.
The ability to endure pain or hardship calmly without complaining or showing emotion. Stoicism is also an ancient Greek philosophy which taught that virtue and self-control lead to inner peace.
Stoicism is a school of philosophy — a way of thinking and living — that began in ancient Greece around 300 BCE and grew into one of the most influential philosophies in the Western world.
To make a feeling or situation stronger or worse, as in "stoking fears of war." Literally, to add fuel to a fire or furnace to keep it burning.

A stole is a long, narrow strip or band of cloth that is worn draped over the shoulders or around the neck. It is not clothing that covers your body — think of it as a decorative, ceremonial, or formal accessory that hangs from the shoulders.
Stolid describes a person who shows very little emotion and is extremely difficult to excite, stir up, or move — no matter what happens around them.

To stomp means to bring your foot down onto something with great force and a loud noise. It is not a gentle, quiet, or accidental action. Stomping is always deliberate, heavy, and powerful. Think of it as the opposite of tiptoeing.

"Stonking" is an informal British English adjective that means impressively large, powerful, or excellent. Think of it as a turbo-charged version of saying something is "really great" or "absolutely massive."
The word "stony" takes its meaning from the nature of a stone itself — hard, cold, rough, and lifeless. This idea runs through every use of the word, whether literal or figurative.
A stooge is a person who is used, controlled, or manipulated by someone more powerful — essentially a human tool. The stooge acts not for themselves, but for whoever is pulling the strings.
"Stoop" means to lower yourself — either physically with your body, or morally with your actions. These two meanings are deeply connected by one simple idea: going down from where you normally are.

A stoppage is an event or period in which something that was moving, flowing, working, or happening comes to a halt. It names both the moment of stopping and the stretch of time during which something remains stopped.
Storage means keeping something somewhere so you can use it later.

When you call something storied, you are saying that it has a long, impressive, and celebrated history — one so full of remarkable events, achievements, and memorable moments that people have been talking about it, writing about it, and telling stories about it for years or even generations.

Every use of "storm" as a verb borrows energy from the weather. Think about a real storm — it moves fast, it hits hard, it doesn't slow down for anything, and it carries a kind of violent, unstoppable force.
Storytelling is the act or skill of sharing stories with other people — in a way that holds their attention, stirs their feelings, and leaves something meaningful in their minds.
Stout always means solid, substantial, and not easily pushed aside — whether it's describing a body, an object, or a person's spirit.
When someone does something stoutly, they do it with firm, unshakeable determination — without backing down, without hesitating, and without letting anyone or anything push them off their position.

A stowaway is a person who secretly hides on a vehicle — most often a ship, airplane, train, or truck — without a ticket, without paying, and without the knowledge or permission of the crew or authorities, in order to travel somewhere.
The most direct meaning of straddle is to sit or stand with one leg on each side of something.
To strafe means to attack a target in a sweeping, continuous motion — moving across it while firing, rather than shooting at it from one fixed spot.
To straggle means to move, spread, or grow in a scattered, irregular, and untidy way — often falling behind, drifting apart from a group, or spreading out without any order or neatness.
A straggler is a person (or animal) who falls behind the rest of a group — moving more slowly, arriving later, or finishing after everyone else.

"Straggling" describes things — groups of people, plants, buildings, or any arrangement — that are spread out in a loose, irregular, and untidy way, with parts trailing behind, scattered unevenly, or growing without neat shape or order.

When something is described as straightforward, it means it is uncomplicated. There are no hidden traps, no confusing steps, no puzzling layers. You can understand it or do it without much difficulty.

Pressure or tension that causes worry or difficulty, as in "under great strain." It can also mean an injury from overstretching a muscle, a variety of a plant, animal, or virus, as in "a new strain of flu," or a trace of a quality in someone's character.

To make a great effort, as in "straining to hear." It also means to injure a muscle by overstretching it, to put too much pressure on something, as in "straining the budget," or to pour food through a sieve to separate liquid.
Tense and uncomfortable ("a strained silence"); forced and unnatural ("a strained smile"); or injured by overstretching ("a strained muscle").

To straiten something means to restrict it, confine it, or put it under severe limitation — especially in a way that causes hardship. Think of it as squeezing something into a tighter and tighter space until it struggles.
When you call someone straitlaced, you mean they are extremely strict about morals, proper behavior, and social rules — and often uncomfortably so.

A strait (or straits) is a naturally formed narrow strip of water that sits between two landmasses and connects two larger bodies of water. It is nature's corridor — land pressing in from both sides, water flowing through the middle.
A strand is a single, long, thin, and usually flexible piece of something — something that is much longer than it is wide, like a thread, a wire, or a fiber.
To strand someone (or something) means to leave them stuck in a place or situation from which they cannot escape or move forward, usually with no help available and no clear way out.

To be stranded is to be left in a place or situation from which you cannot escape or move on — usually because of an outside force or an unfortunate event — and typically with no immediate help available.
To strangle someone means to squeeze their throat tightly so that air cannot pass through. The throat carries air to the lungs. When something compresses it hard enough, breathing becomes impossible.
A stranglehold means a tight, overpowering, and suffocating control over something — control so complete that the thing being controlled cannot move freely, grow, escape, or breathe.
To strap something means to fasten or secure it firmly using a strap — a narrow, flat strip of strong material like leather, nylon, or cloth.
When you describe someone as strapping, you mean they are tall, strongly built, and physically impressive in a healthy, robust way.
Strata means distinct layers — separate, horizontal levels of something, stacked one on top of another, where each layer is noticeably different from the one above and below it.

A stratagem is a clever, carefully planned trick or scheme used to outsmart someone or to get what you want — especially in a situation where there's some kind of opponent, competition, or obstacle. The key ingredient is cleverness.
"Strategic" is an adjective that describes anything connected to a careful, deliberate plan designed to achieve an important, often long-term goal.

To strategize means to carefully think through and plan the best way to achieve a goal — especially when the path forward is not simple, when resources (time, money, effort) are limited, or when you are competing against others or facing challenges.
A strategy is a carefully thought-out overall plan for achieving an important goal, especially when the path to that goal is not simple or straightforward.
Arrangement into separate layers or levels, as in rock, or in society divided into classes.
Stratified means organized or divided into distinct layers or levels, where each layer is separate from the others, sits either above or below them, and is meaningfully different from them.
The stratosphere is a specific layer of Earth's atmosphere — the invisible blanket of gases that surrounds our planet.

A stratum is a single, distinct layer within something that is made up of multiple stacked layers, where each layer is clearly separate from the ones above and below it, and each has its own characteristics.

Straw refers to the dry, hollow stalks of grain plants — such as wheat, rice, barley, or oats — that are left over after the grain (the edible seeds) has been harvested. Think of it this way: when a farmer grows wheat, the goal is the seeds at the top.
A straw man is a fake or distorted version of someone's argument, created specifically because it is easier to attack and defeat than the real argument.
A straw man is a fake, weakened, or distorted version of someone's real argument — one that's been twisted just enough to make it easier to attack and "defeat."

A straw poll is an unofficial, informal vote or survey taken to quickly get a rough sense of what people think or prefer — but without any official weight or binding consequence. It is not a real decision. It is a temperature check.
When you call something stray, you are saying that it has moved away from where it belongs, or that it exists alone and separated from the group it should be part of. It is out of place.
To stray means to move away from where you are supposed to be, or from what you are supposed to be doing — usually gradually and without a strong intention to do so.
A streak is something long, thin, and distinct — whether it's a visible mark, a flash of light, a run of events, or a quality inside a person.
To streamline something means to make it simpler, faster, and more efficient by removing anything that is unnecessary, redundant, or creates unwanted friction.

Street smarts is a noun (always used in plural form) that refers to the practical intelligence and real-world wisdom that helps a person survive, navigate, and succeed in tough, unpredictable, or challenging real-life situations — without needing formal education or textbooks to figure things out.

When something is strenuous, it demands a great deal of physical or mental energy and effort. It pushes you, tires you out, and requires you to work hard. Think of it as the opposite of easy or relaxed.

When you do something strenuously, you do it with great effort, force, and energy — you are not being casual, mild, or half-hearted. You are putting in everything you've got, pushing with full intensity.

A feeling of mental or emotional pressure caused by difficult or demanding situations. It can also mean physical pressure on an object, special importance given to something, or extra force on a syllable or word when speaking.

When you stress something, you give it special importance. You say it, or signal it, in a way that makes other people take notice. You are essentially telling your listener: "Pay attention to this. This part matters more than the rest."
In English, when you say a word, you don't give equal force to every syllable. Some syllables are said with more force, higher pitch, and longer duration. That's called stress.

To stretch means to extend something beyond its current state — to pull it, move it, spread it, or push it so that it becomes longer, wider, reaches further, or goes beyond its usual size, shape, or limit.
To strew means to scatter or spread things loosely over a surface or area, in a way that is random, untidy, or wide-spread — not neat or organized.
Striate means: marked with, or having, a series of parallel lines, grooves, bands, or ridges running in the same direction.
Striated means marked with a series of parallel lines, grooves, streaks, or bands running across or along a surface.

A striation is a narrow groove, scratch, channel, or stripe on a surface — and crucially, striations almost always appear as a set of parallel lines running side by side in the same direction, rather than as one isolated mark.

When someone or something is stricken, it means they have been severely and deeply affected by something painful, harmful, or devastating — to the point where they are overwhelmed, weakened, or incapacitated by it.
Demanding that rules be obeyed exactly, as in "a strict teacher." It can also mean exact and precise, as in "in the strict sense of the word."

A stricture is a strong, pointed criticism — usually formal, official, or written — directed at someone's behavior, work, or conduct. It isn't a gentle suggestion or a mild complaint. It is a sharp, authoritative verdict of disapproval.
To stride means to walk with long, deliberate, and confident steps. But it's much more than just "walking with big steps." The word carries a strong sense of purpose and confidence.
Strident means something that is harshly forceful in a way that is unpleasant, grating, or aggressive.

To stridulate means to make a sharp, high-pitched, chirping or scraping sound by rubbing two body parts together. This is something certain insects do — and it is the precise, scientific word for exactly that action.
Strife means serious, bitter conflict or struggle between people, groups, or forces — especially when it is intense, prolonged, and causes real damage or suffering.
"Strike a nerve" means that something someone said or did triggered a strong emotional reaction in a person — because it touched on something sensitive, personal, painful, or deeply felt.

Something is striking when it is so noticeable, so vivid, or so impressive that it immediately grabs your attention — almost like it reaches out and hits you before you even decide to look at it. It is the quality of standing out powerfully.

To string someone along means to deliberately keep someone believing in something that is not true — usually a promise, a relationship, or an opportunity — with no real intention of ever following through.
The enormous number of possible universes allowed by string theory, each with different physical laws, depending on how the extra dimensions of space are shaped.
Stringent means extremely strict, precise, and demanding — with little or no room for flexibility, exceptions, or errors.
To remove a covering or layer from something, as in "stripping paint off the door." It also means to take off clothes, or to take something away from someone, as in "stripped of his title."

You'd leave a long, narrow band of color — that is a stripe. A stripe is a long, narrow band that stands out from what surrounds it, usually because of a difference in color, shade, or sometimes texture.

A stripling is a boy or young male who is on the edge of becoming a man — but isn't quite there yet. Think of a teenager, roughly 13 to 18 years old, who has started to grow tall but still looks young, lean, and undeveloped compared to a full-grown adult man.
To strive means to put in serious, sustained, and determined effort toward a goal — especially when it is difficult or takes a long time to achieve.

A sudden loss of blood flow to part of the brain, which can cause paralysis or death. A stroke is also a single movement of a brush, pen, oar, or arm, a gentle touch, or a lucky or clever event, as in "a stroke of luck."

To stroke something means to move your hand gently and smoothly over a surface, usually in one repeated direction. Think of what you do when you pet a cat — you place your hand on its back and slide it forward, slowly and softly, again and again.
To stroll means to walk slowly and in a relaxed, easy way — usually because you are enjoying yourself or simply have no reason to hurry.

"Strong" describes something — a person, object, smell, argument, feeling, or situation — that has a high degree of power, force, or intensity, and that holds up well or makes a significant impact as a result.
A stronghold is a place that is so well-protected, so deeply rooted, or so dominant that it is extremely hard to attack, remove, or change.
A structure is something — or the internal arrangement of something — where multiple parts are organized in a deliberate, meaningful way to form a coherent whole.

A struggle is a hard, sustained effort against something that resists you or works against you. It is not just "difficulty" — it is active opposition over time. You are not passively suffering; you are trying, pushing, fighting.
To struggle means to try hard to do something that is difficult, while facing resistance or opposition.
To strum means to sweep your fingers or a pick across the strings of a stringed instrument in one smooth, flowing motion — brushing over multiple strings at once rather than picking them one by one.
To strut means to walk in a proud, confident, and deliberately showy way. It is not ordinary walking — it is performing while walking.

A stub is something that is cut short, broken off, or left over — a small piece that remains after most of something is gone. Think of it as the leftover, the remnant, or the short blunt end of something that was once fuller or longer.
Stubble refers to short, stiff, rough bristles or stalks that are left behind after something has been cut down or shaved off.
Stubborn means refusing to change your mind, your opinion, or your behavior, even when there is a good reason to do so. The key word here is "even."
Something is stubby when it is short and thick at the same time — shorter than you'd normally expect, and wider or chunkier than its own length would suggest.

A stud here is a small, rounded piece of metal that is attached to or pressed into a surface — usually leather or fabric — to decorate it. Think of those shiny silver dots you see on biker jackets, belts, or boots. Those dots are studs.
When "studied" is used as an adjective, it means deliberately done, carefully thought out, and intentional — the opposite of natural, spontaneous, or accidental.

When you call someone studious, you mean they spend a lot of time studying, reading, and learning — and they do it with genuine focus, care, and dedication. A studious person doesn't just open a book reluctantly; they actively engage with learning.
"Stuffy" has three main meanings. What's beautiful about this word is that a single idea quietly connects all three: the feeling of something being closed off, blocked, or airless.
To stultify something or someone means to drain them of vitality, intelligence, or effectiveness — to smother, dull, or make them look foolish and incapable.

Something stultifying is so dull, repetitive, or mentally restrictive that it actively deadens your mind — it doesn't just bore you, it slowly suffocates your thinking, creativity, and sense of aliveness.

Stumble means to lose smooth control — whether with your feet, your words, or your progress in life. Think of it as something going slightly wrong when it was supposed to go smoothly. That single idea connects all the different ways this word is used.
A stumbler is a person who stumbles — meaning someone who trips, makes mistakes, or moves through something clumsily, either physically or in a more general sense of life and effort.
When something stumps you, it means you are completely unable to answer a question, solve a problem, or figure something out. You are stuck. Your mind has no answer. You give up.
To stun means to hit someone so hard — physically or emotionally — that they temporarily lose their normal ability to function.

Stunned describes a state where someone is so overwhelmed by something sudden and unexpected that they temporarily cannot think, speak, or react normally. Their mind goes blank. Their body freezes. They are caught completely off guard.
Extremely beautiful or impressive, as in "a stunning view." It can also mean extremely shocking or surprising, as in "a stunning defeat."
A stunt is an act that is done to get a strong reaction from people — either by thrilling them, impressing them, or simply grabbing their attention. That reaction is the whole point.
To stunt something means to slow down, hold back, or limit its natural growth or development — so that it ends up smaller, weaker, or less developed than it would have been under healthy conditions.

Something that is stunted has not grown or developed as fully as it naturally should have — because something got in the way of that growth. The essential idea is: there was a natural path forward, and something blocked or damaged it.
A childhood in which a child's normal physical, emotional, or social development is held back, by poor nutrition, neglect, abuse, or having to take on adult responsibilities too early.

When someone is stupefied, their mind has been hit so hard by something — by shock, amazement, disbelief, or even a drug or extreme exhaustion — that it temporarily stops working the way it normally should. They can't think straight. They can't react.

To stupefy someone means to affect their mind so powerfully that they are left unable to think, react, or respond normally — at least for a moment. The person is mentally frozen. Think of it as hitting a mental "pause button" on someone. Their jaw might drop.
When something is stupendous, it is so impressive, so large, or so remarkable that it almost stuns you — it leaves you wide-eyed and momentarily speechless.
A stupor is a state where a person's mind and body have "shut down" to a severe degree — they are not fully unconscious (not in a coma), but they are nowhere near normally awake and aware either.

"Sturdy" describes something that is strong, solid, and well-built — something that can handle force, weight, pressure, or rough treatment without breaking, collapsing, or giving way. The heart of the word is dependable, reliable strength.

A sturgeon is a large, ancient species of fish. Not just one specific fish — it's actually a family of around 27 related species of fish that all share the same basic design, all referred to as sturgeons.
A stutter is a disruption in the smooth flow of speech. When someone has a stutter, they cannot speak words out in one clean, continuous stream.

To stutter means to speak with involuntary, broken interruptions — where sounds, syllables, or words get stuck, repeated, or stretched out before the speaker can move forward. The speaker is not choosing to do this.
Stygian means profoundly, oppressively dark — the kind of darkness that feels absolute, suffocating, and deeply sinister, like the darkness of death itself.
A particular way of doing something, as in "a style of writing." It also means elegance and sophistication, as in "she has style," or a fashion in clothes or hair, as in "the latest styles."

When you call something or someone stylish, you mean they have an impressive, attractive sense of style — a quality that makes them look or feel noticeably good, put-together, and refined in a way that draws admiration.

When something is stylized, it means it has been represented or depicted in a deliberately non-realistic way — shaped, simplified, or exaggerated to follow a particular artistic style, rather than trying to look exactly like it does in real life.
A stylus is a small, pen-shaped tool with a pointed or fine tip, used to write, draw, mark, or interact with a surface through direct physical contact.
To stymie someone or something means to stop them from making progress — to block, prevent, or obstruct them in a way that leaves them stuck, unable to move forward.
Suasion means persuasion — the act of influencing someone to think or act in a certain way through words, reasoning, or appeals, rather than through force, threats, or legal commands.
Suave describes a person — almost always a man — who is charming, smooth, confident, and socially polished in a way that looks completely effortless. He never seems nervous or awkward.
Suavity is the quality of being smooth, charming, and polished — especially in the way a person behaves, speaks, and handles social situations.

When something is done sub rosa, it is done in strict secrecy or in strict confidence — privately, away from the knowledge of outsiders, with the clear understanding among those involved that the matter must not be disclosed or revealed to others.

A subaltern is someone who is beneath another person — or beneath a whole system — in terms of rank, power, and social standing. Not just "less powerful," but structurally subordinate: meaning society itself is organized in a way that keeps them below.
The part of the mind that works below conscious awareness, holding thoughts, memories and feelings that affect us without our knowing.

A subcontinent is a very large, geographically distinct piece of land that is part of a continent but stands apart from the rest of that continent so clearly — because of natural boundaries like mountains, seas, or deserts — that it is treated as its own separate landmass.
Subcutaneous means situated, existing, applied, or administered beneath the skin — specifically in the layer of tissue that lies just below your skin but above the muscle underneath.
Subdue means to bring something powerful, wild, or resistant under your control — usually by force, effort, or pressure — so that it becomes weaker, quieter, or no longer a threat.

Subdued means toned down, quieter, or less intense than usual or than expected. Think of it as a volume knob or a brightness dial being turned down — whatever it describes is still there, but its energy, force, or vividness has been reduced or held back.
Subfusc means dull, dark, and dreary — especially in color or appearance. It describes things that are murky, dim, and lacking any brightness, vividness, or cheer.

The adjective subject almost always appears in the phrase subject to, and it expresses one central idea: something is not fully free or independent. Whatever is subject to something else is either vulnerable to it, controlled by it, or dependent on it.

A topic being discussed or studied, as in "change the subject," or a field of study at school. A subject is also a person under a ruler's authority, someone taking part in an experiment, or, in grammar, the person or thing doing the action of a verb.
To subject someone or something to something means to cause them to go through an experience — usually one they did not choose and often one that is unpleasant, difficult, or demanding.
Subjection means being under the power or control of someone or something else — with little or no freedom to act on your own terms.

Subjective describes something that comes from a person's inner world — their feelings, opinions, personal experiences, tastes, or point of view — rather than from facts that exist in the outside world independently of anyone.

To subjugate someone means to bring them completely under your power or control — usually by force — and keep them there. The person or group being subjugated doesn't just lose a battle; they lose their freedom, their independence, and often their dignity.

Subjugation means the act of bringing a person, group, or nation completely under the power and control of someone else — usually by force, threat, or overwhelming authority — in a way that takes away their freedom, independence, and dignity.

In psychology, to redirect a strong impulse, especially a sexual or aggressive one, into a more socially acceptable activity, such as art or sport. In chemistry, for a solid to turn directly into a gas without first becoming a liquid.

In psychology, the redirecting of strong impulses, especially sexual or aggressive ones, into socially acceptable activities, such as art or sport. In chemistry, the process of a solid turning directly into a gas without first becoming a liquid.
"Sublime" means something so extraordinarily beautiful, grand, or powerful that it almost goes beyond what you can fully grasp or put into words.
Something is subliminal when it exists or operates below the threshold of your conscious awareness.
Sublimity is the quality of being so overwhelmingly great, vast, or powerful that it fills you with a deep sense of awe — a feeling that is bigger than ordinary admiration or pleasure.

Sublunary means belonging to the world beneath the moon — that is, the earthly world. It describes anything that exists within the realm of ordinary human life on Earth: physical, mortal, changeable, and imperfect.
A submarine is a watercraft — a vehicle built to travel — that can operate fully underwater, beneath the surface of the sea.

To submerge something means to put it completely under the surface of a liquid — or for something to go under the surface of a liquid on its own. The liquid is almost always water, but it can be any liquid.
When something is submerged, it is completely beneath the surface of a liquid — most commonly water. The key idea is that it has gone under and is now below the surface, hidden from plain view.

When you describe something as submersible, you mean it is designed and built to work while fully underwater — not just near water, not just splashed by water, but completely beneath the surface of water.
Submersion means the act, process, or state of going completely under a liquid — or putting something completely under a liquid — so that it is fully covered beneath the surface.

Submission is about one party yielding to the power, authority, or judgment of another. Think of it as the moment when someone (or something) stops resisting and accepts that another person, force, or system has control or the final say.

If someone is submissive, it means they tend to give in to the will, authority, or wishes of others — willingly, without much resistance. A submissive person does not fight back, does not push their own agenda, and does not assert their own desires strongly.

"Submit" means to place something or yourself under someone else's authority or judgment. Think of it as a deliberate act of going "beneath" someone — giving them the power to decide, judge, control, or receive what you are offering.

The noun subnivean (also commonly called the subnivean zone or subnivean space) refers to the hidden, insulated air pocket — and the ecosystem living inside it — that forms between the ground and the underside of a deep snowpack during winter.

When something or someone is subordinate, it means they are lower in rank, importance, or power compared to something or someone else. Think of it as "coming second" or "being beneath" in a system where things are ranked from high to low.
A subordinate is a person who is below someone else in rank or authority within a structured system — like a company, the military, a government, or any organization with a clear hierarchy.
A part of a sentence that has its own subject and verb but cannot stand alone as a complete sentence, such as "because it was raining" in "We stayed in because it was raining."
To suborn someone means to secretly persuade, bribe, or pressure them into doing something illegal or morally wrong — something they wouldn't necessarily do on their own.
Subpar means below the expected standard or level of quality. When something is subpar, it has failed to reach the bar that was set — it fell short of what was needed, expected, or acceptable.
A subplot is a secondary story that runs alongside the main story inside a larger narrative — a novel, film, TV show, play, or any other form of storytelling.

A subpoena is an official legal document — issued with the authority of a court — that commands a specific person to do something in connection with a legal case. It is not a request. It is not an invitation.

To subpoena someone means to officially and legally command them — through a written court order — to either show up and give testimony in a legal proceeding, or to hand over specific documents, records, or other evidence. It is not a request.

Subrogation is the legal act of one party stepping into the exact legal position of another party — inheriting their rights, claims, and ability to pursue legal remedies — after compensating that other party for a loss that was actually caused by someone else.

Subscribe means to formally commit yourself to something on an ongoing basis — whether that means committing your attention, your money, your agreement, or your signature. Think of it as saying "I'm in, and I'm staying in."
Subsequent means coming after something else in time or order.

Subservience means the state of being completely obedient and submissive to someone or something else — to the point where your own will, opinions, and needs are pushed aside entirely to serve another's.

Subservient means placed below something or someone else, and acting in a way that fully serves, obeys, or gives way to that thing or person. It carries the sense of being secondary — either in rank, importance, or behavior.

To subside means to gradually become less intense, less strong, or less severe — and settle down into a calmer, quieter state. Picture something that was high, active, or powerful slowly coming down and becoming milder.

When you describe something as subsidiary, you are saying it plays a supporting, secondary role — it sits below or behind something more important, and its purpose is to assist, supplement, or back up that more important thing.
A subsidiary is a company that is owned and controlled by another, larger company. The company that owns it is called the parent company (sometimes also called a holding company).
To subsidize something means to give it financial support — usually money — so that it can survive, grow, or become cheaper for people to use.

A subsidy is money given — usually by a government — to a person, a business, or an industry to help them financially, so that they can either survive, grow, or offer their goods and services at a lower price than they otherwise could.
Subsist means to continue to exist or stay alive, but almost always with the underlying suggestion of barely, minimally, or with great difficulty.
Subsistence means the bare minimum that a person or group needs in order to simply stay alive. Not to live comfortably. Not to thrive. Just enough to survive and keep going — nothing more.
"Substance" always refers to what is real, actual, and fundamental — the real "stuff" of something, rather than its surface or appearance.

Substantial means large enough or strong enough to truly matter. It points to something that is not minor, not trivial, not just a little bit — but genuinely significant in size, amount, strength, or importance.
"Substantially" means to a large, meaningful, real degree — not in a small or trivial way, but in a way that genuinely matters.
To substantiate something means to prove that it is true by providing solid evidence.
"Substantive" means real, meaningful, and having actual weight or importance. Something substantive is not hollow, not empty, not just surface-level. It has genuine content, depth, or significance.
A substitute is a person or thing that steps into the role or position of another person or thing — taking their place, doing their job, or serving their purpose.
Substitute means to put one thing (or person) in the place of another. Something goes out, something else comes in to fill that role. Think of it as a swap.

To subsume something means to pull it inside something larger — to take a smaller thing and absorb it into a bigger category, group, system, or idea, where it then exists as just one part of that bigger whole.

Subterfuge means a trick, scheme, or dishonest tactic that someone uses to hide their true intentions, avoid a difficult situation, or get something they couldn't get through honest means. It is deliberate deception — carefully crafted, not accidental.
Subterranean describes anything that exists, is found, or happens below the surface of the earth — essentially, underground.
Subtext is the hidden meaning beneath the surface of words — the real message that isn't directly stated, but is clearly meant and expected to be understood.

A subtitle is something secondary that adds clarity to something primary. The word "sub" means "below" or "under," and that's exactly where subtitles appear — either physically below the main title on a page, or at the bottom of a screen.

So small or delicate that it is hard to notice or describe, as in "a subtle difference." It can also mean clever and indirect, as in "a subtle hint," or able to notice fine details, as in "a subtle mind."
The quality of being delicate, understated, or hard to notice, as in "the subtlety of her humour." A subtlety is also a fine detail or distinction, as in "the subtleties of the language."
Subtly means doing something in a way that is quiet, indirect, and not immediately obvious — but still real, still present, and still having an effect.
To subtract means to take away one amount from another, so that you are left with what remains.
A suburb is a residential area that exists on the outer edges of a city — close enough to the city to be connected to it, but separate from the busy, dense city center.
Subversion is the act of secretly, gradually, or cleverly undermining, weakening, or destroying something that holds authority, power, or accepted standing — usually from within it.

"Subversive" describes something — a person, idea, piece of writing, artwork, organization, or behavior — that works to quietly undermine, weaken, or destroy an established system, authority, institution, or widely accepted set of beliefs and values.

To subvert something means to secretly, indirectly, or gradually weaken and destroy it from within — especially something that is established, powerful, or authoritative, like a government, a system, a set of rules, or a set of values.
When you succeed, you reach your goal. You tried something, and it worked. Think of it as the direct opposite of "fail."
"Successful" describes someone or something that has achieved the goal it was meant to achieve — that it worked, it went well, and the desired result was reached.
Succession carries one big idea: one thing following another, in order. Think of it as a chain — each link comes after the previous one, and before the next one.
Successive means following one after another, in order, without skipping.
A successor is someone or something that comes after another person or thing — specifically by taking over their position, role, or place.

Succinct means expressing something fully and clearly, but using as few words as possible. When something is succinct, it covers everything that needs to be said — no more, no less. Nothing important is left out, and nothing unnecessary is added.
Succinctly means: in a way that is brief, clear, and complete — using only the words that are truly needed, and nothing more.
Succor means help, relief, or support given to someone who is suffering, in serious trouble, or in urgent need.
To succor someone means to go to their aid and give them help, relief, or comfort when they are suffering, in danger, or in serious distress.

Succulent means full of juice, richness, and satisfying goodness. It is always a positive word — it never describes something bad or unpleasant. When you call something succulent, you are saying it is not just good, but pleasurably, almost irresistibly good.
"Succumb" means to stop resisting something that is stronger than you, and give in to it — usually because you have no choice, or because the force is simply too powerful to fight off any longer.
When something is described as sudorific, it means it causes sweating or promotes perspiration. That's the whole idea in a nutshell.

To sue someone means to take them to a court of law and formally demand that they compensate you or fix a wrong they have done to you. It is a legal action that one person or organization initiates against another.
Suede is a type of soft, velvety leather with a fuzzy surface. It is used to make shoes, jackets, bags, and many other products.
Sufferance means passive, reluctant tolerance — allowing something to happen or continue not because you approve of it or want it, but simply because you are not actively stopping it.

Suffering is the experience of going through something deeply painful, difficult, or distressing — and having to endure it. It is what a person (or animal) feels inside when they are in pain, deeply hurt, or burdened by hardship.
To suffice means to be enough for a particular purpose or need. That is the heart of it. When something suffices, it meets the requirement — it does the job, it covers the need, it is adequate.
Sufficiency means the state of having enough — enough of something to meet a need, fulfill a purpose, or satisfy a requirement.
Sufficient means enough to meet a need or purpose — not too little, and not necessarily more than needed. Just the right amount to satisfy a requirement.
To suffocate means to die, or to nearly die, because of a lack of air — or to cause someone else to die that way.
Suffrage means the right to vote — specifically, the legal right of a citizen to participate in choosing their government or leaders through voting in elections.

A suffragette is a woman who actively fought for women's right to vote — not just by signing petitions or writing letters, but through bold, disruptive, and sometimes illegal actions designed to force governments to pay attention.
A suffragist is a person who campaigns for the right to vote to be extended to people who currently don't have it — especially to those who have been unfairly excluded.
To suffuse something means to spread slowly, softly, and evenly through it or over it — until that thing is completely filled or covered with a color, light, warmth, or feeling.

If someone is suggestible, it means they are easily influenced by what other people suggest — their ideas, opinions, instructions, or even just hints — often without stopping to think critically about whether those suggestions are actually true, correct, or right for them.
Suggestive means hinting at something without actually saying it directly.
Sui generis is a Latin phrase that means "of its own kind" or "unique in its nature."
"Suit" means to be right for someone or something — to fit well, not in a physical sense, but in the sense of being appropriate, convenient, becoming, or a good match.
Suitability is the quality of being right or appropriate for a specific purpose, role, situation, or person.
"Suitable" means right for a particular purpose, person, or situation. Something is suitable when it fits what is needed or expected — when it matches the requirements of a specific context.
A suitor is someone — typically a man — who pursues another person romantically, with a serious intention of winning their love, often with the goal of marriage.
When you sulk, you become silent, withdrawn, and cold towards others because you are upset, hurt, or angry about something — but instead of expressing that feeling openly, you close yourself off.

When someone is sulky, they are in a quiet, withdrawn, moody state because they are unhappy, resentful, or feel they have been treated unfairly — and they are showing that unhappiness not by talking about it, but by going silent, pulling away, and refusing to engage normally with others.
When a person is sullen, they are in a dark, resentful mood — and instead of talking about it or expressing it openly, they go quiet, withdrawn, and gloomy.

Sullenly describes how someone behaves when they are silently, heavily uncooperative — not because they are calm or fine, but because they are angry, hurt, or resentful, and have chosen to shut down instead of expressing it openly.
To sully something means to damage or spoil something that was previously clean, pure, or good — making it look bad, dirty, or shameful.
A sultan is a sovereign ruler — essentially a king or monarch — of a Muslim country or territory. The title represents the highest level of political and military authority in a state.
Of weather, hot, humid, and uncomfortable, as in "a sultry afternoon." Of a person, attractive in a way that suggests passion and sexual desire, as in "a sultry voice."
To add numbers together; usually "sum up": to give a brief summary of the main points ("To sum up, we need more time").

When someone is described as a summa cum laude graduate, or when a degree is awarded summa cum laude, it means that person achieved the absolute highest level of academic excellence possible at their institution.
Summarily means: quickly and without going through the usual steps, procedures, or formalities.
To summarize means to take a large piece of information — a long text, a speech, an event, a discussion — and restate only its most important points in a much shorter form, leaving out the details.
When "summary" is used as an adjective, it describes an action that is carried out immediately, without going through the usual steps, formalities, or procedures that are normally required.

A summary is a short, condensed version of something longer — whether that "something" is a book, an article, a speech, a meeting, an event, or even a situation. It captures only the most important points and leaves out everything that is less essential.
Summation means the act of bringing many things together into one complete whole — either by adding numbers, or by pulling together ideas, points, or facts.
A meeting between the leaders of two or more countries, as in "a summit in Geneva." Literally, the highest point of a mountain or hill. Figuratively, the highest level of achievement.

To summon means to officially and authoritatively call someone — or something — to come to you, or to do something. It is not a casual call between equals. It carries a clear sense of power, authority, and expectation that the call will be obeyed.

A summons is an official, authoritative order that requires someone to appear somewhere or respond to something — and because it comes from someone with power or authority, it is not optional. You cannot simply ignore it without facing consequences.

The adjective sumptuary describes something — almost always a law, rule, or regulation — that is designed to control or limit how much people spend on personal luxuries such as clothing, food, parties, or other signs of wealth and extravagance.

When you call something sumptuous, you are saying it is deeply, impressively luxurious — in a way that feels lavish, indulgent, and pleasing to the senses. It is not just expensive. It is gloriously expensive. It is not just beautiful.
To sunder means to forcefully split, tear apart, or violently separate something into parts — or to forcefully separate two things that were connected or united.

When you use "sundry" as an adjective, it means various, several, and of different kinds. It describes a group of things that are diverse and mixed — things that don't all belong to one neat category, but are being mentioned or grouped together anyway.
