To relax after a period of work or stress. Literally, to undo something that has been wound or twisted, as in "unwinding a ball of yarn."
"Unwitting" describes a person who is involved in something — or does something — without knowing what is really happening, or without realizing the true nature or consequences of their actions.
Unwittingly means doing something without realizing what you are truly doing, or without understanding the real nature, significance, or consequences of your action — at the time you do it.
"Unwonted" means not customary, not habitual, or out of character for a particular person or situation.
Firm and determined, not giving way to pressure or persuasion, as in "unyielding opposition." Of a material, hard and not bending.
To release animals, such as oxen, from a yoke. Figuratively, to set someone free from a burden or restriction.
When something is "up in the air," it means it is uncertain, undecided, or unresolved. Nobody knows yet what will happen. No final answer or decision has been made.

"Up to one's neck" means being deeply, overwhelmingly involved in something — usually a difficult, stressful, or unpleasant situation. It describes a state where you are so buried in something that you can barely manage.
Upbeat means cheerful, positive, optimistic, and full of hope or energy. When someone or something is upbeat, they have a "things are good — or going to be good" kind of feeling about them.

To upbraid someone means to scold them harshly and openly for something they did wrong. When you upbraid a person, you express strong disapproval of their behaviour, words, or failure to act — often in a serious, direct, and forceful way.
Upbringing is the way a child is raised — everything that parents, family members, or guardians do to shape a child as they grow up.

To upend something means to turn it completely upside down — either in a real, physical sense, or in a deeper, more powerful sense: to completely overthrow, disrupt, or overturn something so that it no longer functions or exists the way it used to.
To upgrade something means to move it from a lower level to a higher one — to replace or change it so that it becomes better, more capable, more powerful, or of higher quality than it was before.
An upheaval is a sudden, large, and disruptive change that throws things into disorder — turning what was stable and normal completely upside down.

To upheave something means to lift it up or push it upward with great, forceful energy from below. Think of it as a powerful, violent rising — not a gentle lift, but something being thrust or shoved upward by a strong force underneath it.
An uphill battle is something that is very difficult to do, especially because you are working against strong opposition, unfavorable conditions, or a situation that keeps working against you.

To uphold something means to actively support, defend, or maintain it so that it remains standing, valid, and respected — especially when it is being challenged, questioned, or at risk of being ignored.

To upholster means to cover a piece of furniture — typically a seat like a chair, sofa, or bench — with soft padding and a protective outer material (such as fabric or leather), making it both comfortable to sit on and attractive to look at.
Upholstery is the soft, padded covering that is fitted onto furniture to make it comfortable and visually appealing.
Upkeep means the ongoing work, effort, and money needed to keep something in good condition over time.
An upland is a piece of land that sits higher than the land around it, but is not so tall or steep that you would call it a mountain.

"Uplift" as a noun refers to a raising or elevation of something — whether that "something" is a physical object, a person's mood, a group's quality of life, or even someone's ability to do something.
To uplift means to raise something or someone to a higher state — whether that "higher state" is emotional, moral, social, or physical. Think of it as the opposite of dragging something down.

When someone calls a person "uppity," they're saying that person is acting too bold, too confident, or too assertive for someone of their social position. In other words: "You're behaving as if you're more important or powerful than you actually are.
When something or someone is upright, they are positioned straight up and down — perfectly vertical, not leaning, not tilted, and not lying flat.

An uprising is when a large group of ordinary people collectively stand up and actively resist or fight against those who hold power over them — most often a government, a ruler, an occupying force, or an oppressive system.

An uproar is a situation where a large number of people react very loudly, angrily, or with great shock to something — all at once. It carries a sense of things erupting, boiling over, spinning out of control.
"Uproarious" is an adjective that describes something so intensely loud, wild, or funny that it creates — or feels like it's about to create — complete chaos from sheer energy.
To uproot something means to pull it out forcefully from where it is firmly fixed or deeply embedded — leaving it completely displaced and disconnected from the place it was anchored to.
When you describe something as upscale, you're saying it belongs to a higher, fancier tier — noticeably better, more refined, and more expensive than what is ordinary or average.
Unhappy, disappointed, or worried, as in "she was upset by the news." An upset stomach is a slight illness of the stomach.

Upset means to disturb something that was in a stable, calm, or ordered state — whether that something is a person's feelings, a physical object, a plan, a stomach, or a competition. Imagine a neat stack of books sitting perfectly on a table.
Upshot means the final result or outcome of something — especially after a series of events, discussions, arguments, or complicated steps have played out.
To upstage someone means to draw attention away from them and onto yourself — making them look less important, less impressive, or less noticeable, while you shine more brightly.
When you describe a person as upstanding, you are saying that they are honest, morally good, and genuinely worthy of respect. It is always a compliment, and a strong one.

An upstart is a person who has risen quickly from a low or humble position to a higher one — in wealth, power, fame, or social status — but who is seen by others as not truly deserving that position, or as acting with too much confidence and boldness for someone who only just "arrived."

An upswing is a period of noticeable improvement or increase in something — a phase where things start moving in a clearly positive direction, especially after being low, slow, or difficult. It is not just a single good moment.

"Upsy daisy!" is something you say out loud at the exact moment when you lift someone up, or when you help someone rise after a fall. It is a cheerful, warm, encouraging little exclamation — a vocal sound that accompanies the physical action of going upward.

Uptake means the act of taking something in, absorbing it, or making use of it. Think of it as the process of something being "received" — whether by a body, a cell, a plant, or even a group of people.

When someone is uptight, they are too tense, too serious, or too rigid — and because of this, they cannot relax, enjoy themselves, or go with the flow. The word almost always carries a slightly negative or critical tone.
When "upward" is used as an adjective, it means directed toward, moving toward, or tending toward a higher place, level, or position.

Urban means relating to, found in, or characteristic of a city or town. When you use the word "urban" to describe something, you are saying that it belongs to, exists within, or is typical of a city environment.
Urbane describes someone who is smoothly sophisticated, refined, and socially graceful in a way that feels effortless and natural.
Urbanity is the quality of being polished, refined, and graciously smooth in the way you behave and interact with people — especially in social situations.
Urbanization is the process by which a growing share of people in a society come to live in cities and towns, and by which those cities and towns grow larger, denser, and more complex over time.

The most common everyday use of "urchin" refers to a child — usually a small boy — who is scruffy, poorly dressed, and often up to some mischief. The word carries a sense of the child being a little wild, cheeky, or hard to control.
An urge is a strong feeling that rises from inside you and pushes you toward doing something. It is not a calm thought or a carefully made decision.
When you urge someone to do something, you are strongly and earnestly encouraging them to do it.

Urgency is the quality of something that makes it demand immediate attention or action — because it is both important and time-sensitive. When a situation has urgency, it is essentially telling you: "This cannot wait. Deal with it now."

Something is urgent when it requires immediate attention or action — it simply cannot wait. If you delay dealing with it, something bad happens: a deadline passes, harm occurs, an opportunity is lost, or a situation gets significantly worse.

An urn is a container — but not just any container. It has a specific, recognizable shape and carries a sense of formality, ceremony, or importance. Think of it as a dignified, purposeful vessel, as opposed to a plain bucket or box.
Ursine means of, relating to, or resembling a bear.

Usage means the way something is used, or the act and habit of using it. Think of "usage" as "use" with more weight — it usually points to a pattern, a practice, or a convention, not just one single act.
An usher is a person whose role is to guide, direct, or escort other people — usually at a formal event, an official venue, or an institution. They are not in charge of the event itself.

To usher means to guide or lead someone somewhere — but not in a casual, pointing-the-way kind of manner. It implies doing so in a careful, deliberate, and often formal or respectful way, usually by physically accompanying the person.
That arrangement — your right to use something you don't own, and to benefit from it, as long as you don't destroy or fundamentally alter it — is the essence of usufruct.
A usurer is a person who lends money to others and charges them back an outrageously high — and often illegal — rate of interest in return.
Charging extremely high and unfair rates of interest on loans, as in "usurious lenders."
To usurp something means to take power, a position, or a right that does not belong to you — usually by force, by trickery, or simply by pushing the rightful person aside.

Usurpation means the act of seizing power, authority, a position, or a right that does not rightfully belong to you — doing so without legal permission, without being chosen, and often by force, trickery, or sheer boldness.
A usurper is a person who takes power, a position, or a right that does not belong to them — by force, trickery, or simply acting as though they have authority they were never given.

Usury is the practice of lending money and charging the borrower an unreasonably high rate of interest — interest so excessive that it is exploitative, meaning it unfairly takes advantage of the person who borrowed the money.

A utensil is a simple, handheld tool that helps you do a practical task, most commonly in the kitchen. The key word here is practical — a utensil exists purely to make a job easier, faster, or more effective.
Utilitarian means focused on being useful and practical, rather than on being beautiful, fancy, or pleasing. Something utilitarian exists to do a job — nothing more, nothing less.
Utilitarianism is the philosophical belief that the right action is the one that produces the greatest good for the greatest number of people. That's the compass.
Utility means usefulness — the quality of something that makes it capable of serving a purpose, satisfying a need, or providing a benefit to someone.
To utilize something means to make practical, purposeful use of it — to put it to work in a way that gets real value out of it.

Utmost means of the greatest possible degree, amount, or level. When you describe something as "utmost," you are saying it has reached the absolute ceiling — the highest point that can possibly exist.

A utopia is an imagined place or society that is perfect in every way — where people live in complete happiness, justice, equality, and harmony. There is no poverty, no war, no crime, no suffering, and no corruption.

Utopian describes something that imagines, proposes, or relates to a perfectly ideal world — a flawless society where all human problems are solved, everyone is happy, there is no suffering, no injustice, no poverty, and no conflict.

"Utter" means complete, total, and absolute — to the fullest possible degree, with zero exceptions and no room for anything in between. When you describe something as "utter," you are saying it is 100% that thing. Not mostly. Not almost. Entirely.

To utter means to produce a sound, word, or words from your mouth. It is the act of giving voice to something — taking something from inside you (a thought, a feeling, a sound) and releasing it out loud through your voice.
An utterance is anything a person says out loud — a word, a phrase, a sentence, or even a sound — treated as a single, complete act of speaking.
"Utterly" is an adverb. Its job is to mean completely, totally, or to the absolute fullest possible degree — with zero exceptions and zero room for doubt.
Uttermost means the absolute greatest, highest, or farthest point possible — with nothing beyond it.

Uxorial means "of, relating to, or characteristic of a wife." Whenever something is described as uxorial, it belongs to, comes from, or is typical of a wife — her role, her behavior, her feelings, or her position within a marriage.
Uxorious describes a husband who is excessively devoted, submissive, or indulgent toward his wife — so much so that it becomes a weakness or a flaw.
A vacancy is an empty space, position, or slot that is available to be filled.
"Vacant" means not occupied — it describes a space, a position, or even a person's expression that has nothing or no one in it, or that shows no thought or feeling at all.

"Vacate" means to leave something and make it empty or available. Whether it's a physical place, a job position, or a legal ruling — when someone vacates something, they move out of it, give it up, or clear it away.

To vaccinate someone means to put a special substance called a vaccine into their body — almost always through a needle (an injection/shot) — so that their body learns how to fight a specific disease before they ever actually get it.

Vaccination is the act of giving a person (or animal) a vaccine — a specially prepared substance — to protect them from a specific disease. The goal is to make the body ready to fight that disease before it ever actually encounters it.

To vacillate means to go back and forth between two or more choices, opinions, or positions — again and again — without being able to settle on one. It describes a kind of restless, repeated indecision.
Vacillation is the act of going back and forth between two or more choices, opinions, or positions — again and again — without being able to settle on one and stick with it.
Vacuity means emptiness — but not just any ordinary emptiness. It is a very specific, deliberate kind of emptiness: the absence of meaningful content, thought, intelligence, or substance.
Showing a lack of intelligence, thought, or meaning, as in "a vacuous smile" or "vacuous chatter."

The word vacuously comes from "vacuous," which means empty or hollow. So when you do something vacuously, you do it in an empty, hollow, or meaningless way — it looks like it counts, but there's nothing of real substance behind it.

A vacuum is a space that has been emptied — a place where the usual content (most importantly, air or any other matter) is completely or partially absent. Think of it as a "nothing space" deliberately created within a "something world."
A vade mecum is a small, portable book or guide that a person finds so useful and so frequently needed that they carry it with them everywhere.
A vagabond is a person who has no fixed home and wanders from place to place, often with no steady job, no clear destination, and no plan to settle down.

Vagarious means unpredictably changeable, erratic, and wandering — without a fixed or consistent pattern. When something or someone is vagarious, their behavior, movement, or nature shifts in ways that are hard to anticipate or follow.
A vagary is an unpredictable, erratic change or occurrence — something that happens without following any clear rule, logic, or pattern, and therefore cannot easily be anticipated.
Vagrancy is the state of wandering from place to place with no home and no job or money to live on.

Vagrant means wandering without a fixed home, a clear purpose, or a settled direction. Think of a leaf blown by the wind — it has no destination, no roots holding it, and no predictable path. That leaf is behaving in a vagrant way.
A vagrant is a person who has no permanent home and wanders from place to place, typically with no steady job, no reliable income, and no fixed community to belong to.
Vague means not clear, not specific, and not precise enough to be fully understood or pinned down.
Vaguely means in a way that is unclear, imprecise, or not fully formed. When something happens vaguely, it lacks sharpness, definition, or detail — like a shape you can barely make out through fog.

Vagueness is the quality of being unclear, imprecise, or lacking definite boundaries. When something has vagueness, it doesn't give you a sharp, clear picture — it leaves things open, fuzzy, or undefined.
A vain person is someone who thinks too highly of themselves — particularly about how they look, how talented they are, or how important they are. It goes beyond normal confidence.

Vainglorious describes a person who is excessively proud of their own achievements or abilities — and, crucially, cannot stop showing it off. It's not just about thinking highly of yourself privately. A vainglorious person performs their pride.
Vainglory is an excessive, hollow pride in yourself and your achievements, combined with a burning desire to show that pride off and be admired for it by others.

A valance is a short, decorative strip of fabric — or sometimes wood or metal — that is attached along the top edge of something (usually a window or a bed) to make it look neat and attractive, and to hide things that aren't meant to be seen, like rods, rails, or frames.
A vale is a valley — a low-lying stretch of land that sits between hills or areas of higher ground, usually with a river or stream running gently through it.
A valediction is a farewell — but not just any casual goodbye. It is the formal, deliberate, often deeply felt act of saying goodbye, or the actual words spoken or written to do so.
A valedictorian is the student who graduates with the highest academic rank in their entire class.

If something is valedictory, it is related to, or has the character of, a farewell — specifically a formal, intentional, and often emotionally significant goodbye that marks the end of something important.

A valedictory is a farewell speech — but not just any goodbye. It is a formal, carefully prepared address delivered at an important occasion to mark the end of a significant chapter in people's lives.
A man's personal servant who looks after his clothes; or a worker who parks guests' cars at a hotel or restaurant.
A valetudinarian is a person who is excessively and obsessively preoccupied with their own health — someone who makes their physical well-being the central, defining focus of their entire life.
Valiant means showing great courage and determination, especially when facing something difficult, dangerous, or overwhelming — and choosing to push forward anyway, without giving up.
When someone does something valiantly, they do it with great courage, determination, and strength — especially when the situation is difficult, dangerous, or when they are likely to fail or suffer.

Valid means genuinely acceptable, well-grounded, and able to withstand scrutiny. When something is valid, it meets the required standard — it holds up when examined closely. It cannot be rightfully dismissed or ignored.
To validate something means to confirm that it is true, correct, legitimate, or acceptable — either by checking it against a standard, proving it with evidence, or officially approving it.

A valise is a small bag used for carrying personal belongings — clothes, toiletries, and other essentials — when you travel. Think of it as a compact, hand-held travel bag, somewhere between a handbag and a small suitcase.

A valley is a low, stretched area of land that sits between higher pieces of land — such as hills, mountains, or cliffs — on its sides. Think of it as a natural "dip" or "hollow" in the Earth's surface, like the space between two bumps.
Valor means exceptional courage — specifically the kind of courage shown in the face of serious danger, most often in battle or life-threatening situations. It's not just being brave.
To valorize something means to deliberately give it value, worth, or importance — or to raise its value. The key word here is deliberately. It's not about something naturally being valuable.
Valorous means showing great courage and bravery, especially when facing danger, difficulty, or fear.
A valuation is an answer to the question: "What is this worth?"
To vamoose means to leave a place quickly and suddenly — to get out, take off, or depart in a hurry. It's not just any kind of leaving.

A woman who uses her sexual attractiveness to manipulate men. In music, a vamp is a short, repeated passage played as an introduction or until a singer is ready. It is also the upper front part of a shoe.

A vampire is a creature that takes life from others to sustain its own. That idea — feeding off the living, never dying — sits at the heart of every use of this word, whether in ancient folklore, modern fiction, or everyday speech.
A vandal is a person who deliberately damages or destroys property that does not belong to them — especially public property or someone else's belongings — for no good or constructive reason.
Vandalism is the deliberate act of damaging, destroying, or defacing someone else's property — without the owner's permission — for no productive or justifiable reason.

To vandalize something means to deliberately damage or destroy property that belongs to someone else, or that belongs to the public — not for any practical gain, but simply to damage it, often out of anger, carelessness, or a desire to cause trouble.
The vanguard is whoever or whatever is at the front, leading the way into new or challenging ground.
To vanish means to disappear suddenly and completely — in a way that often feels surprising, mysterious, or difficult to explain.
At its most common, vanity is the feeling of being too pleased with yourself — particularly with how you look, but also with your talents, status, or achievements.
To vanquish someone or something means to defeat them completely and decisively — leaving absolutely no doubt about the outcome. It is not a close win. It is not just barely coming out ahead.
Vantage means a position that gives you a superior view or a better understanding of something compared to other positions.
A vantage point is a position — either a physical place or a mental standpoint — from which you observe, examine, or understand something.
Vapid means empty of real substance, thought, or life. When something or someone is vapid, they offer nothing meaningful, stimulating, or interesting.

Vapidity is the quality of being completely empty of real meaning, depth, or substance. It describes a kind of hollow dullness — the state of something (or someone) that looks like it has content but actually has nothing worthwhile inside it.
Vapor is a substance in gas form — but it's a very specific kind of gas. It's the gas form of something that is normally a liquid or a solid at everyday temperatures.
To vaporize means to turn into vapor (gas) — or to cause something to turn into vapor. Vapor is the gas form of a substance that is normally a liquid or solid at room temperature.
Vague, insubstantial, or fanciful, as in "vaporous ideas." Literally, full of or like vapour, mist, or steam.
A vaquero is a skilled horseman and cattle herder from the Spanish and Latin American ranching tradition — essentially, the original cowboy of the Americas.

Variance means a difference, a gap, or a degree of disagreement between two or more things — specifically, how much something varies (departs or differs) from what is expected, standard, or agreed upon.
A variant is a version of something that is mostly the same as an original or standard form, but differs in at least one specific way.
A variation is a difference from something that is considered standard, original, usual, or expected.
A swollen, twisted vein just under the skin, usually in the legs, caused by weak valves that let blood pool.
When you describe something as varied, you are saying it contains many different types, kinds, or forms within it. It is not all the same. It is not repetitive. It has real range and diversity.
To variegate something means to make it varied in appearance by giving it patches, streaks, spots, or areas of different colors or markings.
Variegated means marked by patches, streaks, or spots of different colors in an irregular, natural-looking way — or, more broadly, having a rich and interesting variety of different things.
Variegation is the quality or state of having two or more distinct colors appearing together on a single surface or organism — typically in the form of patches, streaks, spots, blotches, or bands.
A varmint is a wild creature — usually a small or medium-sized animal — that people consider a nuisance, a pest, or a threat.
Varnish is a clear or slightly amber-colored liquid that you paint onto surfaces — most commonly wood — to protect them and make them look polished and shiny.

When you varnish something, you apply a liquid substance called varnish onto a surface — typically wood, metal, or a painting. This liquid dries and hardens into a thin, clear, glass-like protective layer sitting on top of the surface.
Vary means to be different — either across different situations, different things, or different points in time — or to deliberately make something different.
Vascular is an adjective that means "relating to, made of, or involving vessels that carry fluid through a living body."

A vassal is a person who is formally under the power and authority of someone more powerful than them, and who has pledged loyalty and service to that more powerful person — in return for protection and land.

Vassalage is the word for a relationship of dependence and submission between a weaker party and a more powerful one — where the weaker party gives loyalty, service, and obedience in exchange for protection or land.

Vast means extremely large in size, area, amount, or degree — so large that it is difficult to fully take in or imagine. It is not just "big." Something vast is big in a way that feels overwhelming, almost beyond easy comprehension.
A vat is a large container designed to hold liquids — think of something much bigger than a bucket or a pot, often the size of a small room, and typically open at the top or wide-mouthed.
Vatic means having the quality of a prophet or prophecy.

To vaticinate means to prophesy — to declare or announce what will happen in the future, but with the solemn, weighty authority of a prophet or oracle. Not a casual guess. Not an informed estimate. A proclamation.

A vaticination is a prophecy — a statement that claims to reveal or predict what will happen in the future, often delivered with a sense of deep authority, solemnity, or as if inspired by some higher power or mysterious insight.
Vaudeville is a style of live theatrical entertainment that was enormously popular in the United States and Canada from roughly the 1880s to the 1930s.

When "vaulting" is used as an adjective, it describes an ambition, desire, or aspiration that is so extreme, so aggressively overreaching, that it goes well beyond what is reasonable or even safely achievable.
To vaunt something means to boast or brag about it in an excessively proud way — to talk it up loudly, showily, and with more pride than most people around you think is warranted.
In maths and physics, a quantity that has both size and direction, such as velocity or force. In biology, a vector is an organism, such as a mosquito, that carries disease from one host to another.
To veer means to suddenly change direction — to shift away from the path, course, or direction you were on before.
When something is described as vegan, it means it involves no animal products whatsoever — not in its ingredients, not in its making, and not in what it comes from.
A vegetarian is a person who does not eat the flesh of any animal. This means they avoid beef, pork, chicken, lamb, fish, shrimp, and the meat of any other creature.
To vegetate means to live or spend time in a way that is dull, inactive, and mentally empty — doing very little, thinking very little, and barely engaging with life.

Vehemence is the quality of being extremely forceful, passionate, and intense — especially in the way someone feels, speaks, or acts. It describes an energy that is so strong it almost feels like it cannot be contained or held back. It bursts out.
Vehement describes something expressed or done with intense, forceful emotion and strong conviction — not quietly, not mildly, but with unmistakable passion and energy.
Vehemently means with great force, intense emotion, and strong conviction — in a way that is energetic, passionate, and hard to ignore.

A veil is something that covers or hides — but not completely. This is the most important thing to understand about the word. A veil doesn't block something out entirely like a wall does. It softens it, obscures it, makes it unclear or mysterious.
A vein is a narrow channel, strip, or thread that runs through something larger — like a line running through a bigger body, usually carrying something or marking a distinct quality.
To mark something with lines like veins, as in marble or a leaf.

Velleity is a wish so faint and weak that it never leads to any action — and deep down, you never really expect it to. It sits at the absolute lowest end of wanting something. It's not quite a desire. It's barely even a wish.

Vellum is a very fine, smooth writing material made from animal skin — most commonly the skin of a calf, though the skin of lambs, kids (young goats), or other young animals was sometimes used. It is not paper, and it is not leather.
Velocity means the speed at which something moves in a specific direction.
Velvety means: having the smooth, soft, rich, and deeply pleasing qualities that remind you of velvet. It is always a compliment. It carries a sense of luxury, depth, and refinement.

Venal means willing to act dishonestly or corruptly in exchange for money or personal gain. When you call someone or something venal, you are saying that their honesty, decisions, or loyalty can be bought. They don't act on principle — they act on payment.

Venality is the quality of being willing to use your power, position, or duties dishonestly in exchange for money or personal gain. It is the condition of being corruptible — of having a price tag on your integrity.

To vend means to sell something, particularly by offering it to people in a public setting. Think of someone standing at a stall, a cart, or a booth and handing products to customers in exchange for money.
A vendetta is a long-running, deeply personal campaign of revenge that one person — or one group of people — carries out against another. It is not a single act of revenge.
A vendor is a person or a company that sells something — goods, services, or both.
A veneer is a thin layer placed on top of something to make it look better than it really is.
Venerable means deserving of deep respect and admiration, usually because of great age, long history, wisdom, or a distinguished and honorable character.

To venerate someone or something means to regard them with the deepest possible respect — a kind of respect so profound that it borders on worship. It goes far beyond the everyday respect you might show a colleague or a teacher.

Veneration is a feeling of very deep, almost sacred respect for someone or something. It's not just ordinary respect — it is respect raised to its highest, most intense form. Think of it as a mix of profound admiration, awe, and reverence all rolled into one.
Vengeance means the act of harming or punishing someone because they harmed you first — or because they harmed someone you deeply care about.
Vengeful describes a person (or sometimes a group, a god, or even a force of nature) who has a strong, burning desire to get back at someone who hurt them.
Venial means minor, pardonable, and easily forgiven.

Venomous describes a living creature that produces a toxic substance called venom inside its body — and is capable of actively delivering that venom into another creature's body, typically through a bite, sting, or scratch.

A vent is an opening — a hole, gap, or passage — through which something can pass through or escape. That "something" is usually air, gas, smoke, liquid, or even emotion. The opening exists on purpose: it is there to allow or control that movement.

When you vent, you release built-up feelings — usually anger, frustration, stress, or irritation — by talking, complaining, or sometimes yelling. The key idea is that these feelings had been bottled up inside you, and now you're letting them out.

When you ventilate a place, you cause fresh air to flow into and through it, pushing out the stale, stuffy, or polluted air that was trapped inside. The key idea is exchange and circulation — air must come in and go out.
"Ventral" describes the belly side or front/underside of a body or body part. It is the side that, in many animals, faces toward the ground — the soft, exposed underbelly.
A ventricle is a small, hollow chamber or cavity inside a body organ — a space that is built to hold fluid and, in many cases, to actively pump it somewhere.
Ventriloquism is the skill of speaking in a way that makes your voice seem to come from somewhere — or something — other than your own mouth.

A ventriloquist is a performer who can speak — or more precisely, produce the sounds of speech — while keeping their own mouth almost completely still and closed, so that their voice appears to be coming from somewhere else, usually from a puppet or a doll they are holding.
To dare to go somewhere or do something risky or unfamiliar, as in "venture out into the storm." It can also mean to cautiously say something, as in "venture an opinion."

If someone is venturesome, they are willing to take risks and try new, uncertain, or challenging things — especially when the outcome is not guaranteed. They don't let fear of failure, danger, or the unknown stop them.

Venturous describes someone who is willing to take risks and face the unknown — especially in pursuit of something exciting, new, or worthwhile — without being held back by fear, caution, or uncertainty.
A venue is the specific place where a particular event or activity takes place — or is planned to take place.
Veracious simply means truthful. When you call someone or something veracious, you are saying that they consistently tell the truth, deal in facts, and do not deceive.
Veracity means the quality of being truthful or accurate. It describes truthfulness — either as a character trait in a person, or as a property of information, claims, or statements.
A veranda is a covered outdoor platform attached to the outside of a building. Think of it as a large, sheltered walkway or sitting area that hugs the exterior wall of a house or other structure.
To verbalize something means to put it into words — to take something that exists inside your mind (a thought, a feeling, an experience, an idea) and express it through spoken or written language.

When something is described as verbatim, it means it is an exact, word-for-word copy of an original piece of spoken or written content — every single word preserved, in the exact same order, with nothing added, removed, or changed.

When you do something verbatim, you reproduce, repeat, or report something using the exact same words as the original — every single word, in the exact same order, with nothing added, nothing removed, and nothing changed.
Verbiage means an excessive amount of words — using far more words than necessary to say something that could be expressed simply and clearly. Think of it as verbal clutter or linguistic waste.
Verbose means using far more words than are actually needed to express something.
Verbosity is the quality of using far more words than are needed to express something. It is the state of being wordy, long-winded, or unnecessarily drawn out in speech or writing.

"Verboten" is an adjective meaning strictly forbidden — something that is absolutely not allowed, usually because an authority, a rule, or a powerful unwritten social expectation has drawn a firm, uncrossable line around it.
Verdancy is a noun that means the quality or state of being lush, fresh, and richly green — specifically as seen in living plant life, nature, and landscapes.

Verdant means richly and freshly green with living, thriving plant life. It describes a place — almost always a landscape or a stretch of land — that is so covered with healthy, growing vegetation that green is the overwhelming impression it gives you.

A verdict is a final, considered decision or judgment that someone reaches — or a group reaches — after carefully weighing evidence, facts, or experience. The key word here is final. A verdict isn't a gut reaction or a passing thought.
Verdigris is the blue-green or greenish coating that naturally forms on the surface of copper and copper-containing metals like brass and bronze, when they are exposed to air and moisture over time.

Verdure means the lush, fresh greenness of living plants and vegetation. Picture a meadow bursting with green grass on a spring morning, or a dense forest with its thick canopy of leaves glowing in the summer sun.

Verge means an edge, border, or the very limit of something — the thin line where one thing ends and another begins. Think of it as the last possible point before something changes, starts, or crosses over.
When something verges on something else, it means it is so close to that thing that it's almost crossing the line into it — but hasn't quite.
Veridical means corresponding to reality — truthful, accurate, and genuinely reflecting what actually exists or what actually happened, rather than being imagined, distorted, or false.
Verifiable means: capable of being checked, confirmed, or proven to be true.
To verify something means to check and confirm that it is true, accurate, or correct.

"Verily" means truly, certainly, or in truth. When someone uses this word, they are making a firm, confident assertion — essentially saying, "What I am about to say (or what I just said) is absolutely true. No doubt about it."
Something is verisimilar if it appears to be true or seems like it could be real — even if it hasn't been proven to actually be true or real.
Verisimilitude means the quality of seeming real, true, or believable — even if something is not actually real or true.
Veritable means truly being what it is called — completely, without exaggeration, and in every sense of the word.
A verity is a truth — but a very specific kind of truth. It is a truth that is deep, fundamental, and lasting.

Verklempt is an adjective that describes being so overwhelmed by emotion that you become momentarily speechless — choked up, throat tight, eyes welling up, teetering right on the edge of tears but not quite crying.

"Vermicular" means worm-like. Everything this word describes traces back to the image of a worm — its shape, its movement, and the marks it leaves. It can also refer directly to something caused by or relating to worms.

When you call something vermilion, you are describing its color. Specifically, it means a bright, vivid red that leans slightly toward orange — not a pale red, not a dark red, but a bold, warm, eye-catching red with just a hint of orange warmth baked into it.
As a noun, vermilion refers to two closely connected things: a specific color, and the pigment (a coloring substance) that produces that color.

Vermin refers to animals — and sometimes insects or parasites — that humans consider harmful, dangerous, or unwanted because they cause damage, spread disease, destroy food or property, or are simply very difficult to control or get rid of.

When you call something vernacular, you mean it belongs to ordinary, everyday people in a specific place — it is local, native, and natural, rather than formal, official, or imported from somewhere else.

Vernacular refers to the natural, everyday language that ordinary people in a particular place or group actually use in real life — as opposed to a formal, official, or "proper" version of a language.

Vernal simply means of, relating to, or characteristic of spring. When you see or use the word "vernal," it is pointing to something that belongs to spring, happens during spring, or shares the qualities that we associate with the spring season.
A vernissage is an exclusive, invitation-only preview event held at an art gallery or museum, just before an exhibition opens to the general public.
Able to do many different things well, or able to be used in many different ways.
Versatility is the quality of being able to do many different kinds of things well, or the ability to be used in many different ways.
Writing arranged in lines with a rhythm, as in poetry. A verse is also a group of lines forming a section of a poem or song, or one of the numbered sections of a chapter in the Bible.
When someone is versed in something, it means they have a deep, solid level of knowledge and experience in that particular subject or area.
To versify means to write something in the form of verse — that is, in the structured, rhythmic lines that make up poetry.
A version is one specific form of something — where that thing exists (or could exist) in more than one form.
The left-hand page of an open book, or the back side of a sheet of paper. The opposite is the "recto," the right-hand page.
When you describe something as vertebrate, you are saying that it has a backbone — a column of bones running along the inside of its back.
The point where two or more lines meet to form an angle, as in the corners of a triangle. In general use, the highest point or peak of something.
Extremely high or steep, causing a feeling of dizziness, as in "vertiginous cliffs." It can also mean feeling dizzy, or changing so quickly that it is bewildering.

Vertigo is a false sensation of spinning or movement — a trick your brain plays on you, making you feel like either you or the world around you is rotating, tilting, or swaying when, in reality, nothing is actually moving.
Verve is the noun for a kind of energy that is not just strong, but inspired and exciting. It is the force of enthusiasm meeting skill, producing something that feels vivid and alive.
Vesper means evening. It is a word that belongs to the quiet, fading part of the day — the time after the sun has gone down but before the world is fully dark.

Something is vespertine if it belongs to, happens during, or is associated with the evening — specifically the stretch of time around dusk, when daylight fades but true darkness hasn't fully arrived yet.
A vessel is something that holds, carries, or channels something else. Think of it as a container or a passage.

When you call something or someone vestal, you mean they are pure, chaste, and sacred — particularly in the sense of being wholly devoted, untouched, and morally spotless, like a person who has consecrated themselves to a higher cause and guarded their body and character accordingly.

Vested means firmly established, fully granted, and belonging to someone in a way that cannot easily be taken away or made conditional. Think of it as the opposite of "tentative" or "provisional." When something is vested, it is locked in.
A small entrance hall or lobby just inside the front door of a building. In anatomy, a vestibule is a chamber at the entrance to another, such as part of the inner ear.
A vestige is a small, faint trace or remnant of something that once existed fully but has since mostly disappeared, faded away, or stopped functioning as it used to.

Vestigial describes something that is a leftover trace of something that once existed and had a purpose, but has since lost that purpose (or most of it) over time — yet still physically remains. It didn't disappear completely.
A vestment is a special, ceremonial garment worn by a member of the clergy (such as a priest, bishop, deacon, or minister) during a religious service or sacred ritual.
A doctor who treats animals; a veterinary surgeon. In American English, a vet is also a veteran, especially of the armed forces.

To vet something or someone means to carefully examine and investigate them — checking their background, history, claims, or suitability — before deciding whether to trust, approve, use, or accept them.

When "veteran" is used as an adjective, it describes a person who has spent a long time doing something and, as a result, has become deeply experienced, highly capable, and battle-tested in that area.
A veteran is someone who has a lot of real experience in something — usually gained over a long period of time, and often in tough or demanding conditions.
A veterinarian is a trained medical doctor — but for animals, not humans. Just as a doctor examines, diagnoses, and treats sick or injured people, a veterinarian does the same for animals.

The adjective veterinary means relating to the medical care, health, and treatment of animals. Whenever you see this word, it is simply telling you: "this thing belongs to, or is connected with, the world of animal medicine."
A veto is an official power or act of saying "No — this will not happen" in a way that is strong enough to stop or block a decision, even if everyone else agrees to it.
When you veto something, you officially and authoritatively reject or block a decision, plan, or law — stopping it from happening — even if other people have already agreed to it or voted for it.
To annoy, frustrate, or worry someone, especially over trivial matters, as in "the delays vexed him." A vexed question is one that is difficult and much debated.
Vexation means a feeling of irritation, frustration, and inner disturbance — usually caused by something that is persistently annoying, difficult to fix, or beyond your control.

Vexatious means causing persistent annoyance, frustration, or distress — usually in a way that feels unnecessary, unreasonable, or hard to escape. If something is vexatious, it doesn't just bother you once and go away.
Annoyed, frustrated or worried; or (of a question) hotly debated and difficult ("a vexed issue").
Vexing describes something that causes a feeling of persistent annoyance, frustration, or worry — especially when that thing is difficult to deal with, solve, or make sense of.
Viable means capable of working, surviving, or succeeding in the real world — not just in theory, but in actual practice.

A viaduct is a long, elevated, bridge-like structure made up of a row of arches or spans, each one supported by tall columns or pillars, built to carry a road or railway across a valley, a stretch of low ground, or uneven terrain.

A vial is a small container — usually made of glass or clear plastic — designed to hold a small amount of liquid, powder, or other substance. Think of it as a tiny bottle built for precision and care, not for everyday drinking or storage.

A viand is simply an item of food — one single dish or food preparation, especially one that is considered fine, choice, or delicious. Think of it as a formal, elevated way to refer to a particular food that is served or eaten.

Vibrant means full of strong, lively energy that you can almost feel. When something is vibrant, it doesn't just exist quietly — it pulses, it stands out, it feels powerfully alive. Think of the difference between a candle flame and a bonfire.

Vibrato is a musical effect where a held note doesn't stay at a perfectly fixed pitch — instead, the pitch wobbles slightly and rapidly above and below the intended note, over and over, in a steady, controlled rhythm.

"Vicar" means a person who acts as a representative or substitute for a higher authority. Think of a vicar as an official stand-in: someone doing the work and carrying the responsibilities of a greater power, on that power's behalf.
Feeling, enjoying, or experiencing something through another person rather than doing or experiencing it yourself.
When you experience something vicariously, you are not the one actually doing or going through it — but you experience the feelings of it through someone else who is.

A vice is a bad habit, a moral weakness, or a form of behavior that is considered wrong, harmful, or shameful — especially one that a person keeps repeating because they find it pleasurable or hard to resist.
"Vice versa" means "with the two things reversed" — the other way around, or with the roles swapped.

A viceroy is a person who is appointed by a king, queen, or emperor to rule over a country, colony, or large territory on their behalf. Think of it this way: the monarch cannot be in two places at once.
Vicinity means the area around or near a particular place.
"Vicious" means extremely harmful, cruel, or violent — often with a sense of deliberate intent and raw ferocity. It is not a mild word.

A vicious circle is a situation where one problem causes another problem, and that second problem turns around and makes the first problem even worse — and this keeps happening again and again in a loop, making everything progressively harder to escape.
Viciously means in a way that is savage, brutal, or deliberately cruel — with intense force and little to no mercy.
A vicissitude is an unpredictable change in circumstances — especially a shift between good and bad fortune — that is simply a natural part of life, work, or any long journey.
A victim is a person who suffers harm, loss, injury, or damage because of something that happens to them — something they did not choose, want, or deserve.
To victimize someone means to deliberately treat a person cruelly, unfairly, or harmfully — especially by targeting them, taking advantage of them, or causing them to suffer in some way.
A victor is someone who wins — especially in a fight, war, competition, or any serious struggle against an opponent.

When someone or something is victorious, it means they have won — they came out on top after a competition, battle, struggle, or contest of any kind. A victorious person, team, or side is the one that defeated the other side and claimed the win.

Victory means the act of winning — of coming out on top in a contest, fight, struggle, or challenge. It is the moment (or the result) when one side succeeds and the other side is defeated or overcome.

Victual means food — specifically, food that is prepared, ready to eat, or set aside to nourish people. Think of it as a word for food viewed through a practical lens: food as fuel, food as sustenance, food that keeps people alive and going.
To vie means to compete eagerly with others to get or achieve something that everyone wants but only one (or a few) can have.
A viewpoint is a person's particular way of looking at a topic, situation, or issue based on who they are, what they believe, what they have experienced, and what they value.

A vigil is a period of staying awake — usually through the night or for a long stretch of time — to watch over someone or something, to wait for something, or to honour someone, often in a serious or solemn situation.
Vigilance means the quality or state of being carefully watchful and alert, especially to spot danger, problems, or anything that could go wrong — before it actually causes harm.
Vigilant means being carefully and constantly watchful — especially for danger, threats, or anything that could go wrong.
A vigilante is a person who decides to punish wrongdoers or enforce justice on their own, without any official legal authority to do so.

A vignette is a small, vivid, carefully focused thing — a brief snapshot that gives you a sharp impression of something bigger: a moment, a scene, a mood, or a person. It doesn't try to tell the whole story.

Vigor means active, lively, forceful energy — combined with strength and good health. It's not just energy sitting quietly inside you. It's energy that shows up in the way you move, work, think, or act.
Vigorous means full of strength, energy, and active force — and applied with real intensity and effort. It's not just about having strength.

Vigorously means doing something with a lot of energy, force, and determined effort — physical, mental, or both. When someone does something vigorously, they are not doing it half-heartedly or gently. They are putting full power and liveliness into it.
"Vile" means so deeply offensive or bad that it produces a strong feeling of disgust or moral outrage. It is never a mild word.

Vileness is a noun that means the quality or state of being vile — that is, being so deeply bad, repulsive, or morally corrupt that it provokes strong feelings of disgust, outrage, or revulsion in anyone who encounters it.
Vilification means the act of saying very harsh, damaging, and often false or exaggerated things about a person or group — publicly, and with the intention of making others think badly of them.
To vilify someone means to say very harsh, damaging, and often unfair things about them — publicly — in order to make other people see them as evil, dangerous, or completely worthless.
A villa is a large, comfortable, and usually luxurious house that stands on its own — meaning it is not attached to or sharing walls with other buildings.

A villain is a person who does evil, harmful, or deeply wrong things — usually on purpose, and often without genuine remorse. The word doesn't just describe a bad action; it describes a bad person, or at least someone acting in a fundamentally harmful way.

Villainous is an adjective. It describes someone or something as deeply wicked, evil, or morally corrupt — belonging to or characteristic of a villain (a person who deliberately does cruel, harmful, or dishonest things).

Villainy means extreme wickedness, evil behavior, or deeply immoral conduct. It is the quality of being a villain — someone who deliberately does harmful, cruel, or morally wrong things with full awareness and intent.

A villanelle is a type of poem that follows a very specific, rigid structure. It has precise rules about how many lines it contains, how those lines rhyme, and — most distinctively — which lines must be repeated.
Villatic means "of, relating to, or typical of a village, farm, or the countryside." It is a formal, literary way of saying rural or rustic.
Vim means a lively, enthusiastic energy — the kind that makes a person seem almost sparkling with life and eagerness as they do something. It is not just plain energy (like fuel in a tank).
To vindicate someone or something means to prove, after a period of doubt or accusation, that they were right, innocent, or justified all along.
When someone is vindicated, it means they have been proven right, justified, or cleared of blame — but crucially, after a period where they were doubted, criticized, accused, or not believed.

The word vindication has a very specific and satisfying meaning: it is the proof — delivered by events, evidence, or investigation — that you were right about something or innocent of something, after others had doubted, criticized, or blamed you.

If someone is vindictive, they have a strong, burning desire to get back at someone who has hurt or wronged them. They want to punish that person — and they often go far beyond what is fair or reasonable.

Vindictiveness is the strong, deep desire to hurt, punish, or get back at someone who has wronged you — and this desire goes far beyond what is fair, reasonable, or necessary. It is not just wanting justice.
Viniculture is the farming of grapevines specifically to produce wine grapes.
Vinous is an adjective that simply means of, relating to, or characteristic of wine. Think of it as a sophisticated, single-word way of saying "wine-like" or "having to do with wine."
Vintage means old, but in the best possible way. It's not just about age — it's about quality, value, and a kind of timeless appeal that has survived the test of time.

Vinyl is a type of synthetic plastic material. It is smooth, somewhat shiny, flexible yet durable, waterproof, and relatively cheap to produce. Its full scientific name is polyvinyl chloride, which is why you'll often see it shortened to PVC.

A vinyl record is a flat, circular disc made of plastic that stores sound in the form of tiny physical grooves carved into its surface. When you place a needle on it and spin it, the needle traces those grooves and produces music or sound through a speaker.
Violate means to cross a boundary that should not be crossed. That boundary could be a rule, a right, a place, or a person.

A violation is the act of breaking, ignoring, or failing to respect something that is supposed to be followed or protected — whether that is a rule, a law, a right, an agreement, a boundary, or something considered sacred or private.
A violator is a person — or sometimes an organization, company, or government — that breaks, ignores, or goes against something that was meant to be respected, followed, or protected.

Violence means the use of strong, harmful physical force against a person, animal, or thing. When someone hits, punches, stabs, shoots, or physically attacks another person with the intent to hurt them, that is violence.

"Violent" describes something that involves great, overwhelming, and often uncontrolled force — especially the kind of force that causes or is very likely to cause harm, damage, or destruction. Think of it as the opposite of "gentle."

A viper is a type of venomous snake — one that can inject poison into its victim through its fangs. But not every venomous snake is a viper. The word refers to a specific family of snakes with particular traits that set them apart from other snakes.

"Viperous" describes someone or something that is dangerously spiteful, malicious, and treacherous — like a venomous snake. A viper is one of the most feared snakes in nature: it strikes suddenly, it injects poison, and it can cause serious harm.
A loud, aggressive, domineering woman (insulting). In older or literary use, a strong, brave, and heroic woman.
Of an image, video, or story, spreading rapidly and widely online by being shared from person to person. In medicine, relating to or caused by a virus.

A vireo is a small songbird belonging to a group of roughly 50 species found exclusively in the Americas — meaning they exist nowhere else on Earth. They are grouped together in one bird family called Vireonidae.

Viridescent means slightly green, or in the process of becoming green, or having a greenish quality. It describes something that is either turning green or carrying a soft, partial shade of green — not a bold, full green, but a greenish tinge or hue.
Virile is an adjective that describes a strong, powerful, robust masculinity — the kind that feels active, energetic, and full of life force. Think of it as the opposite of weak, frail, or passive.
Virility is a noun that refers to the qualities, characteristics, and powers that are traditionally associated with being a fully developed, capable, and strong adult male.
A virologist is a scientist who specializes in the study of viruses — what they are, how they work, how they spread, how they cause disease, and how they can be stopped or used for good.
Virtu refers to objects — usually small, rare, beautiful, or artistically crafted things — that are prized and collected by people with refined taste.

Almost or nearly, for all practical purposes, as in "a virtual stranger" or "a virtual certainty." In computing, existing or done online or through software rather than physically, as in "a virtual meeting."
"Virtually" means: so close to something that the remaining gap doesn't matter in practice.
A virtue is a quality of good character — a positive trait that a person consistently has, which makes them morally good and admirable.

Virtuosity means an extraordinarily high, almost breathtaking level of skill and technical mastery in performing or doing something — usually in music, art, sport, or any craft that requires years of dedicated practice.

A virtuoso is a person who has reached such an extraordinarily high level of skill in something — usually a performing art — that watching them feels almost magical. We're not talking about someone who is simply good, or even great.
Virtuous describes a person, action, or way of life that is morally excellent — genuinely good, honest, upright, and ethically sound.

Virulence is the degree of harmfulness or destructive power of something — most commonly a disease-causing microorganism like a virus or bacterium — and how severely it can damage or kill a living host.
Extremely bitter and hostile, as in "virulent criticism." Of a disease or poison, extremely severe, harmful, and fast-spreading.
A virus is something that gets inside a system — whether a living body or a computer — and causes harm, often by spreading and multiplying without permission.
As a noun, "vis-à-vis" refers to a person who is directly paired with, opposite to, or corresponds to another person — either physically or in terms of role and position.

"Vis-à-vis" is a word that positions two things in front of each other — it creates a relationship between them, so you can think about how they connect, compare, or interact. Every time you use it, there are always two "sides" involved.
A visa is an official permission — granted by a country's government — that allows a foreign person to enter, stay in, or pass through that country for a specific purpose and for a limited time.
Visage simply means a person's face. But it's not just any ordinary word for "face" — it carries a little more weight.
Viscera refers to the soft, internal organs of the body — the organs tucked inside the large hollow spaces (called cavities) of your body, particularly your chest and abdomen (belly).
Something visceral is felt so deeply in your gut — so raw, so immediate, so instinctive — that it bypasses your thinking brain entirely and strikes you at a primal, almost physical level.
Viscid means thick, sticky, and semi-fluid — like honey, tree sap, or warm tar.
Viscosity is the measure of how much a fluid resists flowing. In other words, it tells you how "thick" or how "resistant to movement" a liquid or gas is.
A viscount is a member of the nobility — meaning a person who holds an official title of high social rank, usually inherited from their family or granted by a monarch.

A viscous liquid is one that is thick, flows slowly, and resists movement. Think of honey. When you tip a jar of honey, it doesn't pour out quickly the way water does — it stretches, drips slowly, and seems almost reluctant to move.

A vise is a gripping tool — a device designed to hold an object tightly and steadily in place so you can work on it with both hands free. Think of it as a pair of powerful, mechanical jaws that you can tighten or loosen at will.
Visionary describes something or someone that shows the rare ability to see far into the future — to imagine possibilities, ideas, or solutions that most people around them cannot yet see.

A visionary is a person who can imagine a future that is better, different, or entirely new — and can do so with unusual clarity, originality, and depth. While most people focus on what exists right now, a visionary focuses on what could exist.
A visitant is a visitor — a person, creature, or being that comes to a place temporarily and then leaves. But this word carries depth and flavor that the ordinary word "visitor" simply does not.

Visitation refers to an act of visiting — but not in the casual, everyday sense of popping over to a friend's house. The word almost always carries a sense of formality, authority, special purpose, or significance.

A visor is a flat or curved shield — part of something you wear on your head — whose sole job is to protect your eyes or face from something, most commonly sunlight, but also rain, wind, or physical impact.
A vista is a wide, impressive, and often beautiful view of a scene — particularly one that stretches far into the distance and opens up dramatically before your eyes.
Visualization is the act of forming or producing a clear, concrete picture of something — either in your mind, or as an actual physical or digital image that others can see.
To visualize something means to form a clear, detailed picture of it in your mind — to see it with your "mind's eye," even when it isn't physically in front of you, or doesn't exist yet at all.
"Vital" means something is so important that everything depends on it — like the way your heart is important to your body. Without your heart, nothing else works.
At its most essential, vitality means the state of being full of life, energy, and strength in a way that is lively, active, and sustained.
To vitalize something means to fill it with life, energy, or a sense of living purpose — to make something feel alive, active, and dynamic.

A vitamin is a natural substance that your body absolutely needs to survive and stay healthy — but cannot make on its own (or cannot make enough of on its own). Because of this, you must get vitamins from outside sources, mainly food.
To vitiate something means to damage, weaken, corrupt, or spoil it — in a way that undermines its quality, effectiveness, or validity from the inside out.
Vitiation means the act or result of spoiling, corrupting, or undermining something — making it defective, impure, or invalid.
Vitiligo is a long-term skin condition in which certain patches of skin permanently lose their natural color and turn white or very pale.
Vitreous means "of, relating to, or resembling glass."
To vitrify something means to transform it into glass, or into a glass-like substance. It also means to become glass-like. Think of it as the process of "turning into glass." That is the heart of it.

A vitrine is a glass display case — an enclosed cabinet or box made largely of glass, built specifically to show off valuable, delicate, or beautiful objects while keeping them protected and untouched.
Extremely bitter, cruel, and hateful criticism or language, as in "a stream of vitriol." Literally, an old name for sulphuric acid and other corrosive chemicals.

Vitriolic describes language, criticism, or tone that is savagely harsh, bitterly cruel, and deliberately meant to hurt or destroy. It is not just "harsh" or "critical" — it is the most corrosive, burning kind of verbal attack.

To vituperate means to attack someone or something with harsh, bitter, and abusive language. When someone vituperates, they don't just criticize — they unleash a flood of angry, often morally charged words, condemning the target sharply and at length.

Vituperation means a prolonged, bitter, and intensely harsh stream of verbal abuse or condemnation directed at someone or something. It is not just criticism — it is angry, scorching, relentless language meant to attack, denounce, and tear down its target.
Someone or something described as vituperative is characterized by harsh, bitter, and aggressively abusive language, especially when blaming or criticizing someone.
Spoken aloud rather than written, as in "a viva voce vote." In British universities, a viva voce (or "viva") is an oral examination, especially for a doctoral degree.
Vivacious describes a person who is full of life, energy, and a warm, lively spirit — someone who seems to glow with enthusiasm and make the space around them feel more exciting and alive.
Vivacity means a quality of being lively, animated, and full of bright, sparkling energy — especially as part of someone's personality or manner.

A vivarium (plural: vivaria or vivariums) is an enclosed space — such as a glass tank, a sealed container, or a specially built room — that is carefully set up to house living animals, plants, or both, in conditions that closely mimic their natural habitat.
Vivid means intensely clear and striking — so powerful that it feels real and immediate, almost jumping out at you.

To vivify something means to give life to it — either literally (in the sense of making something actually alive) or, far more commonly, in the sense of making something feel alive when it was previously dull, flat, or lifeless.

Viviparous is an adjective that describes a living organism — most commonly an animal — that produces offspring which develop and grow inside the parent's body and are then born alive, rather than being laid as an egg that hatches outside the body.

To vivisect something means to cut open or perform a surgical operation on a living creature — while it is still alive — for the purpose of scientific study or experimentation, not to treat or heal it.

Vivisection is the act of performing surgical operations or scientific experiments on a living animal (or, historically, a living human being) for the purpose of research, medical study, or observation of biological processes.
A bad-tempered, spiteful, or quarrelsome woman. Informally, a sexually attractive woman. Literally, a female fox.
"Viz." is an adverb that means "namely" or "that is to say."
A vizier was a powerful chief minister — essentially the number-one official serving under a ruler in certain historical governments, especially in Islamic empires.
All the words that a person knows or uses, as in "a wide vocabulary." It can also mean all the words in a language, the words used in a particular subject, or a list of words with their meanings.
Expressing opinions loudly and forcefully, as in "a vocal critic." Literally, relating to the voice, as in "vocal cords."
To vocalize something means to give it a voice — to take something (a thought, a feeling, a sound, an idea) and express it out loud using your voice.

A vocation is a deep, powerful sense that you are called to do a certain kind of work — not just that you chose it, but that it feels like your true purpose in life. It is the feeling that a particular type of work is not just what you do, but who you are.
The adjective vocational means relating to a job, trade, or occupation — especially one that requires practical, hands-on skills learned through specific training.
To vociferate means to shout or cry out loudly, forcefully, and persistently — especially when expressing a complaint, protest, demand, or strong disagreement. It is not just about being loud.
Vociferation means the act of shouting, crying out, or screaming loudly and with great force — especially when driven by strong emotion such as anger, frustration, protest, or desperation.

Vociferous describes someone (or a group) who expresses their opinions, demands, or feelings in a way that is very loud, forceful, and impossible to ignore. It is not just about volume — it is about the intensity and persistence of that noise.
Vogue means whatever is fashionable, popular, or widely admired at a particular moment in time.

Voguish means fashionable, trendy, or currently popular. If something is voguish, it is "in style" right now — people are drawn to it, talking about it, and following it because it feels current and modern.

When you voice something, you take a thought, feeling, or opinion that lives quietly inside you — and you bring it out into the open by putting it into words. To voice something means to express it openly, deliberately, and out loud.

A void is a space where nothing exists — a total, complete emptiness. Not just a small gap or a minor absence, but something that feels vast, dark, and absolute. Think of the darkness stretching between stars in outer space.
To void something means to officially cancel it or wipe out its existence so that it has no power, no effect, and no legal standing — as if it was never real or never happened.
Volatile describes something that is unstable, unpredictable, and prone to sudden, dramatic change. It is the opposite of stable, calm, or steady.

Volatility means the tendency to change quickly, suddenly, and unpredictably. When something has high volatility, it is unstable — it does not stay in one state for long, and when it shifts, it shifts sharply and dramatically.
To volatilize means to turn into vapor or gas — or to cause something else to turn into vapor or gas.
Volition means the act of making a conscious choice or decision through your own free will — or the power/ability to do so.

Something is volitional if it comes from a person's own will — meaning it is done by conscious choice, on purpose, and with awareness. If you do something volitional, you decided to do it. Nobody forced you. Your body didn't do it automatically.
A number of bullets, arrows or questions fired at once ("a volley of questions"); in sport, a hit of the ball before it bounces.
Volubility is the quality of talking a great deal, very easily, and with a smooth, uninterrupted flow of words.

If someone is voluble, they talk a lot, easily, and quickly — words flow out of them like a fast-running tap that you can't quite turn off. A voluble person never seems to struggle to find something to say.

Voluminous means occupying or containing a very large amount — whether that's physical space, written content, or sheer quantity. Think of it as "impressively, sometimes overwhelmingly, large in size or extent."
A voluptuary is a person who has made the pursuit of pleasure — especially rich, sensory, physical pleasure — the central organizing principle of their life.
Voluptuous describes something that gives a deep, rich, full sense of pleasure — especially the kind of pleasure you feel through your body and senses.
Voluptuousness means the quality of being deeply, richly pleasing to the senses — in a way that feels full, lush, and indulgent.

Voracious means having an extremely strong, almost uncontrollable desire to consume something — and consuming it in very large amounts. The key idea packed inside this word is intensity. It is not just "wanting a lot."

Voracity means an extreme, almost uncontrollable eagerness or greediness — a consuming desire that is intense, urgent, and very hard to satisfy. Think of it as desire or appetite turned all the way up to the maximum.
A vortex is a body of fluid — either liquid or gas — that is spinning rapidly in a circular or spiral pattern around a central point or axis.
A votary is someone who is so deeply devoted to something — a religion, a cause, a belief, a person, or a pursuit — that their commitment feels almost like a sacred vow.
Something is votive when it is connected to a vow — a solemn, heartfelt promise made to God, a saint, or a divine being — either as a way of making that vow, or as a gift given in fulfillment of it.

When you vouch for someone or something, you are making a personal, confident declaration that they are trustworthy, honest, genuine, or good — and you are doing so based on your own direct knowledge or experience.
To vouch for someone or something means to confidently say, based on your own personal knowledge or experience, that someone is trustworthy or that something is true, correct, or of good quality.
A voucher is a piece of paper or document (or its digital equivalent — a code, an email, a file) that stands in place of something of value or acts as proof of something.
To vouchsafe something means to grant it, give it, or bestow it — but with a very specific and powerful attitude woven into the act.
A vow is a solemn, deeply serious promise — but not just any promise. It sits on a completely different level from the promises we make in everyday life.

A voyeur is a person who gets sexual pleasure from secretly watching other people who are naked, undressing, or doing something intimate or sexual — without those people knowing they are being watched.

Voyeurism is the practice of watching other people — particularly in private, intimate, or sexual moments — for personal pleasure or gratification, usually without those people knowing they are being observed. The watcher stays hidden and uninvolved.

Voyeuristic describes something that involves — or feels like — secretly watching other people, especially during private or intimate moments, and getting some kind of pleasure, thrill, or satisfaction from that watching.
To vulcanize something means to treat raw rubber with heat and sulfur (sometimes other chemicals) in order to make it significantly stronger, tougher, more elastic, and longer-lasting.
"Vulgar" describes something — a word, joke, gesture, comment, behavior, or even an object — that is crude, offensive, or in very poor taste.

A vulgarian is a person — almost always someone with money or social status — who behaves in a crude, tasteless, and offensive way. They are coarse, showy, and lack any sense of refinement or good taste.

A vulgarism is a specific word, phrase, or expression that is considered crude, coarse, indecent, or socially unacceptable — the kind of language that educated or polite people typically avoid, especially in formal or respectable settings.
The quality of being crude, rude, or offensive, or lacking good taste. A vulgarity is also a rude word or remark.

When you vulgarize something, you take something that was once dignified, elegant, or artistically valuable — and you drag it down. You strip away its quality, refinement, or good taste and replace it with something crude, indecent, or cheap.

The Latin translation of the Bible made mainly by Saint Jerome in the 4th century, used by the Catholic Church for over a thousand years. In general use, a common or widely accepted version of a text.
Vulnerability is the state of being open or exposed to the possibility of being hurt, harmed, damaged, or taken advantage of — whether physically, emotionally, socially, or in any other way.
When someone or something is vulnerable, it means they are in a position where harm, damage, or attack can easily reach them — and they don't have enough protection to stop it.

Vulpine means of, relating to, or characteristic of a fox. It can describe something that is fox-like in the literal, physical sense, or — far more commonly — fox-like in personality and behavior, meaning cunning, crafty, and sly.
Greedy and predatory, taking advantage of others' weakness or misfortune, like a vulture. Literally, resembling a vulture.
A wad is a compact, tightly pressed mass or lump of soft material — something that has been squeezed, rolled, or pressed together into a rough ball or chunk.
To waddle means to walk by swaying your body from side to side, taking short steps, shifting your weight left and right with every step you take.
